name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Winner of Oklahoma’s U.S. Senate race next week could take office next month, AG rules
text:
The U.S. Capitol on Oct. 9, 2024. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)OKLAHOMA CITY – The winner of the U.S. Senate race can take office once the Nov. 3 election results are certified, according to an Oklahoma Attorney General’s opinion released Thursday.
Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond’s decision means the winner of Oklahoma’s U.S. Senate race will likely take his or her oath of office well before Jan. 3 when the current U.S. Senate term ends. 
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt and Alan Armstrong pose for a photo after the governor held a press conference announcing Armstrong as his appointment to the U.S. Senate on March 24, 2026 at the state Capitol. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
That means current U.S. Sen. Alan Armstrong’s term would immediately end. 
Gov. Kevin Stitt in late March appointed Armstrong, a Republican, to fill the remainder of former U.S. Sen. Markwayne Mullin’s term. Mullin resigned March 23 to serve as President Donald Trump’s Secretary of Homeland Security.
NPR affiliate KOSU reported in September that Armstrong wanted to continue serving until January, but U.S. Rep. Kevin Hern, R-Tulsa, wanted the winner of  Tuesday’s election to take office as soon as the election results were certified. 
Hern, who is widely favored to win, is running for Oklahoma’s U.S. Senate seat against Democrat N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, Libertarian Sevier White and independents Ron Meinhardt and Curtis Stinnett.
Stitt and Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, asked Drummond to determine whether state law allows Armstrong to finish the term or if the newly elected senator can assume office once the State Election Board certifies the results of Tuesday’s general election.
Because the seat was already on this year’s ballot for a full six-year term, state law does not call for a separate special election, according to the opinion.
Instead, the winner is considered elected to both the remainder of the current term and the new term, the opinion said.
“Oklahoma law and the U.S. Constitution point to the same answer: the voters fill this seat,” Drummond said. “Oklahomans will choose their next senator at the polls Nov. 3, and that person will be eligible to take office once the election is certified.”
If the election is uncontested, the State Election Board will meet at 5 p.m. Nov. 10 to certify the results.
An opinion from the state Attorney General’s Office has the force of law unless challenged in court.
Hern’s campaign issued a statement that said the opinion confirms that Stitt’s appointment ends when a successor is elected.
“This is consistent with the clear language of the statute and ensures Oklahoma will have an elected voice in the Senate without delay,” the statement said.
Armstrong’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: New campaign aims to help NC Medicaid recipients keep coverage under new rules
text:
Congresswoman Deborah Ross (left) sat on a panel with Nicole Jorwic, Kirk Adams (center), Rep. Sarah Crawford, D-Wake, and Jamie Richmond (right) in Raleigh on Oct. 29, 2006. (Photo: Keep Your Care)A new campaign launching in North Carolina aims to help Medicaid recipients navigate upcoming federal requirements and avoid losing coverage because of confusing paperwork or reporting rules. 
Keep Your Care, a national campaign focused on helping people maintain Medicaid coverage, launched its North Carolina effort Thursday at a Raleigh roundtable with recipients, caregivers and lawmakers. 
“No one should lose health coverage because of confusing paperwork or red tape,” said Nicole Jorwic, a co-lead of Keep Your Care.
Beginning Jan. 2027, most adults covered through Medicaid expansion will need to document at least 80 hours of work a month, education or community service or qualify for an exemption. States will also be required to check eligibility at least twice a year, rather than annually. 
The Keep Your Care campaign plans to use digital advertising, community outreach and partnerships with local organizations to help people understand the rules, identify exemptions and meet deadlines. Enrollees and caregivers can sign up through the website to find information and get the latest updates on rule changes. 
More than 700,000 North Carolinians enrolled through Medicaid expansion will be subject to the new rules. Gov. Josh Stein’s office estimated that more than 250,000 people could lose coverage under the changes. 
Stein says NC counties will shoulder costs of new Medicaid rules, urges Congress to reverse cuts

Even as the deadline approaches, the rules are still in flux. On Thursday, a federal court ruling narrowed how the requirements can be applied to some very ill patients. 
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson announced that a judge has struck down a federal rule that would have required patients with cancer and other serious illnesses to prove their conditions prevented them from meeting the work requirements. The state estimated the restriction threatened coverage for 64,000 North Carolinians.
Although the ruling blocks enforcement of that restriction, the other Medicaid work and reporting requirements will remain in place for now, though another legal challenge is underway in Maryland. 
At Thursday’s roundtable, caregivers and advocates described how losing Medicaid coverage could affect families already struggling to afford care and disability services. 
Jamie Richmond, a family navigator at the Tammy Lynn Center, described balancing her work supporting families with care for her 7-year-old son, who has autism, and her mother, who lives in Florida and relies on Medicaid. 
She said her son’s speech, music and other therapies cost about $1,400 a month out of pocket. Medicaid also helps families access services like respite care, she said. 
“Families need help before they reach a crisis,” she said. “And it looks like the crisis is coming faster.” 
Campaign organizers said they want to reach people before the new requirements take effect, including those who may qualify for coverage but struggle to understand or comply with the reporting process. 
Congresswoman Deborah Ross, a Raleigh Democrat who participated in the roundtable, said outreach and education will be important as the state prepares to implement the requirements. 
Ross said Democrats could pursue changes to the law if they regain control of Congress, though she did not outline any specific proposals.  
“One good thing about some of these changes is that they don’t go into effect immediately,” she said. “People are terrified, but we can reverse it. We can extend some of the deadlines, and we can change things around.”
The federal requirement applies specifically to Medicaid expansion enrollees. However, advocates at the event raised concerns about additional funding cuts to the Medicaid program that could also affect people with disabilities, seniors and the families who care for them.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Idled WA coal power plant generates a natural gas fight
text:
The steam plume from the TransAlta coal power plant outside Centralia, Wash. could formerly be seen from 30 miles away on cold, clear days. But it’s been absent since mid-December when the plant shut down for conversion to natural gas. (Photo by Tom Banse)
The owner of the only remaining coal power plant in the Pacific Northwest is doggedly proceeding with a plan to extend its life by converting to natural gas fuel over the next two years. TransAlta Corporation got political support, signed a utility to take the electricity and is accumulating the necessary permits to remodel the currently idled power station near Centralia. 
But the coal-to-natural gas conversion is coming into question after a coalition of environmental groups challenged the energy production contract. Now the future of the hulking Centralia coal plant – a generous employer in Lewis County – is wrapped up in a contentious Puget Sound Energy rate increase case. It will be dissected beginning Tuesday, Nov. 3, with expert testimony and cross-examination in front of the Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission in Lacey.
The saga of the big power station matters far beyond Centralia because it encapsulates many themes bedeviling policymakers, ordinary ratepayers and utility managers these days: How to control rising electricity rates; where to get the juice to serve a growing population and attract new industry; and, does natural gas belong on the menu anymore?
TransAlta and its utility customer Puget Sound Energy assert that their contract for natural gas-fired generation is necessary to meet surging electricity demand and fill resource gaps. But the environmental coalition contends the 17-year power deal flies in the face of Washington’s goals to move beyond fossil fuels.
“There are far more less expensive, more efficient and cleaner resources to meet the demand that PSE is anticipating that they have written off,” Earthjustice Senior Attorney Victor Zertuche said in an interview.
Zertuche didn’t name specific alternative projects, but spoke about renewables being cheaper. Besides solar, wind and large-scale battery storage, the green groups also favor giving customers incentives to cut back during times of peak demand. PSE already does this to a degree.
Zertuche represents five groups in this case: Washington Conservation Action, NW Energy Coalition, Sierra Club, Front and Centered and Climate Solutions. Together, the challengers want state utility regulators to throw out PSE’s proposed contract for gas-fired electric generation.
The argument for conversion
Puget Sound Energy’s argument to state utility regulators reiterates that it needs to rapidly address forecasted shortfalls in electricity supplies. The utility said it is aggressively pursuing new clean energy projects, but that is not enough to assemble a balanced portfolio of resources. 
PSE testified that local electric demand is surging from wider adoption of air conditioning, heat pumps, electric vehicles and data centers. At the same time, the utility said it is facing increasing competition from data center developers when it seeks to put new wind and solar farms under contract to meet the forecast demand.

PSE is Washington’s largest utility, with 1.2 million electric customers and nearly 900,000 natural gas customers. PSE’s rates and generation asset selection have to pass scrutiny from state regulators since it is a private company with a monopoly in its service territory. During the current rate case, legions of upset customers demanded that the state utilities commission comb through PSE’s books to reduce proposed rate increases.
PSE Senior Vice President (and Chief Development Officer) Craig Pospisil told the regulatory panel that restarting the Centralia power station with natural gas would provide a vital and dependable backstop during periods of high demand such as summer heat waves and winter cold snaps. He said the remodeled plant would not run continuously. 
“Its value lies in providing necessary firm capacity using existing infrastructure, avoiding greenfield development risk, and supporting reliability during periods when renewable resources and storage may not be sufficient,” Pospisil said in written testimony.
PSE’s long-term deal with TransAlta runs from 2028 to the end of 2044. Then it’s curtains for the Centralia power station. That’s because beginning in 2045, Washington’s power grid is supposed to be 100% non-polluting under the state’s energy transition law.
A three-member independent panel will decide whether the coal-to-gas conversion is a prudent investment. Those state utility commissioners gave no indication of their leanings during two public hearings a month ago. The commissioners were variously appointed by Govs. Jay Inslee or Bob Ferguson and subsequently confirmed with bipartisan votes of the state Senate.
The Washington Utilities and Transportation Commission is expected to make a final decision in January to accept, reject or modify PSE’s proposed rates and generation plans.
Opinions and analysis aplenty
A staff analysis of the competing arguments concluded with a recommendation that the commissioners disallow the PSE plan to buy natural-gas fired electricity from TransAlta. If the commissioners don’t want to go that far, the staff suggested they at least demand more proof from PSE that natural gas generation was the lowest reasonable cost option available.
After reviewing the testimony of PSE critics, the Public Counsel inside the Office of the State Attorney General recently came around to the same position of recommending the commission reject the Centralia power contract.
Adding to the pile-on, a trade association for large commercial and industrial electricity users filed skeptical testimony. The Alliance of Western Energy Consumers cited its own consultant’s analysis that power to be supplied from the converted Centralia generating plant ”does not appear to be cost-effective.”
PSE filed rebuttal testimony with confidential financial data that it said showed gas-fired generation was cost-effective once the reliability value of the resource was factored in.
No one testified in favor of the Centralia plant’s coal-to-gas conversion during more than seven hours of spoken comments the utilities commission accepted over two nights in late September/early October.
“It is absurd that anyone would be trying to add fossil fuel capacity now when the early effects of climate change are already apparent and will continue getting worse,” said electric ratepayer Eddy Donofrio of Thurston County when it was his turn to speak at the commission hearing.
A broader range of opinions in favor and against appears in the public comment file of the state Department of Ecology. That state agency accepted comments separately as it prepares to finalize an environmental permit for natural gas-fired power generation by TransAlta.
The Centralia-Chehalis Chamber of Commerce said the planned coal plant conversion would preserve jobs and economic activity, “rather than prematurely abandoning a major piece of existing regional infrastructure.”
“We know we are short on generation. The natural gas plant would help make up for the shortage until sources of clean energy come on line for the grid,” retired IBEW Local 77 lobbyist Bob Guenther added in his comment to the Ecology Department.
TransAlta has generally kept a low public profile in Washington state this year as other parties vigorously debate the future of its coal plant.
“We’re continuing to work through the permitting and regulatory approval processes required for the conversion project to move forward,” a spokesperson for the Canadian company said in an emailed response to questions.
In a September presentation to stock market investors, Calgary-based TransAlta reported that it had completed the preliminary engineering and cost estimating for the Centralia project. The company’s board is holding off on making a final investment decision until sometime in early 2027.
The 730-megawatt Centralia plant hasn’t operated since last December, in accordance with a long-standing agreement with Washington state to phase out coal power. But the big facility is required by order of the Trump Administration to remain on standby in case of extreme power demand.
TransAlta’s Centralia operation is one of at least six coal-burning power plants around the nation that the Trump administration is trying to keep open past their planned retirement dates. However, the thrice-renewed emergency orders to TransAlta are being challenged as unjustified by the Washington State Attorney General and allied environmental groups.
The most recent order issued to TransAlta by Energy Secretary Chris Wright indicated the department is aware of the plan to convert the coal plant. Wright’s order directed the company to provide his department written notice when it receives the required permits to transition to natural gas. Pospisil said TransAlta informed PSE that it did not expect the series of Energy Department orders to delay the planned plant conversion.
The saga of the aging coal plant has become something akin to a three-ring circus for people interested in tracking the outcome, such as Earthjustice’s Victor Zertuche.
“With the rate case and the permits that are involved, there are just so many angles related to this,” he said.
“As we’re getting closer and closer, there is much more suspense,” Zertuche said. “Optimism, a lot of that as well. We’ll see.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: 2 North Dakota interim college leaders to continue as presidents
text:
Allen Burgad, left, is the president of Valley City State University; Lisa Karch is the president of the North Dakota State College of Science. (Photos courtesy of the North Dakota University System)The North Dakota State Board of Higher Education on Thursday named two interim college presidents to the long-term role.
Allen Burgad will lead Valley City State University and Lisa Karch will lead North Dakota State College of Science. 
Burgad was approved unanimously after the board met in a closed-door executive session. In the vote approving Karch as president, two board members – Curtis Biller and Michelle Kommer — voted no. 
They explained after the vote that they had confidence in Karch, but voted no because the board and North Dakota University System did not conduct a search, a departure from its usual process. 
“It is not a dispute over your exceptional performance in the last four months,” Kommer said. “My vote was just a matter of timing, and a sense that, from my perspective, that it was a premature decision.”
Karch has been interim president at NDSCS since July 1. She replaced Rod Flanigan who had announced plans to retire Dec. 31, but the board voted to place him on paid administrative leave through the end of the year.  
Karch is the former NDSCS executive vice president of academic affairs. 
Board President Kevin Black and University System Commissioner Brent Sanford praised her ability to collaborate with business and community partners around Wahpeton, where NDSCS has its main campus, and Fargo, home to its Career Innovation Center. 
“We recognize that traditional norms in higher education are to go through some sort of search process, but what we recognized … is that we have an absolutely exceptional leader,” Black said.
Burgad has been interim president at Valley City State University since December 2025. He had been dean of the college’s Department of Education. 
“Feedback from your own campus has been overwhelmingly positive,” Black said. “The faculty, the staff, and the students have acknowledged that you are a very humble and inclusive and collaborative leader.”
There was a presidential search at Valley City State but the search committee decided to pause its work in April after multiple semi‑finalist candidates withdrew.
Burgad is a 1989 graduate of Valley City State. He has previously served as an administrator in K-12 schools systems, including West Fargo, Stanley, Northern Cass and Napoleon.
He replaced Alan LaFave, who left to become president at  Northern State University  in Aberdeen, South Dakota. 
The board last year also appointed Sanford to lead the North Dakota University System without conducting a formal search. Sanford had been serving in an interim role before the long-term appointment.
The board also did not conduct a search before naming Carmen Simone as president of Lake Region State College in 2025. The board had interviewed Simone for the president’s role at Dickinson State University before she became interim president at Lake Region in Devils Lake. 
Before that, Simone had been CEO and dean at Dakota College at Bottineau.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: During wave of closures, Morrisey says school funding issue will ‘dominate’ 2027 legislative session
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey gives his State of the State address in the West Virginia Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, on Wednesday, Jan. 14, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)While communities across West Virginia face losing their public schools, Gov. Patrick Morrisey stressed that addressing public school funding issues will be front and center in the next legislative session. 
State education officials said eight to 20 schools face closure or consolidation in the next year. This comes after the West Virginia Department of Education approved the closure or consolidation of 20 public schools last year. 
There are also legal challenges to the state’s current school funding formula, calling it inadequate. One of those challenges is headed to the state Supreme Court. 
West Virginia’s school funding formula relies heavily on student headcount, so the state’s shrinking population has considerably impacted county budgets. The growing number of special education students has also put a strain on school finances since districts are required to accommodate needs under federal and state law regardless of funding. 
“I will say that school aid issues and education issues will dominate the next legislative session. I think it’s very important,” Morrisey said Oct. 28 at a press conference in response to a question from West Virginia Watch. 
The governor noted that public education is crucial to improving the state’s low workforce participation, which he sees as West Virginia’s top issue.
Morrisey, Senate and House education chairs, and the state school board will bring ideas to the table for potential changes. Reaching a consensus on possible changes — and what they’re willing to spend — then getting it through the full Legislature will be a process.
Morrisey spoke with State Schools Superintendent Michele Blatt, he said, after she publicly shared the state school board’s proposed school funding changes they’d like to see in 2027 legislation.
West Virginia uses a seven-step formula to determine how much state funding goes to county school systems based on factors including the number of students enrolled.
The state school board wants to restructure the school funding formula to address declining enrollment along with monetary needs in special education, high poverty areas, rural schools and more. 
“We’re trying to digest that, and we’ve been doing a lot of work internally, and we’re having conversations,” Morrisey said.
The state school board hasn’t released a total cost for its school funding proposal; their special education reform piece alone would cost $190 million.
Multi-million dollar price tags attached to proposed school funding formula legislation were a sticking point for lawmakers earlier this year, who ultimately declined to make any changes to the funding formula. A bill in the House of Delegates updating the funding formula would have cost $214 million.
West Virginia is near the national average in terms of per pupil spending, and the Morrisey administration has already cautioned that putting more money into the school system may not be the answer.
Lawmakers allocated around $2.4 billion for public education in the fiscal year 2027 budget.
“I don’t think we have a spending problem in West Virginia,” Morrisey said. “I think a lot of it depends upon how the monies are spent, and so we’re going to be looking closely at that and continuing to engage with legislators because we have to do this the right way.”
Morrisey, who has made government efficiency and rightsizing a hallmark of his tenure, will likely apply the same mentality as he looks to make changes in West Virginia’s struggling public school system. 
“We’re certainly looking closely at the budget because we have to do something that’s affordable for our citizens,” the governor told reporters. “There will be some additional resources that weren’t in the past that we’ve already been taking steps to do, but in terms of the overall proposal, we have to make sure that it’s meeting the needs of West Virginia citizens and that it has to be responsible.”
Morrisey noted that lawmakers earlier this year focused on the Hope Scholarship, the state’s education voucher program. Lawmarks debated potential changes to the program before they signed off on nearly $300 million in funding for it without any major modifications.  
The 2027 legislative session will begin in January.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: It looks like a duck and quacks like a duck. But is it subject to campaign spending limits?
text:
The Rhode Island Democratic Party spent $228,000 on mailers for gubernatorial candidate Helena Buonanno Foulkes, including this one attacking her independent rival, Ken Block. (Scanned mailer by Rhode Island Democratic Party)Independent gubernatorial candidate Ken Block is crying foul over a six-figure spend on attack mailers that support his deep-pocketed Democratic rival, Helena Buonanno Foulkes, while depicting Block as a conservative-minded duck.
Less than a week before the Nov. 3 election, Block filed a complaint with the Rhode Island Board of Elections, alleging the $228,000 the state Democratic Party spent on attack mailers for Foulkes’ exceeds the limit political party committees can spend on TV, radio and print ads for a single candidate in a year. Block’s complaint, filed Wednesday, also demanded that Foulkes return the “illegal” in-kind contribution. 
“My complaint does not concern a bookkeeping error or a small amount of misplaced money,” Block said in a statement. “This is a six-figure political expenditure to fund negative mailers designed to persuade voters.” 
The in-kind contributions, included in Foulkes’ most recent report to the elections board, reflecting donations and spending from Oct. 6 through 26, paid for a series of mailers linking Block to Republican viewpoints. Block ran for governor as a Republican in 2014, after campaigning as the first statewide candidate for the now-defunct Moderate Party in 2010.
A series of three white ducks stand across the center of one mailer, thought bubbles above each.  
“Obamacare is horrible,” the first reads. “I fought against increasing the minimum wage,” a second states.
The third duck, which has Ken Block’s head on its body, states, “I agree, but I hope they think I’m an independent.”
Below the image, black and red text against a yellow background declares, “If Ken Block walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, he must be a Republican…duck.”
Foulkes’ campaign insists that mailers don’t count toward the spending cap on print ads, reducing Block’s allegations to “whining.” 
 “Unfortunately for Ken Block, mailers like the ones that show he is really a Republican who opposes the [Affordable Care Act] do not count towards the $25K in-kind limit, so voters will continue to learn about how he’s really a Republican who called the ACA ‘horrible,’” Eric Hyers, Foulkes’ campaign advisor, said in a statement on Thursday.
State law offers little clarity.
The 1988 statute sets no limit on the in-kind contributions a political party committee can spend on behalf of a candidate of its party, with three exceptions: TV, radio, and print ads. Those expenses must be capped at a combined $25,000, per candidate, per year.
There is no mention of mailers, nor any definition of print advertisements in the law, an omission Block’s campaign manager, Matthew Schweich, acknowledged.
“In our opinion, in the absence of clarity, you use common sense and look at the rules promulgated by the Board of Elections,” Schweich said in an interview Thursday.
In search of answers 
Block’s campaign looked instead to the 83-page campaign finance manual to support his interpretation of the law. The biannual training guidebook for candidates and party committees includes a list of eligible campaign expenses, with definitions, to help candidates categorize their spending when reporting financial activity to the elections board.
Advertising, according to the manual, “includes but is not limited to: printing, brochures, signs, billboards, radio and television advertising, postage and mailings.”
“It’s clear that the intent of the law is to prevent political parties from spending more than $25,000 on mass communications to the public in support of, or in opposition to, a candidate for office,” Block said in the statement. “It makes no sense to say that a small advertisement in a local paper to a few hundred people should be held to a higher standard of campaign finance scrutiny than a political mailer to hundreds of thousands of voters.” 
John Marion, executive director of Common Cause, disagreed with Block’s position. 
“The common understanding of a print advertisement is something like in a newspaper,” Marion said in an interview Thursday. “A mailer is something separate.”
Marion also distinguished the campaign finance manual referenced by Block’s campaign as distinct from state law. The manual’s definition of an advertisement is likely intended to help candidates understand how to categorize expenses in the election board’s online reporting portal, he said.
“This complaint doesn’t seem to be based in the law,” Marion concluded.
A 2014 advisory opinion by the elections board supports Marion’s interpretation. 
Asked by the attorneys for the Rhode Island Democratic State Committee whether direct mail counts toward the print advertisements subject to the $25,000 spending cap, the elections board advised it did not. The advisory opinion, approved by a unanimous vote of the elections panel at its Oct. 22, 2014, meeting, distinguishes between mass market publication like a print advertisement in a newspaper, and direct mail sent to individual households. 
“Because the statute clearly refers to media expenses, and costs related to direct mail pieces are not media-related expenses, direct mail costs are not subject to the aggregate $25,000 limitation,” the opinion states.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Helena Buonanno Foulkes, left, benefited from a recent mailer funded by the Rhode Island Democratic party depicting her independent opponent Ken Block, right, as a duck. (Photos by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)
Schweich, of Block’s campaign, said they could find no evidence on the elections board website that addressed the issue.
“It’s pretty incredible to me the board expects candidates to follow rules based on advisory opinions that aren’t posted onto their website, and have not been incorporated into the campaign finance law and are not in the statute,” Schweich said. “To my knowledge, an advisory opinion is not a law. It’s not even a regulation.” 
Block issued another statement Thursday afternoon, calling on the elections board to reject the interpretation of its own, 2014 opinion.
“That defies common sense,” Block said of the 2014 opinion. “The delivery method does not change what the advertisement is.”
Chris Hunter, a spokesperson for the elections board, said the agency’s website reflects all decisions and opinions since 2018, when it was last updated. 
Hunter declined to comment on the complaint otherwise, except to say that complaints are confidential unless or until the elections board finds evidence of a violation. 
The countdown is on 
Stressing the importance of transparency for voters heading into the general election, Block demanded that the elections board respond to his complaint by noon Friday. The board is scheduled to next meet on the morning of Nov. 3, but there is no public agenda.
Marion didn’t think voters cared much either way.
“I don’t think voters necessarily vote on campaign finance issues, more on bread and butter issues,” he said.
Issues like healthcare and wages for hourly workers, topics which the mailers allege show Block’s conservative underbelly.
Block’s shifting party identity has been criticized by both his opponents, Foulkes and GOP nominee Aaron Guckian.
Block insists his views have not changed, and his unaffiliated status grants him the freedom to advocate for voters, not special interests. In a new attack ad that aired on broadcast networks starting Tuesday, Block accuses Foulkes of being a “puppet” for the powerful labor groups that have endorsed and donated to her.
Yet Foulkes allies have helped to fuel her multimillion-dollar campaign operation, allowing the Democratic nominee to exponentially outspend her opponents. In the three-week period that ended Oct. 27, Foulkes raised more than $446,000, spending more than half a million dollars. Block received $14,700 donations in the same time frame, boosting his campaign with a $20,000 personal loan. He spent $234,000.
Foulkes’ substantial fundraising lead has come with problems of its own, namely, more than $11,000 in individual donations that had to be returned because the donors exceeded the $2,000 limit per candidate per year. The state elections board did not fine Foulkes for the violation on the condition she refund the excess donations, Hunter said. 
Yet Marion saw the acceptance of excess donations, some dating back to 2023, as a serious violation.
“Its a pretty big deal because there were so many contributions over the $2,000 limit, and her campaign did not catch any of them,” Marion said. “It speaks to a lack of internal controls in her campaign.”
He continued, “She has raised an enormous amount of money. She has the resources to hire the accountants and campaign finance experts necessary to make sure that doesn’t happen.”
Another day, another complaint 
Block filed a second campaign finance complaint against the Foulkes campaign Thursday afternoon, contesting $90,000 the state Democratic Party spent on digital ads for Foulkes. He cites the same state law limiting party in-kind contributions on advertising to $25,000 per candidate, per year.
Block acknowledged in the complaint that the law does not identify digital or online communications as a form of advertising because the Internet and cell phones were not widely used at the time.
But given the pervasive nature of social media platforms in campaign communications today, it is “reasonable” to include digital communications in the law, Block stated. He pointed to a 2024 regulation adopted by the elections board that defines “qualified internet or digital communication” as a form of advertising.
“Statutory construction requires harmony within the election laws to avoid conflicts in definitions; therefore, the Board should apply their definition to this matter,” he wrote. “The Board of Elections must find that the black letter law establishes a maximum donation by the RI Democratic State Committee to Candidate of Helena Foulkes, for advertising purposes, of $25,000.00.”
Because the state party has already spent $25,000 on print ads for Foulkes, Block argues that Foulkes needs to refund the party $90,000 for the digital communications placed for her campaign.
Foulkes’ campaign acknowledged, but did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday.
Advisory opinions or other determinations by the elections board clarifying whether digital communications are subject to the $25,000 annual spending cap were not immediately available.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Election 2026: The Race for the Corner Office
text:
ELECTION 2026 · EDITION 6
The Race for the Corner Office

Gov. Maura Healey will head into Election Day with a high-spending opponent, an affordability crisis still raging, and few of her campaign season wish-list items fulfilled by fellow Democrats in the Legislature. Odds are it won’t really matter. 
Poll after poll shows voters by a sizable margin are leaning toward keeping Healey in the corner office for another four years. A CommonWealth Beacon/MassINC Polling Group survey conducted in mid-September found Healey up by a margin of 22 percentage points over Republican challenger Mike Minogue. Another poll from UMass Amherst and WCVB put the governor’s lead in early October at 25 percentage points. Then, a third poll from Suffolk University and The Boston Globe in mid-October followed up with Healey ahead on Minogue by 23 percentage points. 
It’s always a steep climb for a Republican in Massachusetts to try unseating an incumbent Democrat, especially one who holds statewide office. But it didn’t always seem like the blowout that home-stretch polling is now suggesting. 
Healey’s numbers hadn’t always been the strongest. A MassINC Polling Group survey conducted in March found that only 39 percent of voters viewed Healey favorably, compared to 45 percent who viewed her unfavorably. In June, a Suffolk/Globe poll found most voters could not name a signature accomplishment for the governor during her first term. And just this month, the same survey that had Healey up 23 points also found a plurality of voters, 42 percent, saying Massachusetts has gotten worse in the last four years. 






Based on a survey of 800 Massachusetts registered voters collected from March 12 – 17, 2026, via live telephone interviews and text message invitations to an online survey.


Meanwhile, Healey’s Democratic counterparts in the Legislature are not exactly stumbling over themselves to ship her big wins before Election Day. 
The gas-tax suspension she floated just days after Minogue thrust the idea into the spotlight? Dead on arrival in the House. The sweeping energy affordability legislation she filed way back in May 2025, before the war in Iran sent prices spiking? Stuck in House-Senate negotiations since July. How about tackling the eye-wateringly high cost of housing? The Legislature may make some moves after the votes are counted, but so far hasn’tdone all that much since a 2024 borrowing bill, and they’ve been sitting on Healey’s push for more permitting reforms for months. 
Even if Minogue entered the race as an unknown entity who had never held elected office, he has the one asset even veteran candidates would envy: a seemingly unlimited war chest. 
Mike Minogue’s Primary Day win celebration on September 1, 2026. (Emily Glick/CommonWealth Beacon)
When Johnson & Johnson purchased Abiomed, the medical device company Minogue ran, he personally earned more than $240 million, according to SEC filings unearthed by the Globe. Minogue has been happy to tap into his wealth so far, contributing more than $17 million to his own campaign and significantly outspending Healey.  
Yet here we are. Healey’s strategy of nationalizing the election — of using Minogue’s past donations to Donald Trump and other GOP causes to make her reelection a referendum on the president — has, arguably, paid dividends.  
It’s easy to see why: nearly three-quarters of voters in the most recent Suffolk/Globe poll have an unfavorable view of Trump. A third deem him the figure most responsible for the state of the Massachusetts economy, roughly the same share that picked Healey for that title. 
You can see evidence of partisan ideology outweighing any other concerns in most other races, too. US Sen. Ed Markey, Attorney General Andrea Campbell, and Treasurer Deborah Goldberg — all statewide Democrats running for reelection — are up 20 or more points over their Republican challengers in recent polls. Secretary of State Bill Galvin has an even bigger lead than that. 
So there might indeed be some heat in this election season. It’s just aimed down at Washington, DC, instead of the candidates actually on the ballot here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Matt Ritter considered as possible interim UConn president
text:
An emissary of the University of Connecticut’s board of trustees has approached House Speaker Matt Ritter about becoming the flagship state university’s interim president should Radenka Maric depart before her five-year contract expires on June 30, 2027, according to sources familiar with the situation.
The trustees failed to come to terms on an extension with Maric last June, despite a contract requirement that they resolve her status a year ahead of her contract’s expiration. Instead, they negotiated a six-month extension of the deadline for acting on her contract until next month.
UConn trustees met in executive session Wednesday, with one notable absence: the speaker’s father, Thomas D. Ritter, a long-time trustee.
Maric could not be reached for comment Thursday, and Ritter neither confirmed nor denied that he had been approached.
“I know there are stories out there about my future and potential job opportunities. Next Thursday I will be at the House Democratic Caucus seeking reelection as speaker of the House,” Ritter said in a text. “Beyond that, I’m not going to comment on possible or hypothetical job offers. I am 100% focused on getting House Democrats elected and meeting the caucus on November 5.”
With Democrats assured of retaining control of the General Assembly on Nov. 3, Ritter is expected to be endorsed at the Nov. 5 post-election caucus as speaker for an unprecedented fourth term. If Ritter and UConn come to terms, he would resign from the House.
If a formal offer is made and Ritter accepts, UConn would join the growing ranks of state university systems that have looked outside academia to former governors and legislative leaders for leaders.

Gov. Ned Lamont talks with UConn President Dr. Radenka Maric before a news conference celebrating NSF Quantum Technologies Engine being awarded a National Science Foundation federal award at UConn Hartford’s campus on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

An interim appointment of 18 months or more essentially would become a tryout for the 43-year-old Ritter, a partner in the downtown Hartford law firm of Shipman & Goodwin.
House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, said much of the skill set Ritter has displayed running the House for six years would be useful at UConn, though he was less than happy with the prospect of Ritter’s departure.
“The prospect of the House of Representatives without Speaker Ritter would not be a good thing for the institution,” Candelora said. “I think he’s done a lot of positive things for that chamber at a time that was very tumultuous.”
House Majority Leader Jason Rojas, D-East Hartford, is believed to have the votes to succeed Ritter as speaker.

name: VTDigger
title: Voter voices from Rutland’s downtown Walmart plaza
text:
Walmart has operated its downtown Rutland store since 1997. File photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

VTDigger reporters visited a variety of sites across Vermont in recent weeks, asking voters directly about the issues they care most about this election season. This week we’ll bring you those voices as we approach Election Day on Nov. 3.
RUTLAND — Shoppers meandered outside the Walmart plaza parking lot on a fair weather October Friday as the Nov. 3 election approached. 
The gubernatorial race is an animating issue for voters in Rutland County, as Democratic and Progressive candidate Amanda Janoo, a political newcomer, and incumbent Republican Gov. Phil Scott, who is seeking a sixth term, vie for the chief executive seat in Vermont. 
In 2024’s election, Rutland County voters, along with the rest of the state, favored Scott handily. In August, the majority of municipalities in Rutland County voted for childcare advocate Aly Richards over Janoo in the Democratic Primary. Yet, voters interviewed outside Walmart were divided between those who want a change in leadership and those who want to keep a steady course. 
Exiting Walmart, Erin Tiburske, 21, from Castleton, already cast a ballot through early mail-in voting, and filled in the bubble for Janoo at the top of the ticket. Tiburske wants to see Vermont’s healthcare and housing be more affordable, and favors Janoo’s stance on artificial intelligence and deterring data center construction in the state. 
Scott has had a long run, and it’s “time for something different,” Tiburske said. 
In contrast, another shopper entering Walmart, Zach Shively, 29, of Rutland, said he plans to vote for Scott because of his experience in office. 
“He’s been doing a decent job, and he’s a recognizable face,” said Shively, who said he’s not affiliated with a political party. 
Other voters have yet to pick a candidate for the state’s top office. 
Aileen Alinovi, 44, of Rutland, said that she is weighing her options and researching the election but will not be voting for the incumbent this time around. Scott has not done enough in his decade of service to deliver on campaign promises and bring economic vitality to places like Rutland and Vermont as a whole, Alinovi said. 
But Alinovi still wants to know more about the challenger before casting her ballot. “I really hope she’s a candidate that I could stand behind,” Alinovi said. 
Connie Witzing, 72, of Rutland Town, said that she is a Democrat but is undecided about the gubernatorial race. 

READ MORE

Witzing said she is concerned by the Trump administration’s leadership and the erosion of democratic institutions, and part of her wants to vote blue downballot “to send a message” nationally. 
But Witzing worries that the political newcomer, Janoo, is “green,” she said. Witzing views Scott as a more moderate Republican and a seasoned governor who knows how to steer the ship. 
“Our population is really little, and we have a lot of issues that need a good, strong government. We really do,” Witzing said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Voter voices from Rutland’s downtown Walmart plaza.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: How a small, wealthy Connecticut suburb went from red to blue
text:
Construction workers in hard hats and safety vests, hustling to transform a vacant office park in Avon to 176 units of housing, took little notice of the small ceremony celebrating their labors last summer on a project made possible by Connecticut’s controversial affordable housing law, 8-30(g).
“This is an incredible town. It’s been so supportive, and we’ve had such a great experience,” said Dara Kovel, the chief executive officer of Beacon Communities, the developer. “We also landed in the district of one of the state’s most passionate and vocal advocates for housing for people in need.”
That would be Rep. Eleni Kavros DeGraw, D-Avon. 
Opposition to 8-30(g), as well as an omnibus housing bill Kavros DeGraw helped draft and pass last year, has been foundational to a Republican Party desperate for wedge issues that might resonate in suburbs where the GOP has lost its way, places like the Farmington Valley suburbs of Avon, Canton and Simsbury. 
Kavros DeGraw is both a symptom of and contributor to the GOP’s slide in the valley.
With other moms alarmed by Hillary Clinton’s loss to President Donald Trump in 2016, Kavros DeGraw began reorganizing an ineffectual local Democratic Party that did not run full slates for municipal office and had failed to nominate a candidate for the 17th House District of Avon and Canton in 2014 and 2016.
What happened over the next decade in Avon is emblematic of the political shift that has drawn many upscale suburbs in Connecticut away from Republicans, helping Democrats win supermajorities in what was a closely divided General Assembly when Trump opened his first term in January 2017.
It is a story of how politics still are local, even when shaped by national trends, issues and personalities. Trump was a catalyst, but it was on-the-ground organizing that transformed Avon, a comfortable community of 19,000 with a median household income of $154,058, into a small-town Democratic powerhouse.
Kavros DeGraw, now 51, a stay-at-home mother of three with a background in writing, started a grassroots organization after the 2016 election with a friend, Carrie Firestone, called Forward Connecticut. It was organized around four pillars: connect, inform, serve and lead.
“We had, almost overnight, 2,000 members on Facebook,” she said. “They wanted to know what could they do because everybody was like, ‘This is going to be bad.’”
Grief and anger over a presidential election fueled action, first in the 2017 municipal races. 
“We had women all over the Farmington Valley who suddenly stepped up to run,” Kavros DeGraw said, adding they were not universally welcomed at Democratic town committees unaccustomed to new volunteers with new ideas and ambitions. “It was like, ‘Why are you here?’”
Kavros DeGraw said she announced a plan to raise $15,000 for the municipal elections, instantly getting pushback from a Democratic town committee member.
“He goes, ‘Well, we need to raise like $1,800.’ And he goes, “What would you spend on $15,000?’ I said, ‘We’re going to run a full slate of candidates.’ And he goes, ‘Where are you going to get a full slate of candidates?’” she said.
Avon had 3,748 registered Democrats and 4,145 Republicans when they started in late 2016, and the GOP controlled the town council with a lopsided majority. Gains would come slowly. It was the start of a multiyear effort to recruit candidates, teach them how to run and expand the Democratic base. 
“This is what these women did incredibly well,” said Eliza Massaro, a sales and management executive who joined the Democratic town committee in 2018, a move that would become life changing. Massaro now serves as its chair — and her volunteer political work became a career.
In 2021, Massaro abandoned her sales career to open 818 Political, a consulting firm whose name references the date when the constitutional amendment giving women the right to vote was ratified, Aug. 18, 1920. The majority of its clients are women, Kavros DeGraw among them.

Eliza Massaro, the Avon Democratic chair instructs, volunteers at the DTC headquarters. Credit: mark pazniokas / ctmirror.org

After working behind the scenes as an organizer, Kavros DeGraw ran for the General Assembly in 2018 in the two-town House district of Avon and Canton, challenging Rep. Leslee B. Hill, R-Canton. Kavros DeGraw carried Avon, but Hill narrowly won on the strength of the vote in Canton.
The same year, Democrat Ned Lamont won his first term as governor, but he lost to Republican Bob Stefanowski throughout the Farmington Valley. Other Democrats, notably U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy and congressional candidate Jahana Hayes, did better.
Kavros DeGraw ran again and won in 2020, the night Joe Biden was elected president, carrying Connecticut by 20 percentage points and Avon by 24. She won with 52% of the vote. It also was the year that Democratic voter registration passed Republicans in Avon.
The trend would continue. As of this month, Democrats outnumber Republicans, 4,447 to 3,194, an advantage of more than 1,200 voters.  Running full slates of municipal candidates, Democrats won a 4-1 majority on the council last year.
Seeking a second term in 2022, Kavros DeGraw faced a moderate Republican councilwoman from Avon, Heather Maguire, typically a strong vote getter in municipal elections. It was the Joe Biden midterm, but national conservative politics intruded — that June, the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.
“I went out the day it was decided, and every door … was a husband working from home,” Kavros Degraw said. 
She was struck by how unsettled the men were. One told her a story about his wife’s ectopic pregnancy.
“I had one guy, former military, who said, ‘What if you’re 16 and you just make a mistake? And I thought, ‘Oh, he’s got a sibling or a girlfriend or somebody in his past who had confronted an unwanted pregnancy,’” Kavros DeGraw said.
Kavros DeGraw won with 57% of the vote.
As the Democrats have consolidated, the Republicans in the valley have struggled with internal differences over whether to stand with Trump or tack to the center. In 2024, Kavros DeGraw’s Republican opponent was Manju Gerber, a leader of the socially conservative Moms for Liberty. Gerber got less than 38% of the vote.
Two of the three Republicans who preceded her in the 17th House District seat, Kevin Witkos and Tim LeGeyt of Canton, have broken with their party to varying degrees. Both were elected to the Canton Board of Selectmen after leaving the General Assembly and still serve.
Witkos, the first selectman, resigned from the Republican town committee.
“It’s been taken over by the, I’ll say, the right wing of the party, and that just doesn’t go well in the valley anymore,” said Witkos, who also had been a state senator.
LeGeyt, who succeeded Witkos in the House after Witkos’ election to the Senate, went further. The day after Trump’s election in 2024, LeGeyt went to town hall and changed his voter registration from Republican to unaffiliated.
“I just could not continue with some of the crap that I was seeing Trump take part in, and it’s only gotten worse,” LeGeyt said. “And so Republicans, you know, they’ve got their heads down. They’re not proud of what’s going on, in my opinion.”
Witkos said the health of the local GOP is poor.
“I don’t even get a lot of Republicans requesting to serve on a board or commission. There’s apathy there,” Witkos said. “I think we need somebody closer to the local level, the state level, to kind of re-energize the base, give them something to want to fight for, because I think that’s missing in our party.”
Andrew Ziemba, the Republican running against Kavros DeGraw this year, said his party lacks the infrastructure that Kavros DeGraw and the other women built for the Democrats in 2017 and 2018.
“Republicans, they tend to not really have a robust door-knocking effort. They don’t really do the volunteer calls. They don’t really send out these postcards to people. They don’t really have events,” Ziemba said. “I mean, it’s the Democrats who are very well organized. They make the calls, they knock the doors, and they have volunteers who are very aggressive about making those efforts.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Election 2026: Races to Watch
text:
ELECTION 2026 · EDITION 5
Races to Watch

Welcome back to CommonWealth Beacon‘s Election 2026 newsletter run.
The marquee race on the November ballot looks like a matter of margin more than outcome, barring a shocking upset. 
Gov. Maura Healey, seeking a second term, is the heavy favorite over Republican Mike Minogue. Polls through late August showed her leading by roughly 20 points, and a recent CommonWealth Beacon survey put her ahead by 22 points. 
Minogue — a GOP megadonor and former Abiomed CEO who says he plans to govern without a lieutenant governor since the party’s nominee dropped out — has framed his campaign around the cost of living and the argument that state government is “smothering the American dream.” Healey has responded by linking him to President Donald Trump’s agenda, which is deeply unpopular in the Bay State. 


Dive into the data

The state congressional delegation looks likely to sweep through the general election with ease, after a few incumbents waved off primary challenges in September. But there will be at least one new face, filling US Rep. Seth Moulton’s empty seat after his unsuccessful bid to oust US Sen. Ed Markey. Democrat Dan Koh, a former aide in the Biden administration who also worked for Boston Mayor Marty Walsh, is the front-runner in the race for the Sixth Congressional District representing the North Shore. He faces Republican Micah Jones, a US Army veteran who says a “resistance only mindset” from a fully Democratic delegation could cost the state federal resources.  
Democrats are also certain to keep their overwhelming majorities in both chambers at the State House. The majority party currently holds 166 of the Legislature’s 200 seats. But a handful of down-ballot races feature interesting general election contests, based on a CommonWealth Beacon analysis of 2024 presidential results by legislative district: the First Bristol Senate District and the Third, Seventh, and Eighth Bristol House Districts.
First Bristol Senate District 
As chair of the powerful Senate Ways and Means Committee, Sen. Michael Rodrigues of Westport is one of the most influential figures in state government and one of the most trusted deputies to Senate President Karen Spilka. 
He also, despite being a Democrat, represents the single most pro-Trump district in the entire Massachusetts Senate. Two years ago, voters in the First Bristol Senate district that Rodrigues represents broke for the Republican presidential nominee by a margin of nearly 7 percentage points over the Democratic nominee, Vice President Kamala Harris. 
This year, Rodrigues will need to convince those same voters it’s better to keep a high-profile Democrat in the seat against a challenge from Republican Gabriel “Boomer” Amaral of Fall River. Amaral was nearly elected mayor of Fall River last year. He argues that state investments have not kept pace with rising South Shore costs, despite Rodrigues’s leadership position. 
Third Bristol House District 
Another Bristol district will feature a rematch. Democratic incumbent Lisa Field faces Republican Lawrence Quintal in the Third Bristol District, after Field prevailed by just 15 votes in a special election in June 2025. Field filled the seat previously held by Democratic incumbent Carol Doherty, who died earlier that year. 
They are running on essentially identical platforms this time around, with Field promising to continue her efforts to address rising costs of living, protect workers’ rights, ensure affordable and quality health care, create more opportunities for education and workforce development, and promote government transparency.
Quintal says he will prioritize decreasing taxes and energy costs, increasing state aid, and improving housing access for seniors, veterans, and low-income families. 
Harris carried the district — which covers parts of Easton and Taunton — by 5.6 points in 2024. 
Seventh Bristol House District 
A Republican challenging 13-year Democratic incumbent Alan Silvia in the Seventh Bristol District has tried to make hay out of the increasingly partisan politics surrounding state Auditor Diana DiZoglio’s attempts to audit the Legislature. While a solid majority of both parties support the effort, according to polling, Republicans have embraced it as a cudgel against the Democratic leadership. 
Silvia filed a brief supporting DiZiglio’s audit efforts in April, breaking with party leadership and describing their actions as “obstruction.” Silvia said his constituents “continually ask me, ‘Where’s the audit?’ I can no longer sit back and kick this can down the road.” 
Trump carried the district by about 4 percentage points in 2024. Talos Farris, the Republican candidate, accused Silvia of political maneuvering by opposing the audit and then supporting it. Voters, he said, should not have representation that “bows to partisan leadership until their seat is on the line.” 
Eighth Bristol House District 
One of the most Trump-leaning House districts — the Eighth Bristol District covering Westport and parts of Freetown, Acushnet, Fall River, and New Bedford — has been represented by Democrats but teeters on the edge of party alignment. Rep. Steven Ouellette, of Westport, replaced fellow Democrat and 14-year representative Paul Schmid in 2024 by edging out the Republican candidate by just 300 votes. That same year, Trump carried the district by about 11 percentage points over Harris. 
This cycle, Ouellete faces Jesse St. Gelais, a Republican from Acushnet. Both candidates say they are focused on public safety and addressing the soaring cost of living, but St. Gelais has said he would like to see the end of offshore wind and plans to vote “no” on ballot Question 9 in order to repeal the recently passed firearms law. The race looks tighter than a longtime Democratic seat would suggest, according to the New Bedford Light. In the Republican primary, St. Gelais bested by 800 votes the same Republican that Oulette fended off in 2024.

title: Court dismisses former Iowa legislator’s lawsuit against the state
text:
The Iowa Board of Medicine regulates the state's medical profession as part of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. (Photo by Getty Images, board seal courtesy the State of Iowa) A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit brought by a physician and former state senator who sued two Iowa licensing boards after an alleged investigation into his treatment of COVID-19 patients.
Dr. David Hartsuch, an emergency medicine physician and former Republican state senator, sued both the Iowa Board of Medicine and Iowa Board of Pharmacy, alleging retaliation for his exercise of his First Amendment right to free speech, abuse of process, interference with his professional practice, selective enforcement and violations of his due process rights.
Dr. David Hartsuch. (Photo courtesy of the Iowa Legislature)
Hartsuch, a proponent of using ivermectin to treat COVID-19, alleged that in December 2021, Kent Nebel, then the executive director of the Board of Medicine, indicated complaints had been filed against 17 Iowa doctors for spreading false or misleading information about COVID-19.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A few weeks later, the lawsuit claims, Hartsuch received a letter from the board indicating he was under investigation for complaints alleging the “spreading of COVID disinformation.”
According to state records, the Board of Pharmacy had referred the matter to the Board of Medicine after a patient of Hartsuch’s complained that his pharmacist refused to fill the physician’s prescription for ivermectin in the treatment of COVID-19.
Court records show the Board of Medicine’s investigation of Hartsuch focused on three allegations: that he had acted in an unprofessional manner when dealing with a Walgreen’s pharmacist, that he spread misleading information about COVID-19 and its treatment, and that he was prescribing drugs for off-label uses not approved by the FDA to treat COVID-19.
Ivermectin is used in humans to treat infections caused by parasitic worms. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines Panel has recommended ivermectin not be used for treating COVID-19 outside of clinical trials.
In October 2022, the Board of Medicine wrapped up its investigation of Hartsuch and sent him a confidential warning letter reprimanding him for raising his voice to the pharmacist, while indicating it might reexamine the matter at some point in the future.
Two months later, Hartsuch initiated a state-court lawsuit against the two state licensing boards, asking a judge to order the Board of Medicine to expunge its warning letter, which he said had placed him “in fear of communicating with any pharmacist at all.”
In July 2023, the Board of Medicine issued Hartsuch a second letter, rescinding its October 2022 letter. By that point, Hartsuch argued in court, the damage was done — stating he had lost his malpractice coverage, his job at AllMed Inc., and his hospital privileges.
In a series of rulings, the district court found that it lacked jurisdiction over the matter, noting that the board’s action against Hartsuch was “merely a warning letter” that was eventually rescinded, meaning there was no further relief the court could grant.
Hartsuch appealed, but in October 2025, the Iowa Court of Appeals upheld the district court’s ruling, setting the stage for another lawsuit, filed in federal court, alleging the boards’ actions were unreasonable, violated Hartsuch’s rights and destroyed his livelihood.
That lawsuit named as defendants the two licensing boards and 21 individuals, most of whom were board members or part of the boards’ administrative staff. It alleged the defendants “effectively blacklisted” him through their actions and infringed on his First Amendment right to comment on “matters of public concern, including medical opinions, scientific debate, and public health issues relating to COVID-19.”
Recently, U.S. District Judge Stephen H. Locher dismissed Hartsuch’s lawsuit, ruling it had been filed after the two-year statute of limitations had expired and that it had improperly sought damages from individuals who have immunity when acting in their official, quasi-judicial capacity.
“Hartsuch knew enough by July 2023, at the latest, to start the running of the statute of limitations,” Locher stated in his decision.
“He no longer had a timely claim in February 2026” when the lawsuit was filed, Locher added. “Even if Hartsuch’s claims were timely, they would fail on absolute immunity grounds anyway insofar as he seeks damages from defendants in their individual capacities.”
Locher noted that the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals has held in similar cases that licensing board members are entitled to absolute immunity for their work in investigating and adjudicating disciplinary complaints.
Hartsuch’s attorney, Kyle Savage of West Des Moines, declined to comment on the judge’s ruling or the possibility of an appeal.
Hartsuch served as a state senator from Bettendorf from 2007-2010 and ran unsuccessfully for U.S. House in 2008.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana governor rejects brain scans for death row inmate ahead of execution
text:
Death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit is scheduled to be executed Nov. 5 at Indiana State Prison. Gov. Mike Braun's administration declined to authorize additional brain scans sought by his attorneys ahead of a final clemency decision. (Photo courtesy the Indiana Department of Correction)Gov. Mike Braun’s administration will not allow death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit to undergo additional brain scans before his scheduled execution next week.
The decision follows weeks of legal efforts by his attorneys to obtain additional medical evidence for his clemency case.
Braun’s general counsel, Stephanie Flittner, met with Weisheit’s legal team Wednesday to discuss the testing and his pending clemency request.
The governor previously said he would consider the medical evidence if it became available.
The Indiana Supreme Court refused last week to postpone Weisheit’s Nov. 5 execution or order his transportation for testing. But the justices said the executive branch could authorize the scans without court approval.
‘Every single day without them is a struggle’: Mother urges Indiana to uphold death sentence

In a letter to Braun, attorney Joseph Perkovich requested transportation to Franciscan Health in Michigan City for MRI and PET scans. The testing would allow University of Pennsylvania neuropsychologist Ruben Gur to assess whether brain injuries preceded Weisheit’s 2010 murders of 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb.
Indianapolis psychiatrist R. Andrew Chambers separately supported the request, saying modern imaging could help distinguish earlier injuries from one Weisheit suffered during his arrest.
Perkovich also disputed the parole board’s conclusion that jurors had sufficient evidence to impose the death penalty.
The Indiana Parole Board unanimously recommendation Wednesday that Braun deny Weisheit’s request to commute his death sentence to life in prison.
“The jury then decided his fate without reliable scientific information to illuminate the extent of those injuries and their consequences for his behavior,” Perkovich said in a statement.
Braun has not announced his final clemency decision.
Questions additionally remain about the state’s execution drug supply. The Indiana Department of Correction released a $275,000 invoice for execution drugs earlier this month, but has not provided an updated inventory log confirming their receipt.
Previous records showed no pentobarbital remaining after Indiana’s October 2025 execution.
An informal request for a temporary reprieve is also pending before Braun over concerns about Indiana’s lethal injection procedures. Additional information about the state’s execution protocol is expected to be submitted in the coming days.
A reprieve would temporarily delay the execution but would not overturn Weisheit’s death sentence.
Weisheit, 50, was sentenced to death in 2013 for killing the children in a house fire near Evansville. His execution remains scheduled for before sunrise Nov. 5 at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Election 2026: Affordability
text:
ELECTION 2026 · EDITION 3
Affordability
The buzzword that swallowed the 2026 election

Welcome back to CommonWealth Beacon‘s Election 2026 newsletter run.
It all comes back to affordability. 
Gov. Maura Healey, looking likely to skate into her second term come November, has a delicate tightrope to walk: acknowledge that cost-of-living is the major issue concerning voters, and tout the ways she can try to address it without being blamed for the crisis. It’s a precarious position that her Republican challenger is eagerly hammering. 
Massachusetts housing permits lag other states, home electric costs remain high, health care spending keeps rising, and child care costs are among the highest in the nation.  
And that laundry list of expenses has consequences. Between 2020 and 2025, the state experienced a net loss of about 182,000 residents to outmigration. In April, the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce released polling data that showed slightly more than a quarter of young residents in Greater Boston — one of the priciest regions of the state — planned to leave the region in the next five years.  
The culprit: cost, particularly housing costs, which are among the highest in the nation according to state data. 


Dive into the data

When a UMass Amherst poll asked voters in August about the major issues they want their elected leadership to address, cost of living rose to the top. 
“Bay Staters not only see affordability as a pressing problem but also want Gov. Healey and the state Legislature to do something about it, with a whopping 39 percent of respondents identifying the cost of living as the one issue they want these elected officials to tackle in the coming year,” said Tatishe Nteta, provost professor of political science at UMass Amherst and director of the poll.  
As the midterms approach, he said, “Republican candidates may want to center affordability in their campaigns as a way to connect directly with voters’ most pressing concerns and potentially upset Democratic incumbents.” 
A CommonWealth Beacon poll conducted by the MassINC Polling group in September asked likely voters about their high-priority areas when deciding how to vote in November. Thirty percent said inflation and cost of living.  
This economic anxiety has shaped the primaries as well as the general election. A dispute over Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s proposal to reduce property taxes for Bostonians, which hit a dead end in the state Senate, prompted her to back two unsuccessful challenges to the Boston senators who bucked her plan. 

Had it not been tossed by the state’s highest court on a technicality, a ballot measure that would have cut income taxes was expected to pass, though legislative leaders warned that it would pose a ticking revenue bomb.
“There aren’t many people out there that’re going to go to the polls and … not vote to give themselves a tax cut,” Speaker Ron Mariano said in March. “So we think it’s going to pass and creates a whole set of other problems for us that we have to deal with.”  
Another ballot measure that would make it more likely that the state would have to issue refunds to taxpayers is still set to go before voters in November. 
At the top of the ballot, both Healey and Minogue have centered affordability in their campaigns, though they’ve framed it differently. Minogue says one-party state government is to blame and has called for tax cuts, a budget audit, and a gas tax suspension.  
Gov. Maura Healey holds up a hard copy of her fiscal year 2027 state budget proposal at a press conference on January 28, 2026. Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon
The sitting governor is spending more space in campaign materials looking back than laying out a plan forward. Healey has pointed to actions she’s already taken — capping copays, ordering utility refunds, signing a 2023 tax cut. With winter heating costs looming, she has proposed a two-month gas tax suspension of her own this fall and asked Eversource, National Grid, and Unitil to begin issuing ratepayer refunds for a share of the utilities’ profits immediately rather than waiting until the federal deadline next May. 
Housing costs — routinely cited as the most stinging pain point in polling about affordability — have skyrocketed in Massachusetts over the past two and a half decades. According to Zillow’s home price index, median home prices in the Bay State have jumped 73 percent since 2000.  
The state estimates that the average single family home price cost $610,000 in 2024, which would take a salary of about $162,000 a year to afford. Beacon Hill leaders have pointed to major policy shifts like the MBTA Communities multifamily housing law as an example of clearing the way for more units, but such proposals have run into forceful objection from cities and towns who want to retain control over their local character. 
One measure on the ballot, Question 7, is aimed at making it easier to build smaller, affordable single-family homes in more places. Healey has thrown her support behind the measure. 
Mike Minogue gives gives his victory speech after the September 2026 Massachusetts primary election. (Emily Glick/CommonWealth Beacon)
And the increasingly dire cost of health care is hitting residents hard. Massachusetts has the highest family health insurance premiums in the country, according to the state Health Policy Commission.  
Healey has leaned on recommendations from her affordability working group, including backing efforts to direct more money toward the beleaguered primary care system and stabilize in- and out-of-network costs. Minogue says he is focused on reducing waste in the system and prioritizing community-based care. 
Meanwhile, the national environment is intruding into all of these affordability discussions. Democrats are pointing to the Trump administration’s changes to Medicaid eligibility rules that could send hundreds of thousands off the rolls in the Bay State. Plus, tariff disputes and pervasively high inflation are keeping the cost of building new housing at a premium even if state lawmakers manage to ease the permitting process.
