title: ‘No-hire, no-fire’ flat labor market continues. Is a Jackson casino possible?: Mississippi Marketplace
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi’s unemployment rate dropped only slightly in September, from 3.4% to 3.3%, the lowest since July 2024 when it was 3.1.%. 
The unemployment rate has decreased slightly over the last several months after remaining around 3.8% for almost a year. 



September 2026 unemployment numbers released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed the number of jobs in Mississippi held relatively steady, dropping by about 700 jobs compared to August, mirroring the national “no-hire, no-fire” environment.
“We’ve got a steady labor market, not a whole of jobs being added but not seeing declines in employment, either,” said Corey Miller, Mississippi’s chief economist. 
Katherine Lin
Unemployment claims have declined over the past year, but so has the number of people in the labor force, leading to a lower labor-force participation rate, following national trends. 
Mississippi has one of the lowest labor force participation rates in the country. In September, the rate was 54.3%, down from 55.8% a year earlier. The national rate was 61.8% in September.
UMMC building new cancer center
The University of Mississippi Medical Center has broken ground on a new cancer center in Jackson. UMMC, the state’s only academic medical center, said the building is critical to its goal of achieving National Cancer Institute designation and improving patient outcomes. The building is expected to cost $250 million with funds coming from the state, federal government and private donors.
The center could bring more jobs to the area and generate additional economic benefits for the region. UMMC estimates that once it opens, an NCI designated center would generate over $200 million a year in economic benefit.
UMMC has sought the NCI designation for over a decade. Dr. Alan Jones, the medical center’s associate vice chancellor for health affairs said achieving the designation will take more time.
UMMC will need to hire more faculty, perform community outreach and expand its research capabilities. Researchers receive federal grants, but the grants do not cover all the costs associated with running a large, complex research organization.
Is a Jackson casino possible?
Investors want to build a casino along the Pearl River in Jackson and asked the City Council to sell them city-owned land. Rep. Chris Bell, a Democrat from Jackson, said the project would bring in much needed tax dollars for the city. For the project to happen, it would need approval from the Legislature, which Bell has attempted and failed to secure multiple times.
Tax revenue from Mississippi’s gross casino earnings has been flat over the last few years according to numbers from the Department of Revenue. The growth of online gambling and prediction markets, although mobile sports betting outside casinos remains illegal in Mississippi, is an increasing worry for the casino industry. 
Other news

Barge Forest Products is investing $8.3 million to expand its sawmill operations in Macon.
Jackson-area business leaders discussed the impact of data centers on Mississippi communities as the centers face increasing pushback from residents and lawmakers. 
Mississippi, the Federal Trade Commission and 19 other states filed a lawsuit against Dollar General claiming the company has persistently overcharged customers. In 2023, Mississippi had the highest number of Dollar General stores per capita.
Ingalls Shipbuilding received a $99-million contract for testing and upgrades on a Navy destroyer. 
Fairbanks Morse Defense will double its capacity in Pascagoula. The $60-million expansion includes $27 million from the U.S. navy.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Election 2026: Follow the Money
text:
ELECTION 2026 · EDITION 3
Follow the Money

Welcome back to CommonWealth Beacon‘s Election 2026 newsletter run.
It’s not just the cost of living that’s made the 2026 elections in Massachusetts a matter of money. 
Political spending has become one of the primary avenues of attack Gov. Maura Healey is taking against her opponent, Mike Minogue. The Republican earned a fortune leading and then selling medical device company Abiomed; in recent years, he’s donated hundreds of thousands of dollars to the Republican National Committee and to a pro-Trump super PAC.  
That alone would give ammunition to any Democrat. And Minogue has also put his wealth toward his own campaign, donating more than $17 million as of early October and significantly outspending Healey, who herself has raised about $7.6 million since the start of 2025.
Cue the governor’s attack ad. 
Plus, there are a record-tying nine ballot questions set to go before voters, which have already generated millions of dollars in spending and have a solid chance at tying the single-cycle record of $65.8 million set in 2022, when four questions were on the ballot, including a landmark surtax on wealthy households, which passed with 52 percent of the vote. 
Unlike individual candidates for office, who cannot receive more than $1,000 in donations from a single source in a year, there are no limits on what Bay Staters, businesses, and political action committees can contribute to ballot question campaigns. 


Dive into the data

That’s allowed a small fortune to change hands already. Smart Approaches to Marijuana, a national nonprofit that opposes legal drug use, is the single biggest question backer this cycle so far with $3.5 million contributed to the effort to repeal recreational marijuana. The coalition of business groups known as the Massachusetts Opportunity Alliance has offered $1.9 million, all in-kind contributions, to the effort to tweak a state tax cap. And several private-equity hotshots have put big money behind a proposal to change state primary elections, with Randy Peeler — a founding donor to CommonWealth Beacon – kicking in more than $1 million. 

It’s a robust business across state elections, but for the 160-member House and 40-member Senate, less of the money goes directly into campaigning than you might think. 
Consider the tale of two senators. Will Brownsberger had one of the toughest primary elections of all his colleagues, a closely watched race against Boston Mayor Michelle Wu-backed challenger Daniel Lander that he barely survived following a recount. Senate President Karen Spilka was once again unopposed — in fact, she hasn’t faced a challenger for her Senate seat since 2010. 
Since the start of the year, Brownsberger spent nearly $575,000 on the effort to keep his seat, nearly twice as much as Spilka spent in that span. 
But if you count from the start of the two-year term, the order is flipped. From January 1, 2025, through the end of August 2026, Brownsberger spent about $838,000, and Spilka spent $938,000 on a whole host of things from political consulting to travel to a conference to a $2,150 “ice cream reception for Senate staff during budget week.” 
That’s the way money has long worked in the Legislature: lawmakers burn piles of campaign cash even when they don’t need to exert an ounce of effort to secure reelection. In 2024, a study by state campaign finance regulators found, candidates running for the House unopposed spent about $1,700 more on average than candidates running for the House with opponents — a figure probably skewed by routine big spending among the chamber’s most powerful Democrats. 
But if someone doesn’t have an opponent, you might ask, what are they even buying with all that money? 
The answer: A little bit of everything. There’s the maintenance of websites and offices. Consultants and strategists remain on the payroll even in times of smooth sailing. Lawmakers send condolence flowers to friends and constituents and charge it to their campaign accounts. 
Then there are the other expenses. House Speaker Ron Mariano dropped $379.48 on “refreshments for the office” in January 2026. In late August, Sen. Julian Cyr picked up a $417.73 tab at Mac’s Fish House in Provincetown for what he described as a “mtg w/ colleague and supporters.” 
All of that is allowed, technically, because state campaign finance laws governing legislators allow the use of campaign dollars on anything that supports a candidate’s “political future.” 
As election mania hits its peak, don’t expect the avalanche to slow. Minogue set a record in September for the most a gubernatorial candidate spent in a single month, with $6.1 million. Healey, meanwhile, splashed out $4.1 million of her own, the most she personally has spent in a single month of campaigning dating back to her inaugural attorney general campaign in 2014. 
No one ever said politics is cheap.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Lamont and Fazio reveal their playlists, top reads. Spoiler: They both like Dolly.
text:
One of this year’s candidates for governor gravitates toward country breakout Ella Langley and enjoys Beyoncé’s “Cowboy Carter” during a workout. The other has long favored Bob Marley and the Wailers to soundtrack his campaign events, and recently added Bad Bunny to his playlist. Their tastes overlap when it comes to stars like Dolly Parton, though they may disagree on her greatest song. 
Those selections, and what they might telegraph to voters, landed on reading lists and earworm-heavy playlists that incumbent Gov. Ned Lamont and his challenger, state Sen. Ryan Fazio — both of Greenwich — revealed to The Connecticut Mirror ahead of this year’s general election. 
The candidates said books and music have informed their political philosophies, broadened their worldviews, and carried them through gnarly moments on and off the campaign trail.
“Music has a very important place in our soul,” Lamont said. 
The playlist trend was first popularized by President Barack Obama in the summer of 2015. He still releases listening suggestions and a summer reading list each year.
Stephen Dyson, a professor of political science at the University of Connecticut who hosts the “Pop Culture Professors” podcast with fellow political scientist Jeffrey Dudas, offered some skepticism of the candidates’ selections.
Dyson, who grew up in the United Kingdom, recalled a moment in the early 2000s when Conservative Prime Minister David Cameron named the indie rock band The Smiths as one of his favorites, in what many saw as an attempt to appear hip. Around the same time, Labour Party Leader Gordon Brown cited a fondness for the Arctic Monkeys, but couldn’t name a single track.
“So you’re obviously gonna get some political signalling from candidates,” Dyson said. And yet, as an academic who still remembers making mixtapes and burning CDs as a young person, he thinks there’s something endearing about it. 
It’s as if the candidates are saying to Connecticut residents, “Look, I burned you a CD,” he said.
There’s a similar feeling when it comes to a reading list, Dyson said, particularly at a time when the act of reading itself is becoming an increasingly rarefied one.
“If someone recommends a book to you, that’s a generous act,” he said. “It’s an interesting communicative act. It’s not just saying, ‘I read this and related to it,’ … it’s also saying, ‘We have this in common.’” 
The playlists
When Lamont dips into his list of most-loved songs, he said, some of them are simply pieces he grew up with — he will never not include something from the Grateful Dead or the Rolling Stones. Others are songs he’s come to love through his wife, Annie Lamont, children and young grandchildren. That’s how Taylor Swift’s “Cruel Summer,” off her 2019 album “Lover,” found a place on the list.
The governor said he likes to dance, and some of the songs on his playlist are there specifically for when he feels like moving. He called the Black Eyed Peas’ “I Gotta Feeling,” his favorite song to dance to at a Connecticut Association of Realtors conference in 2023. And he said Walk The Moon’s “Shut Up and Dance” is hard to listen to while standing still.
“It’s just a cool dance song,” he said, chuckling at how many people suggested he not dance in public after a video of him dancing at the 2019 inaugural ball went viral.
Some selections were songs that informed his path to politics; others have come to his attention since spending time in the capital city.
For years, he has loved Bob Marley and the Wailers’ “Get Up, Stand Up,” for both the song’s revolutionary message and Marley’s own history. He’s been known to sing it on the campaign trail, from labor union rallies in New Haven to a No Kings Protest in Greenwich last year.
He included Bob Dylan’s “The Times They Are A-Changin’” and Dolly Parton’s “9 to 5″ for similar reasons. He said he sees the latter as a singular ballad of both workplace equity and female empowerment. “It’s really about women standing up and fighting for their rights,” he said. 
Bad Bunny’s “DtMF” was a more recent addition. A director in the governor’s office, Mellaney Castro, turned him on to the artist, whose cultural reach has extended from Puerto Rico to Connecticut and back several times over. In February, he took a break from budget season to watch the musician perform at the Superbowl’s halftime show. 
“Look, I thought the guy was just magic,” he said. 
Fazio’s musical tastes range from “the type of music I fell in love with from a young age” to contemporary country music, with recent favorites like Ella Langley and Toby Keith and veteran musical voices in the genre like George Strait. “I’m an Ella fella!” he said of Langley.
His selections also have a nostalgic bent. Fazio is especially fond of Creedence Clearwater Revival; the Eagles; Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young; Bob Dylan; and Elvis Presley. Often, he said, he reaches for the soulful sound of the 1960s and 1970s, with selections from Otis Redding, Sam Cooke and Billy Preston. 
“I’m mostly listening to music if I’m on a run or working out,” Fazio said. Some of his favorites that keep him going during a workout: Parton’s “Jolene,” Don McLean’s “American Pie,” the Eagles’ “Take It Easy” and Billy Preston’s catchy “Nothing From Nothing.”
While it does not live on his list, he said he also has an appreciation for Beyoncé’s 2024 album “Cowboy Carter,” which became a flashpoint in the country music world. He said he particularly likes the tracks “Texas Hold ‘Em” and “16 Carriages.”
Reading lists
The governor described his reading list as a mix of “aspirational” and well-loved books that he comes back to again and again. He regularly reads “The Little Engine That Could” to his grandson, who gravitates toward anything with trains. And he said he’s returned dozens of times to the first sentences of the Declaration of Independence and to Walter Isaacson’s “The Greatest Sentence Ever Written.” 
Keith Richards’ memoir, “Life,” holds special meaning for Lamont, after he had the chance last March to present the founding member of the Rolling Stones with the first-ever Connecticut Governor’s Award of Excellence. Referring to his music, Lamont told Richards at the ceremony, “You’re one of my top advisors.”
Like many Connecticut residents, Lamont said he has books on his list that he still wants to get to. They include Colson Whitehead’s “Harlem Shuffle” and Barbara Kingsolver’s “Demon Copperhead.” 
“Reading really broadens the mind,” Lamont said. “I read an awful lot of history, and I think it tends to put the consternation of today’s political world into a little bit of perspective.”
Here is Gov. Ned Lamont’s reading list:

“The Little Engine That Could” by Watty Piper
“1929: Inside the Crash” by Andrew Ross Sorkin
“The Greatest Sentence Ever Written” by Walter Isaacson
“Never Stop” by Dan Hurley
“The Rise of Theodore Roosevelt” by Edmund Morris
“Life” by Keith Richards
“Harlem Shuffle” by Colson Whitehead
“Demon Copperhead” by Barbara Kingsolver
“The Great Gatsby” by F. Scott Fitzgerald
“The Overstory” by Richard Powers


Fazio’s reading list is packed with sweeping historical novels, political and economic commentary, spy thrillers and 20th-century history that he was most excited to talk about. That starts, not in Greenwich or Hartford, but with two novels that take place a world away in 19th-century Russia: Leo Tolstoy’s “Anna Karenina” and Fyodor Dostoevsky’s “The Brothers Karamazov.”
“It was so striking to me that the heroes of those books — it wasn’t the most intellectual or the most secular or the most revolutionary [people], it was the ones who were the most steady, the most faithful and focused on protecting their family and their friends and doing what was right, even if it was considered banal or outmoded,” he said. “Anna Karenina is not the hero of that book. She showed that the flouting of basic ethics for dramatic and romantic reasons was bad for the soul.”
When Fazio first discovered the books in his 20s, they became a reminder, if not a blueprint, for how to remain “steady,” he said. For a time, he was for a period spiritually adrift, and they helped bring him back to his Christian faith. In literary characters who remained unwavering in their faith, he saw a reflection of his late maternal grandmother, Anne Gadaleta, who Fazio has often cited as both a personal role model and an example of self-determination. 
Other selections have shaped how he governs and how he sees the world of politics and economics, which he studied at Northwestern University. Alongside texts like Milton Freidman’s “Capitalism and Freedom,” which informed Fazio’s fiscal conservatism, he said he returns to Harry Jaffa’s 1959 “Crisis of the House Divided.”
The book focuses on the spirited verbal sparring of then-Rep. Abraham Lincoln and Illinois State Sen. Stephen Douglas during the 1858 debates for U.S. Senate. When Fazio thinks of the book, he said, he’s especially struck by Lincoln’s unwavering nature and interpretation of the Declaration of Independence.
Fazio’s belief in the American brand of freedom, or at least the idea of it, might also explain his interest in spy thrillers and novels about government overreach and the surveillance state, like John Le Carré’s “Tinker Tanker Soldier Spy” (in an email that strayed briefly to movies, he includes the 2006 film “Das Leben der Anderen,” or “The Lives of Others,” in the same spirit).
Here is state Sen. Ryan Fazio’s reading list: 

“Anna Karenina” by Leo Tolstoy
“The Brothers Karamazov” by Fyodor Dostoevsky
“Gulag Archipelago” by Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
“The Sun Also Rises” by Ernest Hemingway
“Capitalism and Freedom” by Milton Friedman
“The Road to Serfdom” by Friedrich Hayek
“Crisis of the House Divided: An Interpretation of the Issues in the Lincoln-Douglas Debates” by Harry Jaffa
“The Spy and the Traitor: The Greatest Espionage Story of the Cold War” by Ben Macintyre
“Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy” by John Le Carré
“Vision of the Anointed” by Thomas Sowell

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ Assembly OKs bills expanding human trafficking protections and enforcement
text:
Three months after cops rescued 100 victims and arrested 71 offenders, New Jersey lawmakers passed nine bills to bolster human trafficking protections. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey lawmakers approved nine bills Thursday that would expand penalties for human traffickers, protections for victims, public education efforts, and training for truckers and police on how to spot and stop human trafficking.
The measures are meant to crack down on a growing crime that’s typically underreported and hard to detect, with New Jersey considered vulnerable due to its dense population and location along the I-95 corridor.
The bills come three months after human trafficking investigators rescued almost 100 suspected victims and arrested 71 offenders during the World Cup soccer tournament held over the summer in East Rutherford.
One of the most impactful bills would eliminate the statute of limitations for criminal prosecutions and civil lawsuits involving human trafficking and aggravated sexual contact, which now stands at five years in New Jersey.
Bill sponsor Assemblyman Sterley Stanley (D-Middlesex) called the change “long overdue.”
“This is not nearly enough time for someone to process such immense trauma, let alone be able to address it through the legal system. Some may not even understand they were a victim of human trafficking or aggravated sexual contact until long past five years and may have been children at the time of the crime,” Stanley said. “By increasing the amount of time victims have to bring charges against those who have harmed them, we give victims a better tool to seek the justice they rightly deserve.”
Another measure would toughen penalties for people who promote prostitution and create new crimes, making it a second-degree offense to lead a prostitution network and a third-degree crime to participate in one.
A third bill would expand penalties for patrons of prostitution, with fines going to victim assistance funds.
“Enhanced penalties for being a patron of prostitution is a critical way to decrease the demand for this harmful and illegal industry,” bill sponsor Assemblywoman Carol Murphy (D-Burlington) said in a statement.
Other measures would expand criminal and civil penalties for human trafficking and training requirements for law enforcement; require commercial truckers to be trained on how to spot and stop trafficking; mandate that signs advertising a human trafficking hotline be displayed in gas stations, nail salons, staffing agencies, and more; and require public awareness signs to be in Chinese and Korean.
Another bill would require the state attorney general to review statewide policy on human trafficking. The directive now in place dates to 2012.
Stanley’s bill to eliminate the statute of limitations now heads to the governor’s desk, because the Senate unanimously approved it in June. Most of the other bills await votes before the full Senate or in the Senate’s judiciary or law and public safety committees.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: As campaign winds down, Rep. Scott Perry gets biblical with ‘good vs. evil’ pitch
text:
Rep. Scott Perry joins Pastor Edel Santana in prayer at an Oct. 28, 2026 rally in Dauphin County (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)With the November election just days away, six-term incumbent Rep. Scott Perry offered a stark message to voters at a rally with U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.). 
“The devil is everywhere. You can see it in the things we’re talking about,” Perry told a crowd of roughly 200 supporters at an American Legion post in Linglestown, Dauphin County, Wednesday evening.
In his seven-minute speech, Perry talked about what he saw as the successes of the Trump administration — cutting Medicaid spending, sharply curbing immigration and prosecuting the war in Iran — but the devil could be found in the partisan political struggles in Washington, D.C. and the agenda of his opposition.
“The adversary’s not in this room,” he said. “The adversary’s out there trying to destroy our country and take our country down.”
As Perry faces what may be his most difficult reelection fight yet, his rally with one of the country’s most powerful Republicans was about setting high stakes.
“I don’t mean to make light of this. We are in a battle for the soul of our nation,” Perry said just after taking the stage. He encouraged the crowd to think of the election as part of a “battle between good and evil.”

Voter Guide: 2026 Pennsylvania General Election


While Perry framed the election in biblical terms, Johnson, who is third in line for the presidency, warned that if Democrats gain more power — the party is hoping to flip both the U.S. House and Senate — their agenda would be driven by their “Marxist, communist left” flank.
“They’re gonna take over the means of production,” Johnson warned. “They’re gonna eliminate private property ownership. I’m not making this up. It’s not just trans surgeries for children and the abolishment of prison. It’s everything. It’s madness.”
Johnson was referring in part to the platform of the Democratic Socialists of America, which calls for abolishing the Senate, abolishing police, and “public ownership of the largest corporations and essential industries.” Notably, the Trump administration has announced major public investments in 40 private companies in key industries, according to the CATO institute. That includes taking a roughly 10% stake in the computer chip maker Intel and a 35% stake in an oil company with fields in Venezuela.
Perry, a six-term incumbent, faces former WGAL news anchor Janelle Stelson, who he beat by just over 1% the vote in 2024. That was a year when Democrats underperformed up and down the ballot, and many in Stelson’s camp hope voter dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump can help her finally win a majority vote this year.
In a statement provided to the Capital-Star after Perry’s rally, Stelson, a former Republican, said, “I do not see Republicans as evil. I do not see Congressman Perry as evil. I believe that after 30 years, Scott Perry has been in politics too long. And I believe he is out of touch with our area.”
Stelson specifically criticized Perry’s support of the Trump administration’s tariff regime and the war in Iran, and added that she opposes “the policies of a group of far-left members of the Democratic Party who support open borders and defunding police.”
The 10th District race has become the most expensive for a U.S. House seat in Pennsylvania. The two candidates have collectively raised nearly $16 million and Stelson has the fundraising edge. Though recent polling has the candidates locked in a virtual tie.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More broadly, polling shows Johnson’s majority may be in trouble as Democrats make gains even in traditionally Republican districts. Control of the U.S. Senate will also come down to the outcome of a handful of closely-watched elections.
Near the top of his speech, Johnson warned voters not to trust those polls.
“All the pollsters are wrong,” Johnson said. “Let me tell you what’s happening: they’re undersampling Republicans. We know it to be true.”
Johnson alleged some have pollsters that presented “fraudulent numbers … leaning far in favor of Democrats.” He cited a recent Pew Research Center report he described as “admitt[ing] that their polling is inaccurate.”
Johnson was likely referring to a Pew report on how pollsters can weight responses to account for Republicans becoming less likely to participate in them. (As a note of disclosure, the Pennsylvania Capital-Star is part of the States Newsroom network, which has received funding from the Pew Charitable Trusts.)
When Johnson asked the crowd who had participated in a political poll in the last six months, around 10 of roughly 200 attendees raised their hands.
In his nearly 20-minute speech, Johnson also touted Republicans’ legislative accomplishments during Trump’s second term. In particular, he highlighted tax cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including ending taxes on tips and expanded tax deductions for seniors on Social Security.
He also praised the creation of a nationwide school voucher program (participation is up to states, and so far Gov. Josh Shapiro has yet to opt in Pennsylvania) and a prohibition on Medicaid funding going to Planned Parenthood. And he touted historically low crime rates and unemployment as proof of Republicans’ success under the current Trump administration.
But, Johnson stressed that the coming election was about more than policy preference.
“In the next Congress, we’re not going to be having all the traditional arguments about marginal tax rates, and shades of regulation, and slight differences in foreign policy,” he said. “We are going to be fighting to defend the American way, to hold the republic, to keep it and pass it along to our children and grandchildren.”
Rep. Scott Perry speaks at an Oct. 28, 2026 rally in Dauphin County (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“Make sure our voice is heard”
While Perry described the current political landscape as a battle — he compared Republicans and their supporters to American troops in Normandy on D-Day, persevering against seemingly impossible odds — he also reminded supporters that the fight was at the ballot box.
“We don’t have to pick up arms, God bless it, we don’t have to do that,” he said. “All we have to do is make sure our voice is heard. Gently do that by making sure your battle is in and counted.”
Following Trump’s electoral defeat in 2020, Perry was “a key congressional [ally]” as the president fought to block certification of the election, according to a report authored by the Jan. 6 Select Committee. Despite no evidence of widespread fraud, Perry voted not to certify Democrat Joe Biden as the winner after rioters temporarily forced Congress from its chambers on Jan. 6, 2021.
While Perry and Johnson framed the election in existential terms, State Rep. Marc Anderson (R-York), who served as host at the rally, focused his comments on Stelson.
“She doesn’t have a plan,” he said. “She would do exactly what [Minority Leader] Hakeem Jeffries tells her to do.”
State Rep. Joe Kerwin (R-Dauhin) and state Sen. Greg Rothman (R-Cumberland) also spoke ahead of Perry and Johnson.
Rothman, who serves as elected chair of the Pennsylvania Republican Party, urged attendees to remember how much had changed since President Trump took office. Inflation, he said, had drastically lowered since its highs under Biden in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, and illegal immigration has plummeted too.
A pair of pastors opened and closed the rally with prayer.
“This is about spiritual warfare,” York County Bible Baptist Church Pastor Bill Schutt said near the beginning of the rally, urging supporters to engage by helping get out the vote. “We need God’s people to get engaged in this warfare.”
Harrisburg Pastor Edel Santana closed the rally with a benediction. He said he would be in his church overnight Friday and fast all day Saturday ahead of the election.
“God, do not allow these socialists to take control,” he said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Judge blocks Medicaid rule forcing sick recipients to prove frailty
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Chronically ill people on Medicaid won’t be bound by new work requirement rules that the latest Trump administration guidance requires in order to qualify for “medically frail” exemptions, a federal judge ruled Thursday.
U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston gave a partial victory to a coalition of 25 states and the District of Columbia, which sued the Trump administration in June over the new Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services guidance linked to the 2025 law known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” Connecticut was one of the plaintiff states.
The law says the definition of medically frail must include people who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders or disabling mental disorders, have certain disabilities that significantly impair daily activities, or have serious or complex medical conditions. But the CMS rule went further, requiring people in those categories to show that their conditions also “significantly impair” their ability to comply with the law’s work requirements.
The plaintiffs argued that the stricter rule would prevent eligible Americans from accessing the care they need — and oversteps the text of the law itself as well.
“The states have met their burden of showing irreparable harm for which monetary damages would provide inadequate compensation — they face the burden of costly and intensive alterations to their eligibility verification systems,” Stearns said in his 16-page ruling.
In a statement Thursday afternoon, Connecticut Attorney General William Tong said, “This was another web of useless red tape concocted by Trump to deny millions of Americans access to healthcare. We sued and we stopped him, and we’re going to keep fighting to protect access to Medicaid free from arbitrary and cruel bureaucratic barriers.”
[RELATED: About 110,000 poor CT adults could lose Medicaid coverage]
Notably, while the ruling will make it easier for some Medicaid recipients with qualifying medical conditions to obtain an exemption from the new work requirements, Stearns’ decision does not strike down the work requirements as unlawful.
Additionally, Stearns upheld two other federal restrictions on how states can verify medical frailty: including the requirement that states reject proof of patients’ medical frailty if the diagnosis is more than a year old. He also upheld a policy allowing states to accept only one self-attestation per continuous period of enrollment.
Explaining why he upheld the portions in favor of the government, Stearns said “the government provided a non-frivolous rationale for adopting each provision and explained why it did not find the States’ concerns of disenrollment compelling.”
Representatives from the Department of Health and Human Services and CMS did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment.
The new Medicaid restrictions are part of Trump’s big tax and policy law in 2025. The change affects those covered through an expansion in most states that gave more lower-income people access to the government’s safety net healthcare program.
Starting Jan. 1, expansion enrollees aged 19 to 64 must show that they work or do community service at least 80 hours a month, or are in school at least half the time. There are exceptions for those considered medically frail or in addiction treatment programs, among others.
CT Mirror staff contributed to this story.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: I want a cure for brain tumors, so I’m going to vote for it
text:
(iStock / Getty Images Plus)Scientific research is the reason we have treatments for thyroid cancer, surgery options for breast cancer patients, and hope for individuals fighting brain tumors. For five years, I fundraised and ran marathons to raise money for scientific studies researching the causes of, and treatments for, cancers, including an aggressive brain tumor that my stepfather passed away from in 2019.
Now, as a public health scientist, I rely on federal funding to research infectious diseases and the tools that keep communities healthy. This year, instead of running and fundraising for a cure for brain cancer, I’m voting in the midterm elections.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Clinical trials are a crucial component of medical scientific research. These trials test potential treatments for many diseases, including cancers, and rigorously screen for efficacy and safety. Many are funded by the National Institutes of Health, a federal organization whose budget is controlled by, and voted on, by our elected officials each year. Our representatives in the U.S. Senate and U.S. House are decision-makers on NIH funding increases and cuts. When science is deprioritized, funding falls, trickling all the way from Washington, D.C., to the Denver metro area.
Federal funding cuts to the NIH caused chaos and halted pediatric brain tumor clinical trials in Colorado earlier this year. As a result of decisions made by our elected officials, Colorado children and their families fighting the hardest battles at Children’s Hospital Colorado were thrust into the reality of what funding cuts to science mean: loss of potential treatments and loss of hope for patients. When my stepfather was enrolled in a clinical trial for his glioblastoma, our family was given hope and potentially more time. Even after he passed away, his participation in the trial and legacy means that the medical community is one step closer to finding a cure.
Research and hope for patients are at risk of being defunded, deprioritized and devalued by politicians, following trends of NIH delays and reductions since January 2025. I also know that the marathons and fundraising I’ve done cannot make up the entire gap in funding when our elected officials sideline scientific research. I believe that we need politicians in office who understand the value of science and research for the Colorado families that spend their lives in and out of hospitals, fighting for discoveries and cures.
When I cast my vote in the Colorado midterms, I want to vote for candidates who will listen to experts and follow the science for better health for my family and my communities.
I know the systems that dictate whether medical trials for potential cancer treatments are funded or not, because they are the same systems that govern my own scientific work. How our elected officials think about science and evidence now, during campaigns, can tell us exactly how they might support federal and state funding for child cancer research and other important medical studies.
I can’t vote for an immediate cure for brain cancer, but I can be informed when I head to the voting booth this fall about how candidates will utilize evidence in policymaking. Will the people on your ballot prioritize science? Clinical trials? Cures for brain cancer?

name: National
title: Trump administration has slow-walked 380,000 potential immigrant voters
text:
New U.S. citizens sing the national anthem during an August 2026 naturalization ceremony in Chicago. Naturalizations began dropping late last year as the USCIS started a new, longer process for applicants, including screening social media accounts for “anti-American activities.” (Photo by Maggie Dougherty/Capitol News Illinois)The Trump administration cut naturalization sharply over the past year, leading to accusations it’s holding back hundreds of thousands of people who might have voted in the midterms.
It’s hard to say how those people might have voted had they become U.S. citizens. Naturalized citizens voted Democratic for president by a wide margin in 2020, but in a shift almost half voted for President Donald Trump in 2024, according to a Pew Research Center analysis last year. However, recent elections in immigrant areas in Florida and New Jersey show a return to traditional Democratic voting patterns as anger mounts over mass arrests and deportations of non-criminal immigrants.
The most recent quarterly report from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services shows the agency approved about 55,000 requests for citizenship between April and June, compared with more than 230,000 for the same period last year. 
DHS targeting naturalized Americans in voter investigations, civil rights groups say

Naturalizations began dropping late last year as USCIS started a new, longer process for applicants, including screening social media accounts for “anti-American activities,” and requirements for more English language and civics knowledge, USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler told Stateline in a statement. 
The potential impact: Almost 380,000 immigrants might have become citizens — and therefore voters — over the past year had the approval rate stayed the same. Almost all would have been potential midterm voters since only adults can complete the naturalization process recorded in statistics — children can get naturalized citizenship in other ways based on their parents’ status. 
The processing delays come amid broader attacks by the Trump administration related to voting and citizenship, with officials attempting to block some ballots from being counted and threatening election officials with prosecution. This week, a coalition of civil rights groups accused the administration of targeting naturalized citizens, saying legitimate voters might be disenfranchised. 
Had USCIS processed naturalization applications this past year at the rate it has in the past, significantly more new U.S. citizens could be voting on Election Day.
The potential difference of 380,000 voters is calculated by the lag between about 871,000 new citizens approved between mid-2024 and mid-2025 — including during parts of the Biden and second Trump administrations — and the latest year, with about 481,000 approvals. 
Kahler, the USCIS spokesperson, defended the slowdown.
“Naturalization is a privilege, not a right,” Kahler wrote in the statement to Stateline. “U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is reinforcing robust screening and vetting and has implemented reforms to ensure U.S. citizenship is reserved for those who qualify.”  
Changes he mentioned include reestablishment of a civics test, reinforcing English language proficiency requirements, screening applicants’ social media and “ensuring applicants demonstrate good moral character and attachment to the Constitution,” he wrote, adding that “USCIS will not take shortcuts in the naturalization process.” 
GOP redistricting could backfire as urban, immigrant areas turn back to Democrats

An immigrant advocacy group, the National Partnership for New Americans, said the result is fewer immigrants gaining voting privileges and other rights with citizenship.  
“The administration is deliberately extending wait times across the naturalization process — including significant delays between interview approval and the Oath of Allegiance — in an apparent effort to deny otherwise eligible people their civil and voting rights,” the organization wrote in October. 
Nicole Melaku, the partnership’s executive director, told Stateline that “we see a very clear attempt to curb legal pathways, including who gets to the finish line on naturalization. The stark decline (in new approvals) shows that reality.”
About 10% of eligible voters, 25 million, are naturalized immigrants as of 2024, according to an Oct. 27 Pew Research Center report, up steadily since 2000, when it was 6.2%. 
The share of voters is especially prevalent in California (22%), New Jersey (20%), New York (19%), Florida (17%) and Hawaii (16%), according to the Pew report.
In the latest U.S. Census Bureau estimates released Oct. 29, there were large shifts in the way respondents reported naturalized status between mid-2024 and mid-2025 in the opening months of the new Trump administration. 
About 1.2 million fewer immigrants said they were noncitizens and about 1.3 million more said they were naturalized citizens. The change was especially lopsided in Texas, where 155,000 fewer people said they were noncitizens but an additional 244,000 said they were naturalized citizens. 
Judge denies attempt by Trump’s DOJ to exclude 20,000 California ballots from vote count

The monthly survey reached about 1.7 million households last year, fewer than the usual 2 million partly because of government shutdown issues, with a questionnaire requesting names of people in the home. 
It’s hard to read how many people are really new citizens, and how many may have feared telling government surveyors that they are not citizens. 
The change in reported naturalized citizens, 1.3 million, outstrips the 870,000 new naturalizations reported by USCIS between mid-2024 and mid-2025, according to Stateline calculations. 
Lloyd Potter, Texas state demographer, said it’s likely some people were afraid to report their true status this year. 
“We had a change in administration and kind of an uptick in terms of detention and deportation of unauthorized immigrants,” Potter told Stateline. “I think probably that created a situation where people who were noncitizens might say, on a survey, ‘Yeah, I’m a citizen.’” 
About 11% of Texas voters were naturalized citizens in 2024, according to the Pew Research Center report. 
Christopher Dick, a consultant for the University of Florida’s state-funded Bureau of Economic and Business Research, said it’s also possible more noncitizens didn’t respond at all to the survey, which would make it seem like a larger proportion of immigrants were citizens, distorting the survey.  
As far as the cutbacks in new citizen numbers before the midterms, Steven Camerota, director of research for the Center for Immigration Studies – a think tank that favors less immigration – said it’s part of a pattern of extreme presidential power seen in recent decades. He maintains that Democratic presidents have also used their powers to influence immigration policy and that a divided Congress has not used its powers to halt the pattern.
“We’re in a period here of executive dominance,” Camerota said. “When you have a situation where Congress is willing to surrender all its powers, this is the result.”

Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: VTDigger
title: November brings an end to foliage season — but it’s not winter yet
text:
A motorcyclist travels along the Notch Road in Cambridge during stick season on Thursday, October 29, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This year, VTDigger is teaming up with Henry’s Weather Channel to help answer the annual question of when and where peak foliage will make its appearance across the state.
Each week, we’ll bring you an updated look at how foliage is unfolding statewide, paired with a weekend forecast, so you can plan your drive, hike or porch-sitting accordingly. Henry brings meteorological experience and on-the-ground reporting with photos and videos from across the region.

It’s that time of year, folks. The leaves are off the trees, but it’s not quite time to get out your skis. Though the shoulder season is an awkward time of year for Vermont, the sunny and dry streak will continue into the weekend. 
Bare trees and rock are seen along the Notch Road in Cambridge during stick season on Thursday, October 29, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Here’s your final fall foliage and weather outlook of the year. 
Hello to November
Another beautiful weekend is ahead across Vermont. We have had plenty of sunshine lately, and that will continue this weekend as we flip the calendar to November on Sunday. 
Slide to view high and low temperatures
Halloween is Saturday, and the weather looks perfect if a little chilly. Highs will be in the upper 40s to low 50s with calm winds. Low temperatures on Halloween night are expected to drop into the 20s to low 30s. Cold! Sunday will warm up, with highs in the 50s to near 60. Expect plenty of sunshine and calm winds. 
Slide to view high and low temperatures
The first few weeks of November will bring above-average temperatures to New England. The National Weather Service’s Climate Prediction Center’s six-to-10-day outlook and eight-to-14-day outlook both show above-average temperatures through the first few weeks of November.
Don’t forget to set your clocks back 1 hour on Sunday.
Until next year …
Current foliage across the state is past peak as expected for this time of year. It was a fantastic fall foliage season with the perfect conditions to make those colors vibrant. I hope you all enjoyed October’s ideal weather. 






Henry Swenson of Henry’s Weather Channel is a self-taught storm chaser, weather forecaster and drone videographer based in New England. He is known for his live storm coverage and tracking and has been delivering accurate weather forecasts to the region since 2017. For this partnership, Henry brings his mobile weather station and boots-on-the-ground approach to track fall foliage as it moves across the state.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: South Coast could be battleground in governor’s race
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
text:
THE GOVERNOR WAS just getting into her remarks about the redevelopment of Route 79 and this city’s waterfront when a man driving by in a white truck leaned out his window and shouted, “Booooooo! Boo Maura Healey!”
Healey didn’t miss a beat from the podium that was set up in a grassy field between the northbound and southbound sides of Route 79.
“Good morning, [or] afternoon,” the Democrat who is asking voters next week to return her to office for four more years said, glancing quickly in the driver’s direction. Turning back to the crowd of politicians, union workers and state employees, Healey shrugged and continued, “You can’t win them all. It’s OK. If he only knew, all right?”
The governor’s stop in Fall River was her second event of the day in Bristol County, following an energy-focused stop at Attleboro’s senior center Wednesday morning. Wednesday evening, Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll were slated to headline a campaign rally in New Bedford for themselves and other Democrats on the ballot Tuesday, capping off a daylong swing through a part of Massachusetts that Republicans have eyed as fertile ground for their own revival.
“Kim Driscoll and I are running hard all over the state. We are six days out from the election. Early voting is on,” Healey told reporters in Attleboro. She added, “Around the state, I’ve seen a lot of people who’ve already voted, which I think is a good thing. There’s certainly a lot on the line.”
Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue, who spent Wednesday afternoon visiting businesses and residents in Boston’s North End, has held numerous campaign events on the South Coast and plans his own campaign rally in Fall River on Friday.
Republican Party Chair Amy Carnevale told the News Service in May that Bristol County is a particular area of focus for the MassGOP in state legislative races, citing what she said was a trend of unenrolled voters registering as Republicans and a handful of municipal leaders who have switched their party affiliation to the GOP.
The Fall River Herald News reported Monday that this year’s midterms represent the first election in at least 50 years that Republicans have nominated a candidate for every state legislative seat in the greater Fall River area. It is also the first time in a half-century that a Republican is running to be district attorney for Bristol County.
“Bristol County is certainly a region we’re paying close attention to this cycle, particularly in light of some of the movement we saw in 2024 and the grassroots energy and historic slate of candidates,” MassGOP Political Director Aidan Carey told the Herald News.
Healey won every precinct of Fall River four years ago, claiming support from about 56 percent of the city’s voters. But Fall River voters also narrowly sided with Republican President Donald Trump in the 2024 election, one of nearly two dozen Bay State towns where Trump lost in 2020 but won in 2024. Surrounding towns like Westport and Somerset also went for Healey in 2022 and Trump in 2024.
In New Bedford, Healey won all but one precinct (and about 59 percent of the total vote) four years ago, and Democrat Kamala Harris edged Trump by only about 60 votes two years ago. Healey won Attleboro four years ago in her initial run for governor, claiming nearly 9,000 votes or just more than 56 percent of the Jewelry City’s total. In the last presidential election, about 54 percent of the city’s voters backed Harris.
Though her events in Attleboro and Fall River were technically “official” events and not part of her reelection effort, the campaign trail was never far off Wednesday.
“I voted for you,” an elderly woman excitedly told Healey as she grabbed the governor’s hand during a question-and-answer session in Attleboro .

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Morningside University freezes tuition for St. Luke’s College
text:
Morningside University has announced it will freeze tuition at St. Luke's College for the next academic year. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Students attending St. Luke’s College in Sioux City next fall will not see their tuition increase, its overseeing university has announced.
Morningside University, also in Sioux City, stated in a news release Wednesday tuition for the health sciences college will not increase for the 2027-2028 academic year. According to St. Luke’s College’s website, tuition for bachelor’s degree programs sits at $620 per credit hour and associate degree tuition is $555 per credit hour, with varying costs for certificate and internship programs.
Morningside University President Chad Benson said in the release this decision “reflects Morningside’s effort to balance access, quality and growth.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We have an opportunity to expand exceptional healthcare education, prepare more professionals for our region, and remain disciplined about what we ask students to pay. Holding tuition flat is a tangible demonstration of that commitment,” Benson said in the release.
Morningside began the process of acquiring St. Luke’s College in summer 2025, and the college has been operating as a division of Morningside since January with the goal of a full combination by the end of 2026.
According to the release, freezing St. Luke’s tuition reinforces Morningside’s “commitment to affordable healthcare education and Siouxland’s workforce needs” and represents one step in the institution’s continuing work in expanding opportunities and strengthening technology, programs and people.
“There is no substitute for learning in real clinical environments,” said St. Luke’s College Dean and Morningside nursing school director Jackie Barber in the release. “Our students gain extensive hands-on experience alongside healthcare professionals, building the confidence and clinical judgment they need to enter their careers ready to contribute.”

name: National
title: Chrissy Teigen joins Idaho women who needed abortions in final push for ballot initiative
text:
Chrissy Teigen, a former model and business owner, sits next to Melanie Folwell, lead organizer of the ballot initiative campaign, at Neckar Coffee in Boise, Idaho, as part of a final push to pass the ballot measure on Election Day. (Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families)It took two years for Chrissy Teigen to realize she’d had an abortion and not a miscarriage, longer to understand what went wrong in her pregnancy, and not until this week to realize she hadn’t fully grappled with it emotionally.
Teigen, a former model and business owner, came to Idaho on Wednesday to make a final push leading up to Nov. 3 in favor of Proposition 1, the ballot measure that would restore access to abortion in Idaho. The state has a near-total ban that applies to any stage of pregnancy, with exceptions only for rape and incest in the first trimester and to save a pregnant patient’s life. The initiative, if passed, would also protect access to birth control and fertility assistance treatments such as in vitro fertilization.
Opponents to the measure have called the initiative too extreme because it would allow abortions up to fetal viability, which was the law in Idaho prior to the ban, with exceptions after that point when the pregnancy threatens a patient’s health or life. 
Told her baby wouldn’t survive, she had to leave Idaho for an abortion. She’s sharing her story.

Prior to a rally in downtown Boise with Prop 1 volunteers and supporters, Teigen — who lived in Idaho Falls in the early 1990s — met privately at a coffee shop with 12 Idaho women who have been telling their stories for the campaign about needing abortion care in Idaho. The women sat in a circle and told brief versions of their stories: miscarriages that led to septic infections because of hesitant medical providers, travel out of state for fatal anomalies and catastrophic health complications, and memorials to the babies they lost. 
Nonprofit organization Idahoans United for Women and Families, which has led the campaign for the initiative, coordinated the event, and owners of Neckar Coffee donated the space and coffee. 
Kate Campbell spoke of her son, Remy, and the infected placenta that caused her water to break at 20 weeks and begin labor. A fetus generally can’t survive outside of the womb before 22 weeks, and every day that goes by without an abortion procedure increases the risk of a potentially life-threatening infection, which can cause organ damage and lead to fertility loss. 
Since Idaho’s law only allows for intervention to save a patient’s life, doctors decided not to wait until she was close to death and airlifted Campbell to Utah for care. Utah allows abortion until 18 weeks, and after that, the law includes an exception to preserve a patient’s health, not just to prevent death.
“The only ‘cure,’ if you will, for an infected placenta is giving birth,” Campbell said through tears. She now has a 14-month-old daughter.
Rebecca Crozier and other Idaho women sit side-by-side across from Chrissy Teigen to tell their stories of needing abortion care and being unable to access it in their home state because of the near-total ban. (Photo by Chelsea Harada/Idahoans United for Women and Families)
Desi Ballis had a similar story about a virus she contracted early in pregnancy that caused a fatal anomaly that also put her health in danger. A doctor at her 20-week ultrasound told her she needed to get to Utah as quickly as possible, and she and her husband, Morgan, made the five-hour drive and called multiple hospitals and clinics before they found someone who could help.  
“It was just horrific,” Ballis said.
Others included Rebecca Crozier, who received a fatal fetal diagnosis of anencephaly at 11 weeks and told Stateline her story this week, and Abby Nichols, who traveled to Seattle for an abortion after she received a fetal diagnosis of Trisomy 18, a chromosomal abnormality that is often fatal or life-limiting. 
With each story, Teigen grew more emotional, until it was her turn to talk about the baby she lost at 20 weeks in 2020 after a placental abruption, which occurs when the placenta detaches from the uterine wall, causing heavy bleeding and cutting off the oxygen and nutrient supply to the fetus.



Quotation







I had it so easy compared to you guys, I didn’t even have to think about that extra added layer of having to go somewhere or feeling shame for it.


– Chrissy Teigen


“I think I’m so emotional because hearing all of your stories makes you face what actually happened, right?” Teigen said. “And I had it so easy compared to you guys, I didn’t even have to think about that extra added layer of having to go somewhere or feeling shame for it.”
Teigen received multiple blood transfusions and was trying to make it to 22 weeks, but said her doctor eventually told her she was losing too much blood and they needed to induce delivery. Her doctor didn’t call it an abortion, and when Teigen posted about what happened on Instagram, she wrote only that health providers couldn’t stop the bleeding, and that she and her husband, singer John Legend, were “in the kind of deep pain you only hear about.” She included photos from her hospital bed with Legend, holding the baby they’d been calling Jack.
She described some of the backlash she received for posting the photos, accusing her of seeking attention. But two years later, that backlash intensified.
2 states, 2 abortion ballot measures, and the effort to win over Gen Z voters

“When I said, ‘Hey guys, I didn’t miscarry, I had an abortion,’ and then it was almost like, ‘Oh, we felt bad for you before, now we don’t feel bad for you,’” Teigen said. At 20 weeks’ gestation, an induced labor is a type of abortion. 
Campbell told Teigen that she was grateful for how open she’d been with her story, because when she was asked whether she wanted pictures of Remy and casts of handprints and footprints, she remembered Teigen’s story and how she had unapologetically posted the photos.
Teigen told Stateline that in the years since the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in 2022 that allowed states to ban abortion, she has been an advocate for abortion rights, including traveling to Arizona when the state passed its abortion ballot initiative in 2024. But there was something different and deeply affecting about sitting with the Idaho women, she said, and no longer being able to block out the emotions around her experience.
Whether Proposition 1 passes or fails, she said, the stories about abortion will continue to matter outside of politics.
“Going through something like this is so isolating,” she said. “It’s so important to talk about this, and to release it, and to not hold it in like I’ve been doing.”
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan to receive $7.2M in settlement with GM over allegations of selling driver data
text:
The General Motors corporate logo shines from the Hudson's Detroit building Friday, October 10, 2025 after being affixed overnight to the company's future global headquarters in downtown Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by John F. Martin for General Motors)Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced Thursday that Michigan will receive over $7.2 million in a settlement agreement with General Motors, part of a national $220 million settlement over allegations of GM’s sharing of drivers’ private behavior and location data with third parties. 
Those third parties included data brokers, who then shared data with insurance companies which, according to reporting from the New York Times, used that data to set auto insurance rates for some drivers.
“Drivers deserve to know what information about them is being collected and how it may affect their wallets,” Nessel said in a press release. “Discovering after the fact that a company has been tracking and selling their driving data without their consent is unacceptable. This settlement will hold GM accountable for its past conduct and secure meaningful safeguards so drivers have greater control over their information in the future.”
The settlement requires that General Motors “must obtain the relevant Consumer’s Affirmative Express Consent prior to collecting or using such Consumer’s Covered Driver Data, or disclosing such Consumer’s Covered Driver Data to any Third Party,” meaning that they have to get specific permission from drivers to collect or disclose their driving or location data.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Other terms in the settlement require GM to limit the driving data that it collects at all, and to establish a more comprehensive data privacy program. 
GM does not admit to any “violation or liability arising from any state, federal, or local law” in the settlement, which states, “Nothing contained in this Judgment shall be construed as an admission or concession of liability by Defendants, nor to any express or implied allegations relating to current or historical data processing policies or practices.”
The settlement was reached by a coalition of 36 attorneys general from states and the District of Columbia and largely concerned the company’s Smart Driver program, which ran from 2016 to 2024. Nessel’s press release describes that GM “pitched this tool as a way for drivers to improve their own driving safety and told drivers that they would not share their data with insurers without express consent.”
However, the attorneys general argued that GM did not properly obtain that consent or inform drivers that their data was being sold, and in some cases, dealership employees allegedly accepted terms and conditions on behalf of customers without their consent when a car was first being purchased.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Bernalillo County expecting 10 USDOJ monitors on Election Day
text:
Bernalillo County Clerk Michelle Kavanaugh, pictured above outside a polling place May 5, 2026, told Source NM on Oct. 29, 2026, that the county is expecting roughly 10 federal monitors on Election Day. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)The United States Department of Justice will send approximately 10 monitors to polling sites in New Mexico’s most populous county on Election Day, county officials told Source NM on Thursday, amid the federal government’s recently announced expansion of its nationwide election monitoring effort. 
The USDOJ announced this week that it intends to send 1,000 election monitors to polling locations in all 50 states on Nov. 3, marking an expansion of its previous election monitoring efforts. But federal officials declined to say which polling locations they’ll target for the expanded effort.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bernalillo County officials told Source NM on Thursday that the USDOJ informed the county approximately three weeks ago it would be sending monitors, but did not specify why they had selected the county.
In an emailed statement, Bernalillo County Clerk Michelle Kavanaugh noted that the USDOJ has previously deployed monitors to the county and said local officials are “prepared for their arrival” this year.
“This is not unusual for us, and we’ve accommodated DOJ monitors in previous elections without incident,” she said. 
Trump’s DOJ sends 1,000 election monitors to 50 states; locations not yet disclosed

The USDOJ’s expanded monitoring effort has sparked fears of federal meddling in elections across the country during a mid-term election that will determine the balance of power in the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate. 
Other New Mexico locations where  federal monitors may show up remains  unclear. Lindsey Bachman, the secretary of state’s communications, legislative and executive affairs director, told Source NM on Thursday that her office has been made aware only of their presence in Bernalillo County, but the USDOJ has reportedly reached out directly to county clerks in other states. 
Doña Ana County Clerk Amanda López Askin told Source NM on Thursday in a text message that she has not heard from the USDOJ about monitors in the state’s second-most-populous county. The county will also likely process the largest percentage of the votes cast in the closely watched 2nd Congressional District race between incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) and Republican challenger Greg Cunningham. 
During the last mid-term election in 2022, former President Joe Biden’s USDOJ sent 289 monitors to 24 states, including Bernalillo County and San Juan County in New Mexico. San Juan County officials did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Thursday about whether they expect the federal government’s presence at their polling sites again, as much of the county recovers from recent flooding. 
Fears of federal interference in the state’s elections prompted state lawmakers this session to pass Senate Bill 264, which aims to prevent intimidation by federal immigration and others in local elections. The Secretary of State and Attorney General’s Office earlier this month issued a voter advisory that underscored voters’ rights to cast ballots with interference.
The prospect of federal interference has also prompted third party groups and political parties to step up their presence at polling sites across the country.
In New Mexico, the Secretary of State’s Office has credentialed 571 watchers from six different organizations to monitor elections this year. Bachman could not immediately say how that number compares to previous years.
But Carmen Lopez, co-lead for Observe New Mexico Elections, which employs the majority of the state’s election watchers, told Source NM that the group has nearly twice as many volunteer observers this cycle than the 2024 general election. Approximately 325 observers affiliated with her group are approved this year, compared with about 170 in 2024, she said.
“We had more interest in our observation program this year, partly because more people know about it, and also because people want to participate,” she said. “There are all of these other observation efforts, both inside the polls and outside the polls, that have garnered a lot of interest.”
New Mexico poll workers in rural county required IDs to vote during June primary, observers say

The other groups that the Secretary of State’s Office has approved for election observation, Bachman said, are Disability Rights New Mexico, League of Women Voters of New Mexico and Southern New Mexico, Taos United Indivisible and Land of Action. 
Land of Action is a recently formed, nonpartisan civic association and hub for progressive groups throughout the state. Executive director Heidi Li Feldman told Source NM on Thursday that her group of approximately 80 watchers will fan out primarily to rural counties like San Juan, Grant, Luna, Hidalgo, Otero and Rio Arriba counties. 
Li Feldman said the volunteers are on alert for federal monitors on Election Day, especially since the USDOJ has not said where they will be. 
“Since no one really knows, we’ve trained our watchers to be alert to people who are agents, DOJ monitors,” she said, “and to be extra sensitive to whether they are following New Mexico state law about what law enforcement, federal or otherwise, may and may not do at the polls.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ​Federal officials reject ​Colorado’s conditions for election monitors in Adams County
text:
Clerk Josh Zygielbaum is seen at the Adams County Government Center in Brighton on Nov. 7, 2023. (Photo by Kevin Mohatt/Colorado Newsline)The four election monitors the U.S. Justice Department plans to send to Adams County on Election Day will stay at least 100 feet from polling places after the department declined terms set by the Colorado secretary of state’s office on Thursday.
One of the conditions was that monitors would need to be accompanied by observers from the Colorado secretary of state’s office inside any polling location.
“My office provided reasonable restrictions on DOJ monitors, which they refused to accept,” Secretary of State Jena Griswold said in a statement. “As a result, the DOJ will not be allowed to enter voter centers in Adams County. It is illegal for anyone, including the DOJ, to intimidate or interfere with voters outside of voter centers. My office will take any suggestion of voter intimidation seriously and will act accordingly.”
The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division first notified Griswold and Adams County Clerk Josh Zygielbaum last week about its plan to send election monitors to the county to check for compliance with federal voting rights laws around language and accessibility. Under Colorado law, the secretary of state’s office must approve official observers for elections. The office outlined the conditions of that approval in a Thursday letter to the department, which declined a short time later. It said the monitors would stay outside of polling locations and remain 100 feet from buildings, in accordance with Colorado law.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Justice monitors would have been limited to speaking only with the presiding election official at a polling center and taking notes from an area designated by that official. They would not be allowed to speak with voters, touch equipment or go to areas inaccessible to voters.
Those are basically the same conditions that Justice attorney Jake Bachand outlined in his request letter to state officials on Oct. 27. The letter was shared with Newsline by Griswold’s office. Bachand wrote that the four monitors would work in teams of two and cover between six and eight polling locations each. They would check that election materials are provided in both English and Spanish, that bilingual poll workers are available, that voters are allowed to bring someone to help them in the voting booth and that the entire polling location is accessible to people with disabilities.
“Our monitors will not be anywhere near voting machines or the voting area at any time,” Bachand wrote. “Our monitors will not be requesting to inspect machines, equipment, or poll books, and they will not be attempting to speak with voters inside a polling place for any reason. They will not be wearing suits, displaying credentials, or doing anything else that would indicate to the public that they are from the (Justice Department).”
It’s unclear how the monitors can fulfill their obligations outside of a polling center.
Justice wrote that the monitors would be James Freeman, an attorney who has worked at the department for three decades, as well as special assistant Atticus Yondorf, administrative specialist Ana Gomez Becerra and paralegal Charisha Cruz at the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Denver.
It is common for the Justice Department to assign election monitors, but the larger scale of the deployment this year is different, as is the use of employees from the a criminal, rather than civil, office. The department plans to deploy around 1,000 monitors around the country. Adams County is the only jurisdiction in Colorado set to be observed by federal monitors on Tuesday. It is a Democratic-majority county in the state’s 8th Congressional District, site of a toss-up race that will help decide which party controls Congress.
Interference feared
The department said it chose Adams County because of its high number of Spanish-speaking voters, making it covered by Section 203 of the Voting Rights Act. Some state leaders, however, worry that the federal government is using the practice as a shortcut to find counties with significant non-English-speaking voters to investigate. Colorado’s Democratic congressional delegation wrote in a letter last week that the election monitor deployment is concerning amid other escalating actions by the Trump administration to control elections, including its lawsuit to access confidential Colorado voter information and efforts to limit mail-in voting. Many experts view those as an effort to interfere with results as Republicans are widely expected to lose control of at least the U.S. House and maybe the Senate.
“Adams County is committed to making sure every eligible voter has their voice heard, and election workers in my office will be ready to help any voter that needs it on Tuesday,” Zygielbaum said in a statement. “I look forward to serving the people of Adams County and having another great election.”
Earlier this week, Colorado clerks said they were united to protect elections against any interference from the Trump administration.
Election Day is Nov. 3. More information about how to register to vote and cast a ballot can be found at GoVoteColorado.gov.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: After arrests, Republican leaders outline steps they want state to take to combat MaineCare fraud
text:
Senate Minority Leader Trey Stewart reacts to Gov. Janet Mills State of the State address on Jan. 27, 2026. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Republican leaders are doubling down on their call for greater legislative oversight of MaineCare following several arrests earlier this week.
During a Thursday press conference in Augusta, Maine Senate Minority Leader Trey Stewart and House of Representatives Minority Leader Billy Bob Faulkingham accused the state’s Democratic leadership of failing to investigate possible fraud in the state’s Medicaid program. 
“MaineCare should be paying for healthcare, not healthcare that doesn’t happen, and that’s what’s happened,” said Faulkingham, who represents District 12.
“How long has it been since we started talking about this stuff?” asked Faulkingham, adding, “it’s been at least a solid two years of beating the drum.”
The leaders specifically outlined three steps they wanted to see the state take, including an independent third party review of MaineCare focused on waste, fraud and abuse; full public accounting from the state health department about what officials knew about possible fraud and what actions were taken; and a status report on MaineCare providers under payment suspension or investigation. 
Stewart, who represents Aroostook County, said that if millions weren’t going to “fraudsters,” that money could be used to increase the state’s Medicaid reimbursement rate for struggling healthcare providers and help close the projected $1 billion budget gap.
The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Maine announced Tuesday that it had arrested six individuals who had been indicted by a grand jury for healthcare fraud conspiracy. Two of the defendants are also charged with obstructing an investigation while a third is charged with making false statements.
Community Home Health Care, a licensed personal care agency headquartered in South Portland, was also charged in the indictment, which followed the Maine Department of Health and Human Services suspending payments to the agency in August.
The parties, who have not been convicted, are accused of submitting false claims to MaineCare for personal care services that had not been performed, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office. The indictment further alleges that since 2020, the company and its owner, who was among those arrested, submitted numerous claims to MaineCare for services purportedly provided to a single client totaling more than $600,000.
Noting that Community Home Health Care had charged the state a total of $50 million, Stewart asked, “How many other entities around the state are doing the same thing?” 
State and federal Republicans have for months argued the administration of Gov. Janet Mills, a Democrat, was not doing enough to combat fraud. 
Mills administration health officials earlier this year briefed multiple legislative committees on their fraud investigation protocols. Republicans said at the time that they were not sufficient to crack down on what they believed was a rampant problem. In August, the Maine Department of Health and Human Services suspended payments to four providers in addition to  Community Home Health Care and terminated two providers’ contracts due to credible complaints of serious health and safety risks.
After months of GOP criticism, Maine shares details of Medicaid fraud enforcement

“Protecting the integrity of all our federally funded health are programs for those who really need them is paramount,” said U.S. Attorney Andrew B. Benson in a Tuesday press release. 
The investigation was conducted by the FBI, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of the Inspector General, Homeland Security Investigations, and IRS’s Criminal Investigation unit, with assistance from Maine’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit. This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative established by a sweeping Jan. 2025 executive order aimed at immigration enforcement. The task force increases state and federal collaboration in investigating foreign gangs and transnational criminal organizations. 
In the statement, Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey commended “the sustained diligence of both our federal law enforcement partners and the Maine Medicaid Fraud Control Unit in the effort to bring these cases to this point.”
“I hope today’s announcement serves as an important reminder that federal and state officials are working continuously to protect public dollars for the intended beneficiaries,” he added. 
In June, Lead Maine, a group run by Republican Rep. Laurel Libby of Auburn, submitted a petition to prompt the health department to pass tougher MaineCare oversight rules, including reinstating in-person inspections of providers and suspending payments to providers suspected of improper billing, instead holding their reimbursements in an interest-bearing escrow account until investigations are complete. 
In a statement following the arrests, Libby said, “This indictment is exactly why MaineCare needs real accountability. Every dollar lost to fraud is a dollar taken from a Mainer who depends on this program for care.” 
At a September public hearing, providers and advocates cautioned that the proposed rule changes may put patients’ privacy at risk and make it difficult for healthcare agencies to stay in business.
Eesha Pendharkar contributed to this story.
