name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Potential of Missouri River pipelines to Western states opens new front in uptream-downstream fight
text:
A bridge stretches across the Missouri River at Chamberlain, South Dakota, on Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)Downstream Missouri River states have worried for decades about receiving an insufficient flow of water from upstream dams.
Now they’re worried their share of water could be further diminished by potential pipelines for dry Western states.
The concern is the basis of a dispute about the U.S. House version of the federal Water Resources Development Act. A provision in the bill would require approval from all governors in Missouri River states to study or construct a project that moves water from the river or its tributaries to a non-Missouri River state.
The bill has passed the House and awaits action in the Senate, where a Senate version of the legislation lacks the controversial provision.
Missouri lawmaker and group support provision
The House bill’s definition of “Missouri River states” includes not only the seven states where the river flows — Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Iowa, Kansas and Missouri — but also Colorado, Minnesota and Wyoming, which have land within the river’s 530,000-square-mile drainage basin.
A downstream lawmaker, U.S. Rep. Sam Graves, R-Missouri, sponsors the House bill. Supporters of the controversial provision include an organization in his state, the Coalition to Protect the Missouri River.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Shane Kinne is the coalition’s executive director. He said Missourians’ concerns about water shortages are not hypothetical. For the last four years, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has limited water releases from upper Missouri River reservoirs, affecting commercial barge traffic downstream.
Kinne said Missouri River Basin states should collaborate “so we can manage the resource together and protect ourselves from Western states looking for water.”
“If this isn’t the proposal, let’s bring some ideas to address this concern,” he said.
Joint opposition: Dakotas, Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, Utah
Kinne’s view faces opposition in upstream states.
The governors of Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota — where the Missouri River flows through a series of dams and reservoirs — recently joined with governors in the Missouri River Basin states of Colorado and Wyoming on a letter opposing the House provision.
Estimated cost of proposed eastern South Dakota water pipeline is at least $8.4 billion

Also signing the letter was the governor of Utah, which is not part of the Missouri River Basin. Utah relies on the Colorado River for some of its water, and the state’s Great Salt Lake Commission has mentioned the Missouri River as a potential source of imported water for the vanishing Great Salt Lake.
The governors’ letter says the House provision would give each governor in the 10 Missouri River Basin states “absolute veto power” to stop other states from even “studying the feasibility of projects in a watershed that encompasses one-sixth of the continental United States.”
When the House approved its bill by a vote of 415-9, U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, was among the nine votes against the legislation, along with representatives from states including North Dakota, Wyoming and Montana. Johnson said the Missouri River provision would hamstring the Army Corps of Engineers’ management of dams and reservoirs.
“Why should the Corps need unanimous approval of the governors to study a project that provides water across state lines?” Johnson said in a statement to South Dakota Searchlight.
Upstream officials worry about implications
Some South Dakota water officials also oppose the House provision.
Jay Gilbertson manages the East Dakota Water Development District, based in Brookings. He acknowledges the bill language would not impede several currently proposed Missouri River pipeline projects in South Dakota, because they would not transport water outside the Missouri River states mentioned in the bill. But he worries “it’s the start of a process that’s going to limit our ability to do things in the future.”
Gilbertson said the provision’s language requiring approval from all 10 governors is bad policy.
“You can’t get 10 states to agree on anything,” he said.
Darrell Raschke views it the same way. He serves on the boards of the Mid-Dakota Rural Water System and the Upper Missouri Water Association.
“One governor says no, you just shot the whole project down,” Raschke said. “Why would you put that in law?”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Ethics Commission to launch inquiry into Development Fund problems
text:
North Dakota Ethics Commission member Mark Western listens to Executive Director Rebecca Binstock during a Feb. 18, 2026, meeting at the North Dakota Capitol in Bismarck. On Oct. 28, 2026, Western made a motion to initiate an inquiry into the North Dakota Development Fund. (Photo by Mary Steurer/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s Ethics Commission voted unanimously Wednesday to begin its own inquiry into a state-backed business financing program that drew critical audit findings and lawmakers’ concerns about conflicts of interest and a lack of documentation for millions of dollars in transactions. 
The move is the first of its kind for the 7-year-old ethics panel.
Last month, the Legislature’s audit review committee asked Attorney General Drew Wrigley to investigate the North Dakota Development Fund. He declined to do so earlier this month, citing a legal conflict in his office representing current and former Development Fund Board members in a lawsuit.
Lawmakers seek AG probe after audit finds problems with North Dakota business financing program

That left members of the Ethics Commission pondering a probe of their own.
“I would ask the question: If we don’t initiate, who would initiate it, if it wasn’t us?” Chair Pam Sharp said.
The Development Fund was created in 1991 and offers loans and investments as gap financing to new businesses that might not be able to obtain loans from traditional banks. Its board comprises eight members appointed by the governor.
Audit findings for a 2019-2024 period of the Development Fund included a lack of documentation for millions of dollars in transactions, unverified job data reported by borrowers and inconsistent conflict of interest procedures. Commerce Commissioner Chris Schilken told lawmakers improvements are underway or complete and emphasized the problems predate his and Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s tenures.
Ethics Commissioner Kelly Leben, who is the Burleigh County sheriff, wondered why the attorney general did not refer the matter to another entity to investigate. He wondered about the ethics panel setting a precedent in “self-initiating” investigations.
Commissioner Mark Western, an attorney and professional mediator, said the state constitution provides the panel with the ability to initiate an inquiry or investigation “on matters just like what is sitting here.” He wondered about the consequences of pursuing an inquiry and perhaps finding new details, or doing nothing.
“What does that tell our regulated community? What does that tell the people about our desire to get our fingernails dirty?” Western said.
Commissioner Lisa Edison-Smith, an employment and labor attorney, said the Development Fund situation is unique and important enough for at least an inquiry.
Board of criticized North Dakota business financing program plans meeting to address audit

Leben noted the “uncharted territory” of an inquiry, saying, “I want to make sure we go in with eyes wide open.”
An inquiry could take the form of how the Legislature’s audit committee asks people to attend a meeting and testify, or how Congress does investigations with testimony and staff research, Commission General Counsel Logan Carpenter said.
The panel’s inquiry will begin with commissioners reviewing the audit and making a request for documents from the Development Fund, perhaps in coordination with other state agencies that might be pursuing the matter, Western said.
Wrigley told the North Dakota Monitor his office did not investigate the Development Fund because of the conflict in his office representing fund officials in a civil lawsuit. He also said no one has presented credible evidence of a crime to spark a criminal investigation.
“We have nothing to refer,” Wrigley said.
Development Fund CEO Brian Opp declined to comment on the Ethics Commission pursuing an inquiry.
Sen. Jeff Magrum, who chairs the Legislature’s audit review committee, said he is glad the Ethics Commission “is stepping up to the plate here.”
“I’ll help them in any way I can because I think we need to definitely get to the bottom of this,” said Magrum, R-Hazelton.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: California
title: Dolores Huerta ‘stayed in the fight’ for 7 decades, inspiring generations of Californians
text:
At nearly every step of the farmworker movement, from its earliest days organizing in the 1965 Delano grape strike to the 1986 law granting amnesty to nearly 3 million undocumented migrants, Dolores Huerta was there. 
Huerta, 96, died Wednesday at home in Bakersfield. Just two months before, she was at a rally on the steps of the state Capitol. 
California’s political and labor leadership remembered her as a tireless advocate for farmworker rights — one who coined the United Farmer Worker motto and rallying cry, “Si, Se Puede,” or “Yes, We Can.” Every year on April 10, California honors her contributions by declaring the day as Dolores Huerta Day. 
“Dolores’ leadership in fighting for a union for California’s farmworkers, UFW, is only part of her historic story,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Labor Federation. “Dolores stayed in the fight for working people for decades.
She “showed generations of women they had a place in this labor movement.”
Her influence is still evident in the way California remembers its own history: As César Chávez’s name is removed from university buildings and city streets across California after allegations surfaced earlier this year that Chávez assaulted and raped several women, including Huerta, activists in Los Angeles called for Huerta’s name to replace his. 
“I can’t imagine what she’s gone through in those last few months,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom to a group of reporters Wednesday. “The revelations around César, and how hard that must have been for her in these last four months. … We just have to absorb her contributions, her energy, her passions and her contribution to this world.”
Even in her final months, Huerta pressed on. 
“Just this August, she stood with (the California Immigrant Policy Center) and our partners on the steps of the state Capitol to fight federal cuts that are taking food away from immigrant families, children and foster youth,” said Masih Fouladi, executive director of the California Immigrant Policy Center executive director. “She spoke up for the farmworkers who would be hit hardest, the very people who feed this state.”
Huerta was instrumental in ending the Bracero program in the 1960s which granted Mexican farmworkers temporary status in the U.S. while deducting food and lodging from their meager pay while also exposing them to deadly chemicals. 
United Farm Workers leader Dolores Huerta, center, leads a rally with Howard Wallace, president of the San Francisco chapter of the UFW, left, and Maria Elena Chavez, 16, daughter of Cesar Chavez, right, in San Francisco’s Mission District as part of a national boycott protesting what the UFW describes as the dangerous use of pesticides on table grapes on Nov. 19, 1988. Photo by Court Mast, AP
“Her life’s work was to empower her community to face and overcome injustices, and she has left farm workers and the entire Latino community stronger and more organized than she found it,” said UFW President Teresa Romero. “Dolores’ work remains as important now as ever, and it continues with her example and her inspiration before us. The greatest possible tribute to her life is for her work of organizing to continue.”
Huerta’s family said they will be “following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredibly life and legacy.”
Dolores Huerta speaks at the CalMatters event “Farmworker Health: How Can California Protect its Essential Workers?” in Bakersfield on Feb. 22, 2024. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Ex-Utah Supreme Court justice urges voters to retain judges amid push to unseat her former colleague
text:
Justice Diana Hagen speaks as Mormon Women for Ethical Government and The League of Womens voters oppose the Utah State Legislature during oral arguments at The Supreme Court of Utah in Salt Lake City on Wednesday, Sept. 25, 2024. (Pool photo by Jeffrey D. Allred/Deseret News)Former Utah Supreme Court Justice Diana Hagen is speaking out on social media ahead of next week’s election, urging Utah voters to retain judges in order to preserve an “independent, non-political judiciary.” 
“Do you believe in the Utah Constitution’s promise of a fair, independent and non-political judiciary?” Hagen said in a video posted to her LinkedIn account on Tuesday, a week before Election Day. 
“I do. But some people want judges to behave like politicians,” she said. “They want them to make decisions based on their political views instead of based on the law. And those people are going to vote ‘no’ on the judges on their ballot, in the hopes that the next judge who’s appointed will do what they want them to do rather than what the law requires.” 
Hagen urged Utah voters “please don’t let their vote go unanswered.”
Amid affair allegations, Utah Supreme Court Justice Diana Hagen resigns

“If you care about an independent, non-political judiciary, please be sure to vote to retain our judges,” she said. 
Hagen resigned from the bench earlier this year while under pressure from Republican state leaders calling for an independent investigation into previously dismissed allegations that she had an affair with an attorney representing plaintiffs in the state’s high-profile redistricting lawsuit. 
A Judicial Conduct Commission preliminary investigator that looked into the allegations wrote in a report that the complaint against her was “speculative, overstated and misleading” and contained “very little credibility.” Based on the investigator’s recommendations, the commission voted to dismiss the allegations without conducting a full investigation. 
Had she not resigned, Hagen would have been on this year’s judicial retention ballot along with one of her former colleagues on the bench, Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman. 
Now, Pohlman is the only Utah Supreme Court justice up for retention this year — during a time of heightened tension between the state’s judiciary and the Republican-controlled Utah Legislature, in large part due to rulings against lawmakers in high-profile lawsuits over ballot initiatives, redistricting and abortion. 
In the face of campaigns against her, Pohlman has stayed silent. Utah judicial rules prohibit judges from campaigning for themselves.
Earlier this year — months before the controversy over Hagen’s alleged affair came to light — Utah Republican Party leaders urged voters to vote against retaining both Hagen and Pohlman, largely because of how they ruled in the redistricting and abortion cases. 
Utah House speaker ‘extremely disappointed’ in how JCC handled Hagen investigation

“We’re coming for you,” Utah GOP Chair Rob Axson said during the party’s state nominating convention in April. “Justice Hagen and Justice Pohlman, go find a job in the private sector. We don’t want you anymore.”
The July 2024 Utah Supreme Court opinion in the redistricting case that has caught Republican legislators’ ire remanded the previously dismissed lawsuit back to district court, making clear that the Legislature’s power to change “government reform” ballot initiatives has limits. 
That 2024 opinion was unanimous, with all five justices, including Pohlman and Hagen, deciding against the Legislature. 
The ongoing redistricting lawsuit is challenging the Utah Legislature’s repeal and replacement of a 2018 voter-approved ballot initiative known as Proposition 4 that banned partisan gerrymandering and created an independent redistricting process. 
So far, the courts have ruled that the Legislature overstepped when it replaced Proposition 4, turning the independent commission into an advisory body that lawmakers could ignore. They did just that in 2021 when they adopted congressional maps that the plaintiffs in the case allege cracked Democratic strongholds in the state’s urban core of Salt Lake County. 
Ruling that the 2021 congressional map was the result of an unconstitutional process, a district court judge ordered a new map to be used in this year’s elections that turned one of Utah’s previously deep red districts blue, which incensed Republican lawmakers. 
In Utah redistricting case, judge explains why she ruled against Legislature

Another 2024 Utah Supreme Court opinion that upset the GOP upheld an injunction that for years has blocked Utah’s near-total abortion ban from becoming law while the state faces an ongoing lawsuit over it. 
In that 4-1 opinion in the abortion case issued in July 2024, Pohlman, Hagen and two other justices affirmed the district court’s decision to block enforcement of the ban while the case was litigated. Former Chief Justice Matthew Durrant authored a dissenting opinion. 
Hagen’s public comments urging Utahns to retain judges comes as conservative voices have urged a shakeup in the courts. 
One of Utah’s Republican sitting Congress members, Rep. Burgess Owens (who announced he isn’t running for reelection after Utah’s new congressional boundaries were put in place by the court) posted on X earlier this month, on Oct. 20, urging people to vote against retaining Pohlman. 
That same day, the conservative Utah Eagle Forum — which advocates against abortion — also sent an email urging supporters to vote against Pohlman due to how she ruled in the abortion lawsuit brought by the Planned Parenthood Association of Utah. 
Utah Supreme Court says affair allegations against justice were ‘inappropriately’ released

“When the case reached the Utah Supreme Court, the Justices, including Jill Pohlman, voted to uphold the injunction, and babies continued to die,” the Utah Eagle Forum email said. “JUDGE POHLMAN AGREED WITH PLANNED PARENTHOOD.”
In another social media post, Hagen said a “nonpolitical judiciary is baked into the Utah Constitution,” which says judges should be selected “solely based on fitness for office and not based on partisan politics.” 
She said in that video that all of the judges listed on the ballot “were vetted by a bipartisan nominating committee made up of public members, attorneys and a representative of the judiciary. They were found to be qualified for the job before their names were sent to the governor.” 
“So if you believe in the Utah Constitution’s promise of a merit-based, non-political judiciary, be sure to vote yes to retain the judges,” she said. 
The Utah Judicial Performance Evaluation Commission also offers assessments for all judges who are up for retention election, based on surveys. 
That commission determined only one judge, Weber County Justice Court Judge Trent Nelson, does not meet performance standards and did not recommend him to be retained. The report shows those surveyed criticized his temperament, calling him impatient and demeaning, and questioned his legal ability, among other concerns.
Typically, if judges don’t pass the commission’s evaluations, they retire from the bench rather than staying on the ballot. But Nelson is opting to let voters decide whether he should keep his job, The Salt Lake Tribune reported.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Diners applaud ‘smart move’ in Democrat’s final stretch as he tries to make history in SC
text:
State Rep. Jermaine Johnson, the Democratic nominee for governor, campaigns at a lunch buffet at Brookland Baptist Church in West Columbia on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)WEST COLUMBIA — As part of a packed schedule in his last week of campaigning, the Democrat running for governor in South Carolina wore an apron adorned with his “New SC” logo while going table to table, meeting with diners at the lunch buffet of one of South Carolina’s largest Black churches.
State Rep. Jermaine Johnson, who faces an uphill battle in his bid for the governor’s office, stopped by Brookland Baptist Church on Wednesday to serve food and chat with potential voters in the banquet hall where anyone can get some Southern cooking for lunch five days a week. Johnson’s visit coincided with seniors’ discount day.
“It’s a smart move because out here on Wednesday, there’s senior citizens, right? We know what we want,” said Leonard Taylor, 79, who was among roughly 100 people eating lunch at the time. “We have to have people who come and talk with us, hear us.”

For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.

Janice Rumph, 83, also applauded the campaign strategy, while noting she’d already voted for him.
“He could meet a lot of people here, common people, and people our age that really would vote,” said Rumph, who cast an all-Democrat ballot in early voting. “The idea of him stopping by and greeting us made me more relaxed, you know, meeting him in person.”
It was one of seven stops for the day on his public schedule, following a virtual fundraiser Tuesday evening with Vice President Kamala Harris.
Listening in required at least a $100 donation. It’s unclear how much was raised, and the campaign didn’t say how many people joined the online meeting.
Johnson defied odds in the SC gubernatorial primary. Now people want to know if he can do it again.

But for Johnson, who’s relying on personal connections with voters to overcome a fundraising deficit, those numbers matter less than getting people involved.
That’s “the most important thing. It’s a historical moment. This is why people are so excited,” said the 41-year-old former professional basketball player.
A win next week would make him the first Black governor of South Carolina and first Democrat elected to the office in 28 years.
He faces Republican Alan Wilson, the state’s attorney general since 2010, who’s on a two-week bus tour of the state. Guests on his campaign bus include Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp.
Johnson said he wants South Carolinians to “understand they have a real choice and opportunity” this election.
“I’m going to keep getting out there to let them know that their issues are my issues that they will not be forgotten,” he said.
The best part of the call with Harris, he said, was introducing his 13-year-old daughter to the former vice president.
“You are the reason we are all doing what we do. First of all, you have to know how important you are to all of us,” Harris told Khloe, one of Johnson’s three children.
“And one of the things that I would say to all of us, but in particular to you, my young leader, is always remember you don’t have to ask anybody’s permission to lead,” she said. “You were born a leader, and you have clearly already decided to activate your leadership, and that makes us so proud.”
SC Democrats rally with Georgia US senator ahead of early voting

The 10-minute virtual conversation with Harris followed Johnson’s appearances alongside other potential presidential contenders already crisscrossing South Carolina, the first state on Democrats’ 2028 nominating calendar.
Democrats he’s campaigned beside include former White House adviser Rahm Emanuel, California Rep. Ro Khanna, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, and Georgia Sen. Ralphael Warnock.
“Everywhere I go, people are like, ‘I already know who you are. I know who you are. I’m going in here to vote for you’, even if they don’t know other people on the ballot,” Johnson told the SC Daily Gazette. “They’re saying that they know who I am because they know that I’ve been showing up in their communities. So, they’re excited, and I’m excited about the opportunity.”
President Donald Trump is set to rally in Rock Hill on Thursday to boost Republican turnout — his second rally in two weeks in a state considered ruby red.
Johnson will also be in Rock Hill, where he’s rallying hours later with Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett.
Unlike the U.S. Senate contest in South Carolina, polls don’t show him in a tight race with Wilson. But Johnson said he’s optimistic regardless of what the pollsters are reporting.
He pointed to the recent rise in registered voters in the nation’s fastest-growing state.
According to state Election Commission data, 3.4 million South Carolinians were registered to vote as of Oct. 1, an increase of about 73,000 since the year began.
He contends many of those new voters are Democrats, though it’s impossible to know since South Carolinians don’t register by party.
“These are individuals who are fired up about coming to vote for me,” Johnson said. “So, whatever these polls are showing, it is not accounting for all these new voters that are out there. It’s not accounting for the people that are excited.”
Early voting runs through Saturday. Election Day is Tuesday.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho Supreme Court upholds dismissal of legal challenge to state public defense office
text:
Idaho State Supreme Court justices preside over a hearing in October 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Supreme Court) The Idaho Supreme Court ruled in a 3-2 decision Wednesday that a legal challenge to Idaho’s new state public defense system may be dismissed. The ruling upheld a lower court’s dismissal of the case. 
The majority’s decision found there wasn’t enough evidence to demonstrate the statewide system, which began operations in 2024, had similar constitutional concerns of the previous county-based system for defendants in Idaho who couldn’t afford their own legal representation. 
Idaho Supreme Court Chief Justice Robyn Brody at a hearing in October 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Supreme Court)
“We recognize that Plaintiffs presented substantial evidence that the former county‑based and county‑based, state‑assisted systems were plagued by excessive caseloads, inadequate staffing, and improper political and judicial pressures,” Chief Justice Robyn Brody wrote.  “… But that evidence sheds almost no light on whether those shortcomings are likely to persist under the newly implemented state‑based system, thereby warranting prospective injunctive relief. The law requires more than a hunch that the new system will simply reprise the failures of its predecessors.” 
Justices G. Richard Bevan and Gregory Moeller agreed with Brody’s decision. Justices Cynthia Meyer and retired Justice Roger Burdick, who was temporarily filling in for Justice Colleen Zahn, disagreed with the majority. 
The ACLU of Idaho in 2015 filed the lawsuit, arguing Idaho’s then-county-based system for public defense was inadequate and not fulfilling the state’s constitutional obligation to guarantee right to counsel under the Sixth Amendment. 
The organization and attorneys from the law firms Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, Wrest Collective, and Ali & Lockwood have since argued that state’s reforms to the system continue to be inadequate. 
“This ruling is a disappointment for the thousands of Idahoans who deserve the chance to properly defend themselves in court,” Legal Director at ACLU of Idaho Paul Carlos Southwick said in a press release. “Every single day, Idahoans are denied their constitutional right to legal representation because of the state’s persistent failure to fix chronic and widespread public defense issues. Idahoans who are accused of a crime are sitting in jail for months without access to a public defender, and some are even showing up to their court hearings without legal representation. We are evaluating the decision to determine next steps in our fight for a constitutional public defense system.”
The ACLU has the option to appeal the decision. 
The Office of the State Public Defender could not be immediately reached for this story. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 What is the lawsuit challenging Idaho’s public defense system about? 

In 2022, the Idaho Legislature passed House Bill 735, shifting the costs of public defense to the state, rather than having individual counties pay for them. In 2023, the Legislature created the Office of the Public Defender with House Bill 236 to consolidate the state’s public defense system under the state agency. 
In 2024, a district court dismissed the longstanding class-action lawsuit, filed on behalf of people who couldn’t afford legal defense. The court ruled that because the state had made moves to fix the deficiencies in the previous system, the case was moot, or resolved. The judge also ordered that the state not return to the county-based system for public defense. 
Attorneys for the plaintiffs asked the state’s high court to reverse the dismissal, rule that the state’s new system was unconstitutional and require the state to fix the alleged deficiencies. The attorneys cited a mass resignation of public defenders upon the initial launch of the new state public defense office. 
The state Supreme Court’s opinion did not weigh in on whether the state’s changes to the system were constitutional or successful. The ruling reflected that it was the Legislature’s place to fix the system, not the court’s, Brody wrote. 
“Our task is narrower,” she wrote. “We hold only that the district court did not abuse its discretion in enjoining a return to the troubled county‑based models, and permitting the Idaho Legislature and Executive, rather than the judiciary, to supply the prospective remedy Plaintiffs seek.” 
 Two justices disagree, argue the case could still continue 

The dissent, written by Meyer, argued that the issues in the case were potentially still relevant and the case should not be dismissed. 
Meyer wrote that the creation of the new state public defense office didn’t render questions over the adequacy of the legal representation completely moot. 
“… the State’s efforts, while laudable, have not yet been proven to resolve the serious deficiencies identified by appellants in the public defense system,” Meyer said. “… to dismiss a case based on assurances of something different, results in closing the doors to courts of justice prematurely.”

name: WyoFile
title: Barlow laps Bextel on fundraising in Wyoming governor’s race with $2M
text:
When Rebecca Bextel appeared on The Tucker Carlson Show last Saturday, platforming her candidacy to more than half a million online viewers, she told the conservative political commentator she’d be “lucky” to raise “a million bucks” in the race to be Wyoming’s next governor.
Compared to Vivek Ramaswamy, “running a hundred-million-dollar governor run” in Ohio, Bextel told Carlson, Wyoming is “a very cheap state to buy politically,” reflecting previous allegations she’d made that outside money bought Eric Barlow the Republican nomination in August. 
Ultimately, Bextel, a Constitution Party candidate, reported fundraising well below her aspirational target, bringing in approximately $89,000, according to a campaign finance report filed Tuesday, when candidates were legally required to report their finances ahead of the general election. 
AI-assisted analysis showed that roughly 60% of the reported individual donors who contributed to Bextel live outside of Wyoming, while about 43% of all the money Bextel reported raising came from out-of-state donors. About 38% of all Bextel’s reported donations arrived either on or after Oct. 24, when her interview with Carlson was posted on YouTube. 
Bextel did not respond to WyoFile’s request for comment by publishing time.
Bextel’s reported fundraising fell well short of Barlow, who has reported raising more than $2 million since he announced his campaign in 2025. The bulk of Barlow’s fundraising and spending occurred before the primary election, when he faced two Republican challengers. 
Bextel, who describes herself in campaign materials as a Republican with the Constitution next to her name, pledged to run in the general election against Barlow only if Trump-backed Megan Degenfelder and GOP-backed Brent Bien lost the primary.
In the months since the primary election, Barlow raised about $335,000, according to his report filed Tuesday. Of the 125 reported individuals who donated during that span, about 86% were from Wyoming. 
“Kelly and I started this campaign by showing up, listening and asking people to be part of Wyoming’s future,” Barlow said in a Tuesday press release. “Through the primary and into the general election, people have continued to show up for us. We are grateful for their support and for the trust they have placed in us.”
The two candidates also diverged on donations from political action committees. Bextel did not report any PAC contributions, while Barlow reported receiving $90,500 in PAC money since the primary election. Since beginning his campaign, Barlow has received $334,780 in PAC money.
“Less than 10% of total fundraising came from out-of-state individuals and federal or out-of-state PACs, however, those PACs represent businesses that operate in Wyoming with Wyoming-based employees,” according to Barlow’s press release.
Kasner, the Democratic nominee, reported zero contributions or expenditures in his filing. 
The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting is underway.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: La pérdida del seguro de Children’s Mercy llama la atención sobre el sistema hospitalario de Kansas
text:
El logo y las ubicaciones de Children's Mercy se encuentran en toda el área de Kansas City, incluido el Aeropuerto Internacional de Kansas City, donde saluda a las personas que llegan. El hospital fue noticia recientemente cuando anunció que no aceptaría ningún plan bajo la Ley de Cuidado de Salud Asequible a partir de enero, después de que la única empresa con la que contrató retirara sus planes de dos condados de Kansas y seis de Missouri. Un experto de Kansas dice que muchos factores influyen en esta situación. (Foto de Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)Traducido por Claudia Amaro. 
TOPEKA — Cuando Children’s Mercy anunció que los pacientes no estarán cubiertos por el seguro bajo la Ley de Cuidado de Salud Asequible a partir del 1 de enero, los padres afectados se desahogaron en línea y algunos políticos culparon a la negativa a expandir Medicaid en Kansas.
Children’s Mercy, que tiene sucursales en Kansas y Missouri, solo tiene un plan de seguro en el mercado de la ACA este año, Medica, que cubre alrededor de 400 pacientes actuales, dijeron líderes hospitalarios en un comunicado. El plan de la ACA de Medica decidió salir del mercado en los condados de Johnson y Wyandotte en Kansas, y en los condados de Clay, Jackson, Johnson, Lafayette, Platte y Ray en Missouri.
“Los otros planes de la ACA que dan servicio al área metropolitana de KC estaban previamente fuera de la red con Children’s Mercy y han decidido no contratar con Children’s Mercy en 2027”, dijo el comunicado del hospital.
Un vocero de Medica no respondió preguntas sobre por qué la empresa está saliendo del mercado, y en un comunicado dijo solo que reconoce el impacto que tal decisión tiene en los pacientes.
Aunque el comunicado de Children’s Mercy dijo que el personal trabajará con los padres para asegurar la continuidad del cuidado, los padres preocupados recurrieron a Facebook para señalar los problemas que este cambio causará.
“Lo que hace que esta situación sea tan alarmante es que Children’s Mercy es el único sistema integral de salud pediátrica en nuestra región — simplemente no hay un hospital local de respaldo equipado para este nivel de atención especializada”, escribió Destiny Zelsnack, madre de Kansas City, Kansas, en su página personal de Facebook. “Si un niño pierde acceso a la red, los padres no solo cambian a otra clínica a la vuelta de la esquina; se les obliga a buscar a tres o cuatro horas de distancia en ciudades como St. Louis, Omaha o Wichita solo para encontrar especialistas pediátricos dentro de la red.”
La senadora Cindy Holscher, candidata demócrata a gobernadora, dijo que las decisiones tomadas por los republicanos de Kansas de no expandir Medicaid son un factor significativo que contribuye a situaciones como la de Children’s Mercy. Su oponente republicano en la contienda por gobernador, el presidente del Senado Ty Masterson, siempre se ha opuesto a la expansión de Medicaid.
Kansas es uno de los 10 estados que no han ampliado Medicaid.
“La expansión de Medicaid sería el factor más importante para fortalecer nuestro sistema de salud en general”, dijo Holscher en una entrevista. “La expansión cubriría aproximadamente a 150,000 trabajadores de Kansas y personas que trabajan en cuidado infantil, construcción, comercio minorista, agricultura, y algunas de esas son familias que hoy dependen de los planes del mercado.”
 
Múltiples factores
En Kansas, 58 de sus 100 hospitales rurales están en riesgo de cierre, con 21 en riesgo inmediato, según un informe de junio del Centro para la Calidad y Reforma de Pagos en Atención Médica.
“Los hospitales en zonas rurales tienen seis veces más probabilidades de cerrar sus puertas sin la expansión de Medicaid, y sabemos que cuando una zona rural pierde su hospital, no solo pierde acceso a la atención, sino que también pierde buenos empleos”, dijo Holscher.
Masterson no respondió a las preguntas de Kansas Reflector sobre si la expansión de Medicaid afecta temas como la pérdida de cobertura de la ACA por parte de Children’s Mercy y qué haría él como gobernador para fortalecer los hospitales rurales.
Los hospitales y organizaciones de Kansas han apoyado la expansión de Medicaid, diciendo que estabilizaría los hospitales y ofrecería seguro a los habitantes de Kansas que no tienen seguro o tienen seguro insuficiente. Sin embargo, Missouri ha ampliado Medicaid y Medica también decidió salir de los condados de Missouri.
Las compañías de seguros abandonan los mercados cuando determinan que no pueden ser rentables ahí, lo cual puede suceder por varias razones, dijo Cindy Samuelson, vocera de la Asociación de Hospitales de Kansas.
Los hospitales consideran varios elementos al decidir si aceptar el seguro de un plan específico, incluyendo si los pagos por servicios realmente cubren el costo de proporcionar el servicio y si el plan ofrece buen servicio al cliente, dijo Samuelson.
Por ejemplo, los hospitales analizan cuánto tarda un plan en autorizar o negar la atención, lo que puede causar retrasos en la atención de los pacientes, dijo.
 
Ingresos hospitalarios
Samuelson dijo que la complejidad de los seguros y las operaciones hospitalarias dificulta resumir cómo se toman las decisiones. Los ingresos se ven afectados por todo, desde la cantidad de atención caritativa y no remunerada que los hospitales brindan en sus comunidades hasta los programas de medicamentos recetados y el porcentaje de pacientes de Medicare y Medicaid que atienden.
Los ingresos operativos de los hospitales de Kansas, que provienen únicamente del tratamiento de pacientes y no de inversiones u otros ingresos, provienen de pagadores privados y públicos.
Los pagadores públicos son programas gubernamentales como Medicare y Medicaid, mientras que los pagadores privados son los planes de seguro para empleadores, personas que pagan por su cuenta y planes del mercado ACA, según un informe de la Asociación de Hospitales de Kansas.
“En 2024, los pagos de Medicare a los hospitales de Kansas cubrieron solo el 87% del costo total de atención a los beneficiarios de Medicare”, decía el informe. “En ese mismo año, los pagos de Medicaid cubrieron solo el 70% del costo total de tratar a pacientes de Medicaid en los hospitales de Kansas.”
La diferencia se compensa cobrando más a los planes privados para cubrir la brecha creada por los pagadores públicos.
“Para mantener una situación financiera viable, los hospitales intentan negociar tarifas de pago con grupos de seguros privados”, dijo la información de la KHA. “Los márgenes en estos pagos subsidian las pérdidas hospitalarias por pagos insuficientes de los pagadores públicos, deudas incobrables y atención benéfica. Esto se conoce como transferencia de costos y puede resultar en primas más altas para los asegurados privados.”
Para ilustrar lo que sucede, KHA dijo que en 2024, los beneficiarios de Medicare y Medicaid recibieron casi el 54% de los servicios clínicos de los hospitales de Kansas, pero los ingresos de los pagadores públicos representaron solo el 43% del ingreso total de los hospitales.
“En comparación, los pagadores privados recibían el 30% de la atención proporcionada por los hospitales de Kansas y representaban el 49% de sus ingresos netos totales”, dijo KHA.
Samuelson dijo que el 21% de la atención no remunerada en hospitales de Kansas proviene de pacientes asegurados que no pueden pagar sus costos de bolsillo.
 
Entorno cambiante
Aunque Holscher ha dicho durante toda su campaña que ampliará Medicaid, probablemente será una batalla difícil en un estado republicano que antes no había recibido cientos de millones de dólares en incentivos del gobierno federal para expandirse.
“Vengo de un enfoque muy colaborativo”, dijo Holscher. “Soy el demócrata más exitoso en el Senado en términos de lograr que se aprueben proyectos de ley, y de hecho más exitoso que el 90% de los republicanos.”
Holscher dijo que cofundó el Caucus Bipartidista de Mujeres y, como miembro de la Cámara en 2017, ayudó a aprobar la expansión de Medicaid, que fue vetada por el entonces gobernador. Sam Brownback.
Pero ella ve un ambiente cambiante en Kansas, incluido el hecho de que el presidente de la Cámara, Dan Hawkins, no regresará a su escaño. Hawkins, quien fue presidente de la Cámara, y Masterson, quien es presidente del Senado, lideraron los esfuerzos para detener la expansión de Medicaid. Hawkins se postula para comisionado estatal de seguros.
“Estamos trabajando para cambiar algunos de esos escaños, y ahora parece que hay más ciudadanos alzando la voz porque tenemos esta crisis de asequibilidad”, dijo. “La gente está luchando y sufriendo mucho en cuanto al acceso a atención médica asequible, cuidado infantil y vivienda.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: US Justice Department to send election monitors to these NC counties
text:
A voting sign at Chavis Community Center in Raleigh on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)U.S. Department of Justice election monitors will be in Wake, Alamance, and Mecklenburg counties on Election Day, according to the state Board of Elections. 
The Justice Department announced it would send monitors to every state as part of the largest monitoring effort in history, but did not disclose locations.
The DOJ has sent election monitors to North Carolina in previous elections. This fall’s expansive nationwide effort has Democrats, some Republicans, and voting rights advocates wary because it comes as President Donald Trump attempts to influence elections, States Newsroom has reported.  
Monitors are allowed to enter polling places on Election Day before voting starts in the morning to watch the set-up, and to be inside at night after polls close, state elections board general counsel Tim Hoegemeyer told the DOJ voting rights division in an email obtained by NC Newsline. Hoegemeyer cited state law and election rules in the email.
Early voting turnout so far shows enthusiasm among unaffiliated voters in NC

Additionally, monitors are allowed to approach people outside the polling place buffer zone before or after they vote to ask about their voting experience, Hoegemeyer wrote. Monitors may also contact political parties to request interviews with partisan poll observers. 
According to the Campaign Legal Center, monitors are prohibited by federal law from intimidating, coercing or threatening a voter or anyone helping a voter. 
If approached, voters do not have to answer monitors’ questions, said Jeff Loperfido, chief counsel for voting rights at the Southern Coalition for Social Justice. 
“Once the voting act is over, it’s no different from people who do exit polling for candidates,” he said. 
Olivia McCall, Wake’s election director, said the presence of monitors won’t change voters’ experience. 
“I wouldn’t think they would notice anything different,” she said. 
McCall did not know which polling sites monitors will choose. 
The presence of election monitors will give Wake the opportunity to show how well it runs elections and how closely it follows the law, she said. 
“Hopefully, it will be an opportunity for Wake County to shine,” McCall said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lawmaker seeks to scrutinize insurers’ ‘catastrophe models’ used to deny home coverage
text:
New Mexico state Rep. Anita Gonzales (D-Las Vegas) on Oct. 28, 2026, provided early details of a bill she intends to introduce that aims to give homeowners more information about how insurers determine whether a home is at too high a wildfire risk to justify coverage. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A New Mexico lawmaker on Wednesday previewed a bill she said will shed more light on how insurance companies use sophisticated “catastrophe” modeling to justify canceling an increasing number of policies in wildfire-prone areas of the state.
Rep. Anita Gonzales (D-Las Vegas) told lawmakers on the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee that she intends to introduce a bill at the upcoming legislative session that aims to curb a recent trend of rising premiums and insurance non-renewals in the state. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The bill would require insurance companies to provide more information to homeowners about how they evaluate wildfire risk to homes and neighborhoods. It would also require companies to provide premium discounts to homeowners that have taken established risk reduction steps, and give them a means to appeal company determinations homeowners think are in error. 
Faced with a growing number of expensive natural disasters, insurers are increasingly relying on complex and secret so-called “catastrophe” modeling that informs their decisions to raise premiums or not renew policies, Gonzales said Wednesday. 
Christian Myers, chief actuary for the state Office of the Superintendent of Insurance, said Wednesday that the systems insurance companies use to determine risk remain something of a “black box.” 
But he said “catastrophe” modeling generally incorporates simulations of thousands of wildfire or other disaster scenarios to determine average expected losses in particular ZIP codes and also contemplates how a “worst case scenario” — like a once-in-a-1,000-year wildfire — would play out in an area given its insurance rate, housing profile and other factors. 
Gonzales said New Mexico homeowners deserve to understand how insurance companies make such a determination, especially if it costs them coverage. 
“The question isn’t whether insurers should assess risk. They must,” Gonzales said. “The question is whether homeowners and regulators understand how that risk is being assessed; whether investments that reduce risk are being recognized; and whether homeowners have a meaningful path to improve that risk classification.”
The Office of the Superintendent of Insurance, the state’s insurance regulator, recently announced that insurers opted not to renew more than 6,600 policies in 2025, marking the highest-ever number of non-renewals in state history and a near-tripling of that number since 2021. 
Meanwhile, the Fair Access to Insurance Requirements Plan, which offers insurance to homeowners who can’t find coverage on the private market, has seen a steady increase in enrollees, from approximately 7,400 in December 2024 to more than 7,800 in August 2026, according to data from the OSI Gonzales presented Wednesday, alongside the office’s chief actuary.
New Mexico insurers refused to renew policies for record number of homes in 2025, official says

While most FAIR Plan holders live in eastern New Mexico, where wind and hail often make homeowners insurance difficult to procure, data state officials presented Wednesday show the most significant FAIR Plan growth in recent years has been in wildfire-prone areas like Lincoln, Los Alamos, Santa Fe, Mora, and Otero counties. 
Gonzales’ district includes San Miguel County, which the 2022 Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire hit hard. The number of homeowners relying on the FAIR Plan has increased in that county nearly 18% in that 21-month period, Gonzales noted, from 286 policies to 337 policies.
The lawmaker noted the increasing reliance on the “insurer of last resort” in her county and elsewhere, along with increasing number of non-renewals in a state that already has among the nation’s highest uninsured rates, makes it all the more important that homeowners receive more information about their policies and what they can do to keep them. 
Gonzales’ bill would require insurers to disclose information about the catastrophe models they use to state regulators; take into account property- and community-level mitigation in their premium prices; disclose to consumers how high-risk they deem their homes; and outline steps homeowners can take to improve their risk certification.
For homeowners, wildfire mitigation often involves establishing a buffer around homes cleared of brush or other fire fuels and using fire-resistant materials in their roofs or siding. But Gonzales said homeowners currently don’t have guarantees that implementing those changes will reduce their premiums or keep them covered.
New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham approves $8.25M for flooding, seeks additional federal assistance

If the Legislature fails to act during the session beginning Jan. 19 next year, Gonzales said, “Homeowners may continue spending thousands of dollars on mitigation without knowing whether those improvements affect their classification.”
Gonzales also said she is considering language in the bill that would require insurers to be more up-front about modeling in “other hazards that have been indicated in our state, again as recently as the last few weeks,” she said, referring to recent flooding in northern New Mexico.
Insurance Superintendent Alice Kane told lawmakers that her office supports Gonzales’ bill and would lobby for it at the upcoming session. 
Gonzales introduced a similar bill in the 30-day session earlier this year, but it never received a hearing. Bills that are not budget-related need special designations from the governor to be heard during 30-day sessions, and House Bill 204 did not receive one.

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA’s election chief says federal noncitizen voting list includes citizens
text:
A ballot dropbox in Olympia on March 12, 2024. (Photo by Bill Lucia/Washington State Stadard)Washington’s top election official is calling on federal authorities to provide more evidence that the state’s voter rolls include hundreds of noncitizens, as a preliminary investigation reveals U.S. citizens are listed.
The state’s top federal prosecutors on Monday claimed Washington’s voter rolls included 405 ineligible noncitizens who had voted upward of 1,500 times in elections dating back decades. They called on Secretary of State Steve Hobbs to set aside their votes until they could be confirmed as rightful voters, but Hobbs countered that the information they provided contains “several glaring deficiencies,” including duplicate entries and the inclusion of unregistered voters.
“Without individualized proof of ineligibility, it would be both irresponsible and illegal for election officials to decline to process a registered voter’s ballot,” wrote Hobbs, a Democrat. “If you have individualized proof, I invite you to provide it so election officials can take appropriate steps that are consistent with federal and state law.”
Hobbs’ response on Wednesday potentially sets the stage for litigation from the Trump administration, similar to what’s been seen in California where the feds have argued ballots from 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters should not be counted in next week’s midterm elections. 
President Donald Trump has for months been trying to assert more federal authority over next Tuesday’s midterm election, which could see his party lose control of one or both chambers of Congress. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hobbs is trying to stave off litigation so local election officials can focus on their task at hand.
“Rather than distract these dedicated public servants from their important work at this late hour with a meritless lawsuit, I strongly encourage you to re-visit the deeply flawed data you provided earlier this week, identify any actual proof, and work collaboratively with my office in the weeks or months to come,” he wrote.
Hobbs called Monday’s public allegations from federal prosecutors Charles Neil Floyd from western Washington and Pete Serrano from eastern Washington “profoundly disappointing.”
“If you had valid concerns about voter registrations, the time to raise them was months ago,” the secretary of state wrote. “Your decision to wait until the eve of an election and announce those concerns at a press conference instead of timely providing the list and any corroborating evidence to my office is not a sign of good faith to ensure a free, fair, and accurate election.”
Emily Langlie, spokesperson for the U.S. attorney’s office in Seattle, said the response from Hobbs had been received. Floyd and Serrano “will take some time to review it and decide next steps,” she said.
Hobbs claimed the list received from federal authorities included people who aren’t currently registered to vote or whose registrations are inactive. And many are U.S. citizens, a similar finding to other states that have faced similar accusations from the Trump administration. A spokesperson for Hobbs said it’s too soon to say how many exactly are citizens.
Hobbs also said the list of alleged noncitizen voters presented to the state contained no information sources or evidence supporting the claims of fraud.
“Given the Department of Justice’s recent acts of election interference in California, Alaska, and now in Washington, it would be particularly inappropriate for Washington to simply assume the Department’s unsupported allegations here are credible,” Hobbs wrote. 
The Trump administration is aiming to block the results of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if the Republican incumbent narrowly loses.
Voting is underway under Washington’s mail-in ballot system. Over 1.2 million voters have already returned their ballots, with turnout slightly outpacing 2022. One of the most pivotal congressional races in the country is in Washington’s 3rd District.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Public comment period opens as company seeks state permits for uranium mine
text:
The site of the proposed Dewey-Burdock uranium mine in Fall River County, South Dakota. (Courtesy of U.S. Bureau of Land Management)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/102826-Dewey-Burdock-update-web.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
A company that wants to mine for uranium in southwestern South Dakota is restarting its state permitting process and preparing for a public hearing after securing federal permits earlier this year.
Uranium is a metallic, radioactive element used as fuel in nuclear weapons and nuclear power plants. Interest in uranium exploration and mining has risen recently. That’s in response to nuclear energy’s potential to supply electricity for data centers.
The Dewey-Burdock project would cover nearly 20 square miles in Custer and Fall River counties along the southern edge of the Black Hills, 13 miles from the city of Edgemont. Legal challenges have kept the project in a 14-year stalemate since its initial application for a state permit.


Submitting a petition or comment
For information about submitting a petition or comment on the Powertech permit applications by the Nov. 9 deadline, go to danr.sd.gov/public. Scroll down to the Powertech notice under the “Water rights” heading, and click the dates under the “Petition/Comment Deadline” column.


“We stand by our commitments to work together to see that the local communities and State, and our shareholders, benefit from this project as we continue to uphold our commitment to always operate with best practices to protect the people, land, air, and water,” said the executive chair of Texas-based enCore Energy, William Sheriff, in a June press release after the company received federal permits.
Long-lasting litigation around the various permits has meant the project has “come up in waves” for people in the area, said Lilias Jarding, a project opponent and executive director of the Black Hills Clean Water Alliance.
“So, there are actually quite a few people who didn’t know about it, and we’re working to educate those people,” she said.
Jarding fears the project could pollute underground water deposits known as aquifers.
“I’ve talked to thousands of people about this project over the years,” she said, “and when they understand what it is and what it would do to the aquifers and what it would do to our water, they are universally against it.”
Powertech, a subsidiary of enCore, has applied to the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources for permission to draw water from the Inyan Kara and Madison aquifers. The company plans to drill hundreds of wells and use a water-chemical solution to dissolve uranium underground and bring it to the surface. Withdrawals would total billions of gallons per year, but much of the water used for mining would be treated and reinjected later. Some would be used for processing the uranium and supplying local ranchers with water for livestock and domestic use.
The applications will go to the Water Management Board, a seven-member panel appointed by the governor. Adam Mathiowetz, chief engineer of the state’s water rights program, is recommending board approval. His report says the applications meet all of the state’s legal requirements.
The deadline to file a comment, submit a petition or request a delay of the Dec. 2 hearing in Pierre is Nov. 9. The Dec. 2 hearing could be delayed based on that input.
“We’ve been talking to people across the region, and a lot of people are interested in becoming involved in various ways,” Jarding said. “They understand that water rights permits are not just a matter of temporarily using water.”
Lawsuit involving separate uranium drilling project is dismissed
Meanwhile, a lawsuit was dismissed earlier this week that was related to a separate application to conduct exploratory drilling for uranium in the same region of the state.
Clean Nuclear Energy Corp., a subsidiary of Canada-based Nexus Uranium, is seeking a permit to drill dozens of exploratory holes as much as 700 feet deep on state-owned land, while also seeking permitting for an exploratory project on federal land. The proposed sites are near the rim of Craven Canyon in the southern Black Hills.
Tense hearing on uranium drilling tests new language-translation law before its effective date

Dozens of people and some organizations have raised formal complaints about the project to the state Board of Minerals and Environment, which will decide on a permit. Opponents have said the drilling could disturb ancient Native American petroglyphs on the canyon’s walls, disrupt Lakota ceremonies and potentially contaminate groundwater, among other concerns.
A hearing on the permit began earlier this year in Hot Springs. It was cut short after a project opponent filed a federal lawsuit against the company, the board and the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources.
Elizabeth Lone Eagle filed the lawsuit on the third day of what was planned to be a five-day permit hearing. She alleged “systematic, ongoing, and deliberate denial of meaningful participation to Lakota first-language speaking” project opponents.
A judge dismissed the lawsuit, and an appeals court upheld the dismissal this week.
The state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources did not immediately provide an update on the next steps for the permit hearing.

name: VTDigger
title: Accountability court docket to continue in ‘modified fashion’
text:
Windham County State’s Attorney Steven Brown questions a witness during the trial of Cara Rodrigues on Wednesday, Oct. 16, 2024. Reformer file photo

This story by Chris Mays was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Oct. 25, 2026.
BRATTLEBORO — Windham Superior Court Criminal Division’s Rapid Accountability Docket is ramping down to one day a week. 
“I think overall it’s been very successful,” Windham County State’s Attorney Steven Brown said in an interview last week. “It connected some people with services and community resources that may not have been connected.” 
An announcement in July described the docket as “a concentrated, 90-day county surge of dedicated judicial time and space.”
“The strategic goal is swift intervention: dramatically reducing the time between an alleged offense and a defendant’s first appearance before a judge,” the announcement said. “By accelerating this timeline, the justice system can deliver immediate accountability, case resolution, and rehabilitative services close to the event, meaningfully interrupting the cycle of repeat offenses.”
Court records show that the docket resulted in 223 closed cases, with 297 cases still participating in the program moving forward. A total of 105 defendants, with 45 of those being resolved, participated. 
Defendants were able to resolve their cases on “much more favorable terms,” Brown said. He called Health Care & Rehabilitation Services “a terrific partner.”
“They’ve been present at the vast majority of hearings,” he said. “They’ve been a great resource for folks.” 
The Rapid Accountability Docket will continue in “a modified fashion,” Brown said. The plan is to have one morning a week dedicated to the docket. Brown anticipates Judge John Treadwell will continue handling the cases. 
Town Manager John Potter said the town “really benefited from the accountability court by building on the work of the Situation Table and One Brattleboro and finding additional innovative, proactive ways to better connect people in the criminal justice system with services.”
The two efforts he mentioned are ways the town has collaborated with other agencies to help individuals struggling in the community. 
“I’m extremely grateful to service providers, town staff, the judiciary, and the Governor’s Office for supporting these efforts to continuously improve Brattleboro’s public safety effectiveness,” Potter said. 
Brown said the state’s attorney’s office and public defender’s office weren’t designed to have a third court running. Before, the courthouse was set up to handle criminal and family matters. 
“We have to shift resources and take some measures to limit the impact,” Brown said. “But from my standpoint, it is worth the investment.”
Defense attorneys had “a huge increase in their court time because of this process,” Brown said. 
“That needs to be recognized,” he said. 
Brown said Elisabeth Fainberg, deputy state’s attorney, devoted “100 percent of their energy to the docket.”  
“They attend every hearing,” Brown said. “They provided the office with daily updates on what was happening.” 
Brown said Leah James, victim’s advocate from his office, was “able to shoulder a majority of the work generated by the docket.” 
Brown said the court recognized the importance of the docket and agreed to keep it running in conjunction with the governor’s office. 
“We have weekly calls with the governor’s office,” Brown said. “They’ve been terrific partners as well.”
Mimi Brill, supervising attorney of the Windham County public defender’s office, said the program “spread us incredibly thin so we weren’t able to work on other cases, so that was difficult.”
“We had a mandate,” she said. “It was funded, but we don’t have the services here. At least in Brattleboro and locally, we don’t have as rigorous treatment modalities available as in places like Burlington.”
Brill said the program helped with the backlog of cases but not homelessness. 
“I think some people did well with that kind of structure,” she said. “All in all, I think what we need in Vermont is to have real substance use disorder treatment and real mental health treatment like programmed inpatient that are 90 days that can really work. We don’t have that.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Accountability court docket to continue in ‘modified fashion’.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Vance urges GOP base to head to the polls during North Carolina visit
text:
KINSTON, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 28: U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks at a campaign rally on October 28, 2026 in Kinston, North Carolina. Vance is in to North Carolina to campaign for Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo by Tierney L. Cross-Pool/Getty Images)With less than a week until Election Day, and with Republicans lagging other groups in early voting, Vice President JD Vance rallied in North Carolina Wednesday to help get out the vote. 
Speaking to a crowd of about 500 attendees at Kinston Regional Jetport, Vance urged them to vote Republican straight down the ballot.
“In six days, you have an opportunity to vote for North Carolina patriots who believe in real sovereignty,” Vance said. 
He stumped for U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley and Army veteran Laurie Buckhout, who is running for North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, and dunked on their respective Democratic opponents, former Gov. Roy Cooper and U.S. Rep. Don Davis.
Those contests could play a crucial role in control of Congress. The challenging political climate has left Republicans playing defense in more states than expected. 
In the U.S. House, Democrats need a net gain of just three seats to win a majority. In the Senate, Democrats need a net gain of four. Republicans are defending Senate seats in Texas, Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, and Kansas, as well as North Carolina.
“Chances are, I’m going to be, at the end of the day, the 51st Republican senator, or Roy Cooper is going to be the 51st Democrat,” Whatley said. 
The Cooper campaign criticized Whatley for his ties to Washington. Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee, has consistently aligned himself with President Donald Trump.
“It’s no surprise Michael Whatley’s DC insider friends are trying to boost his desperate campaign,” a Cooper campaign spokesperson told NC Newsline. “Roy Cooper is the only candidate with plans to make stuff cost less while Michael Whatley led the charge to give billionaires handouts.”
The enthusiasm gap
Around 2 million North Carolinians have cast their ballots so far during early voting, and while all political affiliations are voting at numbers greater than during the last midterm election in 2022, the growth in Democratic and unaffiliated early voting is far outpacing the GOP’s. 
As of the close of early voting Tuesday, the number of early votes cast by Democrats was 50% higher than in 2022. Early ballots cast by unaffiliated voters saw an even larger jump — 67% higher than in 2022. Republicans were also up over their 2022 numbers, but only by 10%.
 
The growth in Democratic and unaffiliated early voting is far outpacing the GOP’s as of Oct. 28, 2026. (Chart: Michael Bitzer/Catawba College)
 
Historically, Republicans see higher turnout than other groups on Election Day, but Buckhout encouraged attendees to vote early.
“I know we are the traditionalists, we believe in that day being a near-sacred day to exercise your constitutional rights,” she told the crowd. “Here’s the deal: If you go early, it saves people money because then we don’t have to keep sending you those annoying cardboard things that come in your mailbox.”
U.S. Rep. Richard Hudson, who represents North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District and chairs the National Republican Congressional Committee, said the “hard truth” is that Republicans need to head to the polls.
“A lot of Republicans are a little bit hard-headed. The Constitution does say Election Day, and doesn’t say Election Month — I get it, but folks, we have got to get out and vote,” Hudson said. 
Kinston sits in North Carolina’s 3rd Congressional District, served by U.S. Rep. Greg Murphy since 2019.
Democrats see opening for Barringer in NC-13 race against freshman Republican Knott

Republican state lawmakers carved out some GOP voters in the 3rd and moved them into the 1st last year, aiming to displace Davis. That left the 3rd slightly less safe for the GOP, and a blue wave could cause the redistricting to backfire. Cook Political Report shifted the seat from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” last week. 
“Voting is not a privilege,” Murphy said. “It is a responsibility that comes from living in a free country. Do not sit this election out.”
Carteret County resident Dale Gillikin declined to share who she planned to vote for, but said she hoped Republicans would win across the ticket.
“I’m here to see the vice president. I thought he was great,” she said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Outside interests think Alaska’s U.S. Senate race is a cheap date
text:
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks at a candidate forum held Aug. 27, 2026, by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association. Next to him is his opponent, former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)A U.S. Senate seat in Alaska is worth the same as one from any other state when Democrats and Republicans try counting to 51, the number needed to control the chamber. All 100 senators get an equal vote, regardless of whether they represent states of far less than 1 million residents, such as Alaska and Wyoming, or more than 30 million, such as California and Texas.
The men who drafted the U.S. Constitution almost 239 years ago — yes, it was all men, 133 years before women finally won the right to vote — had to find a compromise between the larger and smaller states. They settled on the plan that treated all states the same in the Senate — even Delaware, with about 10% of the population of the biggest state, Virginia, in 1787 — whereas the larger states would get more representation in the House.
Little did the Founding Fathers know that generations later, that compromise would make it a bargain to campaign for a Senate seat in Alaska compared to the more populous states. Alaska, literally, wasn’t even on their map.
Total spending between incumbent Alaska Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat challenger Mary Peltola and their supporters as of last week exceeded $123 million, with more to come before the Nov. 3 election. That works out to almost enough for every two-person household of voters to buy a new set of snow tires, not that anyone could afford to buy gas to use the new tires.
As outrageously costly as that sounds, it’s a steal compared to spending on the Senate races in Texas, at $533 million, and Ohio, at $435 million. State pride aside, an Alaska senator counts the same toward 51 as those other, more expensive races.
Which is why there is so much national attention, and national millions, directed at mailboxes, streaming services, social media feeds and radio and TV commercials in Alaska, pounding our brains in the hope that we will vote for the candidate supported by the loudest, most abusive and frequently dishonest messages. A campaign win here is just as valuable as a win in a big state, only more affordable. 
The Founding Fathers likely never anticipated how obscenely expensive, intrusive, insulting and painfully long political campaigns could be, especially for important Senate races. It took less than four months for the group to debate, draft and approve the entire U.S. Constitution, while U.S. Senate campaigns stretch out for years.
Alaska, in particular, has attracted an outsized rush of Outside money in this election, telling us how to think and how to vote, in hopes of getting to 51 senators to run the country. We resent being treated like a cheap date, or at least cheaper than Texas.
But if we were on a date, the appropriate response would be to throw a glass of cold water into the face of Outside interests and leave the table, telling them we will find our own way home. We don’t need or want their advice, and we don’t appreciate their messages, which are as offensive to Alaskans as ordering farmed salmon for dinner.

name: VTDigger
title: Voter voices: At the Cambridge dump, unease about Vermont’s future
text:
Cheryl Vreeland stands outside the free store she runs at the Cambridge transfer station on Oct. 23, 2026. Photo by Shaun Robinson/VTDigger

VTDigger reporters visited a variety of sites across Vermont in recent weeks, asking voters directly about the issues they care most about this election season. This week we’ll bring you those voices as we approach Election Day on Nov. 3. 
CAMBRIDGE — Benton Donlevy, a 25-year-old mechanic from Jeffersonville, has watched most of the friends he grew up with in Vermont move away. He wants to stay — “I love the state,” he said — but is struggling to find the home he needs to do so. 
“There’s a lot of factors making that pretty difficult right now,” Donlevy said. Few places come onto the local market that are in his “starter home” price range; and even when they do, he hasn’t been able to match the speed of other bidders.
He hadn’t decided yet who he’ll vote for next week, he said, but is certain Vermont needs “somebody to address” the state’s lack of affordable housing. 
Donlevy was one of dozens of people who stopped by the transfer station in Cambridge over the lunch hour on a bluebird Saturday last weekend. Some parked quickly, dropped their trash and left in just as much of a rush. But others stayed and meandered around the dirt parking lot, catching up with friends and neighbors. 

Benton Donlevy of Jeffersonville poses with his truck at the Cambridge transfer station on Oct. 23, 2026. Photo by Shaun Robinson/VTDigger

Almost everyone who stuck around also stopped to chat with Cheryl Vreeland, who has run a free store at the dump for the past two decades. Vreeland described her age as “70-plus” and wore a bright pink coat. She said clothes have been “flying off the hook” at the store recently, something she chalks up to the rising costs of many basic goods. 
For all the talk of a strong national economy, Vreeland said she and many neighbors in the area simply aren’t feeling it. Some older people have savings to rely on, she said, but “working people, they’re having a hard time. You know, it’s very, very difficult.” 
Vreeland thinks Vermont is, in a word, stuck. She brought up the state’s latest push to consolidate education services, which will likely result in schools closing down. Few if any towns want to give up their local schools, she said, while few people seem to want to pay more in taxes to keep those schools viable, even if they have the means. 
Vreeland said she is frustrated by Republican Gov. Phil Scott, who earlier this year backed legislation that would have forced some schools to consolidate. But she also thinks Scott’s Democratic and Progressive challenger, Amanda Janoo, is running on plans for new public services that will require an unrealistic amount of spending.
“We don’t have the money, and nobody wants to take less. That, to me, is the problem,” she said.
Jochen Obert, 71, was standing nearby and agreed that the state faces daunting challenges, top among them the rising property taxes many people are paying to fund their schools. But it all pales in comparison, he thinks, to national politics — and that is what is driving how he votes this year more than any local issue, he said.
The Jeffersonville resident has voted for Scott in the past. But this year, he said he voted for Janoo because he thinks that Scott, while clearly no fan of President Donald Trump, has not spoken out sharply enough against many of Trump’s actions over the past two years.
“It’s hard to look at anything else,” Obert said.
On the other side of the parking lot, Ron Carter, 67, was surveying the contents of his trunk and, after catching a reporter’s eye, introduced himself by his stage name: “Rockin’ Ron.” That’s the “friendly pirate” character, he explained, that he performs for families at nearby Smugglers’ Notch Resort. 
Like Ocher, Carter said he did not vote for Scott this year despite supporting Scott in the past. Many people he knows in Jeffersonville struggle to afford housing, and he said he has a hard time covering medical bills, himself. Carter was compelled by Janoo’s proposal for universal primary care, he said, though thinks many details of the idea need to be vetted and, hopefully, improved upon by the state Legislature. 
“If the basic concept can happen, I think that would be good,” Carter said. “And I think she’s got a good shot, you know? It’s obviously a big year of change.”
