“My whole community works in the fields. They did a sweep on my little town, and my wife called me and said, “It’s empty, babe. It’s empty,” he said. 
He said he’s had no recent interactions with law enforcement. A public records search returned no recent criminal history. 
“I’m a father. You kidnapped me in the morning and took me from my kids,” he said. 
After his arrest, he was held at an ICE office in Fresno and then transferred to Bakersfield. He said he was taken back and forth while his blood pressure climbed until he eventually ended up spending about seven hours in an emergency room in Bakersfield. 
“They asked me, ‘Are you afraid to go back to your country?’ And I said yes, and I figured that was going to hold everything and at least give me a chance in court,” he said. 



First: Luis Arreguin holds his Bible. Last: Luis Arreguin cries in front of the Cathedral of Mexicali in Mexicali, Baja California, Mexico, on Oct. 21, 2026. Photos by Daniel Resendiz for CalMatters
After several days, agents transferred him to Camp East Montana on the outskirts of El Paso.  
“I didn’t know where I was going,” he said.  
The facility has been a focal point for lawsuits from civil rights organizations and detainees, who have complained about harsh conditions, including not getting enough to eat and insufficient medical care. In September 2025, ICE’s own internal watchdogs found dozens of violations, the Washington Post reported. 
Arreguin spent five days there before he says his phone communication was cut off and he was put on the plane to southern Mexico. 
“At least I am safe here, and I’m not behind the walls of a detention center where I could die,” he said.
Crowded deportation flight
Arreguin said his flight carried roughly 300 fellow deportados, all shackled and chained at the wrists and ankles. He counted 22 women and one minor. 
“They shackled a 14-year-old kid,” he said. 
Arreguin described agents restricting people’s access to the bathroom and water during their 36 hours of travel. 
Meanwhile, officers taunted him: “Oh, look, it’s the famous Mr. Arreguin,” they said, holding up their phones with news stories about his arrest and social media videos his daughter made to draw attention to his case. 
Just before they deplaned, he said, agents hurried down the aisles, removing shackles. He interpreted it as an effort to keep Mexican officials from seeing how they had been transported. 
“A lot of people are afraid to even say anything about how they were treated,” he said.
ICE did not respond to CalMatters questions about the flight or the conditions Arreguin described. 
Others on the flight who spoke to CalMatters on condition of anonymity corroborated the details Luis gave. ICE has a long-standing operational policy that mandates passengers in custody are shackled with handcuffs, waist chains and ankle restraints during flights, including during layovers and refueling stops. 
One detail the former Central Valley resident said he’ll never forget: “Everybody on that plane had their work clothes on. Every single one of them.” 
Changing Mexico deportation strategy
Since this spring, the administration has largely stopped sending Mexican nationals back across the land border. Instead, it’s flying them deeper into Mexico, where officials believe deportees dropped near the Guatemala border are less likely to try to cross back into the United States. 
In Tapachula, Mexican officials fed Arreguin and gave him a debit card loaded with 2,500 pesos, about the equivalent of $130. “They didn’t have to give me that,” he said. It got him as far north as Mexico City. His adult daughter paid for the rest of the trip to Mexicali, where, as a teenager, Luis was able to cross the border freely with his Fresno church group. 
The border city is receiving fewer deportees now than it has in the past decade. In 2024, U.S. authorities returned more than 43,000 Mexicans through Baja California crossings at Tijuana and Mexicali, about one in five of all repatriations nationwide, according to Mexico’s Interior Ministry. 
In the first seven months of 2026, just 1,567 people came through the Mexicali crossing, less than 2% of the national total. The numbers fell as the Trump administration shifted to flying Mexican deportees farther south to Tapachula and Villahermosa, which together took 48,000 people over the same time period, nearly half of all returns.
Those figures don’t include people who were removed to Tapachula and then made their own way north again, like Arreguin. 
“You know you can’t just take people away from their family,” he said. 
What now?
“Don’t cry,” Luis tells his oldest daughter, holding his phone outstretched in front of him to FaceTime her in front of the Cathedral of Mexicali in Baja California. 
In Fresno, Luis’ wife is packing up their house to move. The family doesn’t have the money to stay without Luis paying rent as the family’s main breadwinner. His two youngest children, 6 and 10, will have to change schools. 
“I’m tired of crying,” he says. “It takes a lot out of me when I’m speaking about what I had to go through and what I’m going through and how I was treated,” he said. 
An aerial view of the vehicular and pedestrian border between Mexicali in Mexico and Calexico, California, on Oct. 21, 2026. Photo by Daniel Resendiz for CalMatters
But, he’s working on finding a lawyer to help fight his deportation and return to his family. 
“I have to fight,” he said. 
Until then, his daughter is paying for his motel and food. She is maxing out her credit cards. She is looking for a place in Mexicali big enough for the whole family to visit him for Thanksgiving. 
For decades, Arreguin worked to give his children a better life in the United States. Now his daughter Elaina is trying to make him comfortable in Mexico. 
You’ve supported me for years, she told him. “Now I can do that for you.” 
CalMatters photojournalist Larry Valenzuela contributed to this report.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Democrats see opening for Barringer in NC-13 race against freshman Republican Knott
text:
Paul Barringer, the Democratic nominee running for North Carolina's 13th Congressional District, poses with his dogs, Billy and Penny, at an early voting site in Clayton on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)CLAYTON, N.C. — Johnston County resident Jennifer Gibbs cast her first ballot in the 1990s. She said she’s lost track of the number of times she voted Republican, but she’s switched to voting for Democratic candidates lately.
Gibbs, a retired business owner, said she isn’t happy with President Donald Trump or the current Republican Party. 
Some of her complaints are with the cost of living — Gibbs and her husband Charles are helping out their adult children and grandkids with gas and groceries. Others are with corruption in the government, immigration, and reproductive rights.
“I want to make sure that my granddaughter and my daughters keep all their rights,” Gibbs said. “I don’t know if I’ll ever be able to vote Republican again, ever, because of Trump.”
Gibbs continued that streak Tuesday, when she cast a vote for Paul Barringer in North Carolina’s 13th Congressional District.
Barringer, a healthcare consultant and former lawyer, is challenging freshman GOP U.S. Rep. Brad Knott for the seat. Knott, a former prosecutor and Trump-endorsed candidate, won the district after a primary runoff in 2024 against Kelly Daughtry.  
The Knott campaign did not respond to requests for an interview for this story.
U.S. Rep. Brad Knott (Photo: House.gov)
State lawmakers redrew the 13th in 2023 to heavily favor a Republican. It was expected to be a safe GOP seat this year: Trump won it in 2024 by 17 points. 
However, Democrats have recently come to believe that the wave of voter sentiment against Republicans this year might open the door to a possible flip. Barringer started airing TV ads shortly before early voting started. Knott, who had not run ads this cycle, either, quickly followed suit. 
Election forecaster Cook Political report shifted the race from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” last week, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added the seat to its “Districts in Play” program at the start of October. 
The 13th district resembles a backwards “C,” curving around Raleigh and the more liberal parts of Wake County. It covers parts or all of eight counties, spanning from Caswell County in the north to a thin piece east of Raleigh before going down to Lee County, where Barringer lives.
“My thesis from the beginning was that if you took a gerrymandered district and you could run as a moderate candidate, then you might have a chance,” Barringer told NC Newsline at an early voting site in Clayton.
Paul Barringer, the Democratic nominee for North Carolina’s 13th Congressional District, recently went over 350,000 miles on his 2006 Toyota Land Cruiser. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)
Last fall, Barringer rode his bike from his home in Lee County to Yanceyville, in the northwestern part of NC-13. A straight shot as the crow flies would be 66 miles, but through the district, Barringer said he rode for 183 miles, and it would’ve been more if he had touched every corner. 
As a result, he’s spent plenty of time on the road while campaigning. Barringer said he just went over 350,000 miles on his 2006 Toyota Land Cruiser a week or so ago, and he brings along his dogs, Billy and Penny, for company. 
“He is a ball of fire. He has so much energy, and he shows up all over the place,” U.S. Rep. Deborah Ross, a Democrat representing North Carolina’s 2nd Congressional District, said. She’s been campaigning to support Barringer in his race. 
Barringer grew up on his family’s tree farm in Lee County. He graduated from public schools there, as well as Davidson College, the University of North Carolina School of Law and Princeton University. He spent about 20 years living in Maryland and working in Washington before returning to Lee County to care for his ailing mother.
“I’m really running to provide an independent voice for the district because I think the people of the district deserve a representative who will show up for them and represent their interests, as opposed to displaying loyalty to the president or a political party,” Barringer said.
Knott, the incumbent, has voted with the conservative congressional baseline 96% of the time, according to Heritage Action. His campaign website lists his priorities as securing the border, defending gun rights, and supporting school choice. 
Cooper rallies support one week into North Carolina’s early voting

A quadruplet, Knott lives in Raleigh’s North Hills neighborhood. It’s part of the neighboring 2nd Congressional District, represented by Democrat Deborah Ross since 2021. However, congressional candidates do not need to reside in the district they seek to serve.
Several early voters NC Newsline spoke with Tuesday said they didn’t know much about Knott, but planned to vote Republican down the ticket. Others said he’s a good representative.
Garner resident Lauri-Anne Disinger was volunteering for the GOP at an early voting site in Clayton. She said she’s met Knott at some of his events throughout the district.
“He’s very thorough,” Disinger said. “If he gets a question about a committee that he doesn’t know the answer to, he’ll go back and discuss with a member on the committee and get an answer for the person.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Voters urged to use drop boxes as recommended mail-in deadline passes
text:
The secretary of state's office along with election advocates emphasized that a timely postmark alone isn't enough to ensure a mail ballot arrives on time to be counted, and recommended voters return their ballot to a drop box or vote in person after Oct. 27. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)The U.S. Postal Service’s recommended deadline for mailing in ballots passed Tuesday, prompting voting advocates to urge Nevadans who missed the window to return their ballot to a drop box or vote in person.
USPS officials say they are ready to deliver election ballots securely and on time, but recommended voters mail completed ballots at least one week before the ballots must be received by their local election office. 
The agency assured it has the capacity to deliver the nation’s ballots during the final stretch of the election, but has repeatedly advised voters to return ballots by Oct. 27, one week before the Nov. 3 Election Day, to avoid any delivery delays. 
In Nevada, mail ballots sent through the post office can only be counted if they are postmarked on or before Election Day and received by the election department no later than 5pm on the fourth day after Election Day. 
The Nevada Secretary of State’s office warned voters not to wait until the last minute to return completed mail ballots, and has urged voters to mail it as soon as possible or deposit ballots at one of several drop box locations to ensure on time arrival. 
Election advocates also emphasized that a timely postmark alone isn’t enough to ensure a mail ballot arrives on time to be counted, and recommended voters return their ballot to a drop box after Oct. 27 or vote in person.
“If you are unable to mail it back by the 27th, please drop it off at a dropbox or vote in person either early or on Election Day,” said Kerry Durmick, the Nevada State Director for All Voting Is Local.
Emily Persaud-Zamora, the executive director of Silver State Voices, directed voters worried about their ballots being returned on time to use drop boxes, or take them directly to a local election office.
“For voters in Clark and Washoe counties, all polling locations will have a drop box. Voters can also check out the interactive map from the NV SOS to see drop box sites and polling locations throughout the state of Nevada,” said Persaud-Zamora in a statement.
Voters can also track their ballots on the state website to ensure it has been accepted by the state’s election department. 
Nevada has one of the highest shares of voter participation by mail-in ballot, according to a recent report to Congress. In the 2024 general election about 45% of Nevada voters opted to cast mail ballots. 
Athar Haseebullah, the executive director of the ACLU of Nevada, emphasized that “voting by mail is safe and secure,” but warned that “with unprecedented threats to USPS, it’s best to get your ballot mailed back as early as possible.”
The U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling in June that election officials may continue to count mail ballots received after election day, a legal challenge that was part of the Trump administration’s broader attack on most mail balloting.
USPS officials said they are preparing additional measures to speed up ballot deliveries during the final stretch of the election season, including extra mail deliveries and collections, special pickups, expedited sorting at processing facilities and localized handling and transportation of ballots.
“The Postal Service is confident and ready to deliver a successful Election Mail season,” Postmaster General David Steiner said in a statement last week.
USPS officials pointed to the agency’s record during the 2024 general election, when 99.6% of ballots mailed by voters were delivered to election officials within three days, according to the Postal Service’s post-election analysis.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: St. Clair County nurses are speaking up. County leaders aren’t listening.
text:
Nurses listen during public comment on St. Clair County's medical director, Dr. Remington Nevin at a meeting of the county commissioners on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)My fellow St. Clair County Health Department nurses and I work hard to uphold public health principles and provide much-needed services that our community relies on.
But lately, the department has been in the news for all the wrong reasons.
That’s because my fellow nurses and I have been trying to rid our workplace of intimidation, harassment and retaliation – only to be disregarded by the elected officials who run our county.
It’s been a long journey to get to this point.
We followed internal rules to report the cause of this toxic work environment – the conduct of medical director Dr. Remington Nevin.
Two years ago, a panel of county officials recommended the Board of Commissioners arrange an external investigation into multiple employee complaints. County Human Resources called the situation with Nevin “untenable.”
Months went by. Tired of waiting, we – along with many community members – spoke at commission meetings this summer and laid out the need for an independent, impartial investigation and protection from further retaliation.
St. Clair County Commissioner Lisa Beedon, who chairs the Human Services Committee, spoke in favor of an investigation into St. Clair County’s medical director, Dr. Remington Nevin at a meeting of the county commissioners on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)
We contend that Nevin’s behavior toward employees violated multiple county policies. Outside partners also raised issues with his conduct.
Instead of addressing this crisis, commissioners chose to negotiate a new contract with Nevin giving him more authority and money. They claimed they could not act because the complaints were mostly filed anonymously, blaming employees because we followed the county-approved process.
So, we compiled 42 signed complaints from department workers – nurses and non-nurses, union and non-union, dating from two years ago to as recently as last month – and submitted them to the board.
Again delaying, the commissioners gave the complaints to an attorney to evaluate.
This produced a flawed process and a wholly inadequate report:

The attorney works for the same firm defending Nevin and the county in court. This involves a state-level allegation of retaliation against a health department nurse. That’s a conflict of interest; of course the attorney won’t recommend an investigation against a client. At the least, she appears to have framed the issues in a way that got the answers county commissioners wanted.
The multiple allegations of retaliation were completely ignored. The county’s attorney didn’t even use the word “retaliation” in her verbal summary and only mentioned it in her written report to say that many employees stated they were afraid of retaliation.
The report didn’t fulfill its stated goal. We were directed to share complaints about Nevin’s violations of county policies, which we did. Indeed, the county attorney’s report states she was asked to evaluate whether the board “should retain an external investigator to determine whether violations of County policies … occurred.” Yet later she admits she reviewed only whether Nevin broke the law.

It wasn’t the fair, unbiased review county employees were promised, and it wasn’t the review we deserved.
The report and commissioners’ discussion of it implied that nurses and other staff are to blame for the department’s “dysfunction.” Let’s be clear: the “dysfunction” in the department lies solely with Nevin’s behavior.
This is not a matter of whether people disagree about policy. Opinions are separate from behavior – and, in a healthy work environment, professionals can discuss concerns and ask questions without retaliation.
That is especially true of nurses, who have an obligation to speak up for our patients. We need a safe environment in which to do that.
The county-paid attorney concluded by recommending a workplace consultant for the department, focusing on what one commissioner deemed “teamwork.”
St. Clair County defers decision on investigating health director facing workplace complaints

In dismissing the 42 signed complaints, commissioners pointed out that Dr. Nevin was placed on a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) on Sept. 2. That was related to his undisputed comment about having a “grenade launcher in my pants.”
That toothless plan is related to a single incident, which appears to be the one of the few complaints that has actually been investigated. No one – not Human Resources, not commissioners, not a neutral party – has investigated all the 42 signed complaints spanning two years. We know because many employees tell us they haven’t been interviewed.
And there is already a new complaint alleging that Nevin retaliated against an employee, violating his PIP.
Yet the County Administrator has told us the 42 signed complaints have been “reviewed” and that the focus needs to be “forward looking.”
Is all this just going to be swept under the rug?
We need public officials who stand up for public employees. Too often, what we get instead is elected leaders who excuse bad behavior. This is an egregious example of that.
County officials refuse to support St. Clair County Health Department employees – the vast majority of which are women. Instead, they protect and enable a man who abuses his power to belittle the people around him and make it hard to do our jobs. In this way, it seems that public health is under attack in more ways than one.
Nurses Jessica Baker, Kristen Hays and Katie Pringle (left to right) listen during public comment on St. Clair County’s medical director, Dr. Remington Nevin at a meeting of the county commissioners on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)
We applaud community members who have engaged in fact-finding and advocacy alongside us, using the Freedom of Information Act to make up for the county’s lack of transparency, and we encourage them to continue.
Nurses will keep doing our jobs with professionalism and dedication. We will keep respectfully standing up for ourselves, each other and our community.
We will cooperate with any department consultant – knowing it is an ineffective and inappropriate step. But we deserve a voice in choosing a consultant and determining what “consultation” looks like.
In the meantime, this is the message we want people, especially younger people and other women, to hear: It is not OK for a man to use his power to mistreat people, and it’s wrong to blame the victims of his conduct and expect them to fix it.
I don’t want this to be normalized for my daughters or for anyone else’s. So when people ask if all this has been worth it, my answer is yes.
Because it’s always worth speaking up and doing what’s right.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri pastors take opposing sides in fight over abortion amendment
text:
Ahead of the November election, all four Missouri Catholic Bishops issued a letter urging parishioners to vote yes on Amendment 3, which would repeal the 2024 abortion rights amendment. A sign supporting the amendment stands outside Our Lady of Sorrows Catholic Church in St. Louis (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
The Rev. Alex Bryant set a goal for 2026: Talk to 200 Missouri pastors about abortion. 
Bryant, an Assemblies of God pastor in Springfield, began traveling across Missouri to sit across from his peers, often over coffee, and tell them why he would be voting yes on Amendment 3, which would repeal the state’s 2024 abortion rights amendment. 
The measure, which voters will decide Nov. 3, would ban most abortions, with exceptions for medical emergencies, fetal anomalies, and rape or incest within the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. It would also place a constitutional ban on gender-affirming medical care for minors.
Now, less than a week before the election, he’s met with 250 pastors. 
“I just genuinely believe that the votes are in the pews, and the pastors and Christians were informed, and then if they engaged, and we vote our values, we could win.”
Bryant is part of a growing effort by religious leaders to mobilize support for Amendment 3. But clergy opposed to the measure are also organizing, arguing that their faith calls them to protect individual choices from government interference.
The anti-abortion movement failed to organize effectively in 2024, Bryant said, when Missouri voters approved abortion rights by a narrow margin. The amendment passed with 51.6% of the vote.
“Number one, our politicians dropped the ball … number two, the pro-life organizations were fractured for funds and for money, and for who gets the credit,” Bryant said. “And then number three, the pastors and the Christians didn’t engage.”
This year, supporters of abortion restrictions have taken a different approach.  Republican lawmakers voted to put a new amendment seeking to ban most abortions on the ballot. Anti-abortion groups organized early. And a broad coalition of faith leaders have come together in support of Amendment 3. 
The Rev. Alex Bryant, an Assemblies of God pastor in Springfield (photo submitted).
Bryant, who is Black, has focused much of his outreach on Black pastors across the state. He said many lead congregations that lean Democratic and view abortion restrictions primarily as a Republican issue. 
With those peers, Bryant said he’s found success talking emphasizing the portion of Amendment 3 that would place a constitutional ban on gender-affirming care for minors. State law prohibits gender-transition surgery for minors and bars minors from beginning cross-sex hormones or puberty blockers. The restrictions on hormones and puberty blockers are set to expire in August 2027, though lawmakers have discussed making the ban permanent. 
“I’ve had more than one Black pastor tell me, ‘ah, man, every man in my church is against this,’’’ Bryant said. “They don’t want our boys in women’s sports.” 
Amendment 3 does not address participation in school sports.
Bryant saw untapped power in the pulpits early on. He wasn’t the only one. 
Tom Estes, a pastor in mid-Missouri and a leader with Her Health, Her Future, the main campaign in support of Amendment 3, said the 2024 campaign left little time to organize religious leaders. 
“This time,” he said in September, “we’ve just got buy-in like we’ve never seen.”
This week, the Missouri Baptist Convention at its annual gathering voted in favor of a resolution urging members of its more than 1,700 churches across Missouri to support Amendment 3. 
And earlier this month, all four Missouri Catholic Bishops issued a letter urging Catholics to vote yes.
“Every human life is sacred because every person is created in the image and likeness of God,” the letter read. “The protection of innocent human life is therefore a matter of fundamental moral justice.”
The Catholic Church has been involved in other ballot measures. It previously voiced support for Medicaid expansion and opposition for recreational marijuana legalization. In August, the Catholic bishops weighed in on Amendment 5, a failed effort to phase out the state income tax. 
“It’s not that the Catholic Church hasn’t been involved in ballot issues before, but never to the degree that it is certainly this year,” said Sam Lee, a Catholic deacon in the St. Louis area and a longtime anti-abortion lobbyist in Jefferson City. 
This fall, the Diocese of Kansas City – St. Joseph distributed a guide that included suggestions for priests on how to tie Amendment 3 into the Bible readings for the day. Parishioners are out knocking doors. Large Yes on 3 signs have appeared in front of churches. Lee said many of these efforts crossed over into other denominations as Christians worked together to coordinate canvassing efforts and yard sign distribution.
In Nixa, south of Springfield, the Rev. Michael Lacobee, lead minister at River Stone Fellowship, said he’s never had much interest in pushing his more conservative political beliefs from the pulpit. But abortion, he said, is different.
“To me, this is a moral issue,” he said. “I think it’s an attempt to morally destroy the family.”
Since he began preaching about abortion after the 2024 election, Lacobee said several women have approached him to share their experiences  Now he’s working to support them and support other women who might be considering abortion. 
“This isn’t politics,” he said. “These are real things people are suffering with and trying to figure out and problems they’re trying to solve.”
Other Missouri faith leaders say their experiences counseling congregants have led them to the opposite conclusion: Their religious beliefs compel them to speak out against Amendment 3.
The Rev. Kevin Cameron, pastor at Parkway United Church of Christ, was wary of taking political stances that might ostracize any members of his congregation. Then Amendment 3 was placed on the ballot.
“It was a really important and nuanced conversation with our church council,” he said. “We tried to do what we can to stay out of the blurring of church and state. But, in fact, this time, we felt in order to keep that line separate, we needed to speak up to say faith should be separate, so government shouldn’t be mandating through faith lens what decisions can be made.” 
Now, the lawn of his church features a sign that reads: “No on 3. Stop the abortion ban.” The church hosted a canvassing event for the Stop the Ban campaign this fall.
His congregation is welcoming to LGBTQ+ people. The rhetoric around transgender children was one of his main motivations for getting involved this time around, calling pro-Amendment 3 campaign rhetoric “an assault on people who are already ostracized and who already struggle.”
Cameron is among 90 Missouri clergy members who signed a letter denouncing Amendment 3. 
A Stop the Ban sign opposing Amendment 3, which seeks to overturn Missouri’s 2024 reproductive rights amendment, stands outside Eliot Unitarian Universalist Chapel in Kirkwood (photo submitted).
So was the Rev. Krista Taves of Eliot Unitarian Universalist Chapel. In 2024, her congregation helped gather signatures for the reproductive rights amendment. Now, she said, members are frustrated that the legislature is trying to undo their efforts.
After abortion was banned in Missouri in 2022, Taves said a few families in her congregation left the state, including a couple trying to conceive using IVF who worried Missouri’s laws could impede their ability to start a family. 
“What I’m hearing from people, even those who are confused about abortion, is what they’re not confused about is government overreach. They’re not confused with that at all,” Taves said. “There’s a deep respect that people should have the ability to make choices for themselves and not have politicians tell them what those choices are.”
Rabbi Andrea Goldstein of Shaare Emeth in St. Louis County said Reform Judaism emphasizes individual choice and personal responsibility in making moral decisions.
She opposes Amendment 3.
“It’s not about whether you, quote unquote, believe in abortion or not,” she said, “but that people in the state should be able to practice and make their own healthcare decisions without interference from the government.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Weak economy, vanishing federal aid limit CT’s tax-cutting options
text:
Many policy groups, political candidates and others insist Connecticut must cut taxes again next year, particularly on poor and middle-class families, to combat a worsening  affordability crisis.
But despite a decade of huge surpluses, the state’s own projections show a recession would quickly make that unaffordable, especially now that Connecticut has been weaned off the huge pandemic aid it enjoyed in recent years.
State officials could pay for tax cuts, in theory, by cutting government services, something governors and legislators historically try to avoid during a downturn. That option is further complicated by huge cutbacks in federal human services programs that Connecticut already is trying to mitigate.
Or, officials here could finance relief for low- and middle-income households by boosting income taxes on the wealthy — something they haven’t done since 2015 and which likely would expose sharp political divisions.
“Connecticut is capable of enacting bold policies that build an economy that works for all of us, but we have to be willing to change our tax code so that the wealthy start paying their fair share,” said Emily Byrne, executive director of Connecticut Voices for Children.
Byrne’s group, along with the United Way of Connecticut, more than half of the current General Assembly and others, support a new state income tax credit for low- and middle-income households with children.
But that’s just one of the tax-cutting efforts building support for the regular 2027 General Assembly session, which starts Jan. 6.
The Connecticut Project, a nonprofit social and economic advocacy group focused on making the state more affordable, is spearheading efforts for a new credit for renters, also focusing on low- and moderate earners.
The most popular child tax credit proposal would cost state government about $350 million to $400 million per year, according to nonpartisan analysts. Renters’ credit proposals reviewed but not approved by lawmakers last year would cost anywhere from $200 million to $575 million annually.
And Republican legislators’ proposals to cut income tax rates would cost the state almost $1 billion annually by 2028.
Can state government afford tax cuts next year?
At first glance, all these proposals seem affordable without having to raise taxes on anyone.
State finances have finished, on average, with $1.8 billion unspent since new budget caps were installed in 2017. That’s an amount of black ink equal to about 8% to 9% of the General Fund.
The post-2017 surpluses are almost 90 times the size of the 0.1% average cushion Connecticut budgets generated over two decades prior.
A closer look shows those surpluses were not only statistical outliers but are already at risk of eroding.
When this November’s gubernatorial winner is sworn in and the 2027 legislative session convenes in January, it will mark the longest stretch between state income tax increases since the levy was enacted in August 1991.
But the chief reason those huge surpluses are at risk involves the $4.2 billion in emergency federal COVID assistance Congress sent state government here through the Coronavirus Relief Fund and the American Rescue Plan Act.
As spending caps were extracting $1.8 billion yearly from education, healthcare and other core services over the past six years, Gov. Ned Lamont and Connecticut legislators simply replaced many of those lost dollars with COVID grant funds, which weren’t subject to regular budget rules.
But that emergency federal aid largely was exhausted by late 2025, and Connecticut’s finances already are showing the strain.
State officials had to employ an accounting gimmick to divert $712 million headed for surplus into a new program to expand affordable childcare.
And as they ran for reelection this summer, they also formally exceeded a spending cap three times to redirect another $1.2 billion to cover Medicaid shortfalls, soften cuts to federal human service programs and boost town aid by $280 million.
That local aid funding was ordered as a one-time exception, meaning officials have no approved waiver, at least for now, to maintain the assistance next year.
Fears of economic weakness continue
And if Connecticut’s finances are feeling the strain now, what happens if the global economy continues to slip and tax revenues shrink?
In a May 29 interview with Bloomberg, Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, called the U.S. economy “uncomfortably close” to recession, citing high oil prices, inflation and the ongoing war with Iran among other risk factors.
Many economists since then have said they expect a softer economic transition, but problem signs remain.
Connecticut Voices reported in late August that nearly 63,000 Connecticut residents have lost federal nutrition benefits since last July — roughly double state officials’ projections. And more cutbacks to federal human service programs take effect in 2027.
In early September, the United Way found about 40% of households here can’t afford a basic survival budget.
And diesel fuel that powers the trucks delivering most groceries and department store goods to Connecticut hit an all-time high in late September.
States typically respond to a recession by drawing down reserves, hoping to delay program cuts and tax hikes for as long as possible.
Connecticut, which used its recent surpluses to build reserves and pay down pension debt, still holds a record $4.5 billion in its rainy day fund. That represents 18% of annual operating expenses and is almost triple the safety wall the state built just prior to the Great Recession of 2007-09.
Despite that, an analysis by Lamont’s budget office last November showed surpluses would vanish, the reserve would be gone, and the General Fund would be 3% in debt within two years of a severe recession.
A more moderate downturn could just empty the rainy day fund by 2029.
Is a class-based  tax war in CT’s future?
But either scenario likely eliminates the prospect of paying for new tax cuts out of surplus.
Connecticut Voices has urged lawmakers for years to raise taxes on the wealthy to preserve services and finance tax cuts for low- and middle-income households. This enables relief without destabilizing the state budget.
Connecticut For All, a progressive coalition of more than 60 faith, labor and other civic organizations, also supports this option. 
“Connecticut families need relief, and our state can provide it by asking the richest among us to contribute their portion,” said Constanza Segovia, co-director of the coalition.
Others tax-relief advocates are still developing a position.
The United Way of Connecticut hasn’t proposed raising top income tax rates to finance a child tax credit but also has not ruled it out.
The Connecticut Project is “actively considering our position” on whether a wealth-related tax hike should be used to pay for new tax breaks for renters, said communications director Meghan Holden.
But she also noted the advocacy group is closely studying a recent poll it commissioned from the Survey Lab at Wesleyan University.
It found 73% of voters back a tax credit for renters and 70% support a child-based income tax break. It also reported that 76% support “increasing taxes on millionaires and billionaires.”
“We’ll be basing our position on what working class people are telling us,” Holden said, adding her group would again advocate for a renters’ credit in the upcoming General Assembly session.
Any tax redistribution plan next year will face opposition from the governor.
Lamont and Republican gubernatorial contender Ryan Fazio, both from the affluent Fairfield County suburb of Greenwich, share the conviction that taxing the rich would spark an exodus of wealthy households from Connecticut.
“Gov. Lamont is committed to more taxpayers, not more taxes,” has become a mantra for the administration in recent years.
“There’s a reason you see economic growth from people moving to states with low income taxes,” Fazio said.
House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, says legislators have other options to finance relief besides taxing high-earners.
The state could redirect hundreds of millions of dollars annually, he said, by scaling back generous raises for state employees, canceling Medicaid benefits for undocumented residents and cutting budgeted funds reserved for hundreds of positions often left vacant by state agencies and departments.
“The welfare state that’s been created is unsustainable,” he said.
But Rep. Maria Horn, a Salisbury Democrat and co-chairwoman of the Finance, Revenue and Bonding Committee, said her party wants to deliver more relief, preserve key services and maintain healthy-but-possibly-smaller budget surpluses.
That doesn’t mean Connecticut has to raise taxes on some to finance relief for others next year, she said. But it also means that option can’t be quickly dismissed as it was when the state was awash in billions of dollars in federal pandemic grants.
Neighboring Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Maine, New York and New Jersey have met their obligations by boosting state income tax rates on top earners in recent years.
Meanwhile, Connecticut’s own tax fairness studies have shown the combined state and municipal tax systems have disproportionately burdened the poor and middle class.
The lowest earning 10% of Connecticut workers effectively lost 40% of their income to state and municipal tax burdens in 2022, according to the most recent study, done in late 2025 by the Department of Revenue Services. The middle three deciles lost 16% to 20%, and the highest-earning decile lost just 10.6%.
“I think it’s time for us to take a hard look at the context in which we live,” Horn said, adding there’s “a deep sense of unfairness” among the middle-class voters she’s spoken with this fall.
Note: The Connecticut Project is a funder of The Connecticut Mirror.

name: California
title: For LA fire survivors awaiting federal disaster aid, the midterms could be key
text:
In summary
Long-term disaster recovery for the Los Angeles fires depends on federal funding. FEMA has indicated less support for states, but California lawmakers think Democratic wins in November could change things.


Almost two years since the Eaton and Palisades fires in Los Angeles County, many fire survivors are still displaced, running out of money and waiting for long-term federal disaster aid that may not come.
If survivors have received insurance payouts, they may have depleted that money for temporary housing. Some survivors received Federal Emergency Management Agency funding for housing, too. For renters, that aid ran out on Oct. 9. Any future federal aid is up in the air — and could depend on what happens in the midterm elections.
“I’ve never been at a point in my life where I don’t know what to do, where to go, who to turn to,” said Kate Adams, who received money from FEMA toward rent for an apartment in Duarte after the Eaton Fire damaged the Altadena apartment she and her daughters had lived in for 10 years. 
Adams, a real estate agent, also got some money from a local nonprofit and a California Association of Realtors grant. But even with those contributions, the cost of rent and replacing damaged belongings has exhausted Adams’ savings. She and her daughters are running out of options because there’s no more aid coming in.
“I’ve got two teenage daughters who are just starting their lives,” Adams said. “I don’t know how to keep a roof over our heads.”
A construction worker works on a house in a residential area in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. The area was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters
Adams is just one of many survivors, especially renters, facing the prospect of having no place to go.
A recent survey by the Department of Angels, a nonprofit group that’s tracking recovery efforts, found that 28% of all survivors have run out of displacement coverage. The survey also found that survivors want elected officials to prioritize insurance availability and affordability; financial and tax relief; and speeding up permitting and rebuilding. 
Katie Clark, co-founder of the Altadena Tenants Union, said the “situation on the ground is dire,” especially for renters. “People are wondering if they have to live out of their cars, and pull their kids out of school. We need money and housing. This is not rocket science.”
Pushing for federal funding
While officials at every level of government push for federal funding, fire survivors have traveled to Washington, D.C., to do the same. But the Trump administration has been slow to release funding to California, and it’s unclear when the billions of dollars in long-term disaster recovery money the state has requested will come — if at all. FEMA has told states they will need to handle most disasters themselves, according to a recent leaked recording from the National Emergency Management Association’s annual conference. 
That alarms people like Sierra Lindsey Kos, co-founder of national nonprofit organization Extreme Weather Survivors, who said a federal funding gap strains local and state budgets.
“California communities are already confronting devastating wildfires, flooding, extreme heat, and a growing insurance affordability crisis,” Kos said. “Reducing federal disaster assistance would place even more pressure on families and communities navigating these challenges.”
President Donald Trump did not include Los Angeles County wildfire relief funding in his administration’s budget request for Congress this summer. Two members of Congress from California say the outcome of the November elections could be key to unlocking more federal aid.   
U.S. Rep. Judy Chu, a Democrat from Los Angeles whose district includes Pasadena, recently helped pressure FEMA into releasing $6.6 million to pay the state back for services provided by case managers who helped people deal with insurance, FEMA aid permits for rebuilding and more.
The state requested additional funding to continue the program and was denied, but appealed. Chu said almost 1,400 open cases are waiting to be resolved. She called the program essential for survivors’ mental health.
The Department of Angels survey also asked survivors to rank their five most urgent issues right now. Mental health and long-term financial concerns came in first and second, respectively.
Chu and others are advocating for long-term federal funding, too. California has requested $16 billion through the Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery program — $8 billion each for the Eaton and Palisades fires.
“Basic FEMA funding cannot possibly do the job,” Chu said. “(Community development grant) funds will allow for individual recovery plus other essential causes that will help Altadena to rebuild.”
Congresswoman Norma Torres, a Democrat who represents the Inland Empire, lost her Pomona home to a fire more than 20 years ago.
“I know what these families are going through,” Torres said. “Right now we should be trying anything and everything to bring some relief to victims.”
Gil Barel moves the blinds up to let in more light into her living room in Pasadena on Aug. 2, 2026. Barel is currently not living in her apartment because of the Eaton Fire of January 2025.  Photo by Ariana Drehsler for CalMatters
Torres and Chu both said that if Democrats win the House of Representatives in November, federal aid to California and other states hit by disaster could start to flow.
Torres said her office is trying to find Republican lawmakers willing to advocate for disaster aid alongside Democrats. But she said because the president has not called for the aid, they are reluctant to lend their names to any effort to do so.
“I’m hoping after the midterms that my Republican colleagues have a different perspective and try to approach things in a more humane way,” Torres said.
Chu agreed: “My hope is that the mood of Republicans will be quite different when they lose the House and possibly the Senate. And they may see this as their only ability to shape what can come to their members.”
Some Eaton Fire survivors recently went to the nation’s capital to advocate for federal aid. They were joined by survivors of the 2025 floods in Texas and of the storms and subsequent prolonged power outages in Gary, Ind., when they met with staffers of U.S. lawmakers to ask about long-term federal disaster funds. 
“We’re pursuing opportunities to get members of both parties in the room and have them hear directly from survivors,” said Sylvie Andrews, whose Altadena home burned down. “I really hope they were listening to us. They seemed sympathetic.”
Bill Gould, another Eaton Fire survivor who also lost his Altadena home — along with his prosthetics because he’s a left-arm amputee — said some staffers told them it was unusual to have direct contact with fire survivors. Both he and Andrews were underinsured and have yet to rebuild; federal aid could help them. 
“It will be interesting to see how midterms maybe shake some of this up,” Gould said. “At the same time, time is not our friend. For us, with our (additional living expenses coverage) and our insurance, you don’t have forever for these things to resolve.”
Local and state efforts
Last year, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and L.A. County Supervisor Kathryn Barger met with Trump to ask for help for their constituents as well as for the county for its infrastructure needs. Altadena has more than $2 billion worth of infrastructure to repair and rebuild, said Anish Saraiya, Barger’s director of recovery for Altadena. He also said the county is working on establishing a financial assistance program.
“While we wait for federal resources, the supervisor says we’ll find every dollar out there,” Saraiya said.
Anthony Martinez, a spokesperson for Gov. Gavin Newsom, said California has committed more than $100 million toward affordable multifamily housing in the area. He also said the state will keep pressing the federal government for more funding that can support renters, including through the community development program.
The long-term aid program is usually administered by the Housing and Urban Development Department. 
“Over the last 10 years, California has received billions in federal disaster aid for wildfires, but state and local leaders have not been good stewards of those funds to help their communities recover,” HUD said in an unsigned email response to CalMatters. “HUD remains committed to being good stewards of taxpayer dollars, ensuring every cent goes to serving those in need.”
The federal agency did not respond to follow-up questions.

name: California
title: Sacramento-area community college tries to fool voters by claiming bond won’t raise taxes
text:
I’ve lived in the Sacramento region for more than a half-century and paid local property taxes, some of which support the Los Rios Community College District.
My latest property tax bills, received just a few days ago, contain levies to service bonds that the district issued in years past. I’ve never begrudged those taxes, even though neither I nor members of my family have ever attended Los Rios classes. My sense is that its four campuses provide vital, low-cost opportunities to prepare students for transfers to four-year colleges or training leading to gainful employment.
In fact, I would say that California’s more than 100 community colleges overall provide immense bang for the taxpayer bucks they receive.
However, Los Rios demeans itself by trying to fool voters into passing the new $1.1 billion bond issue on next Tuesday’s ballot. The proposal’s summary on the ballot reads like an advertisement rather than a factual statement:
“With funds that cannot be taken by the state, public disclosure of all spending, and no increase in tax rates, shall Los Rios Community College District’s measure to prepare students, workers, veterans for jobs with affordable college and career training facilities; provide safe drinking water; and repair leaky roofs be adopted authorizing $1.1 billion in bonds with legal rates, average levies below $17 per $100,000 assessed valuation ($74,500,000 annually while outstanding), independent audits, oversight, and all funds staying local?”
The summary’s pledge of “no increase in tax rates” is untrue. Issuing bonds triggers an automatic property tax that the summary itself describes as “below $17 per $100,000 assessed valuation” to generate $74.5 million each year until 2051, to repay investors who purchase the bonds.
The assertion that the bonds will not increase tax rates is based on an assumption that the taxes currently being raised to repay previous bond issues will just continue on for additional decades. But whether that occurs depends on variable factors such as interest rates, and even if the current rate just continues it’s still an increase in taxes over what they otherwise would be.
Another troublesome aspect of the Los Rios proposal is found in the lists of potential projects the bonds would finance.
There’s an old adage that long-term debt, either personal or institutional, should not be spent on anything that doesn’t last as long as the repayment period. A number of the projects mentioned in the official voter guide for this bond issue are really maintenance items, such as fixing leaking roofs.
California’s local governments have a bad habit of neglecting maintenance to meet demands for other spending, such as salary increases, and then catching up by issuing long-term bonds.
Robert Jones, a former Los Rios trustee who wrote the ballot argument against the bond proposal, contends the district’s buildings are underused due to rising levels of remote learning.
“Why would the district want to add at least 32 new buildings when half of the existing buildings remain empty or underused,” Jones asks rhetorically. “What kind of logic is this?”
I’m not singling Los Rios out for criticism. It presents Measure H the way other local entities have, violating the spirit and perhaps the letter of a state law banning the use of taxpayer money “to support or oppose the approval or rejection of a ballot measure, or the election or defeat of a candidate, by the voters.”
Earlier this year, a state appellate court upheld a lower court ruling that Hemet Unified School District misleadingly declared in ballot language that a $225 million bond issue would not raise taxes, which hinged on exactly the same tricky rationale that Los Rios employs.

name: Nevada Current
title: Democrats, Culinary call on Station Casinos to heed Supreme Court ruling, negotiate a contract
text:
“It's time for Station Casinos to join with their workers and their union representation, to come together and negotiate a fair contract,” said Ted Pappageorge, Secretary-Treasurer for the Culinary Union. (Photo: Hugh Jackson/Nevada Current)U.S. Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts in September denied an emergency petition filed by Red Rock Casino to stay a lower court’s decision that affirmed the company must bargain with the Culinary Union. 
Nearly two months later, Culinary workers, flanked by Democratic officials, called on Red Rock Casino to come to the table to negotiate a contract.
“It’s time for Station Casinos to join with their workers and their union representation, to come together and negotiate a fair contract,” Ted Pappageorge, Secretary-Treasurer for the Culinary Union, said at a press conference Tuesday, referring to the company that owns Red Rock Casino.
All three state congressional Democrats and Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, joined Culinary workers Tuesday touting union support, arguing for more labor protections at the federal level, and echoing calls for Red Rock to negotiate a fair contract with workers after years of fighting. 
Less than a week away from Election Day, Ford touted his record fighting for collective bargaining rights as a state senator and attorney general, and told union members that he will “always have your backs on the picket line, in the courtroom, and at the bargaining table.”
“We’re certainly going to hold you to that,” Pappageorge replied, adding “I know you’ll be there for us as you always have been.”
The Culinary Union has been fighting with Stations Casinos for decades to allow members to collectively bargain at their properties. 
The National Labor Relations Board found in 2024 that Red Rock had violated national labor laws during the union’s 2019 efforts to negotiate collective bargaining agreements. 
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the findings of the NLRB in June of this year.
Red Rock filed an emergency application asking the Supreme Court to stay the D.C. Circuit’s decision. Red Rock’s request was denied in September.
The long-time back and forth resulted in “nearly seven years of delays in appeals of a company spending on lawyers instead of the people who make that casino run,” Ford said. 
Now that the Supreme Court has ruled, Pappageorge said “it’s time to lay down the sword and pick up the pen.” 
Following the ruling, Station Casinos said the company will comply with the court order but still objected to the NBLR, a spokesperson told the Las Vegas Review-Journal in September. 
The order also mandate Red Rock Casino, Boulder Station, and Palace Station to display notices from NLRB acknowledging the company violated labor rights and attesting that it will not “threaten you with job loss as a result of a strike if you select union representation” or “threaten you that selecting a union representative would be futile.”
The casinos have not posted those notices yet according to the Culinary Union.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Question 5 would lead to deep cuts in services that communities rely on
text:
MASSACHUSETTS VOTERS will face nine different ballot questions next week—a number we haven’t seen in over 30 years. Considering the sheer volume coupled with the varied and complicated issues these questions seek to address, voters have their work cut out for them.   
This is especially true for Question 5. Proposed by an alliance that includes corporate lobbyists and some of the state’s wealthiest residents, this ballot scheme would alter an arcane and rarely triggered element in the tax code dubbed “62F.” 
Question 5 would modify a tax cap law that was enacted 40 years, also through a ballot question, which calls for refunds to taxpayers whenever state revenue exceeds the previous year’s cap by more than the statewide growth in wages and salaries.  
Under the complex changes to this law that proponents want voters to adopt through Question 5, this tax cap would be exceeded far more often than is the case under the current law, which has only triggered refunds twice in 40 years. Passing Question 5 would cause repeated and deep cuts to the services communities and residents rely on. Under their plan, billions of dollars currently used to support our public schools, pay for local police and fire department equipment, keep people healthy through community health centers, make safety repairs to our roads and bridges, and so much more would be declared surplus and lost.  
In exchange, this money would be given out as rebates to residents every time there’s a surplus. When services are cut by $1 billion, residents would receive a roughly $250 rebate, which comes out to about one small iced Dunks a week. That’s tempting, but the reality is that it is not enough to make a significant impact on a majority of households while stripping the systems and programs they rely on of critical resources. 
According to the Center for State Policy Analysis at Tufts University, this ballot question would require spending cuts averaging $2 billion annually. It would cause tremendous uncertainty in the economy, with experts predicting the necessary spending cuts to fund the question would vary wildly from year to year. Often these cuts would be triggered when state budget writers are already well into the year, creating volatility and making it next to impossible for the state to plan ahead or make long-term investments. 
Under this flawed tax code gimmick, the deepest cuts would likely be triggered by damaging recessions. During the times when state spending to support residents is most critical, the money to do so would be depleted. A rebate of a few hundred dollars cannot make up the difference when job training programs are closed and the projects that create jobs across the state are paused. 
Question 5 supporters point to growing state revenue as a cause for the current affordability crisis families are facing. The truth is that state revenue has grown slower than the economy for most of the years this tax code has been in effect. They ignore the fact that the only significant growth we’ve seen in state revenue is because residents passed the Fair Share Amendment in 2022. The “millionaire’s tax,” as it is most often called, has generated $10 billion by adding a four percent tax on yearly personal income above $1 million dollars. 
Thanks to the revenue generated, every child is now provided a free breakfast and lunch at school, residents have access to free bus service through the state’s 15 regional transit authorities that serve 262 cities and towns, $424 million has made no-cost community college available to all residents, $397 million in scholarships have supported low-and-middle-income students at our public universities, nearly $16 million has helped to expand access to early college and career technical education, and every city and town in the state has received critical funding to repair and repave local roads and bridges. 
Our schools remain the best in the nation and our investments in public transit are bringing people back to downtown and easing the commute of working residents. Helping families and communities when they need it most. 
Question 5 is the definition of a corporate-funded ballot question. They want you to think it’s a grassroots campaign of workers, taxpayers, and those most impacted by the current economy when, in reality, it’s the exact same group of funders that poured millions into trying to defeat the Fair Share Amendment.  
Their sleight of hand is a cynical attempt to deceive families struggling to make ends meet by voting against their own interests. With Massachusetts communities at the point where they cannot continue to support the very basic public services residents depend on, this question would decimate the funding municipalities rely on from the state to keep them afloat. It makes no economic sense. 
To be clear, the state’s wealthiest residents behind this proposal don’t stand to see a windfall. They’d get the same amount back like everyone else—meaning they have very little to gain, while the rest of us have much to lose.  
Peter Enrich is emeritus professor at Northeastern University School of Law and served as general counsel within the Executive Office for Administration and Finance under Governors Dukakis and Weld. Jessica Tang is the president of the American Federation of Teachers Massachusetts, which represents over 26,000 educators and staff working in public schools, universities, libraries, and health offices across the state.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New Naugatuck apartments a ‘blueprint’ for transit-oriented development
text:
By next summer, downtown Naugatuck will be transformed, with dozens of new apartments and a new train station.
Naugatuck’s downtown redevelopment has drawn the attention of Gov. Ned Lamont, who said it’s an example of the potential Transit Oriented Developments (TODs) hold.
“I hear a lot of speeches about transit-oriented development,” Lamont said. “You sort of have to sometimes imagine what it means. You don’t have to imagine when you’re here in Naugatuck. You see what it means.”
The new Water Street train station is expected to be completed in the summer.
However, the first of three apartment buildings at the Platform at Naugatuck which abuts the train line has been completed and residents recently began moving in.
Lamont spoke about the developments’ benefits at a ribbon cutting for the new apartments Monday.
“You’ll be able to walk right over to the train station, go to Waterbury, Stamford, or beyond, or people coming in here for work as well,” Lamont said.
The Platform at Naugatuck is now accepting applicants. The building was approved for families to move in less than two weeks ago, according to Karmen Cheung with Pennrose, one of the project developers.
Five families are currently living in the 60-unit building, but it is expected that nearly half of the building will soon be rented out.
“While we have some finishing touches to do, there has been an overwhelming round of interest,” Cheung said. “Today is about more than just the completion of a building. It’s about what can happen when a community comes together around a shared vision and is willing to do the hard work to bring that vision to life.”
Of the 60 units, a dozen are for residents earning 30% of the Area Median Income (AMI). Another 24 apartments are for families earning 50% AMI, including eight reserved for Section 8 voucher recipients.
Another dozen are for residents earning 80% AMI and the final dozen are market rate apartments.
Officials say the project is all a part of a transit oriented plan to revitalize downtown Naugatuck to make the town more inclusive and connected.
“Not long ago, this was a vacant site with just the potential to transform downtown Naugatuck, today that vision has made a big step in becoming reality,” Cheung said.
The second building will begin construction in early 2027 and applications for project funding for the third and final building will begin in January, according to Cheung.
In all, Platform at Naugatuck will have 180 apartments spread across three buildings and be done in 2030, Cheung said.
The state Department of Housing (DOH) contributed more than $8 million to the project.
“At the end of the day, what is important is for the families that are going to be living and are going to call this place home, are the dinner tables where kids are going to be doing their homework, our neighbors walking around, and what a beautiful place to be,” DOH Commissioner Seila Mosquera-Bruno said.
Generations ago, when Naugatuck was an industrial hub, 10,000 people worked downtown daily, Mayor Pete Hess said.
“For years we’ve been talking about bringing people downtown, and now we’re handing out the keys,” Hess said. “What you see is a blueprint for transit-oriented development.”
This story was first published Oct. 27, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New Haven Harbor navigation channel dredging begins
text:
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has begun a long-planned effort to deepen the navigation channel within the New Haven Harbor by five feet — with the goal of allowing bigger ships carrying steel, cement, and oil to travel to and from the city’s industrial port.
That New Haven Harbor Improvement Project began on Friday, according to Troy Darr, the chief of public affairs for the New England District of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE).
The project dates back roughly two decades, and will see the removal of roughly “4.5 million cubic yards of sand, silt, and rock to deepen the entrance channel, main shipping channel, and turning basin from 35 feet to 40 feet below mean lower low water, while widening the critical transit corridor,” according to Darr.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has awarded this project to contractor Great Lakes Dock and Dredge Company.
The work should take place over the course of “two dredge sessions” — from October 2026 to March 2027, and from October 2027 to March 2028.
“This work will allow the port to accommodate modern, deeper-draft commercial vessels—significantly boosting shipping efficiency, lowering transportation costs, and enhancing navigation safety,” Darr told the Independent in an email comment. “Furthermore, a substantial portion of the dredged material will be beneficially reused directly within harbor to improve important fish habitat, enhance oyster grounds and build a new rock reef.”
Sally Kruse, the executive director of the New Haven Port Authority, welcomed the beginning of this project as “very exciting” not just for the port, but also for New Haven.
“It represents a major investment” by the federal and state governments in making ship transportation in and out of the port more efficient, she said. She said that larger vessels tend to be newer, more efficient, “more modern,” and even more eco-friendly — potentially allowing for “the same amount of material coming in” to the port with fewer vessels.
She said that the channel-deepening project should allow vessels to come in to New Haven’s port “without waiting for high tide. The current depth means that some of the largest vessels cannot come in without doing so.”
In an Oct. 21 press release announcing the start of the project, Darr wrote that New Haven is “the largest port of call in Long Island Sound, the third-largest port in New England by tonnage, and Connecticut’s busiest port.”
New Haven’s port is not a so-called “container port.” The products that are transported in and out of the city’s harbor are not, for example, big boxes of furniture or food.
Instead, the city’s port is a way station for “petroleum products, home-heating oil, aggregates, equipment, and scrap metal,” as Darr put it.
The Oct. 21 press release states that roughly 1.7 million cubic yards of dredged material will be used “to support aquatic ecosystem improvement of shellfish and reef habitat, including filling of relic borrow pits that have existed in the harbor since the 1950s.”
In addition to the deepening of the channel from 35 to 40 feet below Mean Lower Low Water (MLLW), this project will also see the widening of the entrance channel from 500 feet to 600 feet outside the breakwaters; the widening of the channel bend between the breakwaters from 560 feet to 800 feet; the widening of the main channel from 400 feet to 500 feet inside the harbor; and the “optimizing” of the turning basin “for more efficient use by larger vessels.”
“The improvements will support energy production with optimized delivery of critical petroleum, products such as gasoline, jet fuel, and heating oil as well as commodities such as road salt, steel and chemicals vital to our nations industry,” Craig Martin, senior project manager with the USACE New England District, is quoted as saying in the press release.
The work has been coordinated with the U.S. Coast Guard, Connecticut Port Authority, and New Haven Port Authority, among others.
Click here and here to read more about the project, including about how the Senate Committee on the Environment and Public Works authorized a feasibility study back in July 2007 regarding navigation improvements for the New Haven Harbor.
This story was first published Oct. 27, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Starkville’s district consolidation is called the state’s most successful. County residents feel differently
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
STARKVILLE — In marbled rooms at the State Capitol, conversations about school consolidation often lead to Oktibbeha County. 
Many state leaders consider the 2015 consolidation of the Starkville city public schools and Oktibbeha County schools a success story. 
That’s because the consolidation — which married a failing district in the county to one that was middling in the city — resulted in more money, a temporary enrollment bump, a new state-of-the-art school with expanded academic offerings and what is now an A-rated district.
But some locals might argue that account leaves out another part of its legacy: Every school that closed belonged to the county district, where 90% of students enrolled were Black. By comparison, the city schools were 30% white.
Jackie Ellis pictured at the site of her former high school in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Jackie Ellis, 70, attended county schools and graduated from B.L. Moor High School, which later became East Oktibbeha High School. Now the old school is home to an events venue and a boutique motel. 
Every time Ellis drives by the motel, she feels what she lost.
Early resistance ends with shared mission
When the consolidation was first introduced — by lawmakers from Hattiesburg, no less — Starkville residents grumbled, Haley Montgomery recalls.
“The community was fairly blindsided,” said Montgomery, who at the time was a volunteer with the local public school parents’ group and freelanced for the school district. She now handles communications for Starkville Oktibbeha Consolidated School District. 
Starkville parents worried how consolidation with the state-managed Oktibbeha County School District would reshape their C-rated schools.

A historical marker for B.L. Moor High School is pictured in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The former East Oktibbeha High School is now an event venue and boutique motel in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today

Families wanted a seat at the table and asked the Legislature to let locals take the lead. Lawmakers formed a committee of Oktibbeha County residents to recommend ways to improve education in their community.
The committee stumbled early on, when it proposed sending Oktibbeha students outside of the county. Rex Buffington, who led the committee, said the group was trying to shorten commutes for students who lived closer to neighboring school districts than to schools in Starkville.
But the proposal was perceived as a rejection of students. “And of course it was,” he said, acknowledging the misunderstanding. “Why didn’t we see that?”
Rex Buffington, former chair of the consolidation committee, pictured in downtown Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Though painful, the incident helped change the committee’s perspective. No longer would they try to split up students. 
“These were all of our children,” Buffington said. “We were going to take responsibility for finding a plan to help children in both districts.”
When the committee visited the county schools, Buffington saw obvious disparities and, more importantly, the opportunities that lay before him.
“They didn’t have a lot of the extracurriculars that we take for granted,” he said. “I saw they were missing out on so much — in the classroom, yes, but even extracurricular activities. They didn’t have the things they needed and deserved. It was a moral issue to me.”
Many of the county students had grown up in the shadow of Mississippi State University but never visited the campus, Buffington said. The committee wanted to change that. 
The idea for the Partnership School was born. 
Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The university would partner with the district to train teachers at the campus, and would give sixth and seventh graders from across the county access to a sparkling new facility and extracurricular offerings that were previously unavailable to them, like an agriculture class and piano class.  
The school, lofty and spilling with light, opened in 2020 and serves 657 students on MSU’s campus. 
When history is erased
Orlando Trainer, who served as the county representative on the local consolidation committee, saw only benefits in merging the two districts. 
County supervisor Orlando Trainer pictured at the Oktibbeha County courthouse in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Trainer attended Starkville schools, but he and his wife, a graduate of the county schools, chose to send their daughter to Oktibbeha County schools for most of her education. Over time, Trainer saw how much help county schools needed — facilities in disrepair, limited extracurricular and academic opportunities and low student morale. 
Trainer, a county supervisor, considered the condition of the county schools as shameful, particularly with a university just a few miles away. 
“Consolidation for us was an act of redemption,” he said. “I only wish we had done it sooner.”
English teacher Kasey Underwood goes over classwork with students at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
But for Ellis, the longtime Oktibbeha County resident and B.L. Moor High alumna, the loss of her school still hurts.
The only buildings that closed during consolidation belonged to the county district. Today, two former county buildings remain in use — an elementary school and another that’s an alternative school for students with behavioral problems.
East Oktibbeha High School was central to the community and a hub for civic life, Ellis said, including Juneteenth celebrations, ball games, fundraisers and concerts.
East Oktibbeha High School alumni and former school staff are memorialized in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Julius Clark, a longtime Oktibbeha County Schools administrator before the consolidation, remembers the reaction when the closures were announced. 
“Of course, everyone felt that their children were being pushed aside or thrown into something that someone else wanted,” he said. 
Though Clark wishes those schools that were closed could have stayed in the community, he eventually came to support the consolidation. That’s because it gave county students access to extracurricular activities they didn’t have at their district, such as band and choir, and access to better resources, such as modern textbooks and technology. 
“They had been missing out on everything,” Clark said. “We didn’t have recognition or opportunities because of the money. Everything was based on money, and money is based upon your student body.”
Ellis, who works on historic preservation in Oktibbeha County, acknowledges that consolidation ultimately benefitted county students, improving their academic offerings and facilities through the Partnership Middle School. But she feels the community lost something important.
“The opportunity for the community to preserve (the East Oktibbeha school) property was given away to someone outside of the community,” she said. “It’s caused a great loss.”
A number of mementos such as class photos and trophies went missing during the consolidation, Ellis said. Some were found two years ago damaged or destroyed, she said. 
Artifacts that make up a school’s history and traditions are often overlooked during consolidation, said Carrie Hahnel, a senior associate with Bellwether, a national organization that works to improve education outcomes. 
The former East Oktibbeha High School is now an event venue and boutique motel in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayA dedication marker for East Oktibbeha County High School is in place at The Hill and Moor boutique hotel Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayRex Buffington, former chair of the consolidation committee, pictured in downtown Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayThe Oktibbeha County courthouse in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayConstruction at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayPartnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayTrophies are on display at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayStudents complete classwork at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayStudents complete classwork at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayEnglish teacher Kasey Underwood goes over classwork with students at Partnership Middle School in Starkville, Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Schools with more Black students are more likely to be closed, research shows. The logic of closing a predominantly Black school and moving students to a modern, well-equipped building makes sense, Hahnel said, it’s important to understand “that facility might be in disrepair because of a history of disinvestment.” 
A consolidation lesson: Listen to locals
