name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia Treasurer Larry Pack defends Hope Scholarship in enrollment decline
text:
West Virginia State Treasurer Larry Pack addresses reporters about his 2026 legislative priorities during a news conference Nov. 17, 2025, in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)West Virginia State Treasurer Larry Pack defended the Hope Scholarship program Tuesday, stating that while it may contribute “a teeny bit” to declining enrollment, demographic changes are more at play in the trend. 
Declining birthrates, people leaving the state and an aging population means less students entering public schools, a phenomenon Pack said began in the 1960s. 
“Every school I went to is closed, so it’s not a new thing,” Pack said. 
But the Hope Scholarship’s impact on this phenomenon is hard to tell, because the Treasurer’s Office doesn’t keep track of it. 
Pack oversees the Hope Scholarship program, which offers families $5,400 per student in tax payer money for families to send them to private school or teach them at home. Last week, the West Virginia Department of Education announced a 3.5% decline in student enrollment, which some county superintendents attributed in part to the Hope Scholarship. 
Pack said when the Treasurer’s Office accepts applications for the Hope Scholarship, it does not ask whether the student is transferring out of public school. 
“We’re not supposed to ask that question,” he said. “I  think we can probably put it on there as optional and see if anybody will answer it.” 
Pack said he wants to work with local school officials to get better data. 
On Monday, Pack’s office released the latest report on the Hope Scholarship’s performance for the 2025-26 school year, which showed nearly 15,000 students participated. He said based on those numbers, he estimates a couple thousand students may have transferred out of public schools. 
Pack said the number of private school students have remained steady in the state over the last five years, as had homeschooling. He said the Hope Scholarship is only a funding source for parents and not seeing growth in either indicates it’s not the driver of declining enrollment. 
Public school advocates who have placed emphasis on Hope’s hand in declining enrollments are looking for something to blame, Pack said. 
“When you’re struggling, you point out other things that you think might be exacerbating the problem,” Pack said. “So I don’t take it personal. I think they’re struggling, so they’re just pointing here, pointing there, trying to figure out how to get out of this mess.” 
“When you weigh $160 million for Hope Scholarship is what we think for this current year versus the $2.4 billion we spend on public schools, we’re spending a lot of money on public schools. So I don’t think Hope has a big impact on them, but it does have a teeny bit,” Pack added. 
Just because Pack is a supporter of the Hope Scholarship doesn’t mean he’s anti-public school, he said. 
“If you’re an elected official in public service in West Virginia, I think it’s mandatory that you’re pro public school,” he said. 
Pack said with the Hope Scholarship being pretty well established in the state, he wants to see lawmakers and state officials turn their attention to working on the financial issues befalling the public school system. 
“The program is working with respect to Hope Scholarship, and what I think is happening now is now we need to focus and turn (to) what is it we can do to improve our public schools?” Pack said. “I think you’re going to see that be the major thrust of the next couple years of discussions.”

name: Delaware
title: Fightin’ Blue Hens earn first road win in over a year behind 28-point first half
text:
Fightin’ Blue Hen quarterback, Nick Minicucci, warming up before UD’s game against Missouri State on October 20. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
The University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens (4-4, 2-2 CUSA) defeated the Western Kentucky Hilltoppers (3-5, 2-2 CUSA), 35-21, on October 27, ending their seven game road losing streak.
 
The University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens and Western Kentucky Hilltoppers combined for 631 yards of total offense and 49 total points in the first half of their game, Tuesday night. The offensive totals would suggest the half’s most impactful plays were orchestrated by the offensive players, yet the most significant play came from Delaware defensive lineman Trace Scott III. 
Hilltopper quarterback Brock Glenn dropped back to pass from the UD 32 yard line, following a Blue Hen touchdown that tied the game a possession earlier. Glenn surveyed the field on second and eight, looking to his right for a receiver to come open. Glenn never saw Scott coming from the left side. Scott sacked the redshirt junior for a loss of eight yards and followed that with another sack on the next play, forcing the Hilltoppers into the first punt of the game with just under three minutes remaining in the first half. 
Scott’s defensive play broke a back and forth offensive flow and helped the Blue Hens defeat the Hilltoppers, 35-21, in Bowling Green, Kentucky. It’s Delaware’s first win in Bowling Green since 1981.
The Blue Hen offense took over from their own ten yard line after the Scott defensive effort and embarked on the half’s final scoring drive.
Minicucci started the drive with a 12-yard completion to receiver Donovan Lewis and followed that with a pair of completions to running back Kaderris Roberts that put Minicucci atop the Delaware record book. Minicucci completed 18 straight passes to begin the game breaking UD’s former single game high of 16 set by former quarterback Zach Marker in 2023. 
Minicucci’s first incompletion came on the next play on a throw to Lewis, but the senior signal caller didn’t let the incompletion bother him. He followed his only incompletion of the first half with two deep passes to junior receiver Sean Wilson totaling a combined 59 yards. The final play of the drive was a Minicucci shovel pass to running back Jo Silver who ran it eight-yards into the endzone for the go-ahead score. 
“I was seeing everything very clear,” Minicucci said in a postgame interview with CBS Sports Network following the game. “I watched a ton of film, so I knew exactly what they were running and I mean we just executed. Shout out to the o-line, to all the boys for just doing their jobs because that’s what we preach everyday. Do your job.” 

OMG Sean 
: CBSSN pic.twitter.com/iQN2oxgbsh
— Delaware Football (@Delaware_FB) October 28, 2026

Minicucci finished the first half with 301 passing yards, three touchdown passes, and a completion percentage over 95 percent. Wilson led the Blue Hens in receiving at the half with six catches for 113 yards and one of the Blue Hens’ three receiving touchdowns in the frame. Roberts hauled in the first touchdown on UD’s first offensive possession and Silver grabbed the go-ahead score that put UD ahead, 28-21, at halftime. Fellow backfield member Viron Ellison Jr. scored Delaware’s only rushing touchdown on a five-yard rush that tied the score with a little over seven minutes remaining in the second quarter.
The offensive fireworks gave way to the defenses in the second half. 
The Western Kentucky defense stopped Delaware on its opening drive of the third quarter forcing the Blue Hens to punt for the first time in six quarters. The Blue Hen defense forced the Hilltopper offense off the field after three plays and WKU’s defense did the same to the Blue Hens on their ensuing possession. 
The Hilltoppers drove into Blue Hen territory, but were held out of the red zone and attempted a 42-yard field goal which was no good. 
The Blue Hen offense took over at their own 24 yard line after the missed field goal and moved the ball to the Western Kentucky 40 yard line in five plays. On the sixth play of the drive, Minicucci threw a deep pass down the right numbers to Wilson who was a step ahead of the Hilltopper defender. Wilson secured the catch and his momentum took him into the endzone for a 40-yard score. 
Those were the only points scored in the second half. 
The Hilltoppers had chances to cut into the Delaware lead, but failed to overcome the Blue Hen defense.
WKU drove into the red zone for the first time since the first half after Glenn completed a 29-yard pass to freshman receiver Jonathan Stafford Jr. to end the third quarter. On the first play of the fourth quarter, defensive end Brandon Gorham pressured Glenn forcing him out of the pocket. Gorham continued to pressure as Glenn ran toward the sideline and in an attempt to make a play for his team Glenn threw the ball toward his receiver. Sophomore safety AJ Graham saw the throw, jumped the pass and caught the first interception of his collegiate career, ending the Hilltopper threat.

 AJ GRAHAM FIRST CAREER INTERCEPTION 
: CBSSN pic.twitter.com/zfNWerBh27
— Delaware Football (@Delaware_FB) October 28, 2026

Delaware’s defense finished the second half allowing 187 yards of total offense and one conversion on third down rebounding from a first half in which they allowed 290 yards of total offense. 
The Blue Hens also recorded three sacks for the first time since losing to Virginia on September 26. Scott set a career-high with his pair in the second quarter and fifth-year defensive lineman Dominick Brogna did the same with his sack. It’s the first time this season Delaware earned three sacks against a conference opponent.
The offense finished the game with 495 yards of total offense, 414 of which came from the right arm of Nick Minicucci. Minicucci’s 414 passing yards moved him into fourth place on Delaware’s career passing yards list and his four passing touchdowns put him only four away from becoming UD’s all-time career passing touchdowns leader. Wilson paced the receiver room with his nine catches, totaling 183 yards and two touchdowns. Silver led the Blue Hens with 49 rushing yards.
“Everyone on our team is just, we’re just fully bought in,” Minicucci said in the CBS Sports Network interview. “You love your culture and the people who lead and the people who talk and it’s just it’s an honor to play for this team and to play for coach Carty and to do it with my best friends, with my brothers. It’s the best feeling in the world.”  
Delaware’s win breaks a seven game road losing streak that lasted over a calendar year — the Blue Hens last road win was against FIU on September 20, 2025 — and increases their conference record to 2-2. 
The Blue Hens have four more Conference USA (CUSA) games remaining on their schedule and sit a game and a half behind Liberty and Jacksonville State in the CUSA standings. Delaware’s next two conference opponents — Kennesaw State and FIU — have a combined conference record of 1-5, meaning UD could pick-up a pair of crucial conference victories before facing New Mexico State (3-4 overall, 2-1 CUSA) and Jacksonville State (5-2 overall, 3-0 CUSA) to end their season. 
UD’s game against Kennesaw State will be a road matchup on Saturday, November 7, at 3:00 p.m.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee toll lane contractor promises to pay state nearly $148 billion
text:
The transportation group that was selected to build a Tennessee toll road project has upped the amount it will pay the state to build the project. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The road construction group building Tennessee’s toll lanes along the I-24 southeast corridor is upping the ante, promising to pay the state nearly $148 billion over 50 years to lock in the deal, six times more than initially guaranteed.
The Tennessee Department of Transportation and DriveTN, a consortium led by Spain-based Ferrovial, announced Tuesday they reached an agreement on the amount the six-company group will pay the state over a half-century to secure the project, dramatically more than nearly $25 billion offered in August when the state approved the bid. The group will take on the $9.2 billion construction job, building toll lanes roughly 30 miles from downtown Nashville to Murfreesboro and along I-440 and I-40 East in Nashville.
The state’s Transportation Modernization Board awarded the project to DriveTN based largely on its promise to concede $24.8 billion in payments to the state over the eight-year construction phase. The consortium would try to recoup its expenses by charging motorists to use the toll lanes in the congested sector of highways over the next half-century.
Under the new financial structure, Tennessee is expected to receive $7.7 billion in payments between a financial closing date slated for the third quarter of 2027 and the completion of construction in 2035, followed by payments totaling more than $140 billion over the 50-year operating period, according to a Department of Transportation release.
The new financial structure comes two weeks after a road-building group that lost out on the project challenged the award. The group called 24 Choice Lanes Partners says in its filing in Davidson County Chancery Court that the Department of Transportation gave its competitor an edge by allowing it to change the terms of a record-setting payout after the bidding took place. 
The group says in its filing that DriveTN was able to make adjustments after the bidding because it could see the proposals of three other consortiums, two of which promised to pay the state about $7 billion in “concessions” to land the deal.
An international bank downgraded Ferrovial’s stock shortly after the bid, citing “higher risks” associated with a promised payment to the state that dwarfed competitors’ efforts to win the job.
Switzerland-based UBS lowered the company’s stock to “neutral” from “buy” in a new analysis, mainly because the company guaranteed the state nearly $25 billion in payments or “concessions” over the eight-year construction timeline. That figure is much lower than the new total announced Tuesday over the life of the 50-year contract.
A Department of Transportation spokesperson did not answer Lookout questions by Wednesday deadline.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: On WV’s Affordable Care Act marketplace, Peak Health enters, Caresource exits
text:
West Virginians who get their healthcare coverage through healthcare.gov will have the option of plans from Peak Health and Highmark Blue Cross Blue Shield for 2027.  (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)A new health insurance company will join West Virginia’s health insurance marketplace for 2027, as another company exits.
The marketplace — a provision of the Affordable Care Act, commonly called Obamacare — is an option for people who want to buy health insurance but don’t have an employer-sponsored plan. Open enrollment for 2027 coverage begins Nov. 1 and continues through Jan. 15.
Peak Health — owned by WVU Medicine, Marshall Health and Valley Health — is joining West Virginia’s marketplace. Caresource will exit. Highmark Blue Cross Blue Shield will continue to offer plans on West Virginia’s marketplace. 
Peak President Amos Ross told West Virginia Watch the company, which formed in 2021, didn’t initially plan to join the marketplace for 2027. They agreed to join “on a very accelerated timeline” when the state of West Virginia asked them in May and asked if they would join in light of Caresource leaving. 
“Having a single carrier in a market is not good from a choice or price standpoint,” he said. “So we had to dig pretty deep to figure out the plan to get into the market by Nov. 1. But happy to say that we are ready here.”
Vicki McDonald, a spokeswoman for Caresource, said the company’s decision to leave the marketplace was driven by rising healthcare costs and an evolving national landscape. 
“CareSource continuously evaluates its programs to ensure they are effective and sustainable, allowing us to deliver the greatest impact on our members’ health and well-being,” she wrote in an email.
Highmark Blue Cross Blue Shield has been a part of West Virginia’s ACA marketplace since its inception. Ellen Galardy, Highmark’s president of federal business, said the company’s priority in the ACA marketplace this year is stability. 
“We know that with CareSource’s exit from the market, a lot of people are going to have questions about their insurance and what’s covered and what doctors are in network,” she said. “And I think the most important message for most West Virginians who have their ACA coverage through Highmark is to expect very little change. I hope that reassures people that while we always encourage people to make sure the plan still works for them. The message is really about stability.”
Caresource customers encouraged to shop around for coverage 
Caresource plans will be effective through the end of the year. People who let their plans automatically renew will be enrolled in plans either Peak Health or Highmark, depending on their location and other factors. 
Jeremy Smith, program director for First Choice Services, which runs West Virginia’s ACA navigator program, said auto-enrolling isn’t the best option. 
“We encourage people strongly to actively re-enroll themselves,” he said. “So go back into their healthcare.gov account, update their application with their new income, and then actively look at the new plans and prices. We strongly encourage anyone and everyone that’s on the marketplace to do that.”
Plan rates will be announced in the coming days.
Highmark Blue Cross Blue Shield has requested an on-average rate increase of 18%. Most of West Virginia’s enrollees get subsidies, which will increase to match the rate increases, said Louise Norris, a health policy analyst with healthinsurance.org.
“For the ones who don’t, unfortunately, premiums are climbing even higher for 2027,” Norris said. “But for the ones who do get a subsidy, the amount of that subsidy will really depend on what those final rates end up looking like in each area.”
Galardy said the approved rate ended up being slightly different than what the company asked for. She said she expects the two companies’ rates to end up being similar.
“What we’re seeing is kind of Highmark and Peak’s rates are really pretty close,” she said. “So it would say that all of us are really kind of ending up in that same space.”
She added that Highmark is glad that the marketplace will have competition with the addition of Peak Health. 
“I don’t think what any community wants is to have fewer choices,” she said.  “So while Highmark feels strongly that we’re offering good products, and I would argue probably the best network access around, I am personally happy to hear that West Virginians will have options, and I think it keeps everyone on their toes.”
Norris said people should pay attention to the premium changes — which could be significant depending on what kinds of prices Peak Health offers. 
Last year, enrollment on ACA plans dropped by about 10,000 compared to the year before after enhanced subsidies for plans expired at the end of 2025, making the plans unaffordable for some. 
“Overall affordability for people who get a subsidy should stay roughly similar in 2027 to what it has been this year, but that’s still significantly less affordable than it was in 2025,” Norris said. “So some folks who were able to make it work in early 2026, might not be able to continue that all the way into 2027.” 
Ross said Peak Health’s goal is to have the lowest prices on the marketplace. The company will offer coverage in 45 West Virginia counties. Ross said they plan to expand in later years. 
Out of pocket limits will also increase next year, Norris said. This year’s plans have an out-of-pocket limit of $10,600 per person. Next year the limit increases to $12,000 per person. 
People who receive subsidies on the health insurance exchange are required to update their income. Those whose income estimates were lower than their actual income may have to pay back excess subsidies.
Local help available for those signing up
People who enroll in plans by Dec. 15 will start their coverage Jan. 1. Those who sign up after that will have coverage starting Feb. 1. 
Smith also warned people to be careful not to enroll with a scam site. The correct website to enroll is healthcare.gov. If it’s not a .gov website, people are probably in the wrong place, he said. 
“There’s been a lot of people that get phone calls and they end up enrolling in stuff that’s not even real insurance, and then they don’t know it till it’s too late,” Smith said. “So be really careful who you trust and who you’re talking to.”
For help enrolling, Smith recommends using a local insurance agent or a local assistor. First Choice is the state’s navigator program for ACA plans. 
People can call First Choice at 304-356-5834 to set up an appointment with a navigator, Smith said. The agency’s website, https://wvnavigator.com, also has information about enrolling.
“We still have some availability in November,” he said. “People can call if they need help.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Initiative process, voter turnout focal points in Arkansas secretary of state’s race
text:
Republican state Sen. Kim Hammer, Democrat Kelly Grappe and Libertarian Michael Pakko are running for Arkansas secretary of state (Courtesy of the Arkansas secretary of state's office)Republican state Sen. Kim Hammer touts his work on changes to Arkansas’ initiative process as he’s running to be Arkansas’ next secretary of state, saying they’ve made elections more secure. 
But Democrat Kelly Grappe and Libertarian Michael Pakko say those changes have harmed direct democracy by making it harder for citizens to get proposals on the ballot.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Hammer’s work on laws restricting the initiative process, including ones that were blocked by a federal judge, has become a focal point of the race to be the state’s top election official. They hope to replace outgoing Secretary of State Cole Jester, a Republican who is running against Libertarian Christopher Olson for the position of land commissioner.
Hammer, Grappe and Pakko are running as President Donald Trump’s efforts to exert more control over state elections has prompted concern from voting experts. The three say they don’t believe the federal government needs to run Arkansas’ elections, and are vowing to work to address the state’s low voter turnout rate.
 
Direct democracy
Hammer, who has served in the state Legislature since 2011, has sponsored several laws restricting the initiative process that have been the subject of legal challenges. A federal judge has blocked several of the laws and ruled them unconstitutional, including ones requiring all canvassers to be Arkansas residents and paid canvassers working on a statewide initiative petition or referendum to be residents living in the state. That ruling has been appealed to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. 
Candidate for Arkansas Secretary of State Sen. Kim Hammer (R) answers questions at the debate aginst opponents Kelly Grappe (D), and Michael Pakko (L) on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
His rivals have criticized the restrictions and said they agreed with the ruling against them. 
“I think that whole raft of legislation that Sen. Hammer sponsored represented a direct assault on direct democracy in Arkansas, an assault on the principle of Regnat Populus,” Pakko said, referencing the state’s motto, which is Latin for “the people rule.”
Grappe said the focus should instead be on helping the public understand the initiative process and expanding training for ballot question committees and volunteers working on ballot measure campaigns.
Republican’s push for initiative restrictions criticized in Arkansas secretary of state debate

“I don’t think that we need to protect ourselves from the people of Arkansas,” Grappe said. “I think we need to make sure that the people of Arkansas have good processes to use their constitutional rights.”
Hammer defended the laws, saying they’re appropriate safeguards that ensure that out-of-state groups aren’t able to take advantage of the process. 
“I think it’s time that they start explaining their position for why they want a weak process that’s been made evident by the flaws in the previous attempts to put initiatives on the ballot,” Hammer said.  
 
Elections, voter turnout
All three candidates said they’d resist an expanded federal role in administering Arkansas’ elections. Trump earlier this year said Republicans should nationalize elections, and the GOP has been pushing for more voting restrictions at the federal level.
Hammer said he doesn’t believe federal involvement in Arkansas is warranted, saying the state already has secure elections. He said he’ll partner with the federal government but won’t surrender constitutional rights.
“Because Arkansas is the leader of the pack among the 50 states, I think that we’re in a much better position than other states,” Hammer said.
Pakko said any effort by the federal government to run Arkansas’ elections would go against the U.S. Constitution, which gives states and localities the authority for conducting them.
Issue Spotlight: What candidates running for Arkansas secretary of state say about paper ballots 

“I think that any movement by the federal government to take a greater role in election processes is vast overreach,” he said.
Grappe said she thinks the secretary of state should push back on any federal efforts to take over the election.
“I will do what I’m required faithfully by the law, but as far as the federalization or nationalization of our elections, that won’t happen on my watch because I think somebody’s got to hold the line on that,” Grappe said. “And I think it’s the secretary of state’s job to do that.”
Arkansas has one of the lowest voter turnout rates in the country, with 53.5% of registered voters casting a ballot in the 2024 presidential election. That’s below the national average that year of about 64%.
Grappe said the state needs to build the public’s trust in the voting process and expand education about the election process.
“We are failing at educating the public on how things work,” she said.
Third party candidate for Arkansas Secretary of State Michael Pakko (L) answers questions during the debate at Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Opponents include Sen. Kim Hammer (R), and Kelly Grappe (D). (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
Statewide outreach would be a priority, Hammer said, saying he’d work with businesses, schools, colleges and civic groups on increasing voter involvement throughout the year and not just near Election Day.
“I think we’ve got to do a better job of utilizing the secretary of state’s office to be out in the state promoting the right to get out to vote,” Hammer said.
Pakko, who chairs the state Libertarian Party, said increasing voter turnout should also involve removing barriers to the political process that’s led to a high number of uncontested races. He said he’d advocate for changes that include ranked-choice voting, establishing a nonpartisan redistricting commission and moving primaries closer to Election Day.
“I have a whole set of reforms that I would like to see adopted that would bring more competition into the election process,” he said.
Red, white and blue banners adorn the front of the Arkansas Capitol in Little Rock in honor of the Fourth of July holiday on Thursday, July 2, 2026 (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)
 
Capitol grounds
Creating more parking for employees and visitors at the state Capitol is also a priority, Hammer said. He said in the short term there are “underutilized” parking spots behind the Capitol that could be opened to the public but said a longer-term solution is needed.
“I don’t know how we can get around additional parking at this time without involving a discussion about a parking deck and where that would go,” he said. Hammer said he’d like such a deck tied to the Capitol building.
Arkansas Explained: Capitol grounds crowded with monuments and some controversy

Pakko agreed more parking is needed at the Capitol. 
“I think however we would go about it, whether it’s a parking garage or expanding some of the areas for public parking around the vicinity, it should be more convenient for Arkansas citizens to visit their legislators to see how government works firsthand,” Pakko said.
Grappe said she’d like to address parking and accessibility at the Capitol, but also said she’d like to use the Capitol to host facilitated civic-dialogue sessions on divisive issues. She cited Braver Angels, a national organization focused on depolarizing politics, as a model for such sessions.
“I think it would be really great if we could bring in people who disagree on big issues, important issues, and we have facilitated dialogue so that we can talk to each other about those difficult issues,” she said.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Ahead of Election Day, control of Daviess County Public Library stays at forefront of politics
text:
The Daviess County Public Library has become the center of a political maelstrom. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Rainesford Stauffer)OWENSBORO, Ky. – On Oct. 1, incumbent Daviess County Judge-Executive Charlie Castlen was at the Rooster Booster forum when he brought up “the major unspoken issue of this campaign.” That issue was the fairness ordinance, which was aimed at protecting  LGBTQ+ individuals but was rejected in 2020 by the fiscal court.
But then Castlen brought up the second, more timely topic: “Our library: I’ve worked to get a more conservative board that has relocated books to the adult section that, if they were made into a movie, would be an X-rated movie.”
In 2024, challenges to books in Kentucky public libraries jumped by 1,061%. The majority of those challenges took place in Daviess County, where the Daviess County Public Library has withstood a firestorm. In 2025, extensive reporting by WKU Public Radio stated that the library was enduring a campaign from “local Christian conservatives and Christian Nationalists” that challenged titles primarily in the children and teen/juveniles section. Since then, 1,087 books have been reviewed, 574 books have been moved, a “limited Teen Pass card” was created, and policies have been revised by board appointees. 
While challenges to books are ongoing, some say that what’s gotten less attention in the lead-up to election day on Nov. 3 is local elected officials’ outsized role in reshaping the library board, including coordination to ensure the board is conservative and aligned with conservative, Christian religious ideology.
“We have an instance where one very small group of people have effectively wormed their way into a position of influence with our county government all over a handful of library books,” said David Norris, who was formerly on the Coalition for an Inclusive Daviess County’s steering committee. 
While politicians like Castlen are proud of reshaping the library system in a more conservative direction, many in the community have pushed back, arguing that the library is not a political institution. 
“I feel strongly that a public library belongs to the public, not a political party,” said Jimmy Lydanne, who said he’s an independent voter and worked as an educator for more than 35 years. 
As a Daviess County resident, he believes this is an important issue heading into elections. It goes beyond disagreements over books, he said, and raises questions about who gets to decide what information the public can access. 
“Our community includes taxpayers with diverse backgrounds, religions, and political beliefs. No single group should have the authority to impose its personal values on everyone else,” he added.

 The background on book bans
According to Dr. Maria McCauley, president of the American Library Association, the organization tracked 5,668 books banned from libraries, and 920 books restricted due to relocation or parental permission requirements, in 2025. McCauley told the Kentucky Lantern that it is the highest percentage of challenged books resulting in censorship since the ALA began tracking in 1990.
A stack of books that have been banned or challenged. (Photo illustration by Sarah Ladd)
92% of those book challenges were initiated by pressure groups, elected officials, boards, or other decision makers. The ALA report noted less than 3% of challenges were from parents themselves.

“Libraries serve everyone in our communities,” said McCauley. When libraries become politicized, “some individuals want to withhold rights and resources to other people because of their own views,” McCauley added.
“I think it’s a question about our democracy,” McCauley continued. “Our democracy protects First Amendment rights of all people in the United States, and our libraries really try to work very hard to honor that, and to provide a wide range of collections and materials and great learning experiences for the entire community.”
King Simpson, director of the Kentucky Public Library Association believes that, overall, Kentucky libraries have been able to have conversations with their communities about the importance of the First Amendment. “There’s no one-size-fits-all library for Kentucky,” he told the Kentucky Lantern, explaining the importance of libraries bringing in the different interests of their communities. 
“While we totally understand people’s concerns about materials that might be in the library, we also exist to serve everyone in the community,” said Simpson. “So, really encouraging folks to make the right decision for them and their family, but not in a way that affects the entire community.”
Beyond the books and to the board
While the Daviess County Public Library has made headlines for several years, one group’s emphasis on what content individuals should be allowed to access predates challenging books. In 2023, Citizens for Decency, a local Christian conservative group, protested drag shows for audience members ages 21 or over at Owensboro’s RiverPark Center. 
Not long after, the group turned its attention to the Daviess County Public Library, protesting Pride Month activities and calling for audits of materials the group found objectionable. In keeping with reports from the American Library Association about challenges to books, the challenges, or calls for relocation, involve material related to race, history, gender, sexuality, and reproductive health. 
According the organization’s recent social media posts, Citizens for Decency isn’t only focused on “sexually explicit titles,” but is now also challenging books involving suicidal ideation, alcohol and drug use, or diversity, equity, and inclusion.

As a library board is appointed, not elected, it’s a nonpartisan board, and libraries themselves are nonpartisan organizations. Crucially, according to the Daviess County Public Library bylaws, the board has power to employ the library director, determine policies to govern library operations, and oversee and evaluate library programs, leading to larger questions about what could happen to the library’s offerings if controlled by one group, or one belief system.
In 2022, lawmakers passed a Senate Bill 167, which let county judge-executives oversee library board appointments, a shift from the state-vetted finalists selected by the library board. Then came Senate Bill 40 in 2026, sponsored by Republican state Senator Gary Boswell, which further refined the alternative appointment process.

According to Simpson of the Kentucky Public Library Association, only about twenty counties adopted the initial alternative appointment process, which they had to opt into. 
In Owensboro, the legislation had a near-immediate effect. Library board meetings grew increasinging “contentious,” as WKU Public Radio described it.  In early 2024, members of the Coalition for an Inclusive Daviess County, a group that has organized to defend the library, filed an open records request. They discovered that the founder of Citizens for Decency, Jerry Chapman, and Judge-Executive Charlie Castlen were exchanging “hundreds of text messages,” according to Norris. (Norris is on the Daviess County Democratic Party’s Executive Committee. He spoke to the Lantern in his personal capacity, not on behalf of the party.)
“The striking thing to me overall was just the level of access,” Norris told the Kentucky Lantern. “You know how many people who have other issues in this county wish they had the ear of their local government like this group did?”

The messages and emails range from discussions of religion to plans around the library, according to records shared with the Kentucky Lantern by Coalition members.

“Gentleman, I know we have an election three days away, but we also have another year from now that will go a long way toward taking our city back,” wrote Citizens for Decency founder Chapman to Judge-Executive Charlie Castlen, former Daviess County Republican chairman Darin Tapp, and state representative for District 13 D.J. Johnson on Nov. 4, 2023. 

On December 22, 2023, Chapman forwarded a message to Castlen mentioning the first meeting of the “Candidate Development Committee,” which was attended by Johnson and Boswell. “Topics of discussion were potential candidates for City Commission, goals of this committee, candidate training and resources and strategy,” he wrote. 

When reached for comment, Castlen told the Kentucky Lantern that he does not have recollection of that communication from Chapman, and noted the above messages were not sent by Castlen himself. In response to him exchanging messages and emails with Chapman regarding the library and library board, Castlen stated that he’s exchanged commentary with “quite a few people” about library board appointments in his time as Judge-Executive, and does not view Chapman’s communications any differently than he does others.
Inside the Daviess County Library, where politicians are influencing the library board and where some books are located. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Rainesford Stauffer)
Chapman declined to answer questions or participate in an interview, reiterated his position as founder and chairman of Citizens for Decency, and said his personal political activities are not those of the organization.
Citizens for Decency’s website currently promotes BookLens, their own website that scans books through a “biblical lens.” The site is similar to BookLooks, a defunct website that was tied to right-wing group Moms for Liberty, according to USA TODAY. Citizens for Decency is listed as a sponsor of Moms for Liberty’s 2026 summit. As reported by BookRiot, BookLens depends on artificial intelligence; the bottom of the BookLens website reads “Content breakdowns powered by ChatGPT.” 
Some sources told the Kentucky Lantern that it’s not a matter of Democrats versus Republicans, but rather points to a bigger issue of coordinated influence serving specific ideologies. 
In late September 2026, the library board did not submit former Republican Judge-Executive Al Mattingly’s name for reappointment. According to the Messenger-Inquirer, it was the first time in a decade a sitting board member in good standing hadn’t been nominated for another term. 
Notably, Mattingly took different positions than Castlen’s other appointments, including pastor Tim Kline, who received support from Citizens for Decency. WKU Public Radio quoted sources as saying his appointment was a “tipping point,” officially giving the board a conservative majority.
Mattingly also voted in favor of the fairness ordinance in 2020—the same one Castlen plugged that he voted against in the October 2026 forum.
“The public has no control over the library anymore; it’s controlled by a very small minority of people in this community,” Mattingly told the Messenger-Inquirer in September.

 Library on the minds of voters ahead of election day
It’s that level of control that has concerned some, including voters like Lydanne. Initially, he wasn’t listening to  “some of the noise” surrounding the library. Eventually, he felt he needed to pay attention, as someone who said he devoted his life’s work to the development of healthy, confident children.
He said that parental rights are important, but noted they don’t extend to everyone else’s children. 
“I think it’s pretty damn obvious that that’s exactly what’s happening,” he said. “We’ve got a political group based on a particular religious belief that’s leveraging power in regards to what’s available to the children and the families.”
Castlen is not the only politician up for reelection who has been involved in coordination on the library. In a forum for candidates for the 8th District Senate seat, hosted by the Daviess County Farm Bureau, incumbent Republican state Senator Gary Boswell also referenced the library. “I support efforts to keep library sections free of sexually explicit materials for children’s sections,” he said. 
Back in 2005, Boswell entered a legal dispute with the library  over property tax rates. As reported by WKU Public Radio, David Boswell, brother of Gary Boswell, is a director of Citizens for Decency. The organization’s 2026 annual report still lists him as a director.
Sen. Gary Boswell, R-Owensboro, presents a bill on the Kentucky Senate floor. (LRC Information Photo)
In October 2025, Boswell emailed the attorney general’s office with a personal complaint about his granddaughter being required to take a “DEI course,” stating that he wanted “the professor fired or worse.”  The conflicts of interest surrounding control of the library are on the minds of some voters ahead of election day. Boswell did not respond to a request for comment.
Before election day, Lyddane said he looks to a candidate’s past actions, and thinks it’s important to recognize what government is for.
“It’s important that they make all the people in the community feel safe and valued,” he said. “Any time that we’re marginalizing a certain group or individuals or whoever it may be, I think that just weakens our community and it weakens our country.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Kentucky’s status as a bellwether depends entirely on Fayette County
text:
Election Day at the Landsdowne Elementary School  precinct in Lexington, Kentucky, on Nov. 5, 2024. Photo by Arden BarnesA week before Election Day, several pundits and prognosticators have predicted that Kentucky’s 6th District congressional race could be a kind of national bellwether for a potential blue wave throughout the country. 
Why? A flip from a 12-year GOP hold on the Central Kentucky district in a very red state would herald just how dissatisfied voters have become with the Republican Party controlled by President Trump. Then there’s Kentucky’s early closing polls – 6 p.m. Eastern Time, a zone the 6th District is fully inside. Kentucky is usually one of the first states reporting on election night with a possible signs of things to come.
There’s one small catch to these predictions. The 6th District race will hinge on its largest county, Fayette, and in the primary, Fayette’s results were not reported to the Secretary of State until well after 9 p.m. 
You can’t be a bellwether at 9 p.m. on election night.
But never fear, says Fayette County Clerk Susan Lamb. Things will be different this time around.
In the primary, two or three precincts out of 127 had trouble uploading the results to the V Drive, which then had to be driven and delivered by hand to the county clerk’s office downtown. Lamb decided to wait for all the results to be in before uploading them to the state.
This Election Day, she said, her office will count all the absentee ballots and in person absentee results right after the polls close at 6 p.m., then upload them to the state.
Then they will wait for the precincts to deliver the rest of the votes. If there are lulls in the action, “we are going to continue scanning and upload the results as they come in,” she said.
Also in May, there were a large number of first-time poll workers and quite a few workers who didn’t show up. 
“What happened in the primary were circumstances we didn’t expect,” Lamb said. “But now we know we have an alternative way of handling this.”
Other populous counties upload results as they come in, so folks watching can have a sense of which way the votes are going. Which everyone appreciates. Anything can go wrong, and the 6th District results are also depending on 15 other counties.
So whether the 6th District makes Kentucky a bellwether or not, here’s hoping it’s a smooth evening for everyone.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: Affordability won’t improve until Colorado communities measure what matters
text:
An aerial view of Steamboat Springs, Colorado. (Getty Images)A ski patroller. A teacher. A cook. A fourth-generation rancher. These are our neighbors, our friends, our coworkers in the Yampa Valley. They are also the people who power our community.
But increasingly, these neighbors, the lifeblood of our community, are being forced to leave, largely because of rising housing and childcare costs. More than half of renters in Steamboat Springs spend more than 30% of their income on housing, and the average family is spending 25% of their income on childcare.
It’s no coincidence that 25-45-year-olds are leaving Steamboat Springs in dramatic fashion. That loss makes it harder for local employers to recruit and retain workers and puts the character of our town at risk.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
This problem is not unique to Steamboat. Communities across Colorado and the country are facing similar affordability pressures. Local governments, nonprofits, employers, funders and community groups are spending time and resources, forming partnerships, and launching programs meant to address the crisis.
But too often, we measure effort rather than whether people’s outcomes are improving. We count meetings, initiatives, dollars spent and housing units proposed without a solid way of assessing whether working people can actually afford to remain, and thrive, in the communities they serve.
That’s why Steamboat For All is taking a different approach.
Rather than starting with the question, “What should we do?” we’ve started with a more fundamental one: “What are the outcomes we want to see?”
At Steamboat for All, the outcome we want to see is an increase in the 25-45 year old population in the city of Steamboat Springs. Then, we asked, “What metrics point to that outcome?” and we identified reducing the percent of income that households pay for housing costs to 30% and childcare to below 14%.
The next step is to measure progress transparently, through community conversations and dashboards. We now have two community dashboards specific to housing in Steamboat Springs and child care in greater Routt County. The goal is a shared public picture of where we currently stand, where we want to go, whether things are getting better or worse, and a tool for helping everyone in our town make better decisions together.
Transparency matters because it creates a common set of baseline facts. If housing costs continue to push workers out, the community should be able to see that. If a new investment improves childcare access or helps more families stay, we should be able to see that, too. And if an approach isn’t working, we should have the ability to change course.
This work must be grounded not only in data but also in people’s lived experiences. That is one reason we created “Dear Steamboat,” an immersive exhibit shining a light on how affordability impacts our everyday lives. Through written and recorded stories and art from the people who live and work here, the exhibit makes visible the choices that affordability pressures force on our friends, coworkers and neighbors: whether to leave town, delay starting a family, take on another job, or give up a profession they love. With an overwhelming response to the exhibit, we have decided to re-open the exhibit in a more permanent location in downtown Steamboat in mid-November.
Steamboat’s affordability challenge did not emerge overnight, and it will not be solved by any one initiative. Talking with community members who vary in stages of life, ability to thrive in the valley and the desire to maintain Steamboat’s unique character provides a blueprint for ideas and policies that can shape our future. If Steamboat continues to lose workers and families, it won’t just threaten our local economy. We’ll also lose the character of the town — the sense of community that makes us so proud to call Steamboat home.
We have a choice: We can continue to react to each new affordability challenge in isolation, judging success by good intentions and disconnected activity. Or we can come together as a community to define clear outcomes, measure progress transparently and hold ourselves accountable for whether the people who power our community can live and thrive here.
That is the kind of town we believe in: a community where prosperity is not measured only by visitor numbers, property values, or new investment, but by whether the people who teach our children, patrol our slopes, prepare our meals and steward our land can build a life here, too.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Wittman’s defense industry ties draw scrutiny as he seeks Armed Services gavel
text:
U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Westmoreland, is seeking reelection to Virginia’s 1st Congressional District and hopes to chair the House Armed Services Committee. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman has received tens of thousands of dollars in campaign contributions from defense contractors and reported stock holdings in companies with military ties, as he seeks another term representing Virginia in Congress and to become chairman of the powerful House Armed Services Committee. 
The Westmoreland Republican, who has supported U.S. military operations in Iran, says his national security decisions are not influenced by campaign donations or personal investments. 
In an email to The Mercury, campaign director Will Dieterich said Wittman’s investments are managed independently and that the nine-term incumbent has never directed individual stock trades or used nonpublic information to make financial decisions. 
“House ethics rules prohibit linking political contributions to official actions,” Dieterich said. “Congressman Wittman is subject to those requirements, including restrictions governing the use of official congressional resources for political activity.”
Dieterich said Wittman has also told his financial adviser that he would like to begin moving his portfolio away from individual stocks and into exchange-traded funds, or ETFs. 
The issue has become part of Wittman’s reelection fight against Democrat Shannon Taylor in Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, where early voting is underway ahead of the Nov. 3 election. 
Long considered a Republican stronghold, the district has attracted increased Democratic attention since Gov. Abigail Spanberger carried it by 2.6 percentage points last year. 
Taylor has criticized Wittman’s stockholdings and defense industry contributions, accusing him of benefitting from the Iran war while Virginians struggle with higher costs. 
Wittman’s campaign disputes that accusation. Contributions are publicly disclosed and legal, Dieterich said, and the congressman’s national security decisions “are not made based on personal financial interests.”
Neither the campaign donations nor the disclosed investments establish wrongdoing or show that donors influenced Wittman’s votes. The financial disclosures also do not show whether his holdings gained value because of the Iran war. 
 Defense money and committee oversight

Wittman currently serves as vice chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, which oversees defense policy and military operations. He hopes to lead the panel if Republicans retain control of the House and he wins reelection. 
His campaign has received contributions from political action committees affiliated with defense contractors, including Lockheed Martin, RTX and Science Applications International Corp. Each PAC contributed $10,000 during the current election cycle, according to a compilation of Federal Election Commission data. 
A separate listing of third-quarter contributions identifies $27,500 to Wittman’s campaign, $36,000 to his leadership PAC, America’s First PAC, and $4,000 to the Wittman Victory Committee from PACs associated with defense-related companies. 
Those committees serve different purposes. The FEC identifies the Wittman Victory Committee as a joint fundraising committee involving Wittman’s campaign, his leadership PAC, the Republican Party of Virginia and the National Republican Congressional Committee. Not all money raised through it necessarily goes to Wittman’s campaign. 
Wittman’s campaign did not provide a breakdown of every entry when asked. 
Dieterich said Wittman’s responsibilities on Armed Services are to “the American people, our servicemembers, and our national security.”
“His legislative, oversight, and policy decisions are based on those responsibilities, not the political contributions received by his campaign,” Dieterich said.
Alex Keena, an associate professor of political science at Virginia Commonwealth University, said members of Congress commonly receive contributions from industries affected by their committee work. Wittman also represents a state with a significant defense industry, he noted. 
The concern, Keena said, is whether lawmakers put those interests ahead of the public. 
“The danger comes when a member of Congress disregards the public interest in favor of well connected, powerful interests,” he said. “This is particularly problematic if a member of Congress personally benefits from doing so.”
 Stock holdings and the Iran war

Wittman’s latest financial disclosure, filed in August and covering 2025, lists investments in Texas Instruments, Broadcom, Accenture, ITT and Trane Technologies. Each holding was valued between $1,001 and $15,000. 
All five companies have some defense-related business, although their operations extend to other industries. 
The filing does not establish the value of Wittman’s holdings during the Iran war or whether he still owns those stocks. His campaign did not answer that question. 
Dieterich said outside finance professionals make investment decisions without consulting Wittman, who has “never personally selected, purchased, sold, or directed the timing of an individual stock trade.”
He also noted that Wittman voted for the federal STOCK Act of 2012, which affirmed that members of Congress are subject to insider trading prohibitions and strengthened financial disclosure requirements. 
Keena said Wittman’s pursuit of the Armed Services Committee chairmanship could bring greater scrutiny to his investments and fundraising. Owning shares affected by defense policy can raise questions about potential conflicts, he said, even without evidence of a legal violation.
Wittman has supported President Donald Trump’s military operations in Iran and opposed congressional efforts to limit the president’s authority to continue the conflict. 
In September, he voted against a House resolution directing the withdrawal of U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran unless Congress authorized them. The measure passed the House, but the Senate later rejected a separate war powers resolution. 
During a July radio interview, Wittman said “some good things” could come from the conflict as Middle Eastern countries looked for alternative energy shipping routes and the United States pursued new energy agreements. 
He cautioned that those developments would take time to affect fuel prices. 
Dieterich said Wittman’s position on Iran is guided by his responsibility to protect Americans, support service members and confront threats to the United States and its allies. 
 A competitive race

Taylor, currently Henrico County commonwealth’s attorney, said Virginians are paying more for gas, diesel and groceries while Wittman accepts defense industry contributions and holds investments in companies with military ties. 
“I’ve got a different plan: I don’t take a dime of corporate PAC money, I’ll ban congressional stock trading, and I’ll vote to end this war,” Taylor said in an email.  
In a recent interview with the Associated Press, Wittman accused Taylor of misrepresenting his financial disclosures, which report assets in ranges and do not provide a precise measure of his net worth. He called her “a liar.” 
Wittman also emphasized that much of the growth in his reported assets came from inheritances he and his wife received after their parents died. 
Additionally, Wittman has defended higher defense spending. He told The Mercury in September that modernizing the armed forces is necessary to deter adversaries. 
His campaign said that, if he becomes chairman, his priorities would include Pentagon oversight, competition among defense contractors and scrutiny of excessive pricing. 
The 1st District has drawn national attention as Democrats try to win control of the House. Some election analysts have since classified the race as a tossup. 
Keena said campaign finance disclosures allow voters to examine who is supporting a candidate, even if those records alone cannot establish why a lawmaker takes a particular position. 
“Voters will have to decide for themselves whether to award him another term based on this information,” he said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia proposes shifting construction funds to tackle $1.7 Billion highway maintenance gap
text:
A view of Route 28 in Chantilly, Virginia, with vehicles traveling along the roadway. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)As Virginia stares down a $1.7 billion highway-maintenance gap, the Commonwealth Transportation Board is considering a plan to close it by shifting funds away from construction and transportation projects.
The plan introduced at the board’s Oct. 13 meeting proposes adding $239 million annually for pavement repairs starting in fiscal year 2028, while redirecting funds and using $300 million in GARVEE bonds to soften construction cuts. 
Virginia law requires the state to prioritize maintaining its transportation assets, including bridges and pavement, which have increased over the past 20 years. Rising highway repair costs and budget decisions that prioritized construction over maintenance last year created the deficit.
Smart Scale funding, a grant program for transportation projects, would decrease by about 25% under the proposed plan. Since the program was established in 2016, it has awarded $7.6 million to transportation projects across the commonwealth.
Laura Dent, councilmember for the city of Harrisonburg, said the program has awarded the city funding for multiple projects. However, she is concerned about the impact the shortfall could have across the commonwealth, especially those responsible for methods of transportation other than relying on vehicles.
“We rely on Smart Scale for local transportation safety, not just highways. We need sidewalks and public transit and other things that make urban living more safer and more sustainable,” Dent said.
The uncertainty for transportation projects and the Smart Scale program were points of heavy consideration during the board’s discussion, as the group considers another idea: to move about $705 million from the state’s priority projects to alternate funding sources, or have six of them compete in the seventh round of Smart Scale, which is currently in the screening and scoring process.
A chart showing how redirecting $705 million from 15 priority projects to alternative sources, including corridor funds, CMAQ, and regional programs, would preserve resources for other transportation priorities while maintaining project delivery through alternative funding strategies. (Photo courtesy of the Virginia Department of Transportation)
The six projects recommended for resubmission to Smart Scale Round 7 include: the Route 288 Southbound Hard Shoulder Running Lane ($67 million) in Goochland County; the Route 17 (Lee Highway) Corridor Safety project ($20.4 million) in Warrenton; the Route 294 (Prince William Parkway) Corridor project ($21.4million) in Prince William County; E. Parham Road Improvements from I-95 to ClevelandStreet ($10.4 million) in Henrico County; the Port of Virginia Interchange/CommerceRoad Streetscape project ($16.1million) in Richmond; and the Meadowville Bridge/Intersection project ($24.3 million) in Chesterfield County.
In November 2025, the previous board allocated approximately $715 million from GARVEE bonds and the Priority Transportation Fund (PTF) to a list of projects. About $10 million has already been spent, leaving roughly $705 million available.
The Office of the Secretary of Transportation recommends using more restricted funding sources for projects totaling approximately $555 million. The administration said this would preserve more flexible funding for other transportation needs.
Members, including Board Member J. Randall Minchew, raised concerns about how reallocating funds could affect other projects and whether adding projects to Round 7 would be fair. 
“I wonder if these six projects were to be injected into that process, that I wonder if that’s unfair to the other applicants who are having their projects reviewed,” Minchew said. “It’s almost like someone being injected into the NCAA basketball tournament in round three.” 
Secretary of Transportation Nick Donohue said all projects would compete on merit, with no scoring preference, and existing projects would not need to be rescored. 
He explained that the priority projects were considered fully funded when Smart Scale applications opened in March, making them ineligible for evaluation. If the board redirects funding to address maintenance needs, he believes the projects should have an opportunity to compete for funding through SmartScale Round 7.
“They’re not jumping to the Sweet 16,” Donohue said. “What we’re doing is we’re expanding the field of 68 to include another six. They will get no preferential treatment other than, effectively, they get to skip the application process.”
The board presentation lasted about an hour, detailing construction cost increases, maintenance funding and forecasts and strategies.
Construction and maintenance costs have doubled in the past 10 years, according to the National Highway Construction Cost Index (NHCCI).
According to NHCCI component contribution data, asphalt accounted for 33% of the overall increase in highway construction costs over that decade. Higher gravel and aggregate costs stemmed from increased fuel and hauling expenses, rising labor costs and quarry blasting expenses.
A chart shows the current CTF budget projects declining investment in pavement maintenance and Interstate pavement conditions, with performance potentially falling to 71% sufficient and approximately 1,200 lane miles lost by 2031. (Photo courtesy of the Virginia Department of Transportation)
The board also discussed a proposed policy requiring explanations for significant changes in pavement and bridge maintenance spending, including reductions of more than 5%. Funding changes could result from completed projects, maintenance decisions, or changes in federal funding. 
The policy would also require a data-based reassessment of road and bridge conditions every four years, forecasting pavement needs over 20 years and bridge needs over 50 years.
The board will take a final vote on the plan on Dec. 9.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: If Virginians approve reproductive rights amendment, a hearing is set for Nov. 13 to challenge it
text:
Abortion rights signs seen during a Democratic Election Night Party in Richmond in 2023. (Photo by Parker Michels Boyce for the Virginia Mercury)If Virginians approve a ballot referendum on Nov. 3 to permanently protect reproductive rights in the state’s constitution, the amendment will be challenged in court on Nov. 13.
The case seeks a preliminary injunction to block the certification of the amendment referendum results by alleging that the process was not properly filed and that ballot language was misleading. 
Founding Freedoms Law Center launched the legal challenge in April, but it has been stalled since June, when advocacy group Virginians For Reproductive Freedom successfully petitioned to join as a co-defendant.
An argument of the case is whether Virginia’s retroactive repeal of old state code concerning constitutional amendment processes can hold. 
The old code would have required House of Delegates Clerk Paul Nardo to have sent copies of the amendment text to all of Virginia’s circuit court clerks to post outside their courthouses. 
The repeal, which kicked in this July after the amendments had already gone through other advancing steps, removed that part of the process. 
A similar case brought forth by Liberty Counsel was dismissed over the summer in a different court, but the group is seeking an appeal. At the time of the dismissal, Senior Assistant Attorney General Erin McNeil emphasized that state lawmakers have authority to adjust the constitution and prescribe how they do it. 
“How can the General Assembly have this authority to prescribe a process but not have the authority to change that process?” McNeil said in court. 
The argument, however, also surfaced as part of a successful effort to strike down a redistricting referendum voters had approved this past spring. That case, like the Founding Freedoms case, was advanced in Tazewell by Judge Jack Hurley. 
“Not only would this proposed abortion amendment be a disaster for policy reasons, but it would undermine trust in our democratic processes because of the flawed and deceptive means by which it will have passed. We cannot allow that to happen,” Founding Freedoms lawyer Josh Hetzler said in a statement. 
Constitutional: The amendment that could permanently protect reproductive rights in Virginia

The organization is also representing a Prince William County pastor in a newly-filed challenge to a ballot referendum to protect same-sex marriages in Virginia, on the same procedural grounds as the reproductive rights amendment challenge.
A 2015 U.S. Supreme Court case protects gay marriage nationwide, but Justice Clarence Thomas suggested revising it and contraception access after the court overturned federal abortion protections. It’s part of why state lawmakers sent the reproductive rights and marriage amendments to voters. 
Plaintiff in that case, Rev. Ben Purves, also co-signed a joint letter with 400 pastors from around the state opposing both constitutional amendments. 
Founding Freedoms Law Center doesn’t intend to challenge the third constitutional amendment, which advanced at the same time and in the same fashion as the two challenged ones.
Ballot Question Three asks voters if voting rights should automatically be restored for people with felony convictions who have completed their prison sentences. 
“We’re not personally concerned about the restoration-of-rights amendment,” Hetzler said in a phone call over the summer. “We don’t have a position on that.”
