name: Maryland Matters
title: Democratic leaders throw support behind Henson in contentious state Senate race
authors: William J. Ford, Danielle J. Brown
text:
Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel) gives remarks at a recent reception at Metropolitan Kitchen and Lounge in Annapolis. Anne Arundel County Executive Steuart Pittman (D), right, and Spencer Jones, a Democrat seeking a county council seat, listen. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel), appointed to fill the District 30 Senate seat in early 2025, is looking to make history this fall by becoming the first Black senator elected to represent Anne Arundel County. And state Democrats are spending heavily to make sure that happens.
In campaign reports filed Friday, the Maryland Democratic Senate Caucus Committee reported $488,399.10 of in-kind contributions to Henson’s campaign in just the past two months.
It’s the latest turn in what was already one of the most-heated legislative races in the general election, with charges of ethics violations and racism and a vocal split by Democrats dismayed by Henson’s more moderate stance on social issues like abortion and LGBTQ+ rights.
The fighting has also boosted the odds on Republican nominee Jessica Haire in a Senate district the Democrats have held for at least 44 years. Haire, a former Anne Arundel County Council member, said she supports abortion access as a matter of “personal freedom.”
But Haire is more focused on what she called Henson’s record of missed votes as a delegate, and on a 2024 letter from the Joint Committee on Legislative Ethics — it urged Henson to apologize to the public and to legislative leaders for her involvement as a delegate in funding requests for a religious organization to which she belonged.
“I think everybody should be talking about Sen. Henson’s ethics,” Haire said in a recent interview. “There are going to be differences in opinion, but it doesn’t change the fact that we have to have honesty. We don’t have that right now from the sitting senator.”
Henson remains focused on the potentially historic nature of her campaign.
Jessica Haire (right), at a political fundraiser in 2022, launched Opportunity Maryland, a free market organization, alongside ex-Hogan aide Kyle Gilbert. (Photo by Josh Kurtz/Maryland Matters)
“We’re doing something that’s never been done before,” she said in an interview during a recent reception hosted by County Executive Steuart Pittman (D) at Metropolitan Kitchen and Lounge in Annapolis. “Anytime you do something that’s never been done before, you better believe you’re going to work hard for it.”
And Henson isn’t taking any chances. She’s running hard: In addition to the caucus funding, she touts support from U.S. Rep. Sara Elfreth (D-3rd), colleagues from the Legislative Black Caucus of Maryland and Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City). Gov. Wes Moore (D), who donated $6,000 to her campaign, was billed as a special guest at an Oct. 20 reception for Henson in Annapolis.
“When I see the support for this campaign, I see a ton of investors. If this was a portfolio, it would be the most diversified portfolio that an investment [has] ever had,” Henson, an attorney, said. “We’ve had an outpouring of support from all across the state fighting for this district and fighting for this seat, and I couldn’t be more grateful.”
Overall, Henson’s campaign reports raising $316,510.19 and spending $267,510.41, in addition to the in-kind contributions from the Senate caucus fund. Haire reported raising $252,453.95 and spending $288,292.96. Her campaign also received $58,437.84 of in-kind contributions from the Senate Republican Caucus Committee over the past two months.
District 30 includes Annapolis as well as the South County communities of Edgewater and Shady Side, which are more conservative.
Henson was serving on the Annapolis City Council in 2019 when she was appointed to fill the seat of the late House Speaker Michael Busch (D), who represented District 30A. She was elected to the House of Delegates seat in 2022 before being appointed to the Senate last year, filling the seat left behind when Elfreth was elected to Congress.
The Senate appointment came after the Anne Arundel County Democratic Central Committee recommended Henson over fellow Del. Dana Jones (D-Anne Arundel) on a 10-9 vote, leaving some political fallout in its wake.
During her time in both chambers, Henson has been an advocate for renters’ rights, including a 2026 law that limits landlords’ ability to consider criminal background when evaluating a prospective tenant, and a 2025 law bolstering protections for tenants against mold. She sides with most Democratic policy measures, including recent legislation to protect Maryland’s undocumented immigrants against federal immigration agents.
But some Democrats have grown skeptical of Henson’s voting record on issues important to the party, such as abortion access and LGBTQ+ initiatives, and say they’re ready for new leadership.
In 2022, Henson voted against the Abortion Care Access Act, which increased Maryland Medicaid coverage for abortion procedures, and was one of a handful of Democrats to vote to uphold Gov. Larry Hogan’s (R) veto of the legislation.
Legislative ethics panel admonishes Henson for conflict of interest, misuse of official title

In 2023, she did not vote on the Trans Health Equity Act, which expanded Medicaid coverage so that low-income transgender Marylanders could receive gender-affirming care, including voice training, hormone therapy, puberty blockers, and several cosmetic and surgical alterations for the face and body. Henson also didn’t vote on a bill in 2024, also while still in the House, to expand protections to providers of gender-affirming care.
It’s why some abortion activists have thrown their support behind Haire, the Republican nominee whose support of abortion access has earned her an endorsement by Reproductive Justice Maryland Action.
“I believe in personal freedom and personal responsibility … across all aspects of life. I don’t see how you can come at this issue from any other way,” Haire said. “These are deeply personal issues and should be dealt with individually, and on that front, the government should largely stay out of it.”
Sharon Blugis, founder and deputy director of Reproductive Justice Maryland, says the upcoming election could be the “last chance” to get Henson out of the Senate seat.
“Henson is not a good partner at the moment, you can’t trust her when she says she’s going to vote or not vote for something,” she said.
But even Blugis admits that some Democrats who are not happy with Henson’s legislative votes may find it hard to cross party lines for Haire.
“This isn’t perfect,” Blugis said. “I tell those people: ‘You can leave it blank or vote for Jessica.’”
‘It’s a clear choice’
Johntel Greene, who runs a consulting firm, said she will vote for Henson,  downplaying criticism of Henson’s voting record in the House. The bills in question were overwhelmingly passed by the Democratic majority in the legislature, Greene noted, so Henson’s vote did not affect the outcome of the bills.
“A lot of them were actually walk-offs, so it’s not a record of voting against, and that’s part of her deliberation with faith,” Greene said of Henson.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Henson has voted in support of some legislation for the LBGTQ+ community and health care protections for women, especially Black women, such as creation of statewide LGBTQ+ commission and enshrining reproductive rights in the state constitution, which voters approved in the November 2024 election.
Greene noted that when Haire ran for Anne Arundel County executive in 2022 against current County Executive Steuart Pittman (D), Democrats accused her of being associated with Rory McShane, a Republican consultant whose firm was associated with the neo-fascist and racist group The Proud Boys. Haire said at that time she ended her association with group when she found out about the group’s extremist connection.
Haire, an attorney, is married to former chairman of the Republican Party of Maryland Dirk Haire, also an attorney.
“To me, it’s a clear choice,” Greene said. “Do you want Annapolis represented by someone who’d be willing to take more rights away, or do you want somebody who’s willing to fight for communities? She [Henson] is somebody who actually goes into communities. She brings a different voice to Annapolis and a needed voice to the Senate.”
Imperfect candidates
Still hanging over the race are the findings of a legislative ethics panel released in April 2024, about two days after the General Assembly adjourned for that year. The report said Henson engaged in what it called an “ongoing practice” to hide her personal and professional relationship with an Odenton-based religious group seeking more than $1 million in state bond money.
The investigation, which began a year earlier, said Henson’s actions created “at minimum, the appearance of a conflict of interest,” and it admonished her for an improper use of her official title in an advertisement for her law firm. The letter asked Henson to publicly apologize to the public, the speaker of the House and other legislative leaders, and it recommended that she be barred from serving on the House Appropriations Committee, which handle capital grant requests.
Sen. Shaneka Henson (D-Anne Arundel) gives remarks at the Oct. 14 unveiling of a Malcolm X Monument near the Michael E. Busch Annapolis Library. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Henson declined to comment on Blugis and others criticizing her work. But she did say the Senate could have a different look come January.
If elected to a full term, Henson would be one of just three Black women in the 47-member Senate. Sen. Mary Washington (D-Baltimore City and Baltimore County) is running unopposed as is Del. Tiffany Alston (D-Prince George’s), the Democratic nominee to replace Sen. Joanne C. Benson, who did not seek reelection after more than three decades in the legislature.
“When I say that to people, they don’t believe that there could only be three Black women in the Senate of Maryland because Maryland is such a progressive state,” Henson said.
“But any time you are doing something that’s never been done before, you are breaking new ground,” she said. “I understand that. I feel that. I see that. I sense that, and I take on that challenge.”
Although the District 30 Senate election is one of the most bitterly fought in the state, analysts say Henson could hang on in a year when Democratic enthusiasm is much higher than that of Republicans.
The district has been competitive in the past but is turning bluer. Former Vice President Kamala Harris (D) won 58% of the vote there during the 2024 presidential election, but the district also voted for former Gov. Larry Hogan (R) during his two campaigns, and has elected both Republicans and Democrats to its legislative delegation over the years.
“The tough thing for Republicans this cycle is it is a midterm election with a very unpopular incumbent president, who is even more unpopular in Maryland,” said St. Mary’s College political science professor Todd Eberly in a recent interview. “When that happens, it tends to drive turnout among the party that’s out of power nationwide, regardless of the fact that Democrats dominate Maryland.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Commentary: Supporting the freedom to marry for all in Virginia is a bipartisan Issue
text:
Blake McDonald (left) and Chad Stewart pose with their daughter, Flora, during the launch of the Virginians for Marriage Equality campaign near the Bell Tower in Richmond’s Capitol Square on Monday, the start of LGBTQ Pride Month. The campaign supports a constitutional amendment referendum that would permanently protect same-sex marriage in Virginia’s constitution. (Photo by Markus Schmidt/Virginia Mercury)As Republicans, we believe in personal freedom, individual responsibility and a government that treats all people – and all families – fairly under the law. And now, as Virginians head to the polls, we all have an opportunity, regardless of our political party, to put those values into practice and affirm the freedom to marry for same-sex couples.
One of the constitutional amendments on our ballot in 2026 is an amendment to repeal our state’s long-outdated but still-on-the-books ban on marriage between same-sex couples. A “Yes” vote on Question 2 would remove that 20-year-old restriction and replace it with a guarantee of the freedom to marry between two people, regardless of sex, gender, or race.
Constitutional: The amendment that could safeguard same-sex marriage in Virginia

Functionally, it would bring our Constitution in line with the current law of the land, and would do so in a way that reflects shared bipartisan values across Virginia.
Tens of thousands of same-sex couples have built their lives here in Virginia, creating homes, raising children, and contributing to their communities. Nearly two-thirds of those couples are married – bringing not only the joys of professing love and commitment, but also the legal protections and financial stability that marriage provides. 
These families shouldn’t have to live with the uncertainty brought on by an outdated policy in our Constitution – or the worry that, should the U.S. Supreme Court ever revisit the landmark 2015 court ruling striking down marriage bans, the legal safety of their families could be called into question. 
Individual liberty, limited government and the importance of family are central to the conservative tradition – and we are grateful to see the many ways that Republicans and conservatives have voiced their support for marriage between same-sex couples.
Recently, George Allen, our former Virginia governor and U.S. senator, publicly shared how his views on marriage changed, stating in an interview, “the prohibition on gay marriage, I am going to vote for that…many years ago I changed my view on it and I don’t see any harm to me if two people of the same sex get married.”  
We have seen that evolution in our own lives, too. In 2019, Denver officiated the wedding of two men, friends who had volunteered for his congressional campaign. It was a straightforward expression of a belief that people who love each other and want to make a lifelong commitment should be able to do so. 
Barbara has also spoken publicly about the benefits of marriage equality, including stronger families, better access to health care, and greater well-being. Those outcomes reflect values that cross party lines. 
The prominent Virginian, the late Ted Olson, who served as an attorney to President Ronald Reagan as well as in his administration as the assistant attorney general for the Office of Legal Counsel and then as solicitor general in the Bush administration, argued the conservative case for marriage equality in a 2009 interview with the Los Angeles Times.
“It is a conservative value to respect the relationship that people seek to have with one another, a stable, committed relationship that provides a backbone for our community, for our economy,” Olson said. 
Other conservatives who have not been expressly or full-throatedly supportive of marriage between same-sex couples also understand that it’s well past time to move on from this issue, which has been settled here in Virginia for more than a decade. 
Many Republicans have made it clear that whether or not they agreed with same-sex couples marrying in the past, the reality is that legal marriage for same-sex couples hasn’t hurt anyone – and, in fact, has provided critical stability for so many families. Why disrupt something that’s working?
Youngkin signs marriage equality measure, takes tougher line against gun control

We saw that in 2024, when Republican Gov. Glenn Youngkin signed legislation repealing a state statute that banned marriage between same-sex couples. It was an important step forward, and we were grateful to see that discriminatory statute repealed. 
In just a few weeks, Virginia has the chance to complete this journey on the freedom to marry and close one of the final loose ends when it comes to marriage equality. When we cast our votes on Question 2, we’ll be thinking about the many ways that Virginians have come to rely on the freedom to marry.
It’s up to all of us, Republican and Democrat, liberal and conservative, to come together, vote yes on Question 2, and ensure Virginia can be a place where all families can build their lives with confidence and security. 
These families experience the same joys, hopes, and challenges as every other family. You could join us in ensuring that Virginia’s constitution will provide their families the same protections as yours and ours.

title: Virginia Beach wastewater facility to turn biogas into power for thousands of homes
text:
A rendering of the biogas collection facility that will be built on alongside a Hampton Roads Sanitation District wastewater treatment plant. (Photo courtesy Morgan Chase/Virginia Natural Gas)Once a new renewable natural gas facility is completed in Virginia Beach, the flush of a toilet could help power homes across the Hampton Roads region, developers say. 
Hampton Roads Sanitation District has partnered with Virginia Natural Gas, who provides power for about 315,000 homes in the area, to build technology that captures the gas that emanates off of wastewater when it is treated.
Currently, biogas is created during normal wastewater treatment operations called anaerobic digestion, when organisms break biosolids down without oxygen. Once the gas is produced, a flare is used to burn off the methane, CO2 and other gases. 
With the new system, instead of burning the gases, machinery will purify the gas, which can then be funneled into VNG pipelines and used for energy generation. A 200-foot interconnection pipe will be built from the HRSD facility property to existing VNG lines.
“There’s an environmental benefit to this in that we are pretty much eliminating that flared gas,” Carl Garofalo with Southern Company Gas said Monday.
The facility that will operate on HRSD’s existing treatment facility in Virginia Beach will create enough gas to power 5,000 homes annually. The project is estimated to cost $30 million, which will be paid by VNG customers.
“This project demonstrates how collaboration can transform a byproduct of wastewater treatment into a renewable energy resource that benefits our environment, strengthens our region’s energy future and advances our commitment to sustainability,” Jay Bernas, general manager and CEO of HRSD, said in a statement.
The company anticipates filing for approval of the cost recovery for the project with the State Corporation Commission in the next four months. The project is expected to increase the average residential customers’ bills by about $0.36 a month.
The project will eventually save customers money, Garofalo said, because it will eventually allow them to purchase less gas.
“We’re monetizing the environmental attributes for the project, and using that to minimize rate impact,” Garofalo said. “We do forecast, in the out years of the project, that we will actually provide a benefit to the customers in the form of possible bill credits.”
This is not the first facility of its kind in the commonwealth. In 2022, Western Virginia Water Authority and Roanoke Gas Company partnered to build a smaller-scale renewable natural gas facility at the Roanoke Regional Water Pollution Control Plant. The plant became fully operational in 2023 and is able to provide enough gas power for 500 homes in the region.
Biogas from wastewater treatment could be harnessed for other power uses, as well.  
Garofalo explained that landfills produce five times as much gas as treatment facilities like the forthcoming one inVirginia Beach, and could be a new avenue into reducing emissions and bringing more power to the grid.
“There’s a lot of organic waste, and this is a way to add a substantial amount of energy to the system while dealing with a problem for existing customers,” Garofalo said. 
Virginia lawmakers have recently examined what to do with the leftover products of wastewater treatment. 
Legislation passed during this year’sGeneral Assembly session put new regulations on the use of biosolids, the sewage sludge that is left after treatment, as fertilizer on agricultural land. 
Residents across the commonwealth have become increasingly concerned about the presence of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances or PFAS, otherwise known as forever chemicals that could pose health risks with exposure, in the biosolids. 
PFAS are in  everyday products like water resistant clothing, fast food packaging, and much more – and the substance ends up in human waste.
A new state law imposed new restrictions on how much PFAS can be present in  biosolids before their use on farmland is limited.

name: VTDigger
title: Build or tax? Vermont’s governor candidates emphasize different elements of housing policy.
text:
Republican Gov. Phil Scott, left, and Democratic/Progressive challenger Amanda Janoo have starkly different ideas about what’s driving the state’s housing problems – and how to fix them. Photos by Brian Stevenson and Joey Palumbo / Vermont Public
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger. 
The high cost of housing is squeezing Vermonters. One in five people have struggled to come up with rent or mortgage payments in the last year, according to recent Vermont Public polling. More than 4,800 people in the state experience homelessness, as of September. Citing the high cost of living, residents are losing faith that Vermont is a good place to build a life.
Both candidates vying for Vermont’s top job want to bring down housing costs and make the state a more affordable place to live. But Republican incumbent Gov. Phil Scott and Democratic/Progressive challenger Amanda Janoo have starkly different ideas about what’s driving the state’s housing problems — and how to fix them.
Scott, who worked in construction when he entered politics over two decades ago, sees the housing issue as one of supply and demand. Vermont’s housing shortage is at the root of many of the state’s woes, in Scott’s view, from declining enrollment in schools to stress on the healthcare system — and that deficit of homes is driving up prices.
“We need more housing, and there’s no governor who has done more for housing than me,” Scott said at Vermont Public’s gubernatorial debate.
Janoo, an economist and political newcomer, speaks less about Vermont’s housing shortage and more about the “financialization” of the state’s housing stock. In her view, more homes in the state are getting bought by “investors, second-home owners, and corporations,” pricing out everyday people. Taxing those kinds of properties at higher rates is a central plank of her campaign.
“For decades, we’ve treated housing as an investment rather than a home,” her campaign website reads.
Scott: Build, build, build
A common refrain of the five-term incumbent is that Vermont doesn’t need more taxes — it needs more taxpayers. Building up the state’s tax base by creating more housing is a key piece of Scott’s governing philosophy. 
He often cites housing initiatives created during his tenure as some of his proudest achievements in office. Those include the Vermont Housing Improvement Program, which doles out small-scale grants to rehab apartment buildings that have fallen into disrepair, and the Community and Housing Infrastructure Program, a financing tool that lets developers borrow money for roads, sidewalks and sewers against the future tax revenue of a housing project. 
Those programs lend government support to for-profit landlords and developers. In VHIP’s case, property owners must rent their units at below-market rates for five to 10 years in exchange for the money. That’s a shift from the dominant approach before Scott, which focused on awarding funds to nonprofits to construct “perpetually affordable” homes — units with requirements that they be rented or sold at subsidized rates forever.
To be sure, Scott has overseen hundreds of millions of dollars flowing toward perpetually affordable housing — most notably with COVID-era federal cash. But he often says that more funding alone cannot meet Vermont’s housing needs.
“That has certainly been a sort of key tenet, as I understand the governor’s philosophy — that we have to work both within the free market system and the government subsidized system to sort of meet the housing continuum,” said Josh Hanford, who worked for the Department of Housing and Community Development under former Govs. Jim Douglas and Peter Shumlin and served as Scott’s housing commissioner until late 2023. 
Scott’s focus on aiding the private sector also drives his push for “regulatory reform” — a catchall term for simplifying the thicket of local and state permits that new housing projects must navigate.

Houses in Websterville, in Barre Town, on Oct. 4, 2026. Daniel McCullum/Courtesy 

Ire over permitting has animated Scott since he was young. When building a motorcycle shop in Morristown in his early 20s, Scott learned that he needed an Act 250 development permit. The delay and cost ultimately scuttled his plans, his otherwise scant campaign website notes. 
In office, Scott has pushed lawmakers to cut back on regulations governing development, most recently focusing on rules guiding construction near wetlands. He regularly chides the Democrat-led Legislature for being too cautious about his deregulatory efforts to promote more building.
“I understand some worry that if we do too much, we could lose some of the character of our communities, some of that rural charm that makes Vermont special,” Scott told lawmakers during his 2026 budget address in January. “But if we want the next generation of Vermonters to afford to live here, we’ve got to treat housing like the crisis it is and make real change this session.”
Some lawmakers contend that Scott too often chooses the bully pulpit over sitting down to work through difficult policy issues. Kesha Ram Hinsdale, the Democratic Senate majority leader, said Scott’s administration could do more to streamline and expedite permitting within state government itself. 
“You have to make government work for people. You can’t just sort of slow its gears down and expect that 10 years later, more good things will be happening,” Ram Hinsdale said.
Janoo: Taxing second homes and big companies
In her platform, Janoo also says that Vermont needs to simplify permitting for housing — while still maintaining “strong environmental protections.” She contends that the state needs to invest more in permanently affordable housing.
Her signature policy centers on a dramatic restructuring of Vermont’s property tax system, one that rewards homes that “strengthen Vermont communities” and disincentivizes others. 
“Most of the people I know, my age, the only way they’ve been able to buy a house is if they had help from their family, and that’s just perpetuated these inequalities,” said Janoo, who rents an apartment in Burlington, during Vermont Public’s primary debate in July. “We really need to limit private equity and large corporate ownership of the housing stock. We need to increase taxation on second homes, luxury estates, Airbnbs, et cetera, to actually reduce the property tax burden for residential Vermonters.”
When asked for more details on her tax plan, Janoo has said that Vermont lacks the property-level information to determine exactly what new tax rates should be and how much revenue they would generate. 
Second home taxes have become a popular topic this campaign season, and Vermont Public polling shows most Vermonters support them. Over the course of her campaign, Janoo has refined her talking points on the subject, saying she supports higher taxes on “luxury second homes” and “commercial vacation rentals,” and does not want to raise rates on “modest family camps” or long-term rentals.
When it comes to large corporations and private equity firms buying up homes in the state, most data available suggests the practice is limited. 
State tax data indicates that there were about 7,400 “corporation owned” residential properties in the state in 2025, or about 3% of all residences, including seasonal homes and apartment buildings. That’s a broad category that includes properties owned by an LLC or a nonprofit or government entity.
The Department of Housing and Community Development is currently studying corporate buying practices in the state. In a preliminary analysis of more than 20,000 single family home and duplex property transfers between 2022 and 2025, Commissioner Alex Farrell said the state has seen little evidence of a mass buying spree. 
DHCD found just over 60 transactions in which a buyer had purchased five or more properties in a year, Farrell said. The company that had purchased the most homes is a remodeling outfit in Newport, Farrell said, that renovated homes and sold them back to individuals as primary residences.
“The behaviors that we’re concerned about on the national scale, where folks or entities, or you know, someone like a BlackRock is coming in and buying single family homes or duplexes, but then trying to squeeze the equity out of them and just turn them into rentals and add them to their portfolio, et cetera. … That’s clearly not happening here,” he said.
Vermont did see a spike in “investor” purchases of homes in 2021, mirroring a nationwide trend when interest rates were low, according to reporting by VTDigger.
Janoo says that Vermont should rein in private equity and large corporate ownership of the state’s homes before such companies consolidate them and drive up prices.
Vermont’s general election day is Nov. 3.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Build or tax? Vermont’s governor candidates emphasize different elements of housing policy..

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: GOP elected officials rush to support secretary of state nominee
text:
Republican candidate Max Engling smiles Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026, during a secretary of state debate against Democratic candidate Beau Bayh at Fox59/CBS4 studios in Indianapolis. Courtesy: Grace Smith/IndyStar pool photoHigh-ranking Republican politicians are pouring money into Max Engling’s secretary of state candidacy as the race comes down to the wire.
U.S. Sen. Todd Young’s leadership PAC sent $50,000 to Engling for a total of $105,000.
Attorney General Todd Rokita transferred $75,000 from his campaign committee for a total of $100,000.
U.S. Rep. Mark Messmer gave $50,000 and Gov. Mike Braun earlier sent at least $500,000 from related campaign accounts.
The state GOP has given $2.7 million in donations and in-kind support to Engling.
Others who have chipped in at least $5,000 include House Speaker Todd Huston, Sen. Chris Garten and U.S. Rep. Jefferson Shreve.
But U.S. Sen. Jim Banks — who hired Engling as a staffer and endorsed his candidacy in the GOP state convention — hasn’t written any direct checks to the Republican nominee.
Instead, he is described as busy working behind-the-scenes — making calls to large donors and connecting the Engling campaign to outside cash.
U.S. Sen. Jim Banks supports Max Engling in his race for secretary of state. (Photo from Engling LinkedIn)
“Senator Jim Banks has played a huge role in helping to rally national GOP donors to step up in a big way in the Secretary of State’s race and help Max Engling compete with the millions pouring into Indiana from Daddy Bayh’s donors and DC special interests,” Tim Edson, a Republican consultant who is working with outside groups engaged in the race, said in a text to the Capital Chronicle.
The biggest group to jump in is the Restoration of America PAC, which sunk $1 million into ads in the race, according to multiple sources. One in heavy rotation over the weekend calls Democrat nominee Beau Bayh a “nepo baby carpetbagger.”
The buy ended Monday and hasn’t yet been renewed.
The PAC is heavily funded by billionaire Republican donors Richard and Liz Uihlein of Illinois and has direct ties to Banks.
The ad notes Bayh’s attendance at a private prep school, his “liberal indoctrination” at Harvard University and being a senator’s son. It leaves out his Marine Corps service.
“It’s unfortunate that Max Engling has to resort to out-of-state billionaires to lie about me and lie about my family, but that’s not inconsistent with what he’s done throughout this entire campaign,” Bayh told the Capital Chronicle.
Banks has remained relatively quiet during the campaign, and he will not be part of the Indiana Republican Party’s statewide campaign tour from Oct. 28 to Nov. 2. The tour will focus on Engling’s race and the comptroller and treasurer contests. Special guests include Braun, Young, Rokita, U.S. Reps. Rudy Yakym, Jim Baird, Victoria Spartz, Shreve, Messmer, and Erin Houchin.
Banks did appear at the Hamilton County Republican Party Fall dinner Monday night alongside Engling.
And he posted his support on Oct. 1 – “Max is serious about doing the actual job. Beau is serious about using the SOS office to immediately run for Governor like his daddy did. (Greg) Ballard is serious about his anti-Trump and anti-GOP hatred. Vote for Max.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Déjà vu all over again in House District 39 as Democratic incumbent faces MAGA Republican
text:
Democratic Rep. Megan Cotter, left, is seeking reelection to her third term in the House District 39 race against Republican Hopkinton Town Councilor Jasmin Roy, right. (Photos courtesy of Megan Cotter and The League of RI Businesses)Editor’s note: This is the third in a three-part series on state legislative races, chosen based on competitiveness between candidates and relevant district issues. Of the 113 seats in the Rhode Island General Assembly, all of which are elected every two years, 24 seats feature at least two candidates on the Nov. 3 ballot.  
They are both moms in their 40s who want to lower energy bills and preserve western Rhode Island’s rural beauty.
The similarities between Democratic Rep. Megan Cotter and her Republican challenger Jasmin Roy end there.
Cotter, the two-term incumbent for House District 39, has a record of legislative accomplishments she can point to while canvassing the 100-square mile district, spanning Exeter, Richmond, and Hopkinton: adding more money to the green bond for forest and farmland preservation, spurring — and leading — a newly begun legislative panel to study how housing developments affect water supply in rural communities; and limiting self-checkouts at grocery stores to preserve jobs.


About House District 39
Represented by Rep. Megan Cotter since 2022
Geography: Richmond, Exeter and a small piece of Hopkinton
Population: 14,828 residents; 11,382 registered voters 
Partisan breakdown: 59% unaffiliated, 21% Republican; 20% Democrat
Demographics: median age: 41.1, 88.6% white; $127,552 median household income (2024)


Roy, a member of the Hopkinton Town Council, has focused her legislative campaign on denouncing various Democratic officials, including Cotter, for promoting “communism” and government overreach, including in education.
“I don’t coparent with the government,” Roy proclaimed in a June 1 episode of local conservative podcast Cumberland Unfiltered. 
A vocal Trump supporter who touts Second Amendment protections and parental rights in education, Roy’s views, as shared on her campaign website and social media, are likely to resonate with many of the voters in the district, which backed Trump in the last three presidential elections. Cotter’s predecessor, Republican Justin Price, attended the Jan. 6 rally outside the U.S. Capitol, though Price said he did not participate in the riots. 
Cotter narrowly lost to Price in her first run for office in 2020, before defeating him by 32 votes in 2022, and again in 2024.
And while Cotter responded immediately to requests for an interview for the story, and follow-up questions, Roy initially asked for questions sent via email. Rhode Island Current responded with a general overview about the topics to be covered, but Roy  then failed to return more than a dozen phone calls, emails and social media messages over a monthlong period.
“Some of our candidates, they don’t want to be pigeonholed by the media,” said Dave Levesque, founder of conservative business group The League of RI Businesses.
Roy is among a dozen candidates endorsed by The League in state legislative races, and has received more than $5,700 from the League through its unconventional multi-PAC fundraising strategy.
“We’ve had business owners specifically request their donations go to her,” Levesque said of Roy.
The vice-chair for the Washington County chapter of Moms for Liberty, Roy criticized state and local policies on education curriculum and cell phone bans. She has also pledged to reduce “smothering” state laws governing economic development, local zoning and property taxes, and to repeal legislation that infringes on gun rights, according to her campaign website. 
Cotter supported the housing package spearheaded by former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi, but said she thinks there is a “fine line” to reducing municipal red tape to development while taking local concerns into account.
Cotter was one of 28 state representatives — 18 of whom are Democrats — to vote against banning the sale of assault-style weapons in 2025. The bill was approved on the final night of the 2025 legislative session, signed into law by Gov. Dan McKee on June 26, 2025.
Cotter has not pledged specific action on future gun-related legislation, but said she will give careful review to any proposals that come to the floor.
Cotter, 42, of Exeter, who works as vice president of sales for Tony’s Seafood in Seekonk, Massachusetts, tries to focus on local issues rather than national politics: healthcare access, affordability concerns and the push and pull between development and preservation priorities. 
“I try to let the community guide me on what they feel is important,” she said.



Quotation







I try to let the community guide me on what they feel is important.


– Rep. Megan Cotter, an Exeter Democrat


A key example: the former A&P supermarket in Richmond, which has sat vacant since 1986. Stop & Shop took over the lease, but kept the shopping center site undeveloped to prevent competitors from opening a rival grocery store.
Not anymore. Advertising for a new tenant has begun, following a new law based on legislation co-sponsored by Cotter in the 2026 session that bans grocery stores from using restrictive covenants to prevent new markets from opening in former grocery store locations. 
Roy called Cotter’s involvement in grocery store legislation that limits the number of self-checkouts a “waste of legislative power” in an Oct. 2 Facebook post. Roy has also used her social media account to criticize Cotter’s work with lawmakers such as U.S. Rep. Seth Magaziner and advocates such as members of the reproductive freedom group, The WomXn project. 
Roy, who said in a podcast interview that she is now unemployed, backed fellow MAGA Republicans like gubernatorial candidate Elaine Pelino, who lost in the primary, and U.S. Senate challenger Ray McKay.
The two candidates have not debated, interacted, or even been in the same room since January, when the Chariho Regional School District held its annual omnibus meeting, Cotter said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Trump approval 37 points underwater in NJ, poll finds
text:
A new poll finds President Donald Trump deeply unpopular in New Jersey just weeks out from midterm elections seen as referendum on the president. (Photo by Tim Hawk/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]President Donald Trump’s approval rating dipped below 30% in New Jersey in advance of midterm elections broadly viewed as a referendum on his second term, a newly released Fairleigh Dickinson University Poll found.
Just 29% of likely voters told pollsters they approved of Trump’s handling of the presidency, while 66% said they disapproved.
“Trump isn’t running for reelection, but he has made himself the face of the Republican Party,” Dan Cassino, the poll’s director, said in a statement. “The fact that he’s this unpopular means that he’s dragging down Republican candidates in a way that a less visible president might not be.”
Trump’s approval showed signs of softening even among Republicans. Just 68% of self-identified conservatives said they approved of his job performance, while 27% disapproved.
The president’s most die-hard supporters, those who identify as MAGA, still overwhelmingly backed him. Nearly all who called themselves MAGA, 95%, said they approved of Trump’s performance in the job. Only 21% of moderates said the same, compared to 7% of liberals and 8% of progressives.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) got higher marks. Nearly half of likely voters, 48%, said they approved of the job she was doing, while 32% said they disapproved.
While her approvals are still well above water, they’ve also descended in the months since she took office. A Fairleigh Dickinson poll released in March found 58% approved of the job she was doing.
The drop doesn’t appear driven by rising disapproval, which has ticked up only two points since the March poll, but the number who are unsure or don’t know about her performance has more than doubled since then, rising from 8% to 20%.
The declines in Sherrill’s approval and the rise in voters’ uncertainty were marked across demographic groups, but the biggest declines came from women and Black and Hispanic voters.
“It’s not clear what Sherrill has done to cause voters who should be among her most loyal supporters to distance themselves,” Cassino said. “But whatever it is, this is a blinking yellow light for the administration.”
The Sherrill administration has faced some controversies early in her tenure, most notably the resignation of her lieutenant governor following allegations of ethics violations and sexual harassment.
Former Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell, who is Black, resigned last month, but it’s not clear that resignation or the allegations against him were driving the rise in uncertainty.
It could also stem from an increase in former unaffiliated and Republican voters now identifying as Democrats, Cassino said, but no explanation was certain.
“For whatever reason, Democrats are not as happy with the governor as they were when she took over,” Cassino said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: We’re drowning in sketchy information. Media literacy can keep you from going under.
text:
A Mirror Indy story revealed a disinformation scheme. An unknown sender sent a message to people in the Indianapolis area March 18, 2026, criticizing IPS leadership. The message included a video edited from snippets of a recent IPS board meeting.  (Jenna Watson/Mirror Indy)
Last year, Indianapolis parents were bombarded with text messages sharing a video that was critical of the superintendent. An unknown source had deceptively edited videos of public comments at school board meetings to criticize school leadership at a time when IPS was making its case for more funding at the state legislature.
That raised red flags for Mirror Indy K-12 education reporter Carley Lanich. She set out to hunt down the source of the text messages and debunk what appeared to be a disinformation campaign aimed at undermining the superintendent.
At the end of her reporting, Lanich was unable to expose who sent the deceptive messages. But she was able to knock down that bad information and provide accurate insight into public opinion.
“We wound up with a story that tried to provide context for what was seen in the video texted to Indy residents, but also show that we at least attempted to run down where this had come from and express that we still don’t quite know,” she said. “But we do know what is true and accurate about what people’s opinions are of the school district superintendent.”
Lanich has been a reporter for more than eight years, and she says Mirror Indy staff discuss debunking viral information much more often recently. The newsroom actively monitors misinformation and disinformation in the community and staff determines when they should step in to clarify and correct the public record.
(Courtesy banner)
“Media and information is around us everywhere we turn,” Lanich said. “If we want to be an informed democracy, we need to know where our information is coming from, what the source of that information is and if those sources are trusted.”
News media play a big role in bridging trust with the public and providing information for people to act on. But so does everyone else. There are a number of ways you can become a more savvy news consumer, including by learning to identify misleading information and manipulation online. Media Literacy Week, Oct. 26-30, focuses our attention on this problem. Keep reading for tools to help you discern the truth and find trustworthy sources of information.
In the wake of deception and misinformation, the role of the press is shifting 
Reporters today have the added responsibility of wading into the fray to set the record straight. 

Lanich’s work both competes in, and serves as a fact-check for, the vast and murky digital universe where anyone can say just about anything. 

“I feel like it has always been a part of our job to pay attention to social media, to pay attention to, in this case text messages, but to pay attention to what’s being communicated in our community,” Lanich said. “I think it’s always been important for us to use our news judgment about when to elevate rumors and when to step in and correct things, versus when to just let a rumor be a rumor.”

That news judgment drives reporters to be more transparent about their own journalistic process as they report their stories. Providing more transparency helps readers establish trust and view the news outlet as a credible source. 

Mirror Indy often explains at the top of its stories why it is investigating a topic. Reporters also post videos on social media explaining how many sources they interviewed or what developments prompted their story.
Media literacy is important for participating in a democracy
Just last week, Mirror Indy service reporter Sophie Young posted a public service announcement on Instagram debunking a viral Facebook post that misinformed Indy residents about voting in the upcoming midterm elections.

“A reader sent us this meme floating around on Facebook that says if a poll worker marks your ballot, it won’t count,” Young said. “That’s not true, and the Election Board shared a press release that explains poll workers have to initial your ballot.”

The Indy Public Editor is a grant-funded pilot project run by the Poynter Institute. This column is edited by Kelly McBride and copy edited by Lauren Klinger. The project is managed by Nicole Slaughter Graham with support from Amaris Castillo.

In addition to getting tips from readers, Mirror Indy’s reporters also actively watch the comment sections of the stories they post to social media for signs readers may be misinformed about a subject.
“If we see people that are commenting on stories, either with questions or maybe misinformation that could be based on good or bad intent — it could just be someone who doesn’t understand something — we have been encouraged as reporters to respond in the comments with what we know to be true from the reporting we’ve done on a story,” Lanich said.

By providing this extra insight, reporters add more context to stories and quash misinformation and disinformation before they spread throughout our community.
What you can do to become more media literate
Indianapolis residents have a number of tools at their disposal to aid media literacy. One is using primary sources to judge the credibility of information.

The city of Indianapolis and Marion County have numerous public records, including meeting transcripts and videos, that anyone can search to verify whether information is true. 

If you see questionable social media posts or other online content pertaining to government agencies, go straight to Channel 16’ssearchable archive of Indianapolis and Marion County government meetings that occurred within the last 60 days. It includes records from numerous public meetings such as the City-County Council, the election board, as well as the hospital, library, and airport boards. After 60 days, the content moves to a searchable historical database.

Next, see what Indianapolis media are saying about your question. Looking up different sources and comparing them is called lateral reading. It’s a media literacy skill that usually involves searching for keywords and pulling up different sources. Be wary of the first entries a search engine displays. Typically, these are ads—someone has paid to have their links appear before the real search results. AI-generated answers are also tricky. They may be true. But AI answers may be repeating the same questionable information that you saw somewhere else. As you scroll through search results, look for the Indy news media sources that you know are legitimate because they’ve served you good information in the past. 

To research photos or images, use Google Lens or go straight to Google’s reverse image search (Google it.). Copy the image link or paste a screengrab into Google Lens to learn where the image first appeared. 

Finally, if you have a question or concern, ask an Indy reporter. Contact details for reporters at all city newsrooms are usually posted in the website’s About section or staff directory. Mirror Indy has text lines for neighborhood and beat reporters to interact directly with the public. And, keep those social media comments coming on stories you’re curious about.

“That’s just one other small way that we’re trying to engage people and meet them where they’re at rather than just letting even a simple misunderstanding of something go unanswered,” said Lanich.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: NH congressional candidates agree on childcare issues, differ on solutions
text:
From left to right: Stefany Shaeheen, Anthony DiLorenzo, Rep. Maggie Goodlander, Lily Tang Williams, Rep. Chris Pappas and former Sen. John E. Sununu offered their thoughts on addressing childcare affordability and governance during an early education forum on Thursday. The election is Nov. 3. (Screenshots)Lowering costs is taking center stage ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections, and New Hampshire’s congressional candidates all discussed how childcare policy fits into their affordability policy at a forum last week. 
The candidate forum, hosted by Early Learning New Hampshire and Save the Children Action Network NH, gave Granite State’s congressional and gubernatorial candidates a chance to speak directly to childcare providers about childcare policy. All major party candidates for the Senate and 1st and 2nd Congressional District races responded live or via pre-recorded video to questions submitted ahead of the event. Over 90 childcare providers were in attendance. 
Childcare and early education are governed at the state level in New Hampshire. However, the state relies mostly on federal dollars for childcare initiatives like the childcare scholarship program, Head Start, quality improvement metrics and more. 
According to a September report from the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute, between 2020 and the end of the current state fiscal year in June 2027, reliance on federal dollars for funding the NH Child Care Scholarship Program will have increased by 62%, while state funding for the program has decreased by 19%.
Childcare receives bipartisan support in the New Hampshire Legislature due to its impact on working families and employers, while at the federal level, congressional Democrats tend to stand alone when pushing for more funding. But with affordability front of mind as people head to the polls, all major party candidates have taken a position in favor of childcare.
2nd Congressional District: Goodlander’s record versus Williams’ aspirations
In New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District, voters will experience repeat choices between Democratic incumbent U.S. Rep. Maggie Goodlander and Republican nominee Lily Tang Williams. Both were their parties’ candidates on the ballot in 2024. 
Goodlander was first elected to represent New Hampshire’s 2nd Congressional District in 2024. She spent her time speaking live at the forum reflecting on her record from her first term, including securing funding for early education programs at community colleges and high schools, childcare centers in the North Country, and for military families in her position on the House Armed Services Committee. 
“It’s been a top priority for me to do everything in my power as your congresswoman to make childcare early education affordable, and a profession that the best among us want to enter into in New Hampshire,” Goodlander said during the forum. 
Goodlander co-sponsored the Child Care for Working Families Act, which would cap family costs for childcare at 7% of their income, the percentage the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services considers an affordable amount to spend on childcare. She also supported and helped to pass the Supporting Early-Childhood Educators’ Deduction (SEED) Act, which expands the federal above-the-line educator expense tax deduction to include pre-kindergarten and early childhood educators.  
“I’d heard from so many childcare professionals, early childhood educators, about out-of-pocket costs for actually doing the job,” she said. “Our teachers are reimbursed for expenses that are just part of doing the job and educating. And we were able to get that across the finish line on a bipartisan basis this year.” 
In an interview with the Bulletin, Goodlander said she hears from families about rising childcare costs “literally every day.” 
“It’s a full blown crisis right now. Families are having to pay as much as a mortgage to afford childcare, as much as college tuition,” she said. “In rural areas, the real crisis is if they could pay.” 
Goodlander also said she was in favor of cutting government red tape around childcare and harnessing unusual funding avenues, like the National Defense Authorization Act, to get dollars out to providers. 
“When you look at where [New Hampshire] falls at the national level in terms of early childhood education in America, we’re number one in many respects, but we’re certainly not one when it comes to early childhood education,” Goodlander said. “This is the opportunity here.” 
Williams, an entrepreneur and educator, has run on a platform of reducing federal spending and regulations, affordability and limited government. 
She spoke live at the forum about her experiences trying to find childcare as a mother. She told providers that if elected, she wants to work to drive down inflation so providers don’t have to pass down operational costs to parents. 
“[Inflation] is going to add all the costs for providers, and providers have to exist and have to make a business make sense, so they pass to the parents who bear the cost. So then childcare becomes unaffordable,” Williams said. 
Williams told providers she would help bring down costs by tackling high energy costs and burdensome federal regulation. She said federal regulations on childcare “add another layer of red tape regulation” on top of state childcare rules. 
“If the state inspect, why do you need the federal government to inspect again?” Williams said. 
New Hampshire lawmakers, in partnership with the Child Care Advisory Committee in 2025, reformed the state’s childcare laws to reduce redundancies, cutting the law from over 200 pages to less than 90. 
Additionally, Williams said she was in favor of increasing the incentives for potential teachers to enter the workforce. She proposed finding a way to urge employers to participate in or expand on tax incentives for the industry. 
The Bulletin reached out to representatives of Williams’ campaign to speak further about childcare policy. The campaign did not meet interview scheduling deadlines.
Both candidates agree that increasing rural and home-based childcare in their district is important to working families. The 2nd Congressional District consists of Nashua, Concord and most of the North Country, which has sparse childcare offerings. 
Senate candidates talk regulation and funding 
In the race to replace retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, Congressman Chris Pappas and former Sen. John E. Sununu expressed two differing approaches to how they would tackle childcare policy in the Senate. 
Pappas, who currently represents New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District, has made expanding affordable access to childcare a part of his campaign, calling it a “critical issue” in April.
In a pre-recorded video of Pappas that played during the forum, he talked about his record supporting childcare issues while serving in the House, including supporting a cap on out-of-pocket childcare at 7% of a family’s median income, reinstating the expanded child tax credit to help families offset household expenses, and workplace childcare for police officers and military officers.
Like other New Hampshire congressional Democrats, he has also pushed for legislation to expand rural childcare and increase childcare programs that offer care for off-shift workers. 
“This is such an important issue, and I’ve been fighting to get resources to New Hampshire childcare providers so they can open more slots, improve wages, and meet the needs of families,” Pappas said. 
Sununu has spoken little about early education on the campaign trail and has focused on affordability, energy, and government programs like Social Security and Medicare. 
In his live appearance at the Early Learning New Hampshire forum, Sununu said he would be in favor of reducing federal regulations around childcare and supporting the state’s affordability and access efforts through training, audits and the background check application process.
“They’ve taken away the waivers on background checks, so that you can’t work while you’re going through the application process, and that’s unnecessary,” Sununu said. “I think it hurts the number of people that we can have in a setting. And again, it’s just a regulation that makes it a little tougher for people in New Hampshire when they’re doing the right things to deliver the services they need.” 
Some New Hampshire childcare providers have complained about the complexity of the state’s background check process, specifically when programs are changing staff over from school year care to summer care. The New Hampshire Child Care Licensing Unit handles background checks for childcare programs and 24-hour residential programs. There are both state and federal background check rules, and providers may be required to comply with both. 
Sununu also said he supported cutting regulations that govern childcare for military families and create red tape. 
“We can do better, serve you better by getting rid of regulations that aren’t necessarily about New Hampshire, and that’s my focus.” 
The Trump administration has been working on lowering regulations and standards for federal-funded childcare programs like Head Start and the Child Care and Development Fund, the main childcare funding source for New Hampshire. Regulation changes have had varied impacts on the Granite State, but have been generally opposed by childcare teachers and business owners. 
Additionally, Sununu said he would support funding towards workforce development and the state childcare scholarship program, and in the long run, support a “fair and reasonable compensation structure,” making sure an “appropriate level of funding’ would be available and consistent for New Hampshire. 
1st Congressional District candidates both support more federal funding 
New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District holds the majority of the state’s childcare programs, as the district covers Manchester, the Seacoast and parts of the Lakes Region. Both nominees, Republican Anthony DiLorenzo and Democrat Stefany Shaheen, spoke about the importance of having affordable childcare for working families in their district, with their approach to handling it in Congress falling on party lines. 
DiLorenzo, an entrepreneur who owns multiple car dealerships on the Seacoast, attended the forum live. He said there are “many benefits” for both families and businesses to have affordable childcare so that families can work and businesses can have employees. 
“When I personally used childcare, it was shocking how expensive it was, and understandably too, because it’s your kid,” he said. “There’s nothing more important than your kids, so you want to make sure they’re cared for, but you also have to be able to justify being able to go to work, and I think many families struggle with that.” 
DiLorenzo said he supported expanding federal child tax credits, encouraging more private-public partnerships to improve childcare and using federal workforce programs, like the new Workforce Pell Grant, to help increase the childcare workforce. He also said as a congressman, he would encourage businesses to utilize business tax credits at the state level to increase childcare capacity. 
“I look at this funding not as a subsidy but as an investment in American families and in American workers,” he said. 
In a pre-recorded video, Shaheen, former Portsmouth city councilor, biotech consultant, and daughter of retiring U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, talked about her experience working in the early education sector and how she would bring it to Congress. Shaheen co-founded Early Learning New Hampshire in 2003 while her mother was governor. She said she would work to fund more initiatives to increase the number of qualified childcare workers through education. 
“It’s clear that we have to do everything in our power to unleash the potential of our workforce and ensure that young families have access to the care they need when they need it, and that young children have access to high-quality early education before they get to school,” she said. 
Shaheen also said she was in favor of expanding the childcare tax credit, reducing early childhood education costs and workforce entry barriers through free community college, and Medicare for All, so that employers don’t have to pay for healthcare. 
“That’s not acceptable in New Hampshire when you’re working full time and taking care of our youngest, most vulnerable citizens, you should be able to go and get the healthcare you need when you need it.” 
Shaheen has previously said that there would be “no greater champion” for early education if she gets elected to Congress.

name: National
title: Told her baby wouldn’t survive, she had to leave Idaho for an abortion. She’s sharing her story.
text:
Rebecca Crozier, 27, of Meridian, Idaho, poses in October 2026 with mementos from her baby, Haven. At 11 weeks, she received a fatal fetal diagnosis of anencephaly, and had to travel out of state to terminate the pregnancy because of her state’s near-total abortion ban. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Stateline)MERIDIAN, Idaho — It didn’t take long for doctors to see that something was amiss with Rebecca Crozier’s pregnancy.
At her eight-week ultrasound in 2025, they mentioned a possible neural tube defect, she said, but after some research, she thought it was something that could be managed or treated. 
“If it was a fixable problem, I was ready to quit my job and full-time care for a disabled child,” said Crozier, who is now 27. “That was something that we were prepared to do.”
In the time between the two ultrasounds, she had a dream that she was carrying a baby girl, and she and her husband named her Haven.
The couple lived in eastern Idaho at the time, and drove two hours to the Boise area to see the maternal-fetal medicine specialists at St. Luke’s, the state’s largest health system. Now at 11 weeks’ gestation, the specialists told her Haven had anencephaly, which occurs when the brain does not develop normally and the skull is left open, exposing brain tissue to amniotic fluid that causes the tissue to dissolve. It is a fatal condition.
Rebecca Crozier takes a photo of her belly during her pregnancy before she and her husband, Kris, were told that the fetus would not survive. (Courtesy of Rebecca Crozier)
“She was missing a lot of brain tissue,” Crozier recalled. “They were very clear that this baby will not go home with you. You will not take this baby home. This baby will die in the hospital if the baby survives that long.”
In many states, even ones with abortion bans, Crozier would have had the option to terminate the pregnancy. But Idaho’s near-total prohibition includes no exceptions for fatal anomalies. It’s one of 11 states that do not have exceptions for anencephaly or other fatal anomalies. 
Next Tuesday, Idahoans will vote to determine whether the state’s near-total abortion ban should remain the law. Proposition 1, the title of the citizen-led ballot measure, would restore access to abortion until fetal viability, which was the state law before the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. 
Idaho is the only state this election cycle with an initiative that would restore access in a state with a ban. In Missouri, voters will consider a different initiative — to reinstate a near-total ban after passing a constitutional amendment in 2024 allowing abortion access until viability. 
If Idaho’s measure passes, patients like Crozier would no longer have to leave the state for an abortion.
According to the Cleveland Clinic, the rate of anencephaly among newborns is about 1 in 10,000, and those babies die within a few hours or days. Most cases end in miscarriage or stillbirth; the fatal birth defect affects about 1 in 1,000 pregnancies. 
Crozier’s was among them. 



Quotation







We called our families and told them: Something is very, very wrong, and we have to decide what we want to do here.


– Rebecca Crozier, recalling the hours after an anencephaly diagnosis


“They told me that I could try and continue my pregnancy and that they would handle my care from then on, or I could just not choose … which was in and of itself a choice,” Crozier said. “We went back to our hotel and we called our families and told them, ‘Something is very, very wrong, and we have to decide what we want to do here.’” 
In a post on Facebook this past July, Crozier’s husband, Kris, disclosed their choice. He wrote that if they had decided to continue the pregnancy, every appointment thereafter could potentially be the one where they discovered Haven had died. 
“For us, our choice wasn’t whether to let her go or whether she would pass. It was when she would die,” he wrote.
‘Because I loved her’
Dr. Duncan Harmon, the maternal-fetal medicine specialist who diagnosed Crozier in Boise, said he counseled about the high risks of miscarriage or stillbirth with the pregnancy and other risks to Crozier’s health with higher levels of amniotic fluid. And while termination was an option, he said, he couldn’t provide it for her in Idaho. She would have to go out of state and navigate insurance, lodging and any other logistics on her own.
“It’s truly awful that patients can’t receive care in their home state, being surrounded by their primary care team, surrounded by their support people in their time of grief,” Harmon, who now practices in the Southeast, told Stateline.
After a few days of discussion with her husband, Crozier recalled, they decided it was best not to continue the pregnancy for the sake of both her health and their future fertility options. 
“I didn’t want my first experience with motherhood to be watching her struggle. I wanted it to be doing something really hard because I loved her,” she said.
Rebecca Crozier holds a print from one of her ultrasounds, showing the top of the fetus’ skull open from a fatal anomaly called anencephaly. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Stateline)
But making that decision was only the first step. Idaho is the only state in the West with a near-total ban, but the travel distances between clinics are vast, and those clinics are often overloaded. Calls to clinics in California, Oregon and Washington all yielded appointments that were several weeks away. 
The couple have family members who live in Utah. Crozier called clinics in Utah, where abortion is permitted up to 18 weeks, and got an appointment at a hospital within two weeks. Her mom flew in from California to be by her side.
“There was a lot of coordinating with the funeral home, actually, because we had to figure out how to get her transported back to Idaho,” Crozier said. 
The funeral home suggested the couple pick out a few items to cremate with the remains, including a security blanket with a white bunny at the top, so that there were enough ashes for the urn. Crozier held the items right up until it was time. 
Rebecca and Kris Crozier have publicly shared their story of leaving Idaho to terminate a pregnancy with a fatal diagnosis because the state’s near-total abortion ban does not contain exceptions for fatal conditions. (Courtesy of Rebecca Crozier)
She spent $3,000 out of pocket for the procedure, which was not covered by her insurance, and another $1,000 for the urn and cremation, including the costs to transport the  remains across state lines. In the recovery room, Crozier asked about footprints and handprints, but learned Haven was too tiny and the tissue too soft.
“I got really upset, and they had to bring my husband in,” she said. 
For the next year, they kept the full story extremely private and only told a few close friends and family members. Everyone else just knew that Haven had died. The couple opened up  over the summer, including on social media, in support of Idaho’s ballot initiative. But Crozier found that some people’s responses were more dismissive than she’d imagined they would be. 
“A lot of people were like, that’s not really an abortion, that doesn’t really count,” Crozier said. 
Since the summer, the Croziers have been vocal online and in person about the initiative, telling Haven’s story and trying to convey that an abortion ban like Idaho’s affects many people in situations like theirs. 
“With Prop 1 being on the ballot, I feel like people have this kind of idea in their brain of what people who have abortions are like, and I feel like I kind of break that mold for a lot of people,” Crozier said. 
“The whole situation was just so heartbreaking, and on top of being in that situation, having to go out of state and to hide what had really happened from friends and family for fear of being judged.”
More babies born with this anomaly under abortion bans
Dr. Kerri Brackney, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist in Tennessee who is a member of the American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine, said anencephaly diagnoses are not uncommon, and they are usually clearly identifiable early in pregnancy. 
The diagnosis does come with risks, Brackney said, including a buildup of amniotic fluid that can cause preterm labor or high blood pressure, but she said it’s typically manageable.   
“The vast majority of patients I care for are able to find some beauty in the hard,” she said. “It doesn’t take away the hard, doesn’t take away the pain, but unfortunately neither does abortion.”
Idaho is losing OB-GYNs. Doctors who remain are trying to shoulder the extra burdens.

Tennessee also has a near-total abortion ban with no fetal anomaly exceptions, and Brackney said more anencephaly babies are being delivered because of the ban, giving doctors a better sense of what it looks like at full term delivery. Brackney said she is honest with patients about the prognosis, and said the longest she’s seen a baby with anencephaly live after delivery is a couple of weeks. 
She has had patients who chose to leave the state and terminate, even though she doesn’t recommend it, and said she will refer a patient to a reputable clinic in another state if that’s what they decide to do.
“But I also really try to encourage my patients that, No. 1, I think they’re stronger than they realize and we can walk through any hard situation with them,” Brackney said. “They’re not alone, and we can help them to find even the small bits of beauty and joy that are found in a very hard journey.”
Brackney said she thinks patients grieve better over the long term when they “follow their pregnancies to their natural conclusion,” whether that’s a miscarriage, stillbirth or death in the hours or days after delivery. She doesn’t think exceptions for fatal anomalies like anencephaly are necessary in states with abortion bans.
“Sometimes moms find stillbirths to be a gift, where they didn’t have to decide and it happened naturally,” she said.
Early on in Idaho’s campaign, polls showed relatively high support for a ballot initiative to restore reproductive rights, including a Boise State University School of Public Service poll last November showing 61% support. A year later, recent polls have tightened considerably or shown more support on the opposing side, after the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints donated $1 million and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise donated $300,000, helping to usher in a wave of messaging against the measure.
A public memorial
Most of the Facebook posts from the Croziers over the summer didn’t make huge waves. But in early October, Rebecca Crozier made another one that was more direct, complete with multiple photos of her pregnant belly, her ultrasounds and Haven’s memory box. 
She wrote that she was affected by Idaho’s abortion laws and recounted her story, and encouraged people to vote yes on the ballot measure. 



Quotation







A lot of people were like, that’s not really an abortion, that doesn’t really count.


– Rebecca Crozier


The post quickly went viral. It was shared more than 2,700 times, with almost as many comments. Although it was a political post, she also felt it was a way she could permanently memorialize the baby she never got to meet. 
“I kept telling my friends and my family that I was scared that people were going to forget about her,” Crozier said. “That we would get pregnant, and we would have other kids, or that time would go on and that she would be forgotten. 
“And it felt like a way that I could remind myself and other people that she was real, and she mattered to me.”  
The Croziers are still trying for a healthy pregnancy.
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.
Editor’s Note: This story will be included in The Aftermath, an upcoming collaborative project with PBS News Hour and Stateline collecting the personal stories of patients harmed by abortion bans since 2022. If you would like to share your story, please email kmoseley@stateline.org.
