(Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)Ahtza Chavez, executive director of Naeva, an Indigenous voter empowerment organization, speaks to protesters Oct. 27, 2026, in front of the office U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM) Protesters gathered Oct. 27, 2026, in front U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich's downtown Albuquerque office to urge him to withdraw his permitting reform bill from the U.S. Senate's consideration. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A protester critical of U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich's permitting reform bill marches Oct. 27, 2026, in Albuquerque. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM) Protesters march from the University of New Mexico toward U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich's office in downtown Albuquerque on Oct. 27, 2026. They were criticizing Heinrich's permitting reform bill and data centers and urging elected officials not to accept donations from Palantir, the data mining and defense technology firm. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)A protester critical of U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich's permitting reform bill marches Oct. 27, 2026, in Albuquerque. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM) Students from the New Mexico School for the Arts in Santa Fe marched to the Capitol for the "Pull Out the Plug" protest on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)
Office staff told the students Lujan Grisham was out of office, but Kaila Rubbel, a visual arts student at NMSA, waited outside for her turn to write and deliver a letter to the governor. She told Source NM that she wants Lujan Grisham “to take action. I want her to stop this. And I think that not showing up or not doing so shows us who she is.”
Michael Coleman, Lujan Grisham’s communications director, told Source NM in an emailed statement Tuesday that the governor “understands that young New Mexicans are frustrated with the American political system, and she shares their concerns about some of the issues raised during today’s protest.” 
Still, the governor urged the protesters to respect public property and not interfere with government employees “simply doing their jobs.” 
“The governor received the letters the students left in our office, and she plans to read and consider them,” Coleman said. “She hopes the students work to stay informed and continue to participate in the political process.”
In Albuquerque, protesters directed much of their ire toward U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), who recently unveiled a sweeping, bipartisan permitting reform bill that protesters say reduces tribal input and empowers fossil fuel companies to quickly break ground on more harmful projects. 
New Mexico US Sen. Heinrich touts bipartisan permitting reform bill amid environmentalist criticism

More than 100 protesters marched from the UNM bookstore down Central Avenue to Heinrich’s downtown Albuquerque office. In front of a large sign that read “Heinrich is a sellout,” protesters with YUCCA, as well as Indigenous and environmentalist groups, described the bill as a betrayal by a longtime champion for tribal and environmental causes. 
Heinrich’s bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, seeks to hasten the federal permitting process for a variety of projects, including data centers, solar arrays, renewable energy transmission lines and more. 
The 400-page bill, cosponsored with U.S. Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) and two other senators in both parties, has drawn praise from labor unions, as well as both the American Petroleum Institute and the American Clean Power Association. Groups touting bipartisan policy have also lauded it as a step forward on a policy matter that has long frustrated advocates for all types of energy production in the United States.
But critics have said the pros of the bill that Heinrich has touted — namely a prohibition on data centers imposing energy production costs onto ratepayers, and hastening the approvals of renewable energy projects — are far outweighed by the bill’s other provisions. Protesters on Tuesday said the bill erodes hard-fought environmental protections like the National Environmental Policy Act and laws requiring tribal input. 
The All Pueblo Council of Governors, which represents 19 New Mexico pueblos, released a resolution on Tuesday that says the bill’s provisions will combine to ultimately “weaken protections for Pueblo sacred places.”
Outside Heinrich’s office, protesters carried signs decrying “data center giveaways” and “fossil fuel sellouts” and chanted “Kill the bill!” in between speeches.
New Mexico State University students and organizers call for statewide ban on data centers

“We need NEPA. We need our Clean Water Act. We need all of these things because they are the bare minimum for what we need to survive on this land,” Ahtza Chavez, executive director of Naeva, an Indigenous voter empowerment organization, told attendees Tuesday. “And this senator has the gall to say that he’s going to rip that out of our hands. I don’t think so.”
Heinrich’s spokesperson Luis Soriano, in a statement to Source NM on Tuesday, said Heinrich’s bill “actually holds data centers accountable for their energy usage while speeding up the approval of clean energy projects that put cheaper and cleaner electricity on the grid.”
As for tribal consultation, Soriano said that Congress needs to pass the bill to ensure that President Donald Trump’s administration is required to heed tribal input instead of ignoring it.
“The legislation also defends against the Trump administration’s efforts to make all Tribal consultation discretionary and eliminate consultation altogether on cultural landscapes. All of this means stronger Tribal consultation protections, lower utility bills, more good-paying jobs, and a path toward unlocking our clean energy future.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA advocates renew calls for state to limit feds’ access to license data
text:
A masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent knocks on a car window in Minnesota on Jan. 12. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)SEATTLE — Chris Megargee volunteers at a Shoreline Home Depot to help day laborers frequently targeted by federal immigration authorities. 
As part of the adopt-a-corner program, Megargee and other volunteers provide breakfast and share information so the workers, who are often noncitizens, know their rights if U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents come. 
Since January, ICE officials have detained half a dozen men there, including one this month, who drove their cars to the Home Depot, Megargee said. 
Before arresting each, ICE agents entered the license plate numbers on those cars into a database, and received car registration information to identify the driver, Megargee alleged.
Advocates gathered in Seattle on Tuesday to continue their push for Washington state officials to do more to restrict the ability of the feds to get information from the license plate database.
“We need you to act and slow down this mass deportation and detention machine by continuing to cut off access to the Department of Licensing data that is being used for immigration enforcement,” said Lucía Vázquez Martínez, field director for Service Employees International Union 775. 
Gov. Bob Ferguson noted his administration has acted to curb unfettered access to the state’s data.
“My team has worked to limit Customs and Border Protection access for immigration enforcement, while maintaining access necessary to protect public safety, such as human trafficking investigations that require real-time access to data to protect vulnerable Washingtonians,” he said in a statement Tuesday. 
“Looking ahead to the next two years, this will be an ongoing process for us to adapt to what (the) federal government does next to work around what we do to protect our data,” Ferguson added.
These concerns date back years, but have intensified as President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign has grown in Washington, with surges seen in recent months.
University of Washington researchers connected 356 arrests to federal queries for license data between August 2025 and Oct. 13 of this year. In the first five months of this year, agencies housed under the U.S. Department of Homeland Security searched state Department of Licensing driver and vehicle data over 1 million times, according to the university’s Center for Human Rights.
Washington is one of 19 states that offer driver’s licenses regardless of immigration status. Others require warrants or court orders for federal agencies to access state-held license and vehicle data for immigration purposes, according to the UW researchers. Washington does not.
Ferguson spokesperson Brionna Aho said Tuesday that “our team is reviewing what other states have done, and what is lawful, to require judicial warrants for civil immigration-related requests.”
What the state has already done
Last November, Washington officials cut off ICE’s ability to get this data. This was later expanded to Homeland Security Investigations, also known as HSI.
Between November 2025 and Oct. 12, the Washington State Patrol blocked over 174,000 search attempts from federal agencies, including 89,000 from Customs and Border Protection, 45,000 from HSI and nearly 40,000 from ICE, according to the governor’s office. However, researchers say millions more searches from the Department of Homeland Security have still gone through. 
Aho said shutting off federal access to Department of Licensing data entirely isn’t an option due to “legitimate public safety reasons.”   
The state has taken numerous steps, some of them unprecedented nationwide, to cut off immigration authorities, she said.
These reportedly include blocking searches of the Nlets platform, which police agencies use to share driver’s license data across states, by ICE. The state has also stopped Customs and Border Protection from seeing photos of people searched in Nlets in Washington. A terms-of-use notice in Nlets now also informs those seeking its data that it cannot be used for immigration enforcement.
Federal agents have repeatedly found workarounds to bypass the state’s restrictions. 
“As the federal government has rapidly changed its tactics and the way it uses state data, Governor Ferguson has continually considered and reassessed state agencies’ data practices and taken quick action when necessary,” Aho said in an email. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Washington has also suspended nine searchers associated with CBP and three with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services that were suspected to be connected to immigration enforcement operations.
In this case, the UW researchers say this work by the state to block individual accounts is “not providing meaningful protection for Washingtonians’ data.” They argued the continued federal access violates the Keep Washington Working Act, the 2019 state law that prevents state data from being shared with federal authorities for civil immigration purposes
The state also suspended the ability of ICE and CBP to renew tabs for license plates on undercover vehicles. The Trump administration is suing Washington, and other states, over this policy.

name: VTDigger
title: After probe, concerns over Barre City officer’s credibility puts dozens of criminal cases in limbo
text:
The Barre City Police Department. File photo by Mike Dougherty/VTDigger

A county prosecutor has issued a Brady letter against a Barre City police officer accusing him of having sexual relations with a woman he had arrested while that criminal case remained pending.
Orange County State’s Attorney Colin Seaman wrote in a two-page letter issued Friday that his office “has reason to believe” that Barre City Police Officer Matthew Frey “committed acts that create substantial issues pertaining to his credibility as a witness and conduct as a law enforcement officer in any capacity.”
Often termed a “Brady” or “Giglio” letter, the names refer to national court cases. The letters are filed by prosecutors when an officer’s credibility is called into question and can effectively end a law enforcement career because prosecutors may decide to no longer take cases the officer had investigated.
“Based on the information I have right now, I would not feel comfortable calling him as a witness,” Washington County State’s Attorney Michelle Donnelly said of Frey in an interview.
Frey could not be reached Tuesday for comment. 
After the allegations against Frey came to light, Vermont State Police conducted an investigation and turned the case over for review by the Orange County State’s Attorney’s Office, who declined to prosecute, Adam Silverman, a state police spokesperson, said Tuesday.
Seaman wrote in the letter that Frey was the arresting officer of a woman charged with reckless or gross negligent operation of a motor vehicle, cruelty to a child and resisting arrest in May.
“During the pendency of the criminal charges,” Seaman added, “Matthew Frey began a discreet relationship with the defendant primarily using Snapchat media to exchange messages, including requesting and receiving partially nude pictures of the defendant.”
On Sept. 13, the prosecutor wrote, Frey “invited himself” to that woman’s house, “purposefully placed his motor vehicle in a not readily identifiable manner in the driveway, told the defendant she must keep this meeting a secret and had a sexual encounter with the defendant.”
That woman, Seaman wrote, expressed concern in an Oct. 1 complaint to law enforcement that she was “coerced” by Frey.
“The above actions outline a pattern of behavior that exploits a dangerous power imbalance inherent in law enforcement with persons subject to their potential testimony against them in a criminal proceeding,” Seaman wrote. 
“The Defendant in the criminal case is placed in the role of a victim in this investigation,” the prosecutor added. “They were placed in a position of vulnerability potentially fearing retaliation, favorable or less favorable treatment in their criminal case, and disbelief should they come forward with allegations against the law enforcement officer placing them in this position.”
Seaman could not be reached Tuesday for comment.
Donnelly said Tuesday the matter was referred to the Orange County State’s Attorney’s Office to avoid any conflicts since it involved a law enforcement officer in Washington County. 
“We never want to give even the appearance of a conflict of interest,” Donnelly said.
Donnelly said since the letter was issued Friday she has reviewed all the active criminal and family cases in which Frey was involved to determine which cases need to be dismissed or if they can move forward without him as a witness. 
She said an initial review shows about 90 active criminal and family court cases involving Frey. “We are still looking at how many of those are going to be dismissals or refusals,” Donnelly said. 
Donnelly also said after receiving the letter she dismissed the case brought against the woman Frey arrested in May.
Donnelly added that the letter not only raises credibility concerns with Frey. “It shows, I think, an extreme lack of judgment in the way that he treated somebody that he investigated,” the prosecutor said. 
Donnelly said that she agreed with the decision by Seaman to not bring criminal charges in the matter.
“I think that it was a lack of judgment,” Donnelly said of Frey’s actions. She added that while she believed that there were “professional obligations” Frey did not meet, it did not rise to the level of a crime.
Frey is on paid administrative leave, Barre City Police Chief Braedon Vail wrote in an email Tuesday in response to questions from VTDigger. 
Vail said that an administrative investigation is set to begin this week following the criminal investigation and decision by the prosecutor not to bring any charges.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  After probe, concerns over Barre City officer’s credibility puts dozens of criminal cases in limbo.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Commentary: The Constitution is the real key to protecting our elections
text:
Brigitte Romoleroux proudly wears her “I Voted” sticker after voting at the Main Library in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The Justice Department has struck out again after U.S. District Court Judge David Barlow dismissed a lawsuit against Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson. While Judge Barlow correctly interpreted federal law, it is important for Americans to know that the ruling helps ensure our elections remain fair and secure.
The Trump administration, to its credit, wants to root out election fraud. But you do not do that by just demanding that states hand over sensitive voter data. The best way to fight election fraud is by following the system outlined in our Constitution.
Article I, Section 4 of the U.S. Constitution says that state legislatures shall determine the time, place and manner of elections to federal office. It also empowers Congress to alter some state election laws. In other words, states take the lead in running elections, Congress plays a secondary role as needed, and the president does what Congress tells him or her to do.
Nowhere does this give the executive branch the authority to make demands beyond those authorized by Congress. Nor does it allow for new election policy to be made via executive order or federal regulation, as recent executive orders and federal regulations around vote by mail (also paused by the courts) would do.
Widespread election fraud is prohibitively difficult to perpetrate in the United States because there are plenty of opportunities to catch it. That is the genius of our constitutionally designed system.
We have 50 state-led election systems administered by thousands of local election officials. These local election officials collect ballots and count votes, while state election officials provide oversight, add local vote tallies together and announce results.
Think about it: To perpetrate voter fraud on a scale that could change the outcome of a federal election, fraudsters would have to overcome the safeguards of dozens of election systems, while getting hundreds (perhaps thousands) of state and local election officials in on their schemes. Even in state races or smaller districts, dozens of state and local election officials would need to be in on the plot for election fraud to sway those elections. Persuading that many individuals from different geographies and independent jurisdictions to get on board with that deception is so difficult it is practically impossible.
Look at Utah if you want to see how difficult pulling off something like that would be.
In the Beehive State, a voter’s identity is verified several times, including when they return a ballot. Ballots themselves contain scannable barcodes so they can be tracked. They also have barcodes on the envelope that, once scanned, can determine whether a voter has already voted in that election. If a signature on the ballot doesn’t match, a voter may also be required to provide a driver’s license or the last four digits of their Social Security number to prove their identity.
In addition, machines are audited for accuracy, have many levels of encryption and are not connected to the internet. There is 24/7 surveillance of ballots, ballots must be handled by at least two election workers, ballots are counted in public and voter rolls are regularly checked and updated to remove ineligible voters.
Federal executive orders that centralize election authority in one or a few federal agencies, by contrast, would mean the number of anti-fraud safeguards shrinks from thousands to a relative handful. This would make election fraud easier to commit because only a single federal system needs to be corrupted instead of dozens of individual state systems, and it can be done from the comfort of Washington, D.C. — far from the eyes of the thousands of state and local anti-fraud checkpoints that safeguard election integrity today.
Both political parties have tried to expand the federal government’s involvement in elections in recent years. Those advocating for these policies should ask themselves a question: Do I want the opposing political party to have greater influence over elections when they take power? If the answer is no, that is a good sign that those federal election policy reforms will not accomplish their goals.
Rather than pursuing proposals that make election fraud easier by centralizing election authority in Washington, D.C., we should strengthen election integrity by enacting measures that further uphold and protect state-led, locally administered elections.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Republicans make plea for unity following ‘hurt feelings’ in US Senate contest
text:
The third-annual Freedom Fry in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)MYRTLE BEACH — At a GOP-energizing event where a long list of Republican nominees took the stage to make their pitch, the underlying theme was a plea for unity in the unexpectedly tight U.S. Senate race.
The third annual Freedom Fry, a title that’s a nod to the host — U.S. Rep. Russell Fry — serves as a fundraiser for the 7th District congressman and get-out-the-vote pep rally for the party faithful.
This year’s event, two months after a special GOP primary for a coveted spot on the ballot, took on the additional mission of bringing together Republicans still upset over the whirlwind race to replace the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham as the nominee. Less than a month after his funeral, his younger sister, Darline Graham emerged as the winner of a 10-way contest, aided by the endorsement of President Donald Trump.
Republican Rep. Russell Fry speaks at his third-annual Freedom Fry in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)
According to polls, she’s in a close battle with Democrat Annie Andrews for the next six-year term.
That’s at least partly due to intra-party GOP feuding. The son of U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, who lost to Graham in the runoff Aug. 25, has publicly endorsed Andrews. Norman himself is refusing to help Graham. And some of Norman’s supporters are encouraging voters to write his name on the ballot. Norman indicated on the night he lost that he’s upset Trump ever got involved.
Attorney General Alan Wilson, the GOP nominee for governor, used part of his allotted time Monday night to address the “hurt feelings” and urge Republicans to vote for Graham.
“I’m just going to say it out loud. It’s the unspoken truth. But here’s the reality we have: this is the only option,” Wilson said after campaigning with Graham elsewhere in Myrtle Beach.
He was addressing about 400 people who paid at least $50 a ticket to hear from candidates at the Hilton Myrtle Beach Resort and eat from the “fry bar.”
“Here’s the thing: Not voting for Darline Graham or voting for Annie Andrews and standing on that election” could put Democrats in control of the U.S. Senate, he said. “You may not intend for that to be the case, but I’m telling you folks,” he continued, that’s “so much greater than the petty differences that we squabble about in our primaries.”
Over the course of two hours, Republicans who took the stage included South Carolina’s GOP nominees for statewide and congressional offices, as well as Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee.
Fry, the primary’s third-place finisher, also spent part of his time to talk up Graham.
“The mission is more important than the personalities, and that’s why everybody needs to get out there and support Darline Graham,” said Fry, who faces Democrat John Vincent on the ballot.
Fry was widely expected to seek the nomination before Trump encouraged Graham to run.
Rumblings over what would happen if Fry ran and won — making him the GOP nominee for both U.S. Senate and the 7th Congressional District — led to the state Election Commission issuing a statement making clear that it is legal in South Carolina for candidates to run for multiple offices simultaneously. Next steps were being discussed: A legislator in the state House was publicly considering running to replace Fry in the U.S. House.
Ultimately, Fry and Norman, who was coming off an unsuccessful run for governor, announced their bids for U.S. Senate after Trump stunned the field by encouraging Graham to run.
After losing, Fry endorsed Graham ahead of the runoff and has appeared with her on stage since, to include introducing her at his event.
U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas speaks at the third annual Freedom Fry in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)
At the Freedom Fry, Cruz applauded Fry for quickly backing her.
“You ran against Darline in a vigorous contest. You didn’t prevail. And you know what? It would be easy to take your ball and go home, and it would be easy to get mad,” said the Texas senator, who’s considered a potential 2028 presidential contender. “You didn’t do that. … We all need to all unify.”
Earlier Monday, the Republican National Committee announced that Trump will return Thursday to rally in South Carolina for the second time in two weeks — this time in Norman’s hometown of Rock Hill.
Fry urged Norman, who did not attend the Freedom Fry, to “step into the sunlight a little bit to help his Republican nominee.”
“As somebody who carried the conservative banner as long as he has, he should step into the arena,” Fry told reporters, referring to the congressman first elected to the state House in 2006. “He didn’t win. I didn’t win either.”
But Norman doubled down on his refusal, telling CNN after the event that the election is “about attempts to ‘force’ a candidate on the voters.”
As he did in a radio interview last week, Norman again suggested the race against Andrews wouldn’t be tight if he’d won the nomination.
“Regardless of the outcome, it didn’t have to be this way as the great people living in South Carolina deserve ‘better!’ Bottom line!! Elections have consequences!!” he wrote in a text to the reporter. As for his son’s op-ed, he wrote, “Warren is EXACTLY RIGHT in his statement!!! My entire family is NOT SUPPORTING her candidacy.”
Norman’s tenure in Congress ends in January, since he chose to run for governor instead of re-election. He placed third in the June primary.
State Sen. Wes Climer, who faces Democrat Mallory Dittmer on the ballot, was among speakers at the Freedom Fry.
Without directly addressing the GOP feuding, he urged attendees to go vote and take friends with them.
“I know that y’all know some friends from church, from work, from the neighborhoods, some good lifelong Republicans who might get a little extra motivation this year,” said Climer, who also lives in Rock Hill. “Right, so just remind them, elections are about choices, and elections have consequences.”
Attorney General Alan Wilson, the GOP nominee for governor, speaks at the third annual Freedom Fry in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)
State GOP Chair Drew McKissick acknowledged the party division as due to the special primary but attributed it to the later-than-normal contest: August instead of June. He indicated there’s still time to unify.
“You have a time span after a primary is over, working to put everything back together again and getting everybody on board and so forth,” he told the SC Daily Gazette. “So we’re in the process of that, and it’s been coming along.”
Trump’s repeated rallies in South Carolina ahead of the general election are unprecedented.
McKissick indicated he’s not worried, despite the polls showing Republicans in trouble in traditional Republican strongholds. Other states Trump’s visiting this week alone include Texas, Ohio, Florida, Kansas and Iowa. Last week, his stops included North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia.
“You are always happy to have the time of the campaigner in chief,” McKissick said. “If he thinks he’s got extra time to come in and make a swing, fine. That helps everybody up and down the team.”
Early voting runs through Saturday. Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Southern Miss plans $25 million renovation and expansion of 42-year-old Pete Taylor baseball park
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
HATTIESBURG — Southern Miss on Tuesday announced a plan to renovate the 42-year-old home of its nationally renowned baseball program, the only Division I program in the U.S. to boast 10 straight 40-victory seasons and 10 straight NCAA Tournament bids.
The school plans to raise approximately $25 million through private and corporate funding to complete a renovation and expansion of Pete Taylor Park/Hill Denson Field.
“Pete Taylor Park represents so much of what makes Southern Miss baseball special,” said Southern Miss Director of Athletics Jeremy McClain. “The history, the atmosphere and, most importantly, our fans have created an environment unlike any other. This project allows us to honor those traditions while making a significant investment in what comes next for our program.”
Jackson-based Weir Boerner Allin Architecture, which has designed numerous athletic facilities across the South including Dudy Noble Field at Mississippi State, partnered with Southern Miss to do master planning for the project. Seating capacity would increase to approximately 6,500. The largest crowd to date was 6,346, which included more than  2,000 standing room only. Southern Miss has sold out its season tickets of approximately 4,600 tickets for four straight seasons.
A planned renovation of Pete Taylor Park at Southern Miss would include this seating down the first base line. Credit: Courtesy of Southern Miss Athletics
The proposed stadium renovation would include all chairback seating and the addition of eight more luxury suites to the existing 12. Said McClain, “We wish we had room for 20 more suites because we could sell that many more.”
The master plan includes an indoor pitching laboratory and hitting facility with  high-tech sports science equipment to improve performance. Southern Miss coach Chrisian Ostrander, who has guided the Golden Eagles to 143 victories over three seasons called the proposed performance center “a game changer for player development, the backbone our our program.”
Southern Miss is calling the baseball stadium project “Where Tradition Meets Tomorrow, ” McClain said.
“The vision is not to change what makes The Pete special. It is to build around it,” he said. “We want our longtime fans to walk into the renovated ballpark and still feel everything they love about Southern Miss baseball, while the next generation of Golden Eagles experience a facility built for the future.”
McClain said he is confident Southern Miss can raise the money.
“We’ve had several preliminary meetings with potential donors,” he said. “We’ve confident we can get to the finish line soon and move forward with the project. Our baseball program is nationally competitive and we want to continue to invest in its future.”
Fund-raising will include naming rights to the performance center, as well as different enhanced seating areas in the ballpark, McClain said. Already this year, Renasant Bank bought the naming rights to the former M.M. Roberts Stadium in a deal that will pay the university $13.7 million over 10 years.
The birds-eye view of the proposed renovation of Pete Taylor Park. Credit: Courtesy of Southern Miss Athletics

name: Nevada Current
title: Conservation group sues feds for failing to protect rare Nevada toad and fish
text:
Amargosa toad, Oasis Valley speckled dace. (Photos: Center for Biological Diversity, Bureau of Land Management)A conservation group sued the federal government Tuesday for failing to make a timely decision on whether to list a rare Nevada toad and fish as endangered or threatened species.
The Center for Biological Diversity sued the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Tuesday for allegedly violating the Endangered Species Act after federal wildlife managers failed to issue a 12-month finding on whether to list the Amargosa toad and the Oasis Valley speckled dace, as required by federal law.
Last year, a review by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service found there was substantial evidence that both the toad and fish may be eligible for listing, after the Center filed petitions to protect both species under the Endangered Species Act. But the agency missed the legally required deadline to issue a final decision on whether to protect the toads and fish.
The Amargosa toad and Oasis Valley speckled dace live in spring-fed habitats along the Amargosa River in Oasis Valley near Beatty in Nye County. The Amargosa toad is only found along a 14 mile stretch of the Amargosa River, with a population estimated at about 2,000 individuals.
The area has also attracted gold mining company AngloGold Ashanti, which has proposed several potential mines in the area.
“The Amargosa toad and Oasis Valley speckled dace are at the center of a bullseye surrounded by gold mining activity that threatens to push them over the edge to extinction,” said Patrick Donnelly, Great Basin director at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Endangered Species Act protections are urgently needed for these species before AngloGold’s mines suck dry the water they need for survival.”
According to the petitions, both the rare toad and fish are threatened with extinction due to groundwater pumping from seven proposed gold mining operations along the Amargosa. Six of those projects are being proposed by British multinational miner AngloGold Ashanti, including what is potentially the largest greenfield gold discovery in Nevada in more than a decade.
AngloGold Ashanti has claimed their Arthur Gold Deposit could contain about 16 million ounces of gold resources, nearly five times as much gold as Nevada produces annually.
AngloGold Ashanti’s North Bullfrog Project, which is currently in the permitting phase, is about nine miles north of the Town of Beatty. The project would span about 5,400 acres of public lands and would withdraw up to 2,500 acre-feet of water per year from Oasis Valley, perhaps enough to serve about 7,500 homes.
The conservation group said “the combined groundwater drawdown from these projects could substantially reduce flows or dry up springs along the Amargosa River that the toads and fish depend on for survival.”
“The Amargosa River is a crown jewel of the Mojave Desert, and we shouldn’t sacrifice it for gold mining,” said Donnelly. “The Amargosa toad and Oasis Valley speckled dace are emblems of Nevada’s remarkable biodiversity. We won’t rest until they get the protections they urgently need and deserve.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: With 1 week until Election Day, Montana absentee votes exceed 225,000
text:
A sign noting where to vote by precinct is on display at the Helena Civic Center during a primary vote on Tuesday, June 2, 2026 in Helena, Montana. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)One week from Election Day, more than 209,000 Montanans have already cast their ballot this midterm. 
The Montana Secretary of State’s office sent out just under 525,000 absentee ballots to registered voters in October and as of Tuesday afternoon, 225,698 have been returned — roughly 43%.  
That number is tracking well ahead of the 2022 midterm election, when the state reported 284,000 absentee ballots were received by the day before Election Day. 
Montana’s electorate has grown every year since 2002, but saw a jump in registered voters in recent years following a surge of in-migration after the COVID-19 pandemic. Montana has roughly 5% more registered voters in the state compared to the 2022 midterm, with the Secretary of State’s Office reporting 805,418 registered voters as of Tuesday.
But overall voter turnout in 2022 was also historically low by Montana standards. Less than 500,000 voters cast ballots, the lowest number of midterm votes since 2004, according to data from the secretary of state. 
Current absentee votes received by Tuesday exceed 48% of the total votes cast in 2022. 
Compared to the 2018 midterm election, during President Donald Trump’s first term in office, absentee ballots returned so far amount to 44% of total votes cast in 2018. 
Sheridan County leads with the highest percentage of absentee ballots with 51% of absentee ballots returned, followed by Lewis and Clark and Fergus counties at 48%. 
Missoula County leads among the state’s most populous counties with 47% of ballots returned. 
Roosevelt, Lincoln, Big Horn and Glacier counties have returned the lowest percentage of absentee ballots, with less than 33% returned to the state. 
Montana doesn’t require voters to register with a party affiliation, so early returns don’t offer much in the way of specific data points for contested partisan races. But nationwide in many states that do have party registration, Democratic voters lead in early returns. 
Absentee ballots must be received by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Nov. 3.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Former teacher fights license suspension over alleged incident with student
text:
A former Davenport elementary school teacher is suing the Iowa Board of Educational Examiners over its move to suspend his teaching license due to allegations of inappropriate contact with a former student. (Stock photo via Getty Images)A former Davenport elementary school teacher is contesting the state’s efforts to suspend his teaching license due to allegations of inappropriate contact with a former student.
Julian Lira is taking the Iowa Board of Educational Examiners to court and seeking judicial review of the board’s recent decision to suspend his teaching license for three years.
In his lawsuit, filed in Polk County District Court, Lira is appealing the board’s Sept. 24, 2026, final order in his disciplinary case. Lira alleges that before the matter was turned over to the board for final action, an administrative law judge on June 30, 2025, issued a proposed decision for the board to consider.
According to the lawsuit, the judge’s proposed decision included a finding that Lira had “briefly touched (a former student’s) chest” at a wedding reception and described this as a “brief, inappropriate interaction.” The lawsuit asserts the judge concluded that a public letter of reprimand was the appropriate sanction in the case.
The judge’s proposed decision was then forwarded to the board, which issued a final order that, according to the lawsuit, “expressly deleted the last three sentences” of the judge’s proposed decision, all of which were related to the seriousness of offense and the appropriateness of a public reprimand.
The board retained the judge’s finding that “Lira had an inappropriate interaction with a former student at a wedding reception,” and then opted to impose a three-year license suspension, the lawsuit claims.
In addition, the lawsuit asserts, the board imposed additional conditions on Lira’s potential license reinstatement, calling for consultation with a doctor for a psychosexual evaluation, as well as a mental health evaluation and possible counseling or treatment.
According to the lawsuit, the board identified “no additional aggravating factual findings” to justify the enhanced penalty it favored, and the board supplied no explanation for not agreeing with the judge’s proposed sanction in the case.
Lira is asking the court to reverse the board’s final decision and dismiss the disciplinary complaint against him. In the alternative, Lira argues, the court should vacate the board’s decision and remand the matter back to the board for a new hearing before a different administrative law judge.
The State of Iowa, which does not comment on pending litigation, has yet to file a response to the lawsuit.
The disciplinary case appears to stem from allegations that surfaced in late 2023, when WHBF TV reported that Lira had been arrested and charged with misdemeanor lascivious conduct with a minor while the two were guests at a wedding reception on Oct. 7, 2023.
Prosecutors later dropped the criminal charge, saying they could not show Lira — who had briefly served as the alleged victim’s teacher in the third and sixth grade — was in a position of authority over the victim at the time of the alleged incident.
Court records indicate that earlier, in 2019, Lira was criminally charged with sexually abusing a young girl who was a relative of his at the time. A jury subsequently found Lira not guilty of sexual abuse in the second degree, court records show.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Watch: How the fatal Senatobia shooting unfolded in 25 seconds
authors: Julie Lee, Sarah Whites-Koditschek, and Mukta Joshi
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Julie Lee is a data reporter at Mississippi Today. Sarah Whites-Koditschek and Mukta Joshi are investigative reporters at Mississippi Today spending a year as New York Times Local Investigations fellows. They report for the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center in collaboration with The New York Times.
Reporters for Mississippi Today closely examined video footage and broke down key moments of the police confrontation that ended with the fatal shooting of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in a Walmart parking lot this summer.
The frame-by-frame review shows how a tip that two women were running out of the store escalated in a matter of seconds, with five officers surrounding their car, guns raised. The video analysis also catalogs the moments cited by several experts who said the police unnecessarily escalated the encounter and put themselves in harm’s way.
The Mississippi attorney general, Lynn Fitch, announced last week that the state would not pursue criminal charges against Hunter Foster, the Senatobia police officer who shot Kohen. The toddler was sitting on his mother’s lap as a second woman drove. Foster fired at the car as it drove in the direction of two officers, and Fitch ruled his actions were justified. 
That decision came after a state investigation that relied heavily on the video shown here.
The footage begins just after 2 p.m. on June 14, inside a small room with video monitors near the store entrance. A Walmart employee steps in, interrupting police officers who are discussing an unrelated incident.

Outside, the two women, one of whom is carrying Kohen, run toward a gray sedan in the parking lot, Walmart surveillance footage shows. Latoya Ferrell, carrying a box of diapers, gets in to drive. Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, climbs into the passenger seat with her son. 
It is unclear if the officers knew who the women were or why they were running. No one in the video accuses the women of a crime, hints at why they are running or mentions a child. 
An incident report that Senatobia officers filed later said baby clothes and a large box of Pampers Easy Ups diapers were stolen. The report says the diapers were “under rang,” a term for when an item is skipped at self-checkout or a cheaper item is scanned instead. Neither woman has been charged.
As the officers run toward the car, it backs out of its parking spot. They shout, “Stop!” 
The first person to draw a gun is a deputy from the Tate County Sheriff’s Office. He points it at the ground and holsters it almost immediately as the car continues to reverse. Meanwhile, Foster draws his gun. He is the first officer to aim at the car, 20 seconds after the Walmart employee alerted the officers.

Jeremy Bauer, a forensic reconstruction expert who reviewed body-worn camera footage from Foster and two other officers, said the car was still backing up when Foster pointed his gun at it.
Russ Hicks, a retired law enforcement officer and instructor from Washington, said, “What concerns me is taking out the gun so quickly on this kind of a case.” Hicks consults with police departments on use of force and de-escalation techniques.
As the driver backs out of her parking space, she hits an SUV, momentarily coming to a stop. The officers close in around the car, continuing to yell, “Stop,” and drawing their weapons. By the time the car accelerates forward, all five officers have drawn their guns.

The car accelerates toward Foster and a sheriff’s deputy. The front wheel appears to turn left, away from Foster. As the car’s bumper approaches Foster’s leg, he fires one shot at the windshield, about 25 seconds after the Walmart employee ran in. He fires at least two more shots into the side window. 
An analysis of body-worn camera footage indicated the audio was at times mismatched to the video by fractions of seconds. The analysis indicated that Foster’s video had a larger lag, though still less than one-third of a second. For that reason, Mississippi Today muted the footage from his camera.

According to Bauer, the forensic reconstruction expert, Foster fires the first shot when his right leg is in front of the bumper and his left leg is beside the car. 
Bauer said it was hard to tell if Foster was grazed by the car. He noted that Foster’s balance was not disrupted and said there was “no definitive evidence of an impact.”

It is unclear in the videos whether any of the other officers who were close to the car were hit, Bauer said. He saw no evidence of possible contact with the other officers beyond one officer who braced his hand on the hood of the car. 
Veronica Roberson, Kohen’s grandmother, said Mississippi Bureau of Investigation officials told her when she viewed the footage that one officer — not Foster — was struck by the car. She said she was told that the officer who was struck was a sheriff’s deputy who was standing in front of the car. 
Walmart surveillance video seems to show him jumping out of the way in time. But the Walmart camera was recording at a lower frame rate than body-camera footage, so it is difficult to determine whether it accurately captured his movement. Other camera angles appear to show the car veer closer to him, and the deputy can be seen lifting his leg and bracing his hand against the car.

The videos released Thursday are a portion of the camera footage collected by state investigators, though they appear to capture the critical moments around the time of the shooting.
Leaked footage published by Darkhorse Press, a Mississippi news outlet, on Oct. 20 included a clip of Foster and another officer talking outside the hospital where Kohen was pronounced dead. In that video, which starts about 20 minutes after the shooting, Foster asks whether the 1-year-old had been hit, saying, “I didn’t even see a baby in her lap,” adding an expletive. That clip was not included in the footage released by the state Thursday. 
Foster was placed on administrative leave by the Senatobia Board of Aldermen on June 16, two days after the incident. He resigned last Wednesday.

name: WyoFile
title: Teton County sheriff’s candidate calls suspension ‘political,’ keeps campaigning
text:
KHOL 89.1 Jackson Hole Community Radio produced this story with editing support from WyoFile.
Teton County Sheriff Deputy Eric Snow is still campaigning for sheriff and bashing the office that suspended him, which he aims to lead.  
Snow’s comments come a week before the election and a week after his suspension for reasons that remain guarded by the sheriff’s office. Snow said he’s being disciplined for “failure to act” during an arrest last week. 
His suspension follows two highly scrutinized DUI arrests. In the first, Snow charged a Jackson man with a DUI and jailed him despite what the Teton County Sheriff’s Office said was a lack of evidence. In the second, he did not charge a DUI despite a field test indicating intoxication. 
In his first interview since being put on leave, the Republican candidate called his suspension a “no-win situation.” Snow denounced the decision by Lt. Mark Priest as retaliation for challenging their boss, Teton County Sheriff Matt Carr, a Democrat seeking his third term as sheriff.
Snow also defended his arrest track record and claimed Carr has turned the office into a “political instrument.” 
Carr said he had no role in putting Snow on leave and denied allegations that he weaponized the office. In the three-way race, which also includes independent Chris Glenn, Carr has also faced scrutiny for offering a job to his one-time primary opponent, a former Jackson police officer, during the election. 
Carr did, however, say that at least two of Snow’s recent arrests “reflect a pattern of behavior that’s very concerning, that is not reflective of the type of law enforcement we want in our community.” 
Carr said that he would release Snow’s personnel file, which would include any past department reviews, only if Snow first agreed to that.  
Snow declined to do so and told KHOL that, “Cops are afforded some level of privacy.” 
Mark Jackowski, Snow’s attorney, said he reviewed what was represented by the sheriff’s office to constitute Snow’s personnel file and was unable to ascertain any “pattern of behavior” and that the suspension “smacks of retaliation.” 
“I will not be surprised if this matter ends up being litigated,” Jackowski said. “While the sheriff was able to rid himself of a Democrat primary opponent by offering him a job, he couldn’t do that with respect to Snow.” 
Teton County Sheriff’s Deputy Eric Snow said he was dismissed for “failure to act” during an arrest, a point he disputes.  (Evan Robinson-Johnson/KHOL)
Why is Snow on leave? 
The sheriff’s and county attorney’s offices have declined to confirm or provide his suspension letter, citing personnel policy. A pending records request filed by KHOL for all records relating to Snow’s suspension has been received by the county clerk’s office.  
In a press release, Snow states that he was cited for a policy called “fail to act” related to an arrest he made early on Oct. 21. Court records show he pulled over a Driggs, Idaho, woman for speeding and, after being told she was on release for a June DUI, administered a portable breath test, which showed her blood alcohol level to be more than twice the legal limit. 
Despite that result, Snow did not conduct a DUI investigation. That would have included a field test investigating signs of intoxication, such as a field sobriety test. Snow said that omission led to his suspension. 
“I know I’m under the microscope,” Snow said. “So, I chose the path that had the strongest legal foundation to support the arrest.”
Snow instead charged the Idaho woman for violating her previous DUI release order. A defense attorney, he said, could “not argue with a release order violation. You can argue with the DUI.” 
Carr declined to comment on how he viewed the case, but said his office is treating Snow as it would any deputy. Lt. Mark Priest, second-in-command at the sheriff’s office, put Snow on leave.
“Every single arrest that our deputies make, every report they write, everything they do, we look at it. We look at everything. We’re not just picking out Eric’s,” Priest told KHOL. 
Snow felt his actions have been under more scrutiny since a July arrest he made, he told KHOL. The sheriff’s office referred that arrest to the state for an independent evaluation. The Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation, in turn, advised elevating the case to the FBI, which determined it did not meet the threshold for a civil rights violation, the sheriff’s office said. 
Snow stands by the arrest of a Jackson man, whom he charged with speeding and arrested on suspicion of drug-impaired driving, he said. 
“[If] you’ve got somebody who’s demonstrating impairment, getting them off the road is the right choice,” Snow said. Jackowski added that the evidence of impairment dissipates over time. 
A field breath test and evaluation by a drug recognition expert found no evidence of impairment. Snow said the sheriff’s office declined his request to test the man’s blood for drugs beyond what the state typically looks into. Carr said the blood is preserved and had been tested for “everything in the world.” Snow declined to state which other drugs he wanted to test for.
Snow’s expertise called into question 
In his press release, Snow claims that Priest tried to have him “decertified” as a drug recognition expert after Snow ran advertisements highlighting the credentials. 
But a phone recording requested by KHOL and provided by the county shows a more complicated request related to Snow’s July arrest. 
In a recording from Sept. 21, months after the first DUI arrest, Priest talked to Lt. Evan Storch for about eight minutes. Storch, who is with the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office, runs the state’s drug recognition expert training. Storch trained Snow.
In the recording, Priest asks Storch to advise Snow to pause conducting DRE evaluations, not outright revoke his ability to do so, until the end of the election or until the Jackson man’s case “clears up.” 
Defense attorneys had “latched onto” a newspaper article covering questions about Snow’s July arrest, Priest said, and at least one party had chosen to exclude Snow’s testimony from a pending case.
“His supervisors immediately noticed it was not a good arrest. There was not any probable cause there,” Priest told Storch in the recorded call. “I’m trying to avoid making him look bad.”  
In response, Storch told Priest he wouldn’t decertify Snow without having “definitive details” but that he would give Snow “some advice about how to proceed.” 
Reached by phone, Storch told KHOL that he was surprised to be asked to intervene with Snow’s capacities “so close to the election.” He said “nothing” in Snow’s July case “would give me pause to decertify Snow.” He declined further comment. 
In the recorded call, Priest acknowledged that the request was a “very slippery slope” during the election season. 
Many sheriff’s deputies appear to back Carr 
In his interview with KHOL, Snow accused Carr of violating a Wyoming law that prohibits a public official or employee from using “public funds, time, personnel, facilities or equipment for political or campaign activity.” 
Snow claims that has happened several times, including at a GOP-sponsored sheriff’s debate on Oct. 5 where more than a dozen officers stood and sat in the back of the library auditorium. Dressed in uniform, the officers clapped intermittently after the two-term incumbent spoke. GOP moderators asked them to hold their applause, though some later continued.
About 14 sheriff’s deputies line the back wall in the Teton County Library auditorium during a candidate forum hosted by the Teton County GOP. (Sophia Boyd-Fliegel/KHOL)
“What you witnessed at the Republican debate was a crime on the part of the sheriff,” Snow said. “By him asking everyone to be there, that’s misuse of office.”
Carr said he didn’t ask deputies to attend. 
“I was [as] surprised as anyone,” Carr said. 
Snow said on-duty deputies should not have attended the forum. 
“If you’re getting paid by the taxpayer, you shouldn’t be going to a political event,” Snow said. 
Lt. Priest confirmed deputies were not asked to attend, adding that he himself is a Republican, who grew up in Wyoming. 
“Everybody wanted to be there,” Priest said.

name: VTDigger
title: Pownal will consider a 5-year permitting pause on data center facilities
text:
Some in the Pownal area are concerned the former Green Mountain Race Track site is being eyed for a data center. The selectboard is considering a moratorium on such projects. File photo by Holly Pelczynski/Bennington Banner

This story by Jim Therrien was first published in the Bennington Banner on Oct. 26, 2026.
POWNAL — The Pownal Select Board is considering a town moratorium on data center facilities amid concerns the former Green Mountain Race Track site is being eyed for a center.
Other towns in Vermont and around the country have enacted or discussed moratoriums for such centers — especially the large-scale facilities associated with artificial intelligence development, which would create a significant new demand for electricity and water for cooling purposes.
The 144-acre former track site off Route 7 near the Williamstown, Massachusetts, line is located along the Hoosic River and believed to have significant groundwater supplies. The property has been for sale, and rumors have surfaced about a possible purchase by an unidentified party, town officials have said.
Five-year pause
Board member Jeannie Alexander noted the data center rumors during an Oct. 22 meeting, and the fact that other communities in Vermont have enacted or proposed data center permitting moratoriums.
She said that after researching data center issues, she has concerns that an outright ban on the centers “might not be legally binding,” adding, “I think a moratorium is probably the way to go.”
Alexander then suggested wording for a five-year moratorium — to be considered by the board and by Pownal residents during a future board meeting.
A moratorium, she said, would give the town time to enact zoning or other regulation aimed at controlling the impacts of a large data center facility.
‘Irresponsible to wait’
Alexander said Monday in an email, “It is my understanding that a number of developers have been interested in that site in particular. It would be foolish and irresponsible to wait until after the fact to try and protect our town’s natural resources.”
She added, “It’s obvious that the powers that be in Montpelier aren’t coming to save us or any other small town in Vermont, and so we had better be prepared to take care of ourselves and our neighbors. There are significant issues with water quality in Pownal, and energy bills are already too high. We must begin taking seriously the impact that today’s decisions will have on our great-grandchildren.”
She said she supports responsible and sustainable growth, adding that the proposed moratorium “would require the Conservation Commission and the Planning Commission to work together to determine what sort of potential development we could work to attract. Moratoriums on (large power- and water-using) data centers are one of the only issues folks on the left and right are in agreement over. If some tech billionaire wants to make more money off of data centers, they can damn well do it somewhere else. Not Pownal.”
Lawmakers supportive
On the state level, Sen. Seth Bongartz, D-Bennington District, and Rep. Jonathan Cooper, D-Pownal, agreed that the town is right to try to protect its interests.
A bill to regulate large data centers “sailed through both chambers on its way to the governor, because it was designed to protect towns like Pownal from situations like this,” Cooper said Monday in an email. “The bill (H.727) had remarkably broad support: It was unanimously passed out of a committee with five Democrats, three Republicans, and one independent. It was subject to just one roll call vote on its way to the governor, and that was 26-3 in favor of the bill.” 
He added, “I applaud the town select board for listening to its residents, but I worry that in the absence of state law the town will not be able to rely on services of the Attorney General’s office if there is a challenge to the moratorium.”
The Legislature will return to this topic in the next session, Cooper said, adding, “What little opposition the bill actually garnered while it was in the Legislature tended to focus on the unlikelihood of the state needing such regulation, and the adequacy of our existing framework to manage this new phenomenon. I don’t think too many Vermonters are taking great comfort in that line of thinking.”
‘A balanced bill’
Bongartz said in an email: “We passed a balanced data center bill this past session. It controlled water usage and noise. It also required that any center be deemed to be in the public interest, either via building new transmission capacity and/or lowering rates for other users.”
He added, “For reasons that are unfathomable to me, (Gov. Scott) vetoed that bill and left us exposed to an application for a data center with no guardrails in place. His explanation made no sense.”
Scott has contended that Vermont already has strong environmental and other regulations in place to consider applications for permits for data centers.
Bongartz said, however, that the Pownal board “is right to be concerned. A moratorium makes sense until we can get a comprehensive bill regulating the environmental and social impacts of data centers through the Legislature and signed by the governor.”
Last year’s final bill version “will likely get reintroduced,” he said. “It will then likely get amended to some degree as it works its way through the committee process. I do not see it getting weaker. People want to be protected.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Key accountability index for CT schools ticked up last year
text:
Connecticut’s Next Generation Accountability Index for public schools showed modest improvement across most categories in the 2025-26 school year, the State Department of Education said Tuesday.
The index combines 12 factors, including test scores and chronic absenteeism, to produce one number representing the performance of Connecticut schools. For the 2025-26 school year, the statewide index came out to 72.2, a slight improvement over the previous year’s 71.8 but below its pre-pandemic 2018-19 score of 74.2.
Among the highlights were the 4-year graduation rate, which reached 91.2%, and the proportion of students demonstrating postsecondary readiness, which reached 49.9%. Both numbers were the highest for their respective categories since the index was introduced for the 2014-15 school year.
CSDE opted to focus on the latter measure during its press conference. 
According to Chief Performance Officer Ajit Gopalakrishnan, postsecondary readiness has been rising thanks to recent state investments in dual credit courses. Connecticut used some of its federal COVID relief funding to expand those courses, and the General Assembly recently gave the program a line item in the state budget, allowing it to continue after federal dollars dried up.
However, Gopalakrishnan said the program needs further investment from the General Assembly to meet demand. His comment drew a laugh from Education Committee Ranking Member Rep. Lezlye Zupkus, R-Prospect, who was also in attendance.
Education Commissioner Charlene Russell-Tucker said CSDE is still determining just how much additional funding it needs for the dual credit programming.
In the 2025-26 school year, 34.6% of 11th and 12th graders earned three or more college credits through dual credit courses. That’s a more-than 12% increase over what it was during the pandemic.
“It’s not a promise of a credit. It’s actual college credit that goes on a transcript,” Gopalakrishnan said.
At the press conference to highlight the impact of dual credit programming were two high school students, Bena Mejia Romero of Stratford and Evan Gaudio of Wallingford.
Romero, who immigrated with her family from Honduras when she was six, said the dual credit courses she’s taken in medicine have encouraged her to explore becoming a nurse practitioner or doctor.
“I feel more prepared to take on that next step because I’ve begun exploring the field,” Romero said.
Gaudio said he learned how to use CAD software in his dual credit coursework to design a load-bearing structure and a 3D-printed car. He said the class taught him how to work on a timeline and was a “phenomenal confidence booster.”

Students also meet the postsecondary readiness threshold if they meet certain benchmarks on ACT, SAT, AP or IB tests. Postsecondary readiness among high needs students has risen 8.9% since the pandemic. Among Hispanic and Latino students, it has risen 10.2%, and among Black students, it has risen 12.2%.
Chris Todd, executive director of the Office of Early College Programs at the University of Connecticut, said last year, 43% of dual credit students at UConn identified as first generation, and 41% received fee waivers to attend at no cost.
One key use of the accountability index for CSDE is to identify schools that need additional support. If schools score particularly poorly, the state offers them administrative support from the department’s turnaround office, and they also become eligible for additional funding through Title I. 
This year, the state identified 72 schools for this enhanced support. Those include nine from Bridgeport and 15 from Hartford — both districts that have been the subject of state intervention regarding their finances. New Haven, which has also reported severe funding challenges, has eight schools on the list.
Although most factors on the accountability index improved, growth in Math and English Language Arts moved in the opposite direction. According to Gopalakrishnan, growth measures how much individual students’ test scores improve from one year to the next. A lower growth number on the accountability index means those scores didn’t rise quite as quickly as they did the previous year.
CT Mirror reporter Sasha Allen contributed to this story.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: Water pipeline discussion is about choosing our future, or letting scarcity choose it for us
text:
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' Omaha District Oahe Project hydropower house on the Missouri River near Fort Pierre is pictured on July 16, 2025. (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers photo by Delanie Stafford)Imagine if Lake Oahe were filled with oil instead of water.
We would treat it as one of the country’s greatest economic assets. Pipelines would be flowing. Industries would be built around it. The cost of moving oil west would be a budget line item.
Water deserves the same kind of thinking. The difference is that we see the price of gasoline every time we stand at the pump, while generations of public investment have masked much of the true cost of water by the time it pours from a kitchen faucet.
Most of us barely notice the water portion of the monthly utility bill. Yet we will pay about $1.50 for a 20-ounce bottle, the equivalent of nearly $10 a gallon.
That is why we should look differently at the Western Dakota Regional Water System’s proposed pipeline. The latest published estimate is about $4.5 billion to move Missouri River water roughly 165 miles west through a massive pipeline and major pumping facilities.
Will South Dakota be ready when other states come for our water?

The conversation is about to become more visible. The system plans to begin a public campaign in January to build awareness of the project. Before the debate centers on the $4.5 billion price tag, we should ask a more basic question: What is the water worth?
The system secured a future-use permit for 20,765 acre-feet of Missouri River water annually, the equivalent of about 18.5 million gallons a day based on projected needs through 2080. Spread $4.5 billion of construction cost across 50 years at that volume, and the simple capital cost comes to roughly 1.3 cents per gallon before financing, treatment, pumping and operating expenses.
A penny or two a gallon does not make a $4.5 billion project cheap. It does make the number look different.
To decide whether it is worth doing, we must also ask what the water would make possible and what happens without it.
Generations of public investment made dependable water affordable. In the process, we forgot what scarcity costs.
The Lewis & Clark Regional Water System offers a useful reminder. It took decades and hundreds of millions of dollars to build and now serves roughly 350,000 people in South Dakota, Iowa and Minnesota. Its system is designed to deliver about 44 million gallons a day, more than twice the capacity proposed for Western Dakota.
Imagine southeastern South Dakota without the Lewis & Clark system. Growth would have been harder, more expensive and increasingly constrained by local water supplies.
The Western Dakota proposal did not emerge from a wish list. A 2019 South Dakota School of Mines study found that existing supplies could meet demand during average years but become less reliable during prolonged drought.
The pressure is easiest to see around Rapid City, Box Elder and Ellsworth Air Force Base.



Quotation







Generations of public investment made dependable water affordable. In the process, we forgot what scarcity costs.


Pactola Reservoir, high in the Black Hills, remains under drought pressure. Rapid City moved it to alert status and extended water restrictions year-round as inflows fell well below normal. The Bureau of Reclamation cut winter releases from Pactola in half to conserve water.
Pactola’s managers are doing what reservoir managers are supposed to do: storing water from wetter years for use during dry ones.
Then add growth.
Not everyone in the Black Hills wants more of it. A new regional water supply would make more development possible.
But the demand projections behind the pipeline are based largely on population and water-use trends planners already expect. Without another supply, growth may slow, become more expensive or go elsewhere. Infrastructure is expensive. Scarcity is expensive, too. The pipeline would not create growth so much as remove water as a limit.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rapid City is already growing, and Ellsworth’s impending B-21 mission is adding to population, housing and infrastructure demand.
Ellsworth has also shown how expensive it can be to lose water you already have. The Air Force is spending roughly $12.5 million on a water system to restore dependable service to residents whose private wells were affected by PFAS contamination while providing additional system capacity. Federal documents estimate the contamination plume extends approximately 25 miles south-southeast along Boxelder Creek toward the Cheyenne River.
Water is remarkably inexpensive until the water you already have is no longer usable.
That brings us back to $4.5 billion.
If this were oil, we would understand the investment almost instinctively. Missouri River water is one of South Dakota’s great assets, and using a portion of it for western South Dakota’s future should not be dismissed simply because getting it there is expensive.
The question is not whether $4.5 billion is a lot of money. Of course it is.
The question is what South Dakota wants the future of western South Dakota to look like, and whether we choose that future while we still have options or allow water scarcity to choose it for us.
Water has a way of settling arguments. Eventually.

name: WyoFile
title: Judge declines to hold Laramie County Sheriff Kozak in contempt, but sets deadline for records dispute
text:
A judge denied Monday a request to hold Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak in contempt of court in a lawsuit concerning immigration arrest records.  
While acknowledging that Kozak and his counsel, Laramie County Attorney Mark Voss, didn’t fully comply with a court order requiring them to produce immigration arrest records, Laramie County Judge Robin Cooley wrote in her decision that there wasn’t clear evidence showing their noncompliance was willful. 
A Colorado law firm requested records from the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office related to a deputy’s April immigration arrest of Mario Fabian Valenzuela-Robles, a Mexican national with three children who are U.S. citizens. The legal practice, Lichter Immigration, is representing Valenzuela-Robles in ongoing immigration proceedings, and the evidence is vital to his defense in federal court, the firm has said. 
Alleging that it faced barriers to obtaining certain records, Lichter Immigration, represented by former Wyoming GOP Chair Drake Hill, sued Kozak and his office in July. Later that month, Cooley ordered Kozak to provide additional records concerning Valenzuela-Robles’ detention. 
But Kozak and Voss didn’t fully comply with that order, missing the agreed-upon deadline by two days. Some documents were in a format the plaintiffs couldn’t open or read. Kozak’s office didn’t provide a log explaining why certain documents were withheld. Because of these shortcomings, Lichter Immigration requested Cooley to hold Kozak and his office in contempt of court. 
But noncompliance alone, Cooley wrote in her decision, “does not establish civil contempt.” 
“Plaintiffs have not proven by clear and convincing evidence that the failure to comply was willful,” Cooley wrote. Kozak also noted this point. “The law says you have to willfully, you know, withhold the evidence, and so of course we didn’t do that,” he said in a phone call to WyoFile. 
That being said, Cooley continued, just because the defendants’ noncompliance wasn’t willful “does not make it acceptable.” 
She noted that the defendants helped draft the terms of the order compelling production of records. Cooley also pointed out that Hill had asked Voss in an August letter to address concerns about the records. 
The defendants’ failure to address those concerns “prolonged a dispute that should have been resolved without the necessity of further Court proceedings,” Cooley wrote. 
While declining to hold Kozak in contempt, Cooley ordered the sheriff and Voss to provide within 10 days a log explaining why certain records were withheld, records in a readable format and written explanations addressing each of the alleged missing records the plaintiffs had identified. 
Kozak said he had talked with Voss and expects to comply with the order in the next couple of days.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Return of the lame-duck session with RI General Assembly set to reconvene after November election
text:
Rhode Island Superior Court Associate Justice Luis Matos stands alongside Gov. Dan McKee during an Aug. 12, 2026, news conference announcing his nomination to the state Supreme Court. McKee has yet to formally submit the nomination to lawmakers for advice and consent. (Photo by Nancy Lavin/Rhode Island Current)For the first time in six years, state lawmakers are set to reconvene after the Nov. 3 election to consider the appointments of five magistrates and potentially four other judges, including Gov. Dan McKee’s pick for the Supreme Court.
Superior Court Presiding Justice Joseph A. Montalbano last week recommended Timothy G. Healy and Kara Hoopis Manosh for magistrate positions in the state’s highest trial court, subject to advice and consent from the Senate. All Rhode Island magistrates serve 10-year terms unlike judges who serve lifetime appointments.
Also up for consideration are Robert A. Ragosta and Therese M. Picard, who Family Court Chief Judge Michael Forte recommended for appointments to become magistrates in August. In addition, Forte recommended the reappointment of Traffic Tribunal Magistrate Erika Kruse Weller in January.
Senate spokesperson Greg Paré confirmed Tuesday that the chamber has received all five nominations.
“We anticipate potentially receiving (other) appointments from the governor and the judiciary,” Paré wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current Tuesday.
McKee in August nominated Superior Court Judge Luis Matos to fill the vacancy created on the state’s high court by Justice Maureen McKenna Goldberg’s retirement in the spring. The governor lost to Democratic rival Helena Bounnano Foulkes in the Sept. 9 primary. 
Foulkes faces independent Ken Block, Republican Aaron Guckian and two other independent candidates in the Nov. 3 general election.
State law requires the governor to formally transmit a Supreme Court nomination to both the House and Senate before lawmakers can provide advice and consent. But McKee has not yet done so, despite praising Matos as the most qualified of five candidates he interviewed — including former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi — during an Aug. 12 press conference.
“The governor has not forwarded a name to the House for a Supreme Court appointment, so there is no return date for the House,” chamber spokesperson Larry Berman wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current.
McKee also has yet to announce his decision to fill two Superior Court vacancies from a total of eight candidates recommended by the Judicial Nominating Commission on Aug. 12. The pair of vacancies opened when Montalbano became presiding justice and Jeffrey Lanphear retired.
The governor is also considering five candidates for a District Court chief judge recommended by the Judicial Nominating Commission on Friday. The vacancy was created by the Oct. 9 retirement of Jeanne E. LaFazia, who stepped down after 16 years on the bench.
The governor’s shortlist includes former state Sen. Stephen Archambault and District Court judges James Caruolo, Mary McCaffrey, J. Patrick O’Neill and Debra Saunders.
McKee’s office did not respond to requests for comment on the status of his judicial picks.
Paré said the Senate may also consider three additional Traffic Tribunal magistrates selected by its chief judge.
The Rhode Island Senate is scheduled to meet Nov. 5 to formally receive appointments and refer them to the Judiciary Committee. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)
When will they meet?
State law requires a seven-calendar-day waiting period after lawmakers receive a nomination before they can consider it. The House and Senate must separately confirm Supreme Court nominees within 60 days of submission, while the Senate has 90 days to confirm other judicial nominees. 
If lawmakers fail to meet those deadlines, the governor must submit another nominee.
Senate President Valarie Lawson outlined five meeting dates in an Oct. 21 email to senators, opening with a reminder that the chamber was “anticipating receipt of judicial appointments” requiring lawmakers’ advice and consent.
The full 38-member Senate is scheduled to meet Nov. 5 to formally receive appointments and refer them to the Judiciary Committee, which is scheduled to hold hearings Nov. 17 and 18. The Senate is set to consider nominations on Dec. 1, with a second session the following day if needed.
Lawmakers last reconvened following a summer recess in December 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic prompted an unusual lame-duck session at Rhode Island College to pass a state budget and consider judicial nominations, including those of Supreme Court justices Melissa Long and Erin Lynch Prata.
“We’ve gotten used to a legislature that once they go home in June they don’t come back,” John Marion, executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island, said in an interview.
Marion said these sessions were more common when turnover in the judiciary created more vacancies or lawmakers returned to override vetoes by Republican governors.
“It’s certainly not without precedent to see lame-duck legislatures do this,” Marion said. “It’s not mischievous — this is their duty under the way the law reads.”
All 38 senators face reelection. Nine House lawmakers chose not to run again for a seat in the chamber.
