name: Rhode Island Current
title: So many RI General Assembly seats are unopposed. But this Senate race is unusually crowded.
text:
Left to right, Republican Sen. Thomas Paolino faces independent John Barr, Democrat Nelly Burdette; and Independent Jina Petrarca i n a four-way Senate District 17 race. (Contributed photos) 

About Senate District 17
Represented by Sen. Thomas Paolino since 2016
Geography: parts of North Smithfield, Lincoln, and North Providence
Population: 28,145 residents; 20,248 registered voters
Partisan breakdown: 57% unaffiliated; 26% Democrat; 17% Republican 
Demographics: median age: 44.2; 84.7% white; $112,017 median household income (2024)


Editor’s note This is the second in a three-part series on state legislative races, chosen based on competitiveness between candidates and relevant district issues. Of the 113 seats in the Rhode Island General Assembly, all of which are elected every two years, 24 seats feature at least two candidates on the Nov. 3 ballot. 
A professional chauffeur, a clinical psychologist, a civil litigator, and a lead paint inspection company owner.
It’s not the beginning of a joke about an unlikely combination of people walking into a bar. It’s the list of candidates vying to represent Rhode Island’s Senate District 17, the only state legislative race with four names on the Nov. 3 ballot. “I find it interesting,” Republican Sen. Thomas Paolino said of the crowd of his challengers: Democrat Nelly Burdette and independents John Barr II and Jina Petrarca.
And unusual. Nearly 80% of legislative candidates are unopposed this year.
Thomas Paolino: A decade of experience on Smith Hill 
First elected in 2016, then as the youngest member of the General Assembly, Paolino, now 35, has always had at least one competitor on the general election ballot. But never three.
Yet he’s confident after a decade of experience on Smith Hill. He lists accomplishments such as bringing money to district schools, supporting creation of an inspector general’s office and mandating financial literacy proficiency for high school students.
Paolino also pointed to his work in support of healthcare reform, including co-sponsoring bills 2026 to regulate artificial intelligence in mental healthcare, and set up a preventive health state Medicaid pilot program.
If reelected, his priorities include removing surcharges from electricity bills related to state taxes and fees — he proposed funding the programs through the state budget instead — and “returning local control” on housing development to municipalities. He did not specify what measures he would propose on housing, or if that would include repealing existing state affordable housing mandates.
“My ideas come to fruition. You cannot deny that,” said Paolino, a licensed chauffeur and lifelong Lincoln resident.



Quotation







My ideas come to fruition. You cannot deny that.


– Republican Sen. Thomas Paolino


Not according to his challengers, all of whom say they are frustrated with the lack of progress on healthcare, energy costs and economic growth.
Nelly Burdette: Backed by progressive group 
“I was waiting for someone else who was more of an entrenched politician to come in and navigate that process, and then I started to look around and realize there was no one who was going to do that,” said Burdette, 50, of Lincoln.
A first-time candidate and clinical psychologist, Burdette pointed to her professional experiences in mental healthcare and her personal background as a Ukrainian refugee and working mom of three children as her qualifications to represent the district.
“The experience of psychology has made me really very comfortable in sitting in different spaces, having different conversations, and actually inviting people in who disagree,” Burdette said.



Quotation







I was waiting for someone else who was more of an entrenched politician to come in and navigate that process, and then I started to look around and realize there was no one who was going to do that.


– Democratic challenger Nelly Burdette


Her platform centers on healthcare reforms, such as integrating mental health into primary care based on the model at Care Transformation Collaborative of Rhode Island, where she works as chief clinical officer,  and creating a state-administered, single-payer healthcare system, akin to legislation under review in Massachusetts. 
Burdette criticized Paolino for missing eight out of nine meetings of a Senate panel charged with studying primary care workforce solutions, including a new medical school at the University of Rhode Island. Paolino only attended the final meeting in January. He cited work conflicts, but said he read all of the relevant material to stay informed on the commission’s progress.
Backed by the Rhode Island Working Families Party, Burdette said she believes in “progressive principles,” including the millionaire’s tax. But she stopped short of identifying as a progressive, also emphasizing her ability to work with people whose views differ from hers.
Burdette distinguished herself as the candidate who can most relate to the affordability struggles of her community. Unlike the two independent candidates on the ballot, Burdette said she cannot afford to self-fund her campaign.
Burdette had just over $4,500 in her campaign account as of Oct. 5, mostly from individual donors plus $1,000 from political action committees representing various unions that have endorsed her.
Petrarca donated $30,000 of her own money to her campaign, according to her campaign finance report. Barr loaned $2,000 to his campaign, and has not raised money from other donors. 
Paolino also has more than $23,000 in outstanding loans from campaigns dating back to 2016.
Jina Petrarca: Working with all sides
Petrarca, 50, a civil litigator with her own law firm in Cranston, has pledged to forgo the $20,922 salary and health insurance benefits that come with the state job, if elected.
Yet Petrarca said she, too, understands the cost concerns of constituents, noting her volunteer work with a food pantry that helps primarily working families.
A self-described conservative Democrat, Petrarca ran as a Democrat for the same Senate seat in 2016, losing to Paolino by less than 2 points.
Petrarca said she has gone back and forth between identifying as a Democrat and independent over the last decade, ultimately concluding there was “too much noise” in both parties.
Yet she was confident she could work with both parties in the Rhode Island General Assembly to get things done.
“I’ve spent 26 years getting unhappy people to the table and making them compromise,” Petrarca said, referring to her job as a civil litigator.



Quotation







I’ve spent 26 years getting unhappy people to the table and making them compromise.


– Independent challenger Jina Petrarca


On her agenda: eliminating the corporate tax and expanding tax relief for seniors.
The mom of two college-aged children, Petrarca also called for education reforms including more autonomy for teachers and more state funding for students with special educational needs.
John Barr: Seeks to return to State House
Barr, 62, who owns a lead inspection business, served as a Democratic state representative for 10 years starting in 1990, helping secure a share of lottery revenue from Bally’s Twin River for the town of Lincoln and formally enshrine coffee milk in state law as the official state drink.
Nearly 40 years after he was first elected, the father of four and soon-to-be-grandfather he said he has more experience, and more time, to build on his past accomplishments.
“I am basically retired, but I still have all my mental faculties, I still have the energy, and I have time on my hands,” Barr said. “I look at how diverse the political landscape is and I know how to navigate it.”



Quotation







I look at how diverse the political landscape is and I know how to navigate it.


– Independent challenger John Barr


Barr denounced the state’s $15.2 billion budget bottom line, suggesting a 5% cut across all departments.
Barr also called for energy reforms, including extending the 2033 deadline for the state’s 100% renewable electricity deadline by at least 10 years, and setting up long-term plans to deal with solid waste management and limited water supplies.
Barr criticized Paolino for “getting nothing done,” during his time in office, and for nonsubstantive campaign materials.
“Reading his literature, it’s like reading philosophy from Immanuel Kant,” Barr said. 
Paolino rejected Barr’s claims, noting that as a member of the minority party, some of his initiatives end up passing with Democratic sponsorship.
How they compare on issues, governor’s race
Like Paolino, Petrarca and Barr opposed the ban on the sale of assault-style weapons that passed in 2025. Burdette supported the law. 
All three challengers said they would have voted in favor of the three-year charter school moratorium approved at the end of the 2026 session. Paolino voted against it.
In the governor’s race Burdette is backing Democratic nominee Helena Buonanno Foulkes, while Petrarca is supporting independent Ken Block. Barr had not decided and Paolino declined to say.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Himes, Goldstein face off in rematch in CT’s 4th District
text:
This is the fourth in a series of stories profiling candidates in each congressional district race. Credit: ct mirror

Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District, in the southwestern corner of the state, has seen somewhat of a political transformation over the past two decades.
The district was a Republican stronghold for 40 years and was represented by more liberal Republicans. But that changed in 2008 when Jim Himes first ran and flipped the seat during the first election of Barack Obama. Himes defeated Chris Shays, a moderate Republican who would often buck his own party.
Shays was the last Republican from Connecticut to serve in Congress.
Since then, the 4th District has been reliably blue and is expected to stay that way after the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Himes has some theories about what happened, pointing to the shifting dynamics within a political party and not so much the electorate itself.
“The nature of the district hasn’t changed that much. The Republican Party has changed radically, and so my district is in the category of educated districts in which independent voters and even some Republican voters have abandoned the Republican Party. And we started to see this, by the way, under George W. Bush,” Himes said, noting that was when the GOP became more socially conservative. (Members of the Bush political dynasty have strong ties to Greenwich and the 4th District.)
While his district’s voting patterns changed over the last two decades, Himes said other places around the country, like pockets of New York City, are drifting leftward among a younger electorate.
“It’s important to know that the change in the 4th Congressional District is like the change that you’ve seen in other older, affluent, educated districts,” he continued. “And I tell people someday, if the Republican Party ever goes back to being the Republican Party of Mitt Romney or John McCain, this will be a lot less blue of an area.”

Kay Maxwell moderates a debate between, from left, Independent candidate Benjamin Wesley, Republican candidate Dr. Michael Goldstein and Incumbent Democrat Jim Himes during the Lower Fairfield County League of Women Voters candidate debate for Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District at the Westport Library on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Himes faces a rematch on Nov. 3 from Republican Michael Goldstein. Independent Party nominee Benjamin Wesley, a mechanical engineer, will also be on the ballot, running for a second time.
It’s the third time that Goldstein, a doctor and attorney, has run for the seat. He lost the Republican primary in 2022 but became the nominee in 2024, eventually losing to Himes. This year, he was the party-endorsed candidate and won the Republican primary in August.
In his own assessment of the district, Goldstein said there’s “probably a larger Democrat presence in the 4th District than there was” and noted it’s economically diverse. He also said Democrats have been more organized and better-funded than Republicans in terms of running campaigns — a sentiment other GOP candidates running for federal office in Connecticut have shared.
Connecticut’s southwestern corner is home to many commuters who work in New York. The district includes some of the wealthiest pockets of the state but also has a massive wealth gap.
Goldstein said he decided to run again despite the growing polarization in U.S. politics. He also raised concerns about more candidates who are affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America.
“One of the things I notice is that I think the society is becoming much more polarized, and I think that that’s a bad trend,” Goldstein said. “People can have their political differences, but the polarization I think is just bad for our democracy, and it just paralyzed things.”
Goldstein said he worries about the leftward pull of the Democratic Party, especially if it takes control of the House majority next year. He called socialism a “failed ideology.”

Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking member on the House Intelligence Committee, arrives for a closed-door briefing by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and others on the military strike on a suspected drug smuggling boat and its crew in the Caribbean near Venezuela Sept. 2, at the Capitol in Washington, Tuesday, Dec. 9, 2025. Credit: J. Scott Applewhite / AP

If Himes wins another term and Democrats take back the House, the congressman hopes to become chairman of the House Intelligence Committee next year. He has served as ranking member for the past three years of a more secretive panel that oversees the intelligence community. Because of that role, he has talked about election security and efforts to undermine faith in the midterms.
His job as the ranking member places him in the “Gang of Eight,” a group that consists of the Republican and Democratic leaders in the House and Senate plus the chairs and ranking members of both intelligence committees. Because of that, he typically gets a heads-up on major military actions, though that wasn’t the case with Venezuela and Iran.
The Intelligence Committee has oversight over U.S. intelligence agencies as well as some issues concerning the Pentagon and other government agencies. As a potential chairman, Himes has previewed oversight of the Trump administration as a main objective.
“What I can talk about is an effort we’re going to make to try to shine a light on some of the entities who have bent a knee to Donald Trump’s demands,” Himes said, referring to law firms, universities and corporations that do business with the intelligence community. “We’re going to shine a light on instances where contractors and others did the administration’s bidding, either illegally or, if not illegally, at least in ways that raise pretty ugly conflicts of interest.”
He also serves on the House Financial Services Committee.

Republican candidate Dr. Michael Goldstein greets a candidate during the Lower Fairfield County League of Women Voters candidate debate for Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District at the Westport Library on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

As a physician, healthcare is a priority issue for Goldstein. He cited concerns over Democratic policy proposals like “Medicare for All,” arguing that healthcare needs more competition and choice. And as he has in past campaigns, he raised concerns about high energy prices amid debate over a natural gas pipeline that could serve the state and frustration over I-95 becoming a “parking lot.”
Goldstein has said he wants to see an expansion of trade schools that could provide “AI-proof” jobs and a requirement that universities disclose to applicants the salary ranges of graduates with each type of degree.
On artificial intelligence, he believes the federal government has a role to play in protecting Americans from misuse and harm but said they need to find a balance on regulation to keep up with other countries.
Himes sees “perennial issues” that come up every two years in his reelection races like housing, infrastructure and cost of living. On the latter, he said there’s an urgency — especially if his party regains the majority — for Democrats to follow through on their rhetoric around affordability and balance that out with their opposition to the Trump administration’s actions.
He said the “21st Century ROAD to Housing Act” — the bipartisan bill to ease the construction of new homes — was a step in the right direction during this Congress but noted it’s “not transformative” and said more work will need to be done on housing.
Himes also highlighted the federal money from the infrastructure law passed during the Biden administration that’s going toward the ongoing WALK Bridge replacement project in Norwalk to help the Amtrak and the Metro North systems.
But Goldstein bemoaned that money from major federal legislation passed in recent years has prioritized Hartford and should have been spread around the state more.

during the Lower Fairfield County League of Women Voters candidate debate for Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District at the Westport Library on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Himes, Goldstein and Wesley squared off in a debate last week that was hosted by the League of Women Voters. Himes’ opponents took aim at his record but from opposite sides of the political spectrum.
Wesley, who’s running as an independent, said he wants an economic agenda that mirrors progressive Democratic candidates running for Senate like Angie Nixon in Florida and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. That includes a single-payer healthcare system like “Medicare for All,” free childcare, paid family leave and, on housing, a national freeze on rent and moratoriums on evictions.
Goldstein, meanwhile, blamed the rising costs of healthcare on the Affordable Care Act. He doesn’t support single-payer options and wants to see more competition as a way to lower costs.
Himes touted his record and kept more of the focus on the Trump administration.
The congressman is one of the most prolific fundraisers of the incumbent lawmakers running for reelection and has the largest campaign account of all the Connecticut Democrats: $2.4 million cash on hand.
Goldstein hasn’t been able to keep pace on that front, raising a total of about $59,000 throughout the entire campaign.
Like his fellow Republicans seeking congressional office, Goldstein said he’s not getting much help from the party and doesn’t have the resources for advertising on the airwaves. Some of that, he said, is due to Republicans at the state level focusing heavily on the governor’s race.
“I think that a more engaged Republican Party would probably be much better for the candidates. But this has been this way for a while. I don’t see it changing soon,” Goldstein said. “We’re using our funds to reach people through other means besides the air.”
In-person early voting began Monday, Oct. 19 and runs through Sunday, Nov. 1. The last day to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: ‘Go to Canada’: Trump touted Americans’ access to cheaper drugs. A new rule threatens it.
text:
The U.S. House approved a measure July 11, 2001, making it legal for Americans to buy prescription drugs from abroad by mail order from pharmacists like Pharmacist Kevork O'Hanian in Montreal, as a means to cut high pharmaceutical costs. A new rule by the Trump administration threatens that ability. (Photo by Darren McCollester/Getty Images)Days before it was to go into effect, the Trump administration pushed back a U.S. customs rule threatening the supply of vital prescription drugs imported by millions of Americans.
Under the rule, Customs and Border Protection and the FDA will require coding on packages that makes it easier to know what’s in them. It is aimed at collecting tariffs on even low-value imports, and at catching illegal drugs like fentanyl. It will also add costs and complex paperwork to each order.
Now the regulation, which was set to start Oct. 22, is delayed until Jan. 20.
While it is illegal to import most FDA-approved prescription drugs, the U.S. has allowed Americans to import legal medications in small quantities for personal use since 2003. The FDA rarely inspects the parcels.
“The information we have is there’s going to be a complete shutdown on Oct. 22,” Tim Smith, general manager of the Canadian International Pharmacy Association, said in an interview in early October. The 51 licensed retail pharmacies in his organization urged their hundreds of thousands of U.S. customers to file extra orders before Oct. 9 to be sure as many medications as possible arrived before the clampdown, Smith said.
“These are people in every case who have gone to the doctor, gotten a prescription for whatever, gone to the pharmacy to fill the order, seen how expensive it’s going to be, and then looked for an alternative,” he said. “Those are the people who’ve been coming to us for years.”
As Donald Trump campaigned in 2016, allowing people to import drugs was part of his platform. In his first presidential term, Trump let states buy cheaper drugs from Canada. He told Floridians at 2020 rallies that their state could “go to Canada” to obtain drugs for them.
But while Florida and Colorado joined the importation program, neither state has brought in any drugs yet.
Patients have, however, and they flooded authorities with at least 109,000 letters urging the FDA to clarify that the rule won’t stop personal-use drug shipments, said Ken Hunter, executive director of the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation. And Trump ally Laura Loomer called the rule a case of stupidity or sabotage, under a headline that asked, “So Why Is Someone in His Administration Trying To Make Prescription Drugs More Expensive Before The Midterms?”
Seventy-one congressional Democrats signed an Oct. 1 petition led by Reps. Jan Schakowsky of Illinois and Mark Pocan of Wisconsin to warn about the potential impact of the rule. Three House Republicans from Florida wrote separately to CBP and the FDA, noting that Floridians, unlike Americans in Northern states, can’t easily drive to Canada to buy medicine.
By cutting off imports, Hunter said, “they are going to lose millions, maybe billions in tariff revenue.”
“Why would you want to cut off this massive revenue source?” he asked. “Why would they want to cut people off from lifesaving medications two weeks before midterms?”
Pressure by advocacy groups may have led the agency to back off, said Lucia Mueller, president of PharmacyChecker, which helps patients find legitimate pharmacies to obtain cheaper drugs.
“Loomer’s political argument is sound,” she told KFF Health News. “We know she’s had Trump’s ear before.”
The agency’s Oct. 14 news release on the delay said it would help “avoid disruptions to certain international postal shipments.” It didn’t specifically refer to drug imports.
“This is an important short-term success,” said Gabriel Levitt, founder of Prescription Justice, a nonprofit that advocates for more-affordable drugs. “However, the underlying threat to personal prescription drug importation remains, and the next 90 days will be critical.”
A 2020 study found that 2.3 million Americans regularly imported medications from abroad, and some surveys show much higher numbers. About 4 in 10 Americans in a recent KFF survey said cost had led them to not take medications as prescribed over the past year.
When he was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation years ago, Leslie Waters learned that a 90-day supply of the blood thinner Eliquis, or apixaban, would cost $486. “Holy crap!” said the retired computer scientist, who said he lives off a monthly $1,886 Social Security check. Waters, of San Jose, California, learned about the Canada option on the internet and has been buying 90-day supplies from a pharmacy there for $57, including shipping.
Under previous administrations, orders worth $800 or less weren’t taxed or saddled with extensive paperwork. The new rule will require shippers of even low-value international parcels to transmit detailed information about their contents to CBP, along with tariff payments, which must be transmitted through a licensed customer broker.
Zonos, a U.S.-based company that handles logistics for mail from Canada and other countries, told clients in early September that its understanding was that CBP would no longer allow in personal prescription drug packages after the rule took effect, said Smith, of the Canadian pharmacy trade group. In an Oct. 6 webinar, Zonos senior broker Angela Macke said that the company would continue to ship the drugs but that it didn’t know whether the agencies would let them reach patients.
The pharmacy announcements have frightened thousands of customers, said Bill Hepscher, whose company, Canadian Medstore, has six Florida storefronts that help patients import drugs.
“It’s really been hair on fire,” he said. “I could spend my entire day fielding phone calls from people saying: ‘Can I no longer get my Eliquis? I could have a blood clot or stroke!’”
Hepscher said about half his clients buy their drugs from Canada, with many of the others buying from Australia, New Zealand, the U.K., or Turkey. He said 2025 was his company’s busiest year ever — changes to Medicare drug plans and increased enrollment in high-deductible Affordable Care Act plans had led seniors and younger people facing higher costs and copays to seek Canadian drugs.
“I only have 23 days’ worth of pills,” Roland Hofferber told KFF Health News in early October. The retired supply chain engineer in Muscatine, Iowa, takes Jardiance, also known as empagliflozin, to slow his chronic kidney disease. “If I don’t get some through pretty soon, I’m going to have to cut back or quit.”
The drug would cost him $641 for three months in the U.S., he said. He buys a generic from an Indian pharmacy for $54.
The FDA “hasn’t given parameters as to what they will approve and what they won’t,” Zonos’ Macke said during the webinar. “We’ve been told there will not be a general ban. But we cannot reassure U.S. patients. We have to see how FDA applies. They could be lenient. They could be very strict.”
When asked whether patients could still import prescription medicines, CBP spokesperson Jessica Turner said that pharmaceuticals remained under the FDA’s jurisdiction and that the FDA “will continue to determine whether imported medication shipments are admissible.” Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard said the FDA would “continue to evaluate personal imports on a case-by-case basis.”
White House spokesperson Allison Schuster did not respond to questions about imports but said Trump “remains dedicated to lowering the cost of prescription drugs.”
Since summer 2025, patients have had to pay tariffs on brand-name medicine shipments. In 2022, the FDA said it typically checked about 1 in 2,000 medication packages passing through U.S. customs.
“A lot of products weren’t even looked at, because CBP and FDA didn’t have full visibility” into what entered the country, Prescription Justice’s Levitt said. The rule requires shippers to post a bond and fill in a complex data form for each package, he noted.
“Let’s say you’re importing 90 days’ worth of Eliquis,” Levitt said. “FDA can now look on a screen and see that. Do they let it in, or refuse it under law?”
“If they don’t, there’s going to be a cohort of people who cannot afford their drugs anymore,” he said. “And those people are going to suffer.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Lowering beef prices requires curtailing ICE activity in Kansas and elsewhere
text:
Dodge City protesters gather at Wright Park on Sept. 25, 2026, to march to U.S. Rep. Tracey Mann's office. They were protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions in the community. (Photo by Morgan Chilson/Kansas Reflector)For the past five years, lawmakers in Washington, D.C., have been trying to lower prices, but every piece of data shows that families are being pushed to the limit by the cost of living. President Donald Trump’s administration has paid particular attention to lowering the price of beef, which has shot up more than 20% since he took office.
In August, his administration unveiled a plan to import more than 660 million pounds of ground beef, which farmers, ranchers, and even his closest allies rightly criticized. Prices have still not fallen. If Trump really wants to lower beef prices, he must stop the mass deportation agenda.
In September, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement showed up here in Kansas and swarmed small towns in the “Golden Triangle of Meatpacking,” where the communities of Dodge City, Liberal, and Garden City produce a fifth of the nation’s beef supply. At UFCW Local 2, we represent three of the four plants in the Golden Triangle of Meatpacking. During ICE’s operations, U.S. citizens were pulled on their way home from work by agents demanding papers, leaving them shaking and crying.
Families took their kids out of school as unmarked cars roamed, driving erratically in the chaos. Fear led hundreds of meatpacking workers to stay home, and the area’s four meatpacking plants were forced to slash production because of the chaos ICE agents brought with them.
It’s no secret that immigrant workers play a crucial role in America’s food supply chain, as they have for decades. When I meet with our UFCW members in southwest Kansas, I see essential workers who were there when our country needed them most during the COVID-19 pandemic. I see workers who work here legally and have been afraid to go to work after all the violence and racial profiling. They are being terrorized both at home and at work by inhumane enforcement, detention, and deportation policies.
But the effect ripples outside of Kansas. The major disruptions to beef production in our state will show up in higher prices for all Americans.
The UFCW is not the only group raising alarms. The Texas Cattle Feeders Association, Kansas Livestock Association and Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association have also spoken out, noting: “These ICE operations are having a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers that put beef on the table and keep the cattle supply chain moving.”
The entire meat industry knows the ramifications of this.
A report from the immigration group, America’s Voice already found that prices of items that required more immigrant labor outpaced inflation. Lettuce up 32.1%, canned fruit rose 7.9%, whole milk up 9%, and the list goes on.
Our nation’s beef, pork, and chicken supply is next if this cruel campaign continues. Production will slow, supply will fall, and prices will rise. It’s estimated that mass deportations could raise prices by 9.1% by 2028, at a time when working people are already struggling with record-high food costs.
Kansans, whether they’re buying beef at the store or working in a packing plant, deserve better.
In cities where ICE arrests increased fastest in 2025, data show that for every arrest made, four jobs were lost. Bringing these operations to small cities and rural communities like ours will cause even more disruptions than what we saw in the streets of major cities over the past 18 months.
A recent report from the AFL-CIO found that if the mass deportation plans being executed by the Trump administration continue, nearly 6 million jobs, nearly half of which are currently held by U.S. citizens, could be wiped out. These would be fundamental changes to our communities and our economy.
Workers are missing out on paychecks, farmers and ranchers are losing millions in lost revenue, and shoppers are paying higher prices. Since the sheer cruelty and inhumanity have not been enough to change immigration policy, perhaps the impact on food prices could be the wake-up call.
We need real immigration reform, but the president has to stop hobbling our food supply chain and put an end to the mass deportation madness.
Martin Rosas is the president of United Food and Commercial Workers (UFCW) Local 2, based in Bel Aire, representing workers in the grocery, retail, meatpacking and food processing industries. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: In 3-way secretary of state race, one candidate wants to take over elections
text:
The Wisconsin secretary of state's office is in the basement of the state Capitol building. (Wisconsin Examiner photo) Three candidates running for Wisconsin secretary of state in 2026 are seeking an office with duties that have been whittled away over the last several decades.
The Democratic Party candidate, JoCasta Zamarripa, and the Green Party candidate, Pete Karas, both focus on how they would do the work that’s still part of the office.
But the third candidate, Republican Jay Schroeder, has centered his campaign on taking back a power that hasn’t been part of the secretary of state’s job for more than half a century — running Wisconsin’s elections.


The Wisconsin Secretary of State’s current duties include maintaining a variety of state records, affixing the state seal to acts of the governor, certifying certain documents for people going overseas, certifying the state’s votes for U.S. President and U.S. Senate, and sitting on the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands.
The public lands board, which also includes the state treasurer and the state attorney general, makes loans for public projects to local governments and distributes the revenues from public lands timber sales to public schools through the state’s common schools fund.
The 2026 election is the first without an incumbent in 40 years. Democrat Doug La Follette, who began a four-decade run in 1983, resigned in 2023 after being reelected in November 2022.
Gov. Tony Evers appointed former state Treasurer Sarah Godlewski to complete La Follette’s term. She opted to run for lieutenant governor on the Democratic ticket this year rather than seek election to a second term as secretary.


JoCasta Zamarripa: Not just ‘ceremonial’
Former Democratic state Assembly member JoCasta Zamarripa seeks to return to state government after having served as a member of the Milwaukee Common Council. Elected to the Assembly in 2010, Zamarripa served five terms, stepping down to run for Milwaukee alder in 2020. She’s now halfway through her second term in that position.
JoCasta Zamarripa. (Campaign photo)
As she’s traveled the state, Zamarripa says, she’s heard from some voters that the secretary of state is a “largely ceremonial” job, but she strongly differs with that assessment.
The role as a member of the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands, which raises revenue from timber sales that go to public school libraries, is important, she says, because “our schools depend on that funding.” The board also provides competitive economic development and public project loans to local communities.
The office provides important services such as authenticating documents for overseas actions, from foreign adoptions to international business deals, Zamarripa says.
As an alder who has had to assist the community members she represents in a variety of contexts, “these are important constituent services that I’m well positioned to take on,” Zamarripa says.
She also favors adding staff and funds to the office.
Zamarripa says she decided to run for secretary of state after learning Gov. Tony Evers would not seek a third term and seeing that “there was going to be some movement” in the Democratic upper echelons of state government.
As the first Latina in the state Legislature and on the Milwaukee Common Council, Zamarripa said she “felt this was an opportunity for me to throw my hat in for a statewide run to galvanize and capture the Latino vote.” She said she believes her presence on the ticket could help curb the drop-off in voting by Latino voters in Wisconsin in the midterms.
“It’s very important that we retain this office in Democratic hands,” Zamarripa says.
Pete Karas: ‘People want more choices’
Long-time Wisconsin Green Party member and activist Pete Karas says he’s joined the race for secretary of state because he believes neither Democrats nor Republicans should have a political monopoly in Wisconsin.
Pete Karas (campaign photo)
“People are just sick and tired over the same two parties,” Karas says. “People want more choices.”
Karas says he’d actually like to see the job become a nonpartisan office, with its election in the spring along with local county board and common council races.
In the office itself, he favors modernization, noting that the incumbent, Sarah Godlewski, has taken steps to make state records more accessible to the public.
To that end, Karas says he’d support some additional funding, as well as partnerships with libraries, universities and nonprofit organizations who could “step up and help us modernize the records.”
Karas says he opposes a maneuver in the 2025-27 state budget that made an exception for  Milwaukee County from a longstanding state provision requiring counties to pay most of their traffic fine and forfeiture revenue into the Common School Fund, overseen by the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands.
The budget allows the county to use those funds to pay local prosecutors and district attorneys. The provision is now the subject of a lawsuit.
“I would have pushed the Board of Commissioners of Public Lands to file a lawsuit” against the funding carve-out, Karas says.
While Zamarripa says she’s confident she can overcome two opponents in the election, she acknowledges she’s concerned that Karas could pull enough votes that would otherwise go to her, thus enabling Republican Schroeder to get the most votes of the three.
Karas rejects that concern.
“I’m not running to take votes away from anybody,” he says. “The Democrats do not own people’s votes.”
Jay Schroeder: Replace the elections commission
Jay Schroeder won the Republican nomination with a vow to eliminate the Wisconsin Elections Commission and move election administration into the secretary of state’s office — as it is in 37 states.
Jay Schroeder, Republican nominee for Wisconsin secretary of state. (Campaign photo)
In the August primary, he got more votes than the candidate who had the party’s endorsement. “I was focused completely on cleaning up the election system — which needs to be done, and that’s why I won,” Schroeder says.
Current and former state elections officials and the other candidates have all rejected the premise of Schroeder’s campaign.
“Those criticisms are more political than anything else,” says Kevin Kennedy, who  served as executive director for two previous Wisconsin election administration agencies before the Republican-led Wisconsin Legislature created the elections commission.
Election administration was separated from the secretary of state’s office in 1974 and handed over to the State Elections Board, an independent agency that operated until 2007, followed by the Government Accountability Board, which the Wisconsin Elections Commission replaced in 2016.
Zamarripa finds Schroeder’s campaign message troubling. “I’m very worried,” she says, predicting that if Schroeder wins, “he will be emboldened and the Republican Party will be emboldened to give him as much latitude as possible” to carry out his agenda.
Karas calls Schroeder’s goal “a ludicrous proposal” — but says he doesn’t think it has any chance of taking effect. “There’s so many holes in what he’s proposing, I cannot believe any Legislature or any governor would sign on to that,” he says.
Schroeder, however, says that if he wins, he expects to make the case to whoever wins the race for governor on the grounds that “my crystal clear platform” focused on taking over election administration delivered his victory.
In that scenario, he doesn’t expect the putative next governor to ignore him. ” I think that’d be kind of hard for them to do that,” he says.
Focus on voter lists
This is Schroeder’s second try for the job as the GOP nominee. He lost the general election in 2018 to long-time Democratic incumbent Doug La Follette. He also ran for the Republican nomination in 2022 but didn’t advance.
Schroeder’s campaign’s central premise is that the Wisconsin Elections Commission is a failed agency, beset by problems that have sowed public mistrust.
The elections commission’s defenders say that’s an unwarranted claim. In 2024, the commission’s executive director, Meagan Wolfe, received awards from two national organizations for public service and for improving its operations.
Schroeder’s criticism emphasizes the state’s practice of preserving the records of people who have been removed from the list of active registered voters.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission maintains a statewide electronic voting database. About 1,850 local clerks across the state register voters and enter their information in the database. When voters die, move away, are found incompetent by a court or are convicted of a felony (preventing them from voting until their sentence is completed), local clerks record that information, too.
Wisconsin law doesn’t allow the elections commission to delete the records of people removed from the active registered list. Instead, their records are switched to “inactive.”
Inactive voters are not included in the lists of registered voters sent to each polling place before Election Day, according to the elections commission.
Inactive voters who qualify — for example, a person who moves out of state and then later returns to Wisconsin — must register again, said Emilee Miklas, the elections commission communications director.
The elections commission staff sends local clerks “Registration Alerts” identifying deceased people, potential duplicate records, and the names of convicted felons to be checked against local registration rolls. The alerts draw on Wisconsin Department of Health Services’ monthly death reports and Wisconsin Department of Corrections daily updates on felony convictions.
The state also gets data from the national Electronic Registration Information Center, which collects it from other states and from federal agencies, including the Social Security Administration. The elections commission staff most recently reported their findings at the commission’s October quarterly meeting.
Records retention suspicion
Wisconsin’s retention of records for inactive voters has been a source of conspiracy claims of widespread voter fraud by some activists. But the elections commission says the practice enables clerks to cross-check a registration against inactive voters — preventing a person registering from impersonating a dead person, for example.
“Basically, you have one database with 7 million records, and there’s a very good reason why we keep records of inactive voter records, deceased voters, because if you got rid of those, you would lose one of your best tools to combat election fraud,” said Don Millis, the commission’s Republican chair, at the Oct. 1 meeting.
Schroeder says he doesn’t see any need to keep the records of people no longer registered.
“There’s more deceased people on the voting rolls than there are alive,” he said in an interview, conflating the records of active voters with the inactive voters whose records are kept separate from the active list. “They don’t need to be in the system.”
Federal laws require all states to retain some records of people struck from the voting rolls, according to Sam Liebert, Wisconsin state director for All Voting Is Local.
Nevertheless, Schroeder says numerous other states are able to produce “clean lists” regularly and that Wisconsin should, too.
“When you’re deceased, you should have nothing to do with any voting system, any recording or anything,” Schroeder says. He calls the idea of using “historical reasons” to maintain a list of inactive voters “a bunch of baloney.”
He suggests that the state could “interface that with Social Security, so when someone’s benefits stop, their name would go off the voting rolls.”
The elections commission already uses Social Security data to identify people who have died and to remove them from the active voter lists, according to the agency.
Schroeder says he first decided to run for secretary of state after reading about Wisconsin’s practice of keeping the records of people no longer registered, then looking up the record for his deceased father and seeing him still listed as registered.
Schroeder says he did not try to contact either the local clerk where his father had lived or the Wisconsin Elections Commission to correct his father’s status, however. 
“I’m like, ‘wait a minute, that’s not right,’” he says, and it triggered his decision to run for secretary of state. Eventually when he looked again for his deceased father’s name, he was no longer listed as an active registered voter.
“All my goal is, why I’m running for this office, is to increase confidence in elections,” he says. “And anything that gets in the way of that in my opinion needs to be changed.”
Incidents including duplicate ballots being sent by the Green Bay clerk to voters two elections in a row and a thumb drive at Milwaukee’s central count in August that had the wrong database loaded on it have convinced him that the system is flawed, Schroeder says.
Both incidents were the subjects of elections commission investigations, and audit logs in the Milwaukee case showed no evidence of tampering, Votebeat reported.   
When Schroeder ran in the Republican primary in 2022 for the office, he told a crowd that he would not have signed “a sheet of paper for the election,” apparently a reference to the certification of electoral votes for Joe Biden, who won Wisconsin in the 2020 presidential election, Bill Lueders reported in a commentary for the Wisconsin Examiner.
In an interview last week, Schroeder didn’t deny the comment but waved it away.
“I think there was other things that maybe could have been checked into,” Schroeder said. “But generally speaking, the system works. Joe Biden [was] the president. I’m not living in the past.”
Before the primary, Schroeder held himself out as an “authentic MAGA activist” and a “MAGA aligned candidate on election integrity.”
Asked Monday about his alignment with the “MAGA” movement associated with President Donald Trump, Schroeder said, “I don’t know that I would. I would try to do what’s right.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Child welfare adviser wrapping up his work this year
text:
Indiana Department of Child Services Director Adam Krupp. (Photo courtesy of DCS)Special adviser Adam Krupp will likely wrap up his state employment by the end of the year after he completes a comprehensive evaluation of the state’s child welfare system.
The report is a follow-up to a 2018 assessment, conducted by the Child Welfare Policy and Practice Group, which was used to make key reforms.
Krupp left his post as head of the Indiana Department of Child Services in April, following a three-month medical leave. He transitioned to a special advisor role for Gov. Mike Braun on abuse and neglect issues while keeping his annual salary of $210,000.
New DCS Director Jennifer Dorfmeyer also makes $210,000.
“I get that a lot of people have criticized the role. They have questions about the role,” Krupp told the Capital Chronicle. “It helps if we look at this as an investment as opposed to an expense or a cost.”
“It’s a heartbreaking circumstance when you’re observing things that you know need to be fixed, but the day-to-day can be so overwhelming that that improvement gets stalled, or those strategic initiatives and priorities get put on the shelf for another 30, 60, 90 days because another crisis pops up,” he said. “Well, this role has allowed me to step away from all of that and just focus on what do we need to do and how are we going to get it done.”
Krupp files a weekly status report with the governor’s office on his activities. The reports indicate the majority of his 37-hour workweeks are being spent on the updated assessment he is crafting.
Other highlights include:

Meeting with experts on how to responsibly incorporate artificial intelligence into the agency
Reviewing legislation and consulting with lawmakers
Internal meetings with Dorfmeyer and other DCS staff
Meeting with foster parents to discuss their experience with the system
Reviewing monthly data on key performance indicators

Krupp said the most significant deliverable will be the comprehensive assessment, which is set to be hundreds of pages long.
“At a really high level, this is not designed to be critical of the past,” he said. “This whole exercise is: how do we make the system better? Because at the end of the day, as I always said as director, it’s about the best interests of the children, and they’re our most vulnerable population.”
He said it’s time to revisit the high-level assessment of the agency; examine where the data is trending and offer dozens of recommendations for the future. Some of those changes can be implemented internally, and others would have to be greenlit by the General Assembly.
In a statement the governor said he “grateful for Adam’s service and his commitment to Hoosier children,” adding, “I look forward to reviewing his final report and recommendations as to how our state can continue to serve and protect our most vulnerable.”
Krupp has also been looking at ways to harness AI: vetting the cost, implementation timelines and uses. He noted immediately that he doesn’t mean allowing AI to make child welfare determinations. Instead, it’s using AI to reduce paperwork and data entry so that caseworkers can spend more time with families and kids in the field.
He said there are programs now that can forecast staffing needs based on rising caseloads and even considering major plant shutdowns in a region of the state. Another tool is using AI to mine large files to identify possible kinship placements.
“You’ve got eight years of notes, you’ve got 11 case managers, and there are names scattered throughout this case management file for that child or that family,” Krupp said. “We want to find a kinship placement. That might take a case manager like a week to do. AI can do it in 60 seconds.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: At rally for David Crowley, Kamala Harris addresses women burdened by high costs
text:
During her speech, former Vice President Kamala Harris spoke about rising costs, criticized Tom Tiffany and told voters that they had the power to change the direction of the state and the country. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Democratic candidate David Crowley often asks his supporters to volunteer the “Three T’s”: “time,” “talent” and “treasure” — or money. But with about a week until the election, he put a new spin on the phrase at a rally with former Vice President Kamala Harris Monday evening. 
“I usually say the last piece is treasure, but we’ll make an executive decision and turn that third T into turnout,” Crowley said. “We may not have billionaires, but we got something better. We’ve got you.”
Harris reinforced that message as she addressed attendees at the Pfister Hotel in Milwaukee.  Harris said she came through Milwaukee to say “thank you” for the work people are doing to help elect Crowley, and she emphasized that the work needs to continue through Election Day. 
“People have been feeling like ‘I can’t do anything about this,’ and I know how much pain people are in,” Harris said, commenting on the “brutality” of the Trump administration and the feeling of powerlessness it engenders. But, she added, “That phase is over. We are now in a moment to turn anger into action.”
Crowley faces Republican candidate U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in the state’s first open race for governor since 2010. 
Harris told attendees that their voices and votes matter.
“You don’t have to put up with this,” Harris said. “They’re putting a whole lot of money to try and convince people either that their vote doesn’t count or to lead them astray, but we have the power of the people on our side, so for the next eight days, let’s get out there and do everything we possibly can in a way that we show people who we are, what we want from leadership, and what we deserve.”
Harris is the latest surrogate to speak on Crowley’s behalf. Other Democrats who have visited the state or plan to include Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Georgia U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. 
During her speech, Harris spoke about rising costs, criticized Tiffany and told voters that they had the power to change the direction of the state and the country. 
Ahead of Harris’ visit, Tiffany criticized the Crowley campaign, saying that he wants to bring California policies to Wisconsin. 
“Wisconsin rejected Kamala Harris once, and now it’s time to reject David Crowley and his tax-hiking, spending spree and toll road agenda,” Tiffany said in a statement. 
President Donald Trump won against Harris in Wisconsin in the 2024 election by fewer than 30,000 votes. During his second term, Trump’s popularity in Wisconsin has fallen to record lows with 60% disapproval in the latest Marquette Law School poll. 
“Let’s talk about the fact that David’s opponent denied the election of 2020,” Harris said. Tiffany voted against certifying voters’ choice of Biden in two states in the 2020 election, and said he would have voted against certifying Wisconsin’s vote. 
“By the way, we won. We won that election,” Harris said. 
Democratic candidate David Crowley takes a selfie with his wife and Harris. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
The rally was targeted at mobilizing women to vote and the economic pressure women are facing was a common theme among the speakers as well as one of the issues at the top of mind of women who attended. 
While waiting for Harris and Crowley, Sarah Bielejeski, a 38-year-old Milwaukee resident, told the Examiner that she was asked to attend by her friend’s daughter. She said she wasn’t too informed about the election, but that she knew “enough to know that Tom Tiffany is not right.” 
During the interview, Bielejeski reached for another attendee standing beside her to join in the conversation.
Megan Czarnyszka, a single mom from the Milwaukee suburbs, said she had decided to attend the rally so her daughter could witness the civic engagement and was looking forward to learning more. She said that while she supported a different candidate in the primary, she was now backing Crowley.
Both Bielejeski and Czarnyszka said they were glad to be in a room with like-minded people. 
Czarnyszka, a small business owner, said she wants Democrats to win control of the Legislature as well as the governor’s office because Affordable Care Act insurance has become too expensive for her and she also wants to see schools fully funded.
“It’s like tripled right now,” Czarnyszka said about her health insurance premiums. “The deductible will be another $1,500. We’re talking $5,000 before my insurance ever kicks in. We’re talking the difference between me thriving, having my medications, and going all the way back to like poverty levels.” 
Harris described cost of living as a women’s issue, as did, Crowley and his wife.
Ericka Crowley gave a speech emphasizing costs before her husband and Harris took the stage.
“I’m a mother of three, y’all. I got a child in college and I’m still trying to figure out how to pay this tuition. I was at the grocery store the other day and I was like, ‘Oh I’m so exhausted of these prices. I’m tired of it, and I know y’all are exhausted,” she said. “We deserve better.” 
Crowley highlighted the same issue when he took the stage. 
“We feel these prices, too, and so when I say I get it, I get it. You know who doesn’t get it though? Congressman Tom Tiffany. He went to Washington, DC, and sold Wisconsin out,” he said. 
Harris said she was used to reporters asking her to speak about women’s issues. “I’d look at them and say, ‘I’m so glad you wanna talk about the economy,’” Harris, the first female vice president and the second Black woman elected to the U.S. Senate, said. Then she pivoted to making a plug for Crowley.
“David had everything to say about what is important to all people, including women. He stands for affordable childcare — only 7% of your income should go to childcare,” she said, referring to one of Crowley’s policy proposals. “He stands for affordable healthcare. We all know his opponent voted for that big bad bill that cut Medicaid by a trillion dollars to help millionaires and billionaires to cut their tax bills.”

title: Once more, with feeling: Time to enter Maryland Matters’ election contest

He could be voting. He could be filling out his entry for the Maryland Matters election contest. Both require some brainpower, some luck and some gut feelings. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Ugly and frightening as election season can get – or is that Halloween? – the reassuring thing is that voters do finally get a chance to have their say. name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Commentary: A wake-up call for ‘We the People”: America needs us to act
text:
The U.S. Constitution, signed in Philadelphia in 1787. (U.S. Air Force illustration/James Borland)America’s future cannot be left to politicians while the rest of us watch.
We cannot condemn money buying influence, hatred dividing communities and loyalty to individuals replacing loyalty to the Constitution, then surrender our responsibility to change course.
As a proud American Muslim who chose this country as my home, I refuse to abandon its promise. But loving America requires the courage to confront its failures and the determination to repair them.
Patriotism demands more than waving a flag. It demands living up to what that flag represents.
Disappointment is not a plan. Outrage is not a strategy. Silence leaves our future in someone else’s hands.
The Constitution begins with “We the People.”
That means us. And on Nov. 3, 2026, those words must become action.
Seeing something and saying something are no longer enough. We must do something: Vote, organize, challenge misinformation, defend our neighbors and demand accountability.
Our ballots must carry an unmistakable message: Public office belongs to the people.
Reclaim democracy from big money. When wealth purchases privileged access, politics begins to resemble legalized bribery. Elect leaders committed to pursuing a constitutional amendment to overturn Citizens United, strengthening donor disclosure and expanding participation by small donors. A citizen’s influence should never depend on the size of a check.
Protect the vote. Demand secure, accessible elections, fair district boundaries and protection for election workers. Voters should choose their representatives; representatives should not manipulate maps to choose their voters. Candidates must accept lawful outcomes after legitimate challenges are resolved. Democracy cannot depend on whether your side wins.
Reject division disguised as leadership. Demand answers about groceries, housing, healthcare, education, energy costs and jobs. A struggling farmer and a struggling city worker deserve solutions, not reasons to hate each other. Reject prejudice against any race, religion or birthplace.
Unity, not uniformity. We can disagree without denying anyone’s dignity or belonging.
Defend constitutional limits. No president or party owns the government. Demand congressional oversight, respect for lawful court orders and protection for whistleblowers. Defend peaceful protest, religious liberty, due process, free speech and a free press, including when those freedoms inconvenience leaders we support.
Rights defended only for our allies will not remain secure for anyone.
Restore trust in the courts. Demand enforceable ethics standards, financial disclosure and clear recusal rules. I support constitutional reform establishing fixed judicial terms and electing federal judges, with strong safeguards against donor influence and political pressure. Judges must remain free to uphold the Constitution even when their decisions are unpopular.
Let the people directly choose their president. Pursue a constitutional amendment replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote, supported by clear counting and recount rules. Every voter should matter, wherever that voter lives.
These changes will require sustained work and broad agreement. One election can begin that work.
Give young Americans real influence. Create a “We the People” Youth Council of high school students from rural, suburban and urban communities, reflecting each region’s racial, religious, cultural and economic diversity.
Make participation accessible regardless of family income. Keep the council independent of campaigns. Give students mentoring and regular access to officials from both parties elected on Nov. 3.
Within its first year, the council should publish a democracy agenda, convene bipartisan forums and publicly track lawmakers’ responses.
Young people deserve more than photographs with politicians. They deserve a voice in the democracy they will inherit.
Before voting, ask candidates: What will you do, by when, and how will we measure your progress?
Then keep asking after Election Day.
Verify your registration. Make a voting plan. Help another eligible voter. Attend town halls. Track commitments.
No party owns patriotism. No politician owns America.
On Nov. 3, turn conviction into votes. On Nov. 4, turn promises into accountability.
“We the People” must mean us, and it must mean now.
God bless America. Let us make it worthy of its promise.
I will do my part. I promise.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Medical debt hit 1 in 4 Americans and 1 in 5 Ohioans last year, even the insured, study shows
text:
(Getty Images)Medical debt hit 1 in 4 Americans and 1 in 5 Ohioans last year, a new study shows, including those who have health insurance.
A recent study by the Urban Institute, supported by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, showed that more than a quarter of American adults reported medical debt for them or someone in their family in 2025, and more than half of those who reported medical debt owed at least $1,000.
Of those who reported debt, 26% were adults with current health insurance.
“Health insurance does not shield people from rising healthcare costs and the crushing burden of medical debt,” Katherine Hempstead, senior policy officer for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation said in a press release announcing the study.
“Historic cost increases and coverage losses are forcing impossible tradeoffs between healthcare and other basic needs.”
The study found that for those with medical debt, 1 in 7 Americans have past-due medical bills or bills they couldn’t pay at all. Adults ages 45 to 54 represented the largest population with medical debt, but 17.6% of those in the study who were on Medicare also reported owing medical debt.
Researchers at the Health Policy Institute of Ohio have also been studying medical debt and the impact it can have on families, as well as overall health outcomes in the state.
“As expected, being uninsured is a major risk for experiencing medical debt,” HPIO researcher Brian O’Rourke told the Capital Journal. “However, recent data in Ohio suggests that this is not just a problem for our uninsured population.”
Citing the Ohio Medicaid Assessment Survey, O’Rourke said more than 1 in 5 Ohio adults were struggling to pay off medical bills in the last year.
While the data shows the highest population of people having trouble paying off medical debt are those who don’t have insurance, a quarter of Ohioans with private insurance were also struggling to pay.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the Urban Institute study, researchers found that hospital services resulted in the largest debt reported, with 52% of adults with medical debt citing hospital costs.
Debts also came from specialists, dental care, and general doctor services, according to the research.
Source: The Urban Institute
O’Rourke said out-of-pocket medical spending is “a significant burden in Ohio,” with the average family’s out-of-pocket medical spending in the state exceeding the national average.
The Ohio institute has released several pieces of research showing the potential impact cuts to Medicaid through the federal budget spending bill (also called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), and reduced subsidies for the Affordable Care Act could have on Ohio’s uninsured population.
Ohio’s population in the ACA Marketplace has already seen a drop of 100,000, and the HPIO projects as many as 300,000 Medicaid participants will be dropped because of newly imposed work requirements, which O’Rourke said will likely leave “many uninsured and with limited resources to pay off medical bills.”
The Urban Institute study also noted anticipated changes, including worsening medical debt, from rising health insurance costs, along with Medicaid and ACA changes.
“This analysis shows medical debt is pervasive, affecting adults across age groups and income levels, and people with and without health insurance,” said the Urban Institute’s Michael Karpman, in a statement.
“It will be important to monitor how the burden of medical debt shifts as policies restricting access to Medicaid and (the ACA) Marketplace coverage take effect.”
More uninsured Ohioans on the books and a higher amount of medical debt certainly causes strain on households, but O’Rourke said state providers, particularly those in rural or underserved areas, will also see impacts.
“More uncompensated care can lead to closures and possibly even raise healthcare prices even further in the state,” O’Rourke told the Capital Journal.
The Ohio legislature is on break until after the Nov. 3 election, but one bipartisan bill that could see action as the lawmakers return is a bipartisan measure addressing medical debt.
Ohio House Bill 257 was introduced in May 2025 by sponsors Rep. Michele Grim, D-Toledo, and Rep. Jean Schmidt, R-Loveland.
The bill would cap the interest rate for medical debt at 3% annually, and bar methods like wage collection to pay the bills.
The bill would also keep healthcare providers or collections agencies from reporting nonpayment of medical debt to consumer reporting agencies.
The bill has seen several hearings in the Ohio House Health Committee, garnering support from groups like the American Lung Association, the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network, and the American Diabetes Association. Gary Dougherty, director of state government affairs for the ADA, said limiting interest on medical debt in particular would help patients like those with diabetes.
“People with medical debt have reported it as a driving factor for delaying care or not filling their prescriptions,” Dougherty wrote in June testimony to the House Health Committee.
“For people with diabetes, it is critical that we eliminate financial barriers that may result in them forgoing the care they need to manage the disease.”
Groups speaking out against the bill include the Consumer Data Industry Association, and  the Association of Credit and Collection Professionals, that argued the bill would “take an overly broad approach to limiting medical billing and collection practices that … would lead to unintended negative consequences for Ohio consumers and providers of medical services in the state.”
The bill has until December to make it through the General Assembly, or it will need to be introduced again in the new year, with the beginning of the new two-year General Assembly term.
