name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Newberry hospital picked for free federal cybersecurity pilot program
text:
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp speaks at the launch of Project Lifeline 250 at Newberry Health Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)NEWBERRY — A group of private cybersecurity companies will offer their services, free of charge, to a Newberry hospital as part of a federal pilot project aimed at better protecting rural healthcare from virtual attacks.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross and U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Chief Counselor Chris Klomp were on hand Monday at Newberry Health, located 40 miles northwest of downtown Columbia, for the launch of Project Lifeline 250.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Thanks to the commitment of the world-leading American industry here today, we’re deploying the greatest American tools and capabilities to defend hospital networks, deploy physical backup devices after an initial incident to ensure an impacted hospital can still provide critical care and identify high-risk devices and replace them,” Cairncross said. “We’ll find what works and we’ll scale it. America’s rural communities and hospitals, they rely on it, and we’ll get it done.”
“We have an opportunity to build a model that every rural hospital across the entire country can rely upon,” Cairncross added.
The announcement was light on details. Officials did not say when the six-month pilot period would start, how it would be maintained and expanded after the pilot period or how that expansion might be paid for. Nor did they say why they selected South Carolina for this initial trial.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross speaks at the launch of Project Lifeline 250 at Newberry Health Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman)
The Office of the National Cyber Director and the South Carolina State Law Enforcement Division’s cybersecurity arm will oversee the program.
Technology companies including Cisco, Cyera, Microsoft, Trellix, Zscaler, Rilian, Dispel, Abnormal AI and Becton, Dickinson and Company, Palo Alto Networks, ServiceNow, Infoblox Security Solutions and Forescout Technologies will provide their services.
The average hospital has more than 26,000 internet-connected devices, all of which could be subject to a cyber attack, Klomp said. And his agency tracked more than 2,200 health-related cyber incidents just last year.
And unlike larger hospital systems, rural providers don’t have the same financial resources to shore up its technological defenses.
“When a family walks through the doors of a hospital, they’re counting on a nurse, they’re counting on a doctor, someone to be there and to help them,” Klomp said. “Those professionals are depending on systems to share the medical records, the labs, the radiology communications, and others to give them the information to coordinate care appropriately. When those systems fail, the consequences can reach the bedside. They impact real lives. They impact the patient, impact their family.”
Klomp told the story of St. Margaret’s Health, a Catholic hospital system in Illinois, which closed in 2023. In their filings to the state, hospital officials cited a cyberattack as one of the reasons behind their closure.
“They couldn’t generate revenue and they couldn’t keep their doors open,” Klomp said.
Closer to home, AnMed in the Upstate saw its operations interrupted for months by a cybersecurity attack in which CEO William Kinley said cybercriminals accessed patients’ health information.
AnMed, with its 461-bed hospital in Anderson and more than 60 physician practices across South Carolina and Georgia, kept its urgent care and emergency services locations open following the July 26 attack. But doctors and patients had limited access to medical records.
It wasn’t until mid-September that the hospital system returned to normal operations.
“Cybersecurity is no longer just an IT issue,” SC Law Enforcement Division Chief Mark Keel said. “It is a public safety issue. It’s an economic issue. And in a healthcare environment, it can be the difference between life and death.”
“South Carolina is not waiting for a next cyber incident to happen,” Keel added. “We are identifying risks, bringing partners together, and putting practical solutions in place to better protect the citizens of our state.”
SC rural hospitals, doctors’ offices receive share of $200M in federal funding amid Medicaid cuts

One of the technologies the Newberry hospital will test out is called Project Code Cart, Cairncross said.
Researchers at the University of California San Diego developed Code Cart, which Cairncross described as an IT system in a box, using a U.S. Department of Health and Human Services grant.
“It’s designed, in the event of a full shutdown of systems in a hospital for a ransomware attack, to completely restore essential functionality within two hours, so that all operations can be maintained,” Cairncross said. “Think essential communications. Think radiology labs, access to critical electronic health records.”
Project Lifeline follows a similar White House-led cyber effort: Project Watershed 250, a pilot project to protect water infrastructure from a cyber attack in Texas. The Office of the National Cyber Director announced that pilot in August.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Struggling Canton school loses its charter
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy has lost its charter and must halt instruction by the end of the year — a first-time penalty for a Mississippi charter school.  
The Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board voted unanimously on Monday to revoke the Canton school’s charter. Two board members, Candace Robbins and Marcy Scoggins, were absent. 
While other charter schools have been cited for breaking federal education law and violating the terms of their contract, no other school has been ordered to effectively shut its doors.
Hearing officer Kim Turner asks questions during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Kim Turner, an assistant attorney general who serves as state agencies director in the attorney general’s office, recommended the board revoke the school’s charter because of numerous instances of noncompliance with federal law, state law and the terms of its 2020 contract.
The authorizer board had waited four months, since a related May 14 hearing Turner presided over, to take action.
The evidence presented during that hearing affirmed a “statutory and contractual basis” for revoking the school’s charter, Turner concluded in her recommendation. “Such a decision would be neither arbitrary nor capricious.”
Earlier in the meeting, Dorlisa Hutton, an SR1 administrator and wife of Chief Executive Officer Tamu Green, made a final plea before board members moved to vote on the fate of the school. 
READ MORE: Charter school in Canton opened with a STEM focus but no full-time STEM teachers. It has had many more problems
Hutton asked the board to hold off on a final decision until the school’s latest audit was available —  an alternative action Turner had suggested. Hutton also asked the board to return the school to good standing. She asked the board to release $300,000 in charter school start-up funding, which had been frozen pending the vote on the school’s fate.
Dorlisa Hutton, vanguard ambassador for SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy, speaks at the Dec. 8, 2025 meeting of the Mississippi Charter School Authorizer Board Meeting in Jackson. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
Returning the school to good standing would mean “we can build the facilities our students deserve and bring to the table the bankers and partners who are ready to invest in Canton,” Hutton said. “And it means the chance for Mississippi’s first college prep and STEM [science, technology, engineering and math] charter school serving children of whom nearly nine and 10 are economically disadvantaged to become the first charter school in this state to earn an A.”
Hutton did not respond to questions from Mississippi Today about whether the school planned to appeal.
Jamie Travis, an attorney for the charter school, suggested in May he would pursue an appeal process if the authorizer board voted to revoke the school’s charter. The appeal should be directed to the Hinds County Chancery Court, Turner said, which is where the board is based.
The board’s vote ends a process that began in December, when the authorizer board reviewed the school’s financial statements, which showed SR1 CPSA had one day’s cash on hand. The school had also over projected its enrollment each year since it opened in 2023.
SR1 CPSA was the only charter to face revocation twice. The authorizer board first cited the school for requesting money to serve 150 students, but enrolling 12. The school spent $816,725 that year, which would break down to about $68,060 per student — five times what the average Mississippi school district spends.
“The record established this revocation proceeding did not arise from one isolated event. Rather, these proceedings were initiated following years of notice, monitoring intervention, corrective action, and requests for and production of documents,” Turner found.
Students head to waiting vehicles and school buses after classes end for the day at SR1 College Preparatory and Stem Academy, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in Canton. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Since then, the school’s fate has been in limbo, which also affected its funding. 
The board could not act without a recommendation from Turner. That board received that recommendation on Oct. 6.
Regulators had reason to worry about the school’s future. A disorganized business office and an allegedly unsafe cafeteria were just some red flags that came up during inspections by authorizer board employees. Visits from other agency inspectors soon followed.
Green severely mismanaged the school, charter board attorney Dillon Pitts argued at the May hearing. Also at the hearing, Green said his “unwritten rule” of  management was: “we just spent.” He claimed to not know that school records had to present the best financial snapshot by the end of the fiscal year. 
Tamu Green, CEO of SR1, confers with Dorlisa Hutton, chief operations officer and vice president for SR1 College Preparatory and STEM Academy, during a hearing about SR1 on Thursday, May 14, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The school was also out of compliance with federal food safety and nutrition guidelines. 
A Mississippi Today investigation found school leadership tried to deceive regulators before inspections by moving furniture and other supplies on site and retagging them. Former employees accused SR1 leadership of deceptive business practices.
The school has experienced significant turnover as well. The school’s top administrator resigned at the end of September, after starting in August. The school is on its third business manager in less than a year. 
SR1 CPSA could still reopen as a private school.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Regulators eye in-state path for out-of-state medical marijuana patients
authors: Katie Castellani | State House News Service
text:
CANNABIS REGULATORS ARE EYEING rules to eliminate residency requirements for purchasing medical marijuana in an attempt to make the product easier for out-of-state patients to buy.
“Simply put, it is a really effective way and a thoughtful way for us to give medical patients across the country more access to treatment for any of the reasons that they’re using marijuana for medicinal purposes,” Cannabis Control Commissioner Xiomara DeLobato told the News Service.
Under a regulatory proposal introduced at an October 22 CCC meeting, individuals 18 and over – regardless of what state they live in – diagnosed with a “debilitating medical condition” by a certified health care provider in Massachusetts can register to purchase medical marijuana. Those under 18 who have been diagnosed with a debilitating condition that is also considered a “life-limiting illness” and certified by two health care providers can get medical marijuana.
Forty-one states and the District of Columbia allow medical marijuana use, as of June 2025, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. And if the regulations are passed, the Bay State would join many others including New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York and Maine, that allow non-residents to get medical marijuana. Massachusetts and Vermont are the only New England states that don’t allow non-residents to access medical marijuana.
Jeremiah MacKinnon, president and executive director of the Massachusetts Patient Advocacy Alliance, said the proposed regulations mark “a step in the right direction to modernize our medical program.”
“We have such a robust health care system here in Massachusetts that people travel from other states to get surgeries, and whether it’s tourism or visiting family or other situations, if an individual wants to seek continuity of their care, accessing medical marijuana, this is a great pathway because it allows them to continue to access medical marijuana tax-free,” MacKinnon told the News Service. 
Also, he said proposal could help get more needed dollars flowing to the state’s medical marijuana industry.
“For the past few years, the medical marijuana market has been struggling, and so to expand the pool of patients that are able to access medical marijuana in the state, I think is a positive thing for the health and long-term stability of the industry,” MacKinnon said.
Medical marijuana products are not taxed in Massachusetts and adult-use cannabis products are available to anyone, from any state, over 21. Recreational cannabis products are subject to a 6.25 percent state sales tax and a 10.75 percent excise tax while municipalities that host licensees can receive a local option tax of up to 3 percent. As of September, the industry has generated $2 billion in state and local taxes since it was enacted in 2016.
According to CCC data, year-to-date medical marijuana sales to patients and caregivers have fallen from $17.9 million in September 2023 to $11.2 million last month.
Ryan Dominguez, executive director of the Massachusetts Cannabis Coalition, said the regulations would create an avenue for out-of-state patients to get marijuana products they may need in Massachusetts if voters here next month support Question 8 repealing the state’s recreational cannabis market. 
Patrick Nestor, a spokesperson for the campaign supporting the ballot question, declined to comment on the proposed regulations.
The proposed regulations are similar to a Senate-approved measure recognizing patient registrations in other states for medical marijuana prescriptions. After talks with the House, that provision was dropped from the bill (H 5350) lawmakers sent to Gov. Maura Healey, which she signed into law in April. 
DeLobato said that commissioners plan to take an initial vote on the regulations on December 10. Then, the commission will take public comments on the regulations from January 1 to February 2 before making any changes and taking a final vote.

name: VTDigger
title: Guard families deserve an answer
text:
Dear Editor,
As a veteran of the Vermont Air National Guard, I understand that military service is not simply about following orders. It also involves sacrifices by those who serve and the families who stand behind them.
I served four years in the Guard. My husband also served while we were raising our family. I chose to leave because I did not want to risk an overseas deployment and its impact on our family. My husband continued to serve.
That experience is one reason I am concerned about Gov. Phil Scott’s apparent lack of response to a letter signed by 27 Vermont veterans, retired military officers and Guard family members calling on him and state legislators to support the Defend the Guard Act. The letter raised concerns about deploying Vermont National Guard members into overseas combat without prior congressional authorization and called for a public legislative hearing. It was publicly reported on Aug. 20. To date, as far as I know, there has been no response from the governor.
Reasonable people can disagree about the legislation, and a governor is entitled to explain his position. But when veterans and military families raise serious concerns, they deserve more than silence.

READ MORE

Leadership does not require agreement. It requires listening. It requires responding. It requires being willing to explain decisions to those affected by them.
I served in the Vermont Air National Guard. I know that service comes with obligations. Our elected leaders have obligations, too.
Lonnie PolandMilton, Vt.
